This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term><note>Works in the "public domain" are those whose intellectual property rights have expired, been forfeited, or are inapplicable, allowing the public to use them freely.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia</term><note>Handwritten notes, stamps, or sketches added to the margins of a book by previous owners or librarians.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ **Maintain attribution** The Google "watermark" you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

### **About this book**

This is a digital copy of a book that for generations has been preserved on library shelves before being digitized by Google as part of a project aimed at making the books of the whole world available online.

It has survived long enough to no longer be protected by copyright and to become <term>public domain</term><note>Works in the "public domain" are those whose intellectual property rights have expired, been forfeited, or are inapplicable, allowing the public to use them freely.</note>. A public domain book is a book that was never protected by copyright or whose legal copyright terms have expired. The classification of a book as public domain can vary from country to country. Public domain books are the link to the past; they represent a historical, cultural, and knowledge heritage that is often difficult to discover.

Comments, notes, and other <term>marginalia</term><note>Handwritten notes, stamps, or sketches added to the margins of a book by previous owners or librarians.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file as a testament to the long journey traveled by the book, from the original publisher to the library, to finally reach you.

### **Usage guidelines**

Google is proud to be a partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them universally available. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. However, this work is costly; therefore, in order to continue offering this service, we have taken some initiatives to prevent illicit use by commercial entities, including the imposition of restrictions on the sending of automated queries.

We also ask that you:

+ *Do not make commercial use of these files* We have designed Google Book Search for use by individual private users, and we ask you to use these files for personal use and not for commercial purposes.

+ *Do not send automated queries* Do not send automated queries of any kind to Google. If you are conducting research in the fields of machine translation, optical character recognition (OCR), or other fields where you need to use large quantities of text, we invite you to contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help you.

+ *Keep the watermark* The <term>watermark</term><note>A digital identifying mark or logo—in this case, the "Google" logo—placed on pages to identify the source of the digital file.</note> that appears in each file is essential to inform users about this project and help them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Do not remove it.

Do not assume that, because a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, it is also in the public domain for users in other countries. The criteria that establish whether a book is protected by copyright vary from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether a specific use of the book is permitted. Do not assume that because a book appears in Google Book Search it means it can be used in any way and in any country in the world. The penalties for copyright violations can be very severe.

## THE WORKS

### OF

# BERNARDO DAVANZATI.

<note>Bernardo Davanzati (1529–1606) was a prominent Florentine citizen, merchant, and scholar. He is best known for his rigorous translation of the Roman historian Tacitus into the Florentine vernacular, a task he undertook to prove that Italian could be just as concise and powerful as Latin. Beyond literature, he was a pioneering economic thinker who wrote influential treatises on the nature of money and exchange.</note>

## TO THE DISCERNING READER.

-><image-desc>ornamental divider consisting of a central oval shape with symmetrical horizontal flourishes</image-desc><-

Among many editions, even elegant ones, of the works of Bernardo Davanzati, you would be hard-pressed to find one that is not copied, more or less accurately, from the Comino prints; <note>The Volpi-Comino press in Padua was famous in the 18th century for its beautiful and scholarly editions of Italian classics.</note> good enough, perhaps, but not as much as was required for this author. For he, through certain of his <term>capestrerie</term> <note>Literally "wildnesses" or "eccentricities," this refers to Davanzati’s famously concise, almost jagged prose style that often defied standard grammatical conventions of his time.</note> which made him stand apart from all others and not too accessible, also required singular care to make him easy for readers without stripping away his native character. This negligence having scattered no few blemishes throughout his works, who knows but that it may have contributed to him being judged less correctly by some. What is certain is that he is not always obscure where they reproach him for obscurity; rather, he has been so corrupted by his editors. Therefore, having been requested to oversee this edition, I wished to thoroughly examine the original prints (hitherto untouched) and what remains of his manuscripts. Thus, I have been able to correct not a few nor slight errors, long-entrenched in all previous editions, and to restore his proper <term>lessigrafia</term> <note>Lexicography, or more specifically here, the author’s idiosyncratic spelling and orthographic systems.</note> which was always neglected due to that wretched habit of modernizing, and of erasing this not-contemptible part of the ancient coloring. And because, if the double "z" did not seem reasonable to Davanzati, and he did not want it, must it be given to him in spite of himself? <note>A reference to a long-standing debate in Italian linguistics regarding whether certain words should be spelled with a single or double "z". Davanzati preferred the simpler, more Latinate single "z".</note> Did it not seem so also to Carlo Dati and Udeno Nisieli? <note>Carlo Dati (1619–1676) was a celebrated Italian philologist and scientist; "Udeno Nisieli" was the pseudonym of Benedetto Fioretti (1579–1644), a critic known for his work on Tuscan style and language.</note> Why, if it pleased him to write *Agusto* [August], *agurio* [augury], *agure* [augur], should he not be respected? Do we not perhaps do the same in *agosto*? The same may be said of *giucare* [to play] for *giuocare* and of other singularities gra- <note>The text cuts off here with the catchword "gra-", which likely continues as "grammaticali" (grammatical) on the following page.</note>

<summary>In this preface, the editor Enrico Bindi argues that previous editions of Bernardo Davanzati’s work have been poorly edited and unnecessarily modernized. He defends his decision to restore Davanzati's original, idiosyncratic spellings and concise style based on a study of original manuscripts and early prints.</summary>

# TO THE DISCERNING READER.

...orthographic characteristics, common also to others, which it did not seem necessary to change. Where he is not consistent, I believed it best, following his example, to exercise some freedom: therefore you will find *after* and *after* <note>original: "dopo" and "doppo"</note>; *public* and *public* <note>original: "publico" and "pubblico"</note>; *everyone*, *between both*, *at the hour*, and *everyone*, *between both*, *then* <note>original: "ogn'uno", "intr' ambi", "all'ora", and "ognuno", "intrambi", "allora"</note>; *with the*, *not it*, *on the*, and *with the*, *not it*, *on the* <note>original: "co 'l", "no'l", "su'l", and "col", "nol", "sul"</note>; *to the*, *of the*, *with the*, and *to the*, *of the*, *with the*, and even *to the*, *of the* <note>original: "a gli", "de gli", "con gli", and "agli", "degli", "cogli", "alli", "delli"</note> etc.; and likewise in other words where he lacked a fixed method. This required warning, so that such inconsistencies, which are found in almost all writers of that time, should not be mistaken for errors. It is well understood, however, that when he writes *temples* [tempij], *gods* [iddij], *to the others* [agl'altri], *to the men* [agl'huomini] etc., these were not to be followed, because such ways of writing—although defended by some at that time (see the *Letters of Claudio Tolomei*, Book VII, page 287 and following, Venice 1566)—are today rightly considered faulty and not to be tolerated.

Regarding the <term>Vernacular Translation of Tacitus</term> <note>Davanzati's most famous work was his translation of the Roman historian Tacitus into a concise, idiomatic Florentine prose.</note>, from a comparison of the original prints and a portion of the manuscript kept in the <term>Magliabechiana</term> <note>The Magliabechiana was the foundational collection of the National Central Library of Florence, named after the scholar Antonio Magliabechi.</note> (see the *Bibliography* hereafter), I have gathered a rich harvest of variants. These arose from the translator's changes and reconsiderations and are most useful for the study of language and style. It is true that these do not extend beyond the first six books of the *Annals*, because the rest of the translation is posthumous and lacks the author’s final refinements; nor is there any guide for it other than Nesti’s poor printing. Nevertheless, it has been no small help to always keep the Latin text before me, using the wonderful edition published recently in Zurich, based on the Laurentian manuscripts, by Baitter and Orelli (*Zurich*, 1846-48).

I will also say a word about the brief notes that I thought to add; these, above all, aim to make this translation readable without having to stop at every turn to consult dictionaries or other references; they explain, without too many...

# TO THE DISCERNING READER.

...philological intricacies, archaic or Florentine words and phrases; noting some inaccuracies of the translator; citing the words of the Latin text, where either curiosity or necessity seemed to require it; noting some grave errors in other editions; reporting, where most appropriate, some variants or changes (most of which we have relegated to the back of the volume); warning where the translator followed readings not accepted by the best texts; explaining (though rarely) certain historical information more necessary for understanding; re-translating—either by myself or with <term>Dati</term> <note>Carlo Roberto Dati (1619–1676), a Florentine philologist and scientist.</note>, <term>Politi</term> <note>Adriano Politi (1542–1611), known for his translation of Tacitus and his work on the Italian language.</note>, <term>Valeriani</term>, or an anonymous 16th-century manuscript—some misunderstood phrases, or those too lowly or too obscure. In the first six books, my short notes are distinguished by an asterisk, so as not to confuse them with the translator's own marginal notes.

I have also preserved the copious indices of subjects, both because they are of great convenience to scholars and because they were written by Davanzati himself, who used terms and phrases there that can greatly benefit the language. The index for the first six books, printed by him in *The Empire of Tiberius Caesar* <note>original: "Imperio di Tiberio Cesare"; this refers to the first six books of Tacitus's Annals.</note>, you will find at the end of this volume; the general index, as it appears in the <term>Nesti</term> <note>Niccolò Nesti, an 18th-century printer.</note> edition, will close the second.

I have brought the same care to the minor works. For the *Schism* <note>original: "Scisma"; Davanzati’s history of the English Reformation, *Lo Scisma d'Inghilterra*.</note> I followed the Roman edition by <term>Facciotto</term> <note>Guglielmo Facciotti, a Roman printer active in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.</note>, published during the author's lifetime, while also taking into account the one edited by <term>Bartolommeo Gamba</term> <note>A noted 19th-century bibliographer and editor.</note>, which was based on a <term>Marcian manuscript</term> <note>A manuscript held in the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice.</note> that offers infinite and, for the most part, excellent variants, which I have noted accurately. For the *Tuscan Cultivation* <note>original: "Coltivazione toscana"; Davanzati's famous treatise on the cultivation of vines and olives.</note> there was no need to search for printed editions, as the original manuscript exists, which gave me the means to correct many errors and to note some of the author’s revisions <note>original: "pentimenti"; literally 'repentances,' referring to places where the author changed his mind or edited his own work.</note>, which are so helpful to those who wish to delve into the secrets of the art. Even the few *Letters* that...

...remain, were collated against the original manuscripts <note>original: "autografi"; documents written in the author's own hand.</note>. These are missing for the other writings; however, there are many manuscript copies which, being from the period, carry no small authority. But more on this in its proper place. You will also find some unpublished material: a few sonnets, some fragments, and little else. I would have provided more, if my efforts had not proved in vain. That little is taken, for the most part, from a thick notebook of various studies, entirely in our author’s <note>The editor refers to Bernardo Davanzati as "the Our" or "Our Author."</note> own hand, which I owe to Pietro Bigazzi <note>A 19th-century Florentine scholar and bibliophile.</note>, a learned and diligent collector of every literary rarity. I am also indebted to him for the opportunity to examine a printed edition of Plutarch's *Essays* <note>original: "Opuscoli di Plutarco"; a collection of shorter works by the Greek philosopher.</note> that belonged to Davanzati, featuring various handwritten marginal notes <note>original: "postille a penna"</note> by him, from which I have chosen the most curious.

Whether in this work I have earned that humble praise of accuracy—which is all one can hope for—I do not know; what is certain is that I have exerted myself as much as possible. I do not presume, however, to have avoided every error; for it is too difficult in these minute tasks for the mind not to become occasionally weary and strained. It is up to you to be discerning, O Reader.

***

# ON THE LIFE AND WORKS

## OF BERNARDO DAVANZATI.

---

Not only nations, but even the cities and peoples within a single nation possess their own distinct character and physiognomy, much like the families and individuals who compose them. However, in a people, these distinctive features appear more or less strong and pronounced depending on the extent to which they have been able to act in accordance with the regulated movements of their own nature—that is, according to their own laws and institutions. For wherever a people has been forced to bend to external laws, these laws act like a Procrustean bed <note>In Greek mythology, Procrustes was a bandit who forced travelers to fit into an iron bed by either stretching them or cutting off their limbs; Bindi uses it here to describe forced conformity.</note>, which stretches or prunes, and reduces all bodies to the same measure and listlessness.

This is seen above all in the Florentines. During the period when they governed themselves and had the opportunity to fully deploy the virtues of their own nature, no other Italian people possessed a more sharply defined, noble, or cheerful character. They possessed a witty spirit and an intellect both agile and profound: poor and modest within their own homes, yet immensely wealthy and magnificent in their public life <note>original: "nel comune"; referring to the shared resources and buildings of the city-state.</note>; they were both playful and severe, simple and magnanimous. They were no less clever (if not always loyal) in the courts <note>original: "curia"; referring to legal and administrative environments.</note> than they were valiant in arms. And, what causes the most wonder, despite having a mercantile soul <note>original: "animo mercantesco"</note>, they possessed such a feeling for beauty as is attested by the Roman-style daring of their buildings and the arts which they brought back to life. Their way of speaking, writing, conversing, and building—everything bears an imprint so distinct that you could never mis—

<meta>catchword "bi." at bottom right</meta>

<summary>This opening passage of the biography of Bernardo Davanzati discusses how the unique character and institutions of Florence shaped its people, highlighting their blend of mercantile pragmatism and artistic brilliance.</summary>

<page-num>VI</page-num>
<header>ON THE LIFE AND WORKS</header>

be exchanged with that of any other Italian people. But these vivid and peculiar features began to fade after the middle of the sixteenth century. Not entirely, so long as the Florentines were subject to a domestic and recent lordship <note>A reference to the Medici family, who transitioned from citizens to hereditary rulers of Florence.</note>. They disappeared completely in the time that followed. And even the language, which appeared so lively, effective, and

->pure in the last artisan,<sup>1</sup><-

degenerated, distorted by foreign jargon, which crept in through fashion, through negligence, and through a lost sense of dignity. Certainly, hearing a Florentine today, you could not say:

->Your speech makes you manifest.<sup>2</sup><-

This fact, observed and lamented by many, has returned more distressingly to my thoughts as I must write these humble words about Bernardo Davanzati, who is the most notable among the last Florentines who preserved a Florentine character through their actions and writings. For this reason, too, he deserves to be held in high regard. However, it is a matter of regret that information about his life is too scarce: because he divided his time between the business of the bank and solitary studies, staying far from literary and civil disputes—sparing with words, having few friends, not a courtier, not ambitious—he made little noise, and few spoke of him, though they did so with the highest praise.

He was born in Florence on August 31, 1529.<sup>3</sup> He considered himself descended from the Bostichi,<sup>4</sup> an ancient and powerful Guelph<sup>5</sup> family,

---

<sup>1</sup> <note>original: "Pura vedeasi nell'ultimo artista"</note> Dante, *Paradise* XVI, 49. <note>In this passage, Dante’s ancestor Cacciaguida describes the old Florence where the bloodline was pure down to the humblest worker.</note>
<sup>2</sup> <note>original: "La tua loquela ti fa manifesto"</note> Dante, *Inferno* X, 24. <note>The famous line where the ghost of Farinata degli Uberti recognizes Dante as a fellow Florentine by his accent.</note>
<sup>3</sup> Here is the birth document, extracted from the archive of the Office of Works of Santa Maria del Fiore: "1529, August. Tuesday, the 31st. — Bernardo Giuliano and Ro (Romolo) of Antonio Francesco of Giuliano of Nicolaio Davanzati, parish of Santa Trinita, born on the said day, at the 8th hour." Rondinelli, and others following him, are therefore in error when they place his birth on August 30.
<sup>4</sup> In his books, printed under his own supervision, he always calls himself Davanzati-Bostichi.
<sup>5</sup> Giovanni Villani, *Chronicle* VI, 33; V, 39. <note>The Guelphs were a major political faction in medieval Italy that supported the Pope against the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>

family already in decline in the times of Cacciaguida <note>Cacciaguida was the great-great-grandfather of Dante Alighieri; he appears in the *Divine Comedy* as a representative of the ancient, virtuous Florence.</note>, and almost extinct in those of Dante and Villani. <sup>1</sup> But today genealogists cast doubt on such a family alliance. <sup>2</sup> It is certain that the Davanzati family was of ancient nobility. It took its name from a Davanzato who fought for the Guelphs <note>The Guelphs were a political faction in medieval Italy that supported the Pope against the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> at the Battle of Montaperti in 1260: and at the beginning of the following century, the family was admitted to the honors of the republic. <sup>3</sup> It produced citizens who were pious and charitable; one Lottieri who founded the monastery of Santa Marta at Montughi in 1336, and a Niccolò, who founded that of Doccia on the hill of Fiesole in 1413: as well as graceful poets, such as Mariotto, Francesco, and Bartolommeo: <sup>4</sup> wise statesmen, such as Manetto, who negotiated the peace with the Pisans in 1397, and a Giuliano, distinguished in the 15th century in the science of law and for many honorable embassies he undertook; "an effective man of great power in speaking," as Scipione Ammirato calls him. <sup>5</sup> Equal honor came to our Bernardo from his mother, Lucrezia de’ Ginori, who belonged to a most noble family. His father, Antonfrancesco Davanzati, is honorably remembered by the historian Benedetto Varchi among those who provided well for the fatherland's liberty during those final moments of the memorable Siege of Florence. <sup>6</sup> From which he reaped that fruit which was to be expected—

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

### OF THE LIFE AND WORKS

...from the broad promises of the happy victor; who, nodding to the new rulers, meant to say (and was understood) "that the security of the new State should be provided for with a vigorous proscription."¹ <note>A proscription is a decree of condemnation to death or banishment, often used by new regimes to seize the assets of political enemies.</note> Confined first in Sicily, then in Pontremoli, his property confiscated, a bounty on his head, it is not known what became of him.² <note>The "him" here refers to Anton Francesco Davanzati, Bernardo's father, who was punished for his republican sympathies after the Medici returned to power.</note>

To Bernardo, born during the death throes of the republic, paternal care was lacking, but not a liberal education, which his mother saw as all the more necessary for him as he revealed his intellect to be early on quite lively and sharp: "for a fertile field, if left uncultivated, produces weeds more vigorously than a sterile one does."³ He learned Latin and Greek excellently; studies which in that strict education—which now seems barbaric—were never separated. But he did not record who his teachers were, and it would be difficult to guess, among such a great and admirable abundance of highly learned men then in Florence, rightly called by our author: "flower of intellects, honor of letters, mistress of arts, mirror of civilization."⁴ The Florentine University <term>Studio fiorentino</term> <note>The "Studio" was the historic University of Florence, a center of Renaissance humanism.</note>, which had declined significantly during the disturbances of war and under the shameful Alessandro <note>Alessandro de' Medici, the first Duke of Florence, known for a brief and controversial reign.</note>, rose again through Cosimo to nearly the splendor of the times of Lorenzo the Magnificent, when scholars like Poliziano, Ficino, Filelfo, and Argyropoulos taught there;⁵ <note>These men were the giants of 15th-century humanism: Angelo Poliziano (poet), Marsilio Ficino (philosopher), Francesco Filelfo (humanist), and John Argyropoulos (who brought Greek learning to Italy).</note> and when the Florentine youth spoke Greek with such Attic—

<page-num>IX</page-num>

# OF BERNARDO DAVANZATI.

...enough to make one believe Athens had been reborn on the banks of the Arno.¹ 
There Pier Vettori <note>A renowned humanist scholar famous for his precise editions of classical Greek and Latin texts.</note> taught the humanities; to him nothing was unknown of classical antiquity, and he was a most graceful writer of both his mother tongue and the learned languages. The chair of Greek and Latin eloquence was held by Giovambattista Adriani, an elegant historian and worthy heir to the literary glory of Marcello;² philosophy was taught by Verino;³ while Gelli and Varchi read Dante and Petrarch there. The Greek classics were taught by Vincenzio Borghini,⁴ a learned illustrator of Florentine antiquities, whom Foscolo—no friend to the sixteenth-century writers—calls (and it is high praise) a non-pedantic writer.⁵

<page-num>X</page-num>

# ON THE LIFE AND WORKS

It is hard to believe that the young **Bernardo** did not listen to these worthy men; though in that abundance of learning, every house was a school, and youth had the opportunity to learn in every place.

Rondinelli <note>Francesco Rondinelli (1589–1665), a Florentine scholar and librarian who wrote a biography of Davanzati.</note> tells us that "with study he coupled business, which in his early years he practiced in Lyon." ^1 I do not believe, however, that he did so in his own name, but rather on behalf of the Capponi <note>The Capponi were one of the most powerful banking and political families in Florence.</note>; and it seems to me that this can be inferred from a *Record* by Benvenuto Cellini, where he is expressly named as the *cashier of the Capponi*; ^2 and from his *Lecture on Exchange*, where the examples he uses to illustrate his subject are drawn from their bank. ^3

Nor should it be a cause for wonder that this most refined mind took the best years of his life away from literature to devote them to business. For in vigorous ages, where there is a public life, one does not find "literary men" by trade; there, studies are either a means to act well in the republic—or they are nothing. To the Romans, solitary studies were not a life, but leisure; and Agricola was barely forgiven for having given himself to the speculations of philosophy with much more passion than was fitting for a Roman and a senator. ^4 And in Florence, the "manufacturers of literature" <note>A term implying those who write as a profession or craft rather than as an extension of a civic or commercial life.</note> began to appear in the age of Davanzati, when there was nothing else for men of genius to do. But before then, you would hardly find a scholar who was not also a statesman, a soldier, or a merchant. But a merchant most of all: because trade was the primary source of wealth and power.

<page-num>XII</page-num>
<header>ON HIS LIFE AND WORKS</header>

Savonarola <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498) was a Dominican friar and preacher who became the moral and political leader of Florence, famous for his "Bonfires of the Vanities."</note>; who, speaking of the education of children, cried out: “The first thing fathers set them to learn is poetry, and afterwards they are sent to the banks to learn exchange and usury; and so they send them to the house of the devil.”¹ To Horace, on the other hand, it did not seem possible that with this "rust" and anxiety for wealth, one could produce good poetry worthy of being preserved in cedar oil <note>The ancients used cedar oil to protect precious papyrus scrolls from insects and decay.</note>; and he rebuked the greedy Romans for it.² But the Florentines, however, knew how: they coupled not only poetry, but all the fine arts, with trade most excellently. This makes me certain that they did not practice trade in a slavish or inhuman way; for beauty cannot be felt in a soul hardened by sordid gain. As for that bad reputation as usurers, the cause is due partly to the envy of other nations, who were then idle; partly to the necessity of protecting themselves against the great dangers of the time—as shown by the bankruptcy of the **Bardi** and **Peruzzi** families, which was a public disaster;³ and partly also to the abuses of a few who, as often happens, defiled the reputation of all.

When Davanzati went to Lyon, this poem by Ottonaio <note>Giovanni Battista dell'Ottonaio (1482–1527), a Florentine priest known for his Carnival Songs (*Canti Carnescialeschi*).</note> was in circulation (Carnival Songs. Cosmopoli 1750; vol. 2, page 550):

> .... it pains us . . . greatly
> That many today devote themselves,
> Who could have been true and good merchants,
> To keeping company even with street-peddlers.
> Everyone keeps warehouses and shacks,
> Everyone buys and resells,
> Wherefore the poor man who spends too much
> Curses the time, the goods, and the money:
> Yet there are not so many greedy people
> Always against us, etc.

<page-num>XIII</page-num>
<header>OF BERNARDO DAVANZATI.</header>
<sig>b</sig>
<meta>catchword I.</meta>

The city [of Lyon] was no less full of Florentine merchants than **Montpellier**, **Nîmes**, **Marseille**, or **Toulouse**. Traces of them remain even today in the name of a street called the **Guadagni** street, named for a powerful family that conducted great trade there.¹ Like everywhere else, they had a consul, their own laws, and broad privileges granted by the king. Above all others, the bank of the **Strozzi** flourished; here, no less than in **Rome** and **Venice**, they maintained a numerous and powerful company. When **Filippo Strozzi**, to escape the suspicions of the *Piagnoni* <note>The *Piagnoni* (literally "the weepers") were the devout followers of the friar Girolamo Savonarola; Strozzi, a wealthy patrician, was a political rival to their influence.</note>, withdrew there for a time, he was able to arm the Florentine merchants and hold firm against the rioting city so effectively that they were nearly exterminated.²

I do not know how long **Bernardo** remained in **Lyon**; but, certainly, it was not for long. Soon I find him back in **Florence**, participating in the academies and continuing his trades, investing his capital in limited partnerships <term>accomandite: a form of business partnership where some partners provide capital with limited liability while others manage the trade</term> (as was mostly done at that time), which did not always gladden him with good profits. I gather this from his own handwriting in his **Marginalia to Tacitus**, where I find one note—canceled by him, but still legible—in which he clearly alludes to a foul trick played on him in one of these merchant companies.

> "I do not know which of my neighbors (he recounts) took from a friend
> "a notable sum of ducats to trade in partnership,
> "and at the end of eleven months, without any accidents or losses in
> "the trade, they fled with forty-four thousand; and
> "they have found help, favors, friends, and ways: so that they
> "walk with their heads held high, and spend cheerfully."

<page-num>XIV</page-num>
<header>ON THE LIFE AND WORKS</header>

> "And they compensate that friend by claiming to have satisfied him before the others, contrary to all truth. And let this be the seal that disabuses everyone."

The following words also hint at the lowly snares of a rival in commercial matters; they were likewise canceled by him in that same autograph manuscript, but not so thoroughly that they cannot be read:

> "A man of worth... so that I might be ruined... he sought, he intrigued, he stirred up many, he wrote to Venice, and he scrutinized the account books. But I, having conducted business with my own capital and never being in debt, remained always *firmly squared against the blows of fortune.*¹" <note>original: "Ben tetragono ai colpi di ventura." This is a famous quotation from Dante Alighieri's *Paradiso* (Canto XVII, line 24), signifying a person who stands firm like a cube (tetragon) no matter how they are thrown by fate.</note>

The fact that he canceled these brief and justified outbursts of resentment shows me a good soul, who forgets or despises offenses.

Even though the most noble minds did not hold the industry of profit in contempt—nor did **Giovambatista Gelli** (the "Attic bee") <note>A reference to Gelli’s eloquent and "sweet" Florentine prose style, likening him to the ancient Greek writers of Attica.</note> disdain the craft of the stocking-maker <term>calzettaio: a maker or seller of hosiery</term>, but rather loved it;² nor did it seem ignoble to **Grazzini**, known as **Il Lasca** <note>"The Roach" (a type of freshwater fish); Grazzini was a celebrated poet and founder of the Accademia della Crusca.</note>, to practice the trade of the apothecary, just as it had not seemed so to **Matteo Palmieri**;³ nevertheless, **Davanzati**—whether because of the aforementioned frustrations or because he loved his studies too much—was not content with the time spent in the troubles of the bank. He felt remorse for being so occupied in the pursuit of wealth. Therefore, he lamented to his very dear friend **Baccio Valori** with these verses full of severe melancholy:

> Not of gold, but of a wretched insect’s⁴ thread
> Are the fibers from which I feel both heat and cold,
> And much I carry my face and gasping side,
> So does greedy desire hunt and tame me.

¹ See this marginal note reported in its entirety on page 134.
² His friends would have liked to take him away from that mechanical craft and give him the leisure to attend solely to his studies; but he, with rare modesty, refused, and wished to live by his own labors. However, I do not believe that he ever abandoned the merchant trade. Rather, he devoted himself ever more intently to his studies. The academies, having become affairs of state, began to lose much time in these competitions, trifles, and courtly formalities. Previously, they were bands of friends who gathered simply within private walls to share and fruitfully develop their studies together, not without the seasoning of frank and homely recreations, as the Florentine spirit required. Such was that learned company of the Platonists <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, sponsored by the Medici in the 15th century.</note>, from which the first dawns of renewed philosophy arose in Italy; such was that of the Oricellari Gardens <note>The *Orti Oricellari*, where Machiavelli and his circle discussed politics and history.</note>, where Machiavelli used to read his *Histories*. <page-num>XXII</page-num>

# OF THE LIFE AND WORKS

» to disseminate.¹ » Although distracted by his private business, he strove to ensure that his consulship <note>The "consul" was the elected head of the Academy.</note> flourished with excellent readings, turning his attention to the very best authors.² For the most part, these academic lectures dealt—with more outward show than actual utility—with broad interpretations of our classics. A sonnet or a *canzone* by Petrarch or Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia, a medieval Italian poet and jurist.</note>, or even by some fellow academician, would be selected, and then they would hold forth with endless empty talk. Davanzati, on the contrary, almost always chose subjects of public utility, treating them without unnecessary flourishes, and without (to use one of his own fine phrases) *breaking the neck of rhetoric by wanting too much of it*.³ Only once do I see that he took it upon himself to comment on Petrarch’s *canzone*, *Italia mia* <note>Petrarch's famous patriotic poem "My Italy," which calls for peace and laments the presence of foreign mercenaries.</note>, etc.;⁴ and such a choice leads me to believe that he spoke of things neither academic nor vain. On other occasions he gave readings, but the subjects are unknown, nor among the many manuscripts of those academicians scattered through various libraries have I happened to find any of his.

Meanwhile, another academy had arisen in 1568, primarily through the efforts of Tommaso del Nero,⁵ who gathered many ingenious young men in his home. These gave rise to the Academy of the *Alterati* <note>Literally "The Transformed."</note>, which was also dedicated to the study of the language, and which later, in 1582, provided the model for the Accademia della Crusca.⁶ And also

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>

### BY BERNARDO DAVANZATI.

Davanzati was welcomed into that academy. Every academician, following the fashion that was popular at the time, renamed himself with some strange name and invented a coat of arms and a motto, which they called an *emblem* <note>original: "impresa"</note>.

> “Modest emblems,” (said our author) 
> “usually suggest, with wit, a noble core 
> of some virtue or fortune beneath 
> a humble exterior of some trait 
> belonging to the one who adopts it. <note>1</note>”

Therefore, following his own inclinations and nature, he called himself THE SILENT ONE <note>original: "il Silente"</note>, and took for his insignia a barrel hoop with the words MORE TIGHTLY, MORE COMPRESSED <note>original Latin: *STRICTIUS ARCTIUS*</note>, to signify that speech—as Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, known for promoting "laconic" or brief speech.</note> desired—must contain a great and abundant meaning in short and simple sayings, <note>2</note> and that he almost wished to make himself understood without speaking. Being a man of action and simple ways, he always aimed at the main objective; if he could reach it by shortcuts, he certainly did not take the royal road; because life is short, and the proverb is all too true: *words cannot be threaded like beads.* <note>The Italian adage "le parole non s'infilzano" suggests that talk alone has no substance or practical value.</note> Searching through his papers where he recorded the most choice maxims of the great ancients, I see that he had noted this one from Plutarch: *Concise speech reaches the point and strikes the mind;* <note>original Latin: "Concisa oratio rem assequitur et mentem ferit"</note> "it catches the point and pricks," as he put it. <note>3</note> And indeed, the ideas that best strike the mind are those presented with nothing more than their own essential meaning: any excess,

the more beautiful it <note>Referring to an ornate literary style.</note> is in itself, the more it distracts attention from the core idea, causing it to pass by either misunderstood, misinterpreted, or too slowly, to the annoyance and frustration of those who thirst for knowledge. Therefore, he would have liked to compress many good but overly rambling books into his small circle, extracting from them a sort of distilled substance <note>original: "stillata sostanza"</note> that might better nourish the mind while saving time. He actually did this for some works, as we shall see; and he would have done so for others, such as the *Discourses* of Vincenzio Borghini, had time and inclination not failed him.¹

Among the *Alterati* <note>The "Altered Ones," a prominent Florentine literary academy.</note>, he held the rank of Regent (for so the head of the academy was called). He was the tenth to hold the position, succeeding Cavalier Vincenzio Acciaiuoli, known as "The Troubled,"² to whom he delivered the playful accusation, as was required by the quirky academic custom. There, he read discourses—some grave, some witty—which were always filled with excellent doctrine and the most refined forms of expression. However, he very rarely graced them with his voice, both because he was slow to write (as are all those who love art and meditate deeply) and because his business affairs <term>negozi</term> <note>Davanzati was a successful merchant and financier; "negozi" refers to his commercial duties.</note> did not allow him to indulge too much in such exercises. > » It is never satisfied with anything I do, and it 
> » exhausts me so much that it harms my health: 
> » which my age, my family, and my necessary duties 
> » strongly warn me to protect: therefore, I cannot 
> » study, nor endure these academic labors, nor join 
> » you except rarely.³ »

# OF BERNARDO DAVANZATI.

<sig>i.</sig>

...questions and academic factions, two of which, above all, caused a great stir at that time. One arose within the Florentine Academy and was provoked by Giambullari <note>Pier Francesco Giambullari (1495–1555), a scholar who attempted to prove the divine and ancient origins of the Tuscan tongue.</note>, who, being learned in Oriental languages and wishing to excessively elevate the nobility of his own, claimed it descended from Hebrew, Chaldean, or another language spoken in the region of Aram <note>An ancient region in the central Middle East, primarily modern-day Syria.</note>, with some mixture of Latin and Teutonic due to the periods of Roman and Germanic rule. He based his theory on the migration of Chaldean peoples into Etruria <note>The ancient region of central Italy, roughly corresponding to modern Tuscany.</note>, as attested by Sanchuniathon and Berosus <note>Ancient historians whose works were often cited in Renaissance debates about origins.</note>; on various etymologies; and on the aspiration or *gorgia* <term>gorgia</term> <note>The "Florentine throat," a distinctive phonetic feature where the hard "c" sound is aspirated or softened between vowels.</note> of the Florentines, which—aside from the Spaniards—is unknown to any other people in Italy or Europe. But if this argument held true, the English (as Foscolo <note>Ugo Foscolo (1778–1827), a major Italian poet and literary critic.</note> rightly observes) should be said to be of Greek origin, because they have the Greek *theta* <note>original: "theta" — referring to the 'th' sound in English which resembles the Greek letter θ.</note> in their pronunciation.^1 Nonetheless, Giambullari found followers, and the faction of the "Arameans" was formed in the academy, which was so roughly handled and defeated by the mocking verses of Lasca <note>The pseudonym of Anton Francesco Grazzini (1503–1584), a playwright and poet known for his sharp wit.</note>.^2 — The other question was national rather than academic, and of such weight that it was not silenced until the time of Monti <note>Vincenzo Monti (1754–1828), who participated in the later stages of this linguistic debate.</note>, and is barely silenced now only out of weariness. This was the "Question of the Language": because the Florentines had in their dialect the greatest abundance of the common language of Italy, they had come to claim that this language should be called "Florentine" and not "Italian," and that to write well, one had to be born in Florence or at least have "drunk from the Arno" <note>A common idiom meaning to be raised in Florence or steeped in its culture.</note>. This caused resentment in the other provinces which, by the admission of the Florentines themselves, could boast the purest writers, such as Bembo, Ariosto, Sperone, Tasso, and many others. Thus, when Girolamo Muzio of Capodistria <note>original: "giustinopolitano" — Muzio was a prominent scholar from Justinopolis, the Latin name for Koper/Capodistria.</note> came to Florence at this time, being no less skilled in gram...

...matics, as well as a learned and elegant writer of religious controversies. When it was said to him there <note>referring to the Florentine Academy</note> that "he could not, being a foreigner, write well or with merit in the Florentine idiom;¹" he responded quite appropriately, that:

->. . . . . . . . . . . . it is not the Tuscan rivers<-
->But heaven, art, study, and holy love<-
->That give spirit and life to names and writings.²<-

Hence arose the bitter disputes and mutual recriminations—on one side for the quips <note>original: "riboboli" — colorful, local Florentine idioms or proverbs</note> and Florentinisms <term>fiorentinerie</term> <note>overly precious or local Florentine expressions</note>, and on the other for "barbarisms" and "clumsiness." From this came that book titled *Battles* (*Battaglie*), where Varchi <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a prominent Florentine humanist and historian.</note> is so badly treated, and Machiavelli is called a writer little better than clumsy and lacking in grammar;³ and hence, finally, those disdainful words of our Author <note>Davanzati</note> against "that Muzio who came from Capo d'Istria to Florence to speak and write of this homeland so villainously, and to teach us how to speak with a whip in hand through those pedantic *Battles* of his.⁴"

Despite this, Davanzati never entered directly into the field of these contentions; for he valued his time too much and hated the gossipy chatter of the idly literary. He contented himself only with saying, whenever some particularly lively Florentinism fell into his translation of Tacitus <note>Davanzati is famous for his incredibly concise Italian translation of the Roman historian Tacitus.</note>, with a smirk: "Hush now, or Muzio will shout at us." And in truth, he had no need to learn the properties of the language from the belligerent man of Capo d'Istria; who, if he was polished and refined, nevertheless lacked spirit and nerve, and was missing that...

<page-num>XXVII</page-num>
<header>OF BERNARDO DAVANZATI.</header>

...great virtue of speech, which places things before the eyes, and in which our Author <note>Davanzati</note> has no equal.¹

This virtue he possessed, partly from a happy natural disposition, partly from being a man of action, and above all from the profound study he devoted to Dante and Horace, the unique masters of sculpting thoughts. Besides those two giants, "he highly esteemed Virgil; and wishing to praise the sweetness and smoothness of his style, accompanied by the gravity and majesty found equally throughout his work, he would say that this master of the loftiest song <note>original: "signor dell’ altissimo canto," a reference to Dante’s description of Virgil in the *Inferno*</note> always rang the great bell; as if he made himself heard more than others, or, like the bass in music, led the chorus of all other poets.²" He lovingly sought out effective simplicity in our writers of the fourteenth century <term>trecento</term> <note>The 1300s, regarded by many scholars as the golden age of the Italian language</note>, and loved to collect many manuscripts from that century. Among these, he held most dear one of the Chronicles of Villani <note>Giovanni Villani (c. 1276–1348), whose *Nuova Cronica* is a foundational work of Florentine history</note>; having always regarded it "as a gem of highest value, he left it as such to his heirs in his last will, binding them with the strongest ties to..."

Afterward, I spent time in Lombardy, Piedmont, France, and Flanders; and I was perhaps forty before Florence ever saw me. And putting together all the time I have been there across several visits, I do not know if it would exceed a year. Thus, I was neither born there nor raised there as a child; and that there is not the slightest trace of 'Florentineness' <term>fiorentinaria</term> <note>A term used by critics to mock the perceived pretension or regional quirks of native Florentines</note> in me is plain enough to anyone who hears me speak. He did not only study dead books, but much more the living book of the people, so fertile with teachings for those who know how to read it. <margin>¹ «Many words that had been held in disgust due to the rust of time, he revived by polishing and cleaning them; and many others, which were considered plebeian and base and thus not admitted into noble writings, he displayed, demonstrating their ancient nobility—almost as if providing proof of their lineage—and placed them within his works, where they shine like sparkling stars.» — Rondinelli <note>Francesco Rondinelli (1589–1667), a Florentine scholar and academician who wrote a biography of Davanzati.</note></margin>

...and lordly writer of antiquity <note>A reference to Tacitus, whose style Davanzati famously emulated</note>, who never travels the beaten path, much less walks through the common square. In this way, he also slightly overstepped the mark in his well-intentioned effort to recirculate many words that had been forgotten through neglect of our own riches and a vain desire for the wealth of others;¹ dragging a few from the grave that were prompted neither by necessity nor by elegance. Yet this is a very minor fault compared to the immense merits this writer holds for our language. Even if his only achievement were that—amidst so much academic empty-talk—he stood apart and, by his example, recalled the Italians to that sinewy <term>nervoso</term> <note>Literally "nervous," but in a literary context meaning vigorous, concise, and energetic prose, stripped of unnecessary ornament.</note> and native way of speaking taught by Dante and lost in the luxuries of Boccaccio; taught also by Machiavelli and lost again beneath the courtly trains <note>An allusion to the long, trailing robes of high-ranking churchmen, symbolizing the slow, formal, and overly decorative prose style of the period.</note> of Giovanni della Casa and Pietro Bembo, both monsignors; it seems to me that this alone would be enough to rank him among our primary models. I do not know if this virtue was appreciated in him by his contemporaries. Certainly, they were the least suited to sense it, judging by their own writings. Indeed, while there is no man of letters in that age, great or small, who does not speak of miracles regarding Varchi <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a central figure in Florentine linguistic debates.</note> and the knight Salviati <note>Leonardo Salviati (1540–1589), a founder of the Accademia della Crusca.</note>, I find few who even mention the name of Bernardo Davanzati; and those few, when they do praise him, remark more upon his linguistic proficiency—a trait common to many—than on the robustness of his style, in which he stood alone. Indeed, in his repertoire or handbook, under the heading "Philosophy and the other arts serve theology,"<note>original: "*Philosophia et cæteræ artes deserviunt theologiæ*"</note> I see that he collected a long series of authorities proving that truth, which today is the cornerstone for anyone who has wished to find the greatest and most dialectical unification in theological studies. Among the Fathers of the Church, I see the maxims of Clement of Alexandria cited most often, perhaps because he was more abundant in erudition.<gloss>1</gloss> Alongside Dante he often cites Saint Thomas Aquinas, of whom he especially notes his sharp and precise definitions. But I find more extensive studies on the Holy Scriptures, of which one sees not only the maxims collected and ordered under certain headings, but also some difficulties discussed that occurred to him during his reading. And since even from small signs the character of a man is revealed, I seem to see the merchant, and the Florentine, where he carefully records that passage of the Bible: "you shall lend to many nations, but you yourself shall borrow from none";<gloss>2</gloss><note>original: "*fœnerabis gentibus multis et ipse a nullo fœnus accipies*"</note> observing that "usury was not prohibited except with those of the lineage of Israel."<gloss>3</gloss> Sometimes he intersperses these notes with some application to his own times. of Pier Vettori, the elder, and nephew to 그 Girolamo, whose name cannot be remembered without the mind rushing to the ardent sermons of the friar from Ferrara <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), the Dominican friar whose charismatic and fiery preaching led to the "Bonfire of the Vanities" in Florence.</note>, and the chants and the dances and the fiercely devout bonfires: with Filippo Sassetti, a shrewd merchant, intrepid traveler, and elegant writer:¹ with Bernardo Buontalenti, an illustrious architect, for whose sake he drew material from the Greek of Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, an ancient Greek engineer known for hydraulic inventions.</note> for those whimsical fountain designs of his which embellished the Boboli and Pratolino gardens, and which contributed to giving him the nickname *Bernardo of the Pinwheels*.² Although austere and "by nature and by study of words, not very abundant <note>original: "poco abbondevole"</note>,³" yet he sometimes loved cheerful company, nor did he disdain to amuse them with writings that were perhaps too lively, according to the bad habit of the time.⁴

He was, however, honest in his life: he longed for the ancient loyalty: he was indignant at the corrupt living and the immoderate luxury of his age.⁵ He was mindful of benefits received, and he did not want to leave the merits of those who had served him with faith to the discretion of forgetful heirs. For shortly before closing his eyes forever, having a good sum of money brought to his bedside, he wished to personally reward his servants and thank them. He was sincerely religious without superstition, which he had defined in his own way in a margin of his Plutarch: "superstition, like foam, rust, or eye-crust."⁶

<page-num>XXXVI</page-num>

### OF THE LIFE AND THE WORKS

And I am pleased to recount the words with which Rondinelli describes his death:

> "He took this last step with supreme religion and Christian piety: so that while sitting up in bed, it seemed he no longer felt or understood anything; but when those standing around him spoke of spiritual things concerning his soul, he would then raise his head as much as he could, listening intently and gathering with great greed those reminders and discourses being made: a sign of how one realizes then how all mortal things are vain; therefore, he acts with great wisdom who, beforehand, does not become overly entangled in them, using them with that moderation which is proper."

After having brought forth from this Francesco Rondinelli <gloss>1</gloss> the most beautiful and important traits found in the short account he titled *Portrait*, it would be a grave mistake not to transcribe (before speaking of our subject's works) the stupendous <term>ethopoeia</term> <note>A rhetorical term for a vivid description of a person's character and manners.</note> with which he gives the final touch to his picture:

> "Bernardo Davanzati was, for those who would wish to know it, small of body; of a brown complexion. He had lively eyes, black hair, a small and sparse beard; his forehead, like his cheeks, was wrinkled; his face, rather severe than not. In his dress, he loved ancient parsimony and civil customs: in eating and drinking, he was sober: in speaking, he was brief, flavorful, and sententious; because words, no differently than coins, are more esteemed when they enclose greater value in a smaller circle. Some called him the *peppercorn* <note>original: "grano di pepe"</note>, led perhaps by his brown color and the wrinkles of his face, but much more by the wisdom, sharpness, and virtue of his soul gathered into a small body. He despised praise for his own things, always judging them imperfect. He more often blamed the errors of others..."

<page-num>XXXVIII</page-num>

### ON THE LIFE AND WORKS

comparing it with Italian, he judged that whereas the latter was flabby, weak-jointed, prolix, and light, the former [French] was virile, robust, grave, and concise. And as proof, he did not compare Dante with Marot or Malherbe, nor Machiavelli with Montaigne or others; instead, he took a speech by Tacitus,<sup>1</sup> and upon that he compared the translation by Giorgio Dati (who had expanded the text on purpose to make its difficulties clear to everyone) with that of Blaise de Vigenère. After having counted the words of both and found nine more in the Italian version, without considering whether this was by necessity or choice, he cried out that the Italian (*which is a great pity* <note>original: "qui est la grand’ pitié"</note>) could not have done it with one fewer without being ruined, *without being constrained* <note>original: "sans estre contrainte"</note>. This boasting, coming from such a man, caused indignation in Italy, and more than anyone else, it stung <note>literally "gave the gnat to"</note> Messer Bernardo. He soon set out *to disprove by deed the ill-spoken words of Henri Estienne*,<sup>2</sup> and began to wrestle with Tacitus for the boast of brevity, as the "absolute master of that omnipotent Florentine tongue."<sup>3</sup> Having completed a sample, he sent it to his friend Gianvincenzio Pinelli in Padua (1591), by whom he was greatly encouraged on that *steep climb*.<sup>4</sup> But being by then old and suffering from failing eyesight, he despaired of reaching the summit. Therefore, he remained content to publish only the first book of the Annals, addressing it to Baccio Valori. To him—after a discourse on the vividness and efficacy of the Florentine tongue over common Italian, which, "like wine begged from door to door <note>original: "vino limosinato a uscio a uscio"</note>, does not seem to sparkle or sting"—he shows that this first book...

book, "with all the disadvantages of articles and other things" [the Italian text] turns out, upon examination, to have five thousand fewer letters than the Latin, and thirty-seven thousand fewer than the French: from which he concludes "one may recognize from this sample, as the lion is known by its claw <note>original: "dall' unghia il lione"; a reference to the Latin proverb *ex ungue leonem*, meaning to judge the whole by a small part</note>, the fierceness of our vernacular." ...corrupt and destroy the purity and elegance of the language of the country, for the strengthening of which others employed all their care and industry. ¹ <note>original: "rompre et faire perir la pureté et l'élégance de la langue du pays..."</note> » These are trifles not worth refuting, except perhaps by a Frenchman for the honor of his nation; a task to which **Egidio Menagio** <note>Gilles Ménage (1613–1692), a French scholar and philologist who defended Italian literature</note> peradventure applied his mind. ² In the 18th century, as linguistic studies continued to decline, it is no wonder if the "Florentine Tacitus" <note>Davanzati's famous translation of the Roman historian Tacitus</note> was met with silence or spoken of with blame. **Fontanini** and **Zeno** <note>Giusto Fontanini and Apostolo Zeno, prominent 18th-century bibliographers and critics</note> do not appreciate him much; ³ **Tiraboschi** <note>Girolamo Tiraboschi, author of a monumental history of Italian literature</note> barely mentions him; and even the two **Salvinis** show themselves somewhat severe toward him. ⁴ But with the resurrection of **Dante**—that is, the dignity of Italian feeling and speech—the star of **Davanzati** was also rekindled in that great fire; nor is this a sign of little worth in him. I will not speak of **Cesari** <note>Antonio Cesari, a leader of the Purist movement who idolized 14th-century Florentine style</note>, as it is well understood how he must have been infatuated with him; nor will I dwell on **Perticari**, who naturally had to criticize him. But **Alfieri**, **Foscolo**, **Giordani**, **Leopardi**, and **Tommaséo** (representing the most vigorous minds of Italian letters in this century) recognized that "he had competed with Tacitus in that force of expression which clearly demonstrates a corresponding force of soul and intellect. ⁵" But no one judged him better than **Foscolo**, who saw clearly that **Davanzati’s** "Florentinism" was a pure illusion of his own and of those who believed him, born of a few scattered <term>riboboli: colorful, local Florentine idioms or proverbs</term> which could be removed with slight care without diminishing anything—indeed, while adding much to the strength, brevity, and beauty—and that he "had the tra-"

» ...the most marvelous production that has ever existed. » The language into which he translated is that understood and written by every cultured Italian, and « in translating, he wrote in such an original manner » that no one has since, nor ever will, be able to imitate him. ¹

To Leopardi <note>Giacomo Leopardi (1798–1837), one of Italy's greatest poets and scholars</note>, after having called this translation "extremely vigorous and highly original" <note>original: *nervosissima, originalissima*</note> and impossible to imitate, it seemed that it did not provide a faithful portrait of Tacitus's character, precisely because of that beautiful air (he says) of familiarity and ease that Davanzati gave it, which is not found in the original, which is entirely austere and grave. ² But if the translation is *extremely vigorous*, it possesses (it seems to me) the most distinctive trait of the Tacitean style: and let us grant that at times it detracts from the gravity with some proverbial speech; this, being infrequent, cannot constitute the entire character of the translation. But most people, having found phrases like *it’s either an ace or a six* <note>original: *o asso o sei*; a gambling metaphor meaning "all or nothing"</note>, *to go off the rails* <note>original: *andare in orinci*</note>, *all in an upheaval* <note>original: *tutt' in bulima*</note>, *a gloomy face* <note>original: *viso saturnino*</note>, and a few other such plebeian expressions, immediately cried out without further consideration: "Behold, the Roman consuls converted into common market-women!" <note>original: *Crezie*; a Florentine nickname for simple or low-class women</note> It is as if all of Tacitus were wrapped in this mud, and did not rather have the occasional splash, which can neither change the quality nor diminish the value of a rich garment. Here the proverb was proven true: "What a few strike up, the others sing." ³ <note>original: *Quello che pochi intuonano, gli altri cantano*. This is a translation of Tacitus, *Annals* II, 12: *quae pauci incipiant, omnes canant*.</note> For if the saying of Quintilian <note>A famous Roman teacher of rhetoric</note> is true—that no word is so lowly that, when placed appropriately, it cannot receive nobility—then it cannot be said that Davanzati always diminished the reverence due to Tacitus with such words, when he used them where nature required them. Consider whether the mutinous soldiers in Germany could have spoken more appropriately, or if a more artful and choice discourse would have been [appropriate] for them...

...better? ¹ He did not use those [plebeian expressions] when he made Arminius, ² Seneca, or Nero speak; ³ nor when he described the death of Libo, ⁴ of Piso, ⁵ of Otho, ⁶ or the burning of Rome; ⁷ nor when he painted the portraits of Galba ⁸ and Poppaea Sabina. ⁹ What is there here, and in a hundred other places, that is merely Florentine? Or rather, what is there that is not illustrious Italian? Or, to put it better, of consular and imperial majesty? Is Foscolo <note>Ugo Foscolo (1778–1827), a revolutionary poet and critic who championed Davanzati’s style</note> not right then? Or should Giordani <note>Pietro Giordani (1774–1848), a classical scholar and friend of Leopardi</note> also have simply believed our Bernardo when he claimed to have wanted to translate « not with the most noble speech of literary writers, but with the common talk of the people of Florence? » ¹⁰ But then why did he not translate Tacitus as Zannoni <note>Giovan Battista Zannoni (1774–1832), known for writing in a very rustic, street-level Florentine dialect</note> later wrote the *Ciane*? That indeed would have been true Florentine, not this.

Nor do I intend by this to defend him where he sometimes fails—out of a desire to be too brief—to fully render the Latin concept; or where he misunderstands (almost always due to a defect in the source text); ¹¹ or where he uses shortcuts that are too violent, and therefore obscure; or where he needlessly exhumes too many dead words. These words, however, he took care to clarify not only in the *Annotations* <note>original: *Postille*; marginal or end notes</note>, but also in an Index, where he exchanged both Florentinisms and archaic terms for "current coin" <note>meaning common, modern equivalents</note> for whoever might want them. If only he had had the time to complete the *Annotations*, so sharp, so lively, so full of noble and sometimes novel thoughts on aesthetics, politics, economics, and morality!

<page-num>XLIV</page-num>
-># OF THE LIFE AND THE WORKS<-

With the history of the *Schism* <note>original: *Scisma*; referring to Davanzati's work *Lo Scisma d'Inghilterra* (The Schism of England)</note> he deserved well not only of literature, but of Catholicism, which had begun to be undermined even in Italy by the innovations of the monk from Wittenberg <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German priest who initiated the Protestant Reformation</note> and by the violent lusts of Henry VIII of England. Florence, protected by the fierce orders of Cosimo <note>Cosimo I de' Medici (1519–1574), who maintained strict religious orthodoxy in his state</note>, was little touched by it; yet some Florentines had approached the new heresy, such as Carnesecchi; others had openly joined it, like Peter Martyr Vermigli and a few others who fled elsewhere. Neighboring Siena had been shaken by the fall of Ochino, who was already renowned for great learning and holiness;² and the two Soccini, Fausto and Lelio, were attempting a new school of error <note>The Soccini family developed Socinianism, a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity</note>. Showing from what base origins the disastrous English discord arose could not help but shed light also on the character of the other enemies of Catholic truth. And perhaps Davanzati, a man of felt and firm faith, aimed more at this than at a pure linguistic exercise. At first, his work was thought to be original; later it was doubted, as the small preface attached to it—which was found by Gamba in the Marciana manuscript—was not yet known; in it, he says clearly that he wanted to attempt, using the history by the Jesuit Nicholas Sanders <note>Nicholas Sanders (c. 1530–1581), an English Catholic polemicist</note>, the same trial already performed *on the first five books of Cornelius Tacitus* <note>Davanzati's famous challenge was to translate the dense Latin of Tacitus into an even smaller number of Italian words</note>. From this, it can be seen that he conducted this small work as an interlude and rest from the heavy labor on the Latin historian. Here, too, one finds the same vigor, purity, and conciseness. However, it is regrettable that he was too severe in pruning the original; having omitted not only every moral and political consideration, but also circumstances of great importance. This makes his [work]...

> ¹ We gladly include here a note that Abbot Michele Colombo placed at the beginning of the *Schism* <note>original: *Scisma*; referring to Davanzati's *Lo Scisma d’Inghilterra*</note> in the 1727 Cominiana edition <note>Books printed by the Comino brothers in Padua, famous for their accuracy</note>; for which we are indebted to the courtesy of the illustrious Angelo Pezzana, librarian of the Parmense <note>The Palatine Library of Parma</note>, where the said copy is kept. — “In the style of Bernardo Davanzati, whether he translates or speaks in his own voice, there is always an originality that makes him stand out from all other writers. No one is more skilled than he in the handling of the language: rich in his parsimony, he knows how to enclose many meanings in few words; he is always polished and refined, expressing himself, even without seeking ornaments, with grace, spirit, and a charm entirely his own. A single word from his pen is sometimes worth an entire phrase, and possesses more strength and loveliness; with such finesse and ingenuity does he know how to employ it.

> ” This excellent writer is not, however, without some faults. It seems to me that he occasionally gives a sentence a turn that is too studied, making it lose some of that fluidity and smoothness that is so pleasing; as, for example, where he says: *How much more useful would it be for men, rather than children; for the heads of Kingdoms, rather than minor Princes; for the royal persons themselves, rather than their children, to marry one another?* (page 19). Sometimes he uses constructions that are a bit strange. Such appears to me the one in the following passage (unless there is an error both in the printing by Massi and Landi cited by the Academicians of the Crusca <note>The Accademia della Crusca is the premier institution for the Italian language</note> in their Dictionary, and in both Cominiana editions, of which I have some suspicion): *Another, named Oppero, when he was a Catholic, spoke ill of the too-much wealth* <note>original: *troppo ricchezza*; an archaic use of 'too much' as an adjective modifying a noun directly</note> *and soft life of the Bishops* (*). (page 107). The phrasing would have been more regular in this way: *spoke ill of the too-rich and soft life, etc.* (**). Another is this: *The other nations outside have always spoken of it freely: and grieved* <note>original: *doltosi*; a plural past participle used here without a supporting 'they have'</note> *that your youth has been deceived by your wise men* (page 20). Since that participle *grieved* cannot be subordinate to *have*, like the other participle *spoken*, regular construction required it to be: *and they have grieved, etc.*; but the writer preferred in this place to serve brevity of expression rather than subject himself to the scrupulous regularity of the phrasing. Furthermore, precisely for the love of brevity, he sometimes subordinates several things to a single verb, to some of which the verb cannot properly belong, as seen in this phrase: *At fifteen years old, she allowed herself to be deflowered by the Cupbearer, and then by the Chaplain of Thomas Boleyn* (page 23). Unless she had miraculously become a maiden again, after the act of the Cupbearer she could not be deflowered also by the Chaplain. Certainly with less brevity, but with greater propriety, the author would have expressed himself by saying: *she allowed herself to be deflowered by the Cupbearer, and then [abused]...*

# XLVI OF THE LIFE AND WORKS

The lectures on ***Exchange*** and on ***Money*** should be judged according to what was then known of public economy; and they will be found laudable not so much for the propriety and purity of the prose, as for the matters they contain. In the first, he restricts himself to describing with beautiful clarity the method of currency circulation, without entering into higher considerations regarding this new and powerful impulse given by the Florentines to commerce. In the second, he discourses eruditely on metals, on the different types of value, and above all, he laments the decline of the Florentine currency in his day, so damaging to trade, and to co—

---

...made himself available to the Chaplain, etc. <note>The author is continuing a list of stylistic "faults" or quirks in Davanzati's writing.</note> Sometimes he passes from one subject <note>original: *nominativo*</note> to another, letting the sense alone determine which of them the various actions mentioned belong to. Here is an example: *the Devil incited him to despoil the Convents: telling them full of rages, lusts, ignorance, ambition, and scandals; and they discovered one another; and gave them in commendam to men of account* (page 66). Here *incited* <note>original: *stigò*</note> refers to the Devil, *telling them* <note>original: *dicendoli*</note> to Henry <note>Henry VIII</note>, *discovered one another* to the Convents, and *gave them* again to Henry. These sudden leaps from one subject to another, and from this to yet another, without the aid of some pronoun to indicate to which of them the action belongs, usually generate confusion in the reader's mind at first glance; and therefore, it seems to me, they are to be avoided.

Sometimes he joins certain words to others without there being a connection between them. We have an example of this in the following passage: *More was a layman: most pleasing to the general public: England did not produce for many centuries a man so great: born noble in London: most learned in Greek and Latin: experienced in magistracies and embassies 40 years* (page 62) <note>Referring to Sir Thomas More</note>. These words *forty years* are attached there in a way I cannot quite explain. One might also perhaps charge him with the vice of tossing out, as he very often does, the various members of a sentence without linking them to one another. I agree that such "unlinking" <note>The stylistic device of asyndeton, or omitting conjunctions</note> is not always to be blamed; I confess further that in some cases it may even deserve praise, as when one makes a person speak who is agitated by some vehement passion; but in our author, they seem too frequent to me, and I do not know if they can all be sufficiently justified. 

Finally, one encounters in this Author some words that are either too Latinate, such as *succedituro* <note>one who is to succeed</note>, *vocato* <note>called</note>, *corampopolo* <note>original: *coram populo*; in public/before the people</note>, etc., or too antiquated, such as *di certano* <note>certainly</note>, *le piacimenta* <note>pleasures</note>, *le peccata* <note>sins</note>, *ammorbidoe* <note>softened</note>, *morette* <note>likely a dialectal form of deaths or perhaps "small moorings"</note>, etc., or too low and popular, such as *la vilia* <note>the eve of a feast</note>, *far belli falò* <note>to make fine bonfires</note>, and other similar terms. But these little blemishes <note>original: *taccherelle*</note> are almost made to disappear by the supreme merits of such a great writer. It seems to me, however, that his style is rather to be held in high regard than to be imitated; since it would be too difficult to achieve its beauties, and too easy to contract its defects.

# BY BERNARDO DAVANZATI. XLVII

themselves who imprudently cause it. If one considers that before Davanzati, there was only Gasparo Scaruffi who had sampled this subject matter;¹ the Abbé Galiani will not seem particularly moderate in the severity with which he judged our author’s doctrines.² Davanzati, as a practical and cultured merchant and as an agreeable academic, intended only to collect the observations of his own experience, embellishing them with curious erudition and the refinements of the language.

I will not dwell long on the two *Humorous Orations* <note>original: *Orazioni facete*</note>, delivered to the *Alterati* <note>The *Accademia degli Alterati* (The Transformed), a Florentine literary society focused on the study of language and drama</note>. I do not call them by their proper name of *Cicalate* <term>Cicalate: literally "chatterings" or "trifles," these were lighthearted, often nonsensical academic lectures popular in 16th-century Italy</term>, so as not to give cause for indignation to the more serious-minded. But if they wished to compare them with the others that idly weigh down the volumes of the *Florentine Prose*, I am certain they would find them not without the flavor of Attic wit and containing some substance of good thought. That pleasant, lively, and whimsical Florentine spirit could not be extinguished even under the scourge of the terrible proscriptions of Cosimo <note>Cosimo I de' Medici, who transformed Florence into a more rigid autocracy</note>. Indeed, seeing how the "merry companies" grew during this time, and how this pastime of "chattering" was more in vogue than ever;³ one might believe that the Florentines wished, through such trifles, to forget themselves and their present ills; if one did not know that almost everyone who had been able to remain in Florence was not the sort to grieve too much over the lost ancient orders of the republic.

Among the works of Fronto, one can read the praises of negligence, of dust, and of smoke. And the celebrated discoverer and editor of this and many other literary monuments, Cardinal Angelo Mai, defends the author with the example of Xenophon, Plato, Favorinus, and many others, who did not disdain such diversions. See *Letters of Marcus Cornelius Fronto and the Emperor Marcus Aurelius* <note>original: *Marci Cornelii Frontonis et M. Aurelii imperatoris epistolæ*</note>, edited by Angelo Mai. Rome 1823, page 324.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Bernardo Davanzati’s minor works, moving from his lighthearted academic lectures to his formal "Funeral Oration for Cosimo I de' Medici."
