->### ON THE LIFE AND WORKS<-

Just as he yielded to those lighthearted trifles <term>cicalate: literally "chatterings," these were informal, often humorous academic lectures</term>, he likewise applied himself to the *Funeral Oration for Cosimo* <note>Cosimo I de' Medici (1519–1574), the first Grand Duke of Tuscany</note>; it is not entirely hollow and wordy like those of the magnificent knight Master Lionardo Salviati and a hundred other academics and gentlemen; but it is certainly not worthy of the translator of Tacitus <note>Davanzati was famous for his concise Italian translation of the Roman historian Tacitus</note>. He praises the crowns, the scepters, and the royal ornaments worn by Cosimo in a dominant city not subject to foreign power: he praises the bonfires lit from the *Mugello even unto the Adriatic Sea* at his birth: he praises the splendor of his house; the beauty of his person; the principality he obtained, *the most desirable and supreme good of all humans*: he praises his intellect and, as proof, cites *the disputes he had with Lorenzo di Pier Francesco*; he praises his enemies who were (and this is true) *the axes and hammers used to build and fix his principality in place*. It is as if, in wishing to praise him, there were no other merits to find in this man—who, not only for his tyrannical spirit but for his cunning nature and statecraft, was called the "Tuscan Tiberius" <note>A comparison to the Roman Emperor Tiberius, known for his reclusive and suspicious nature</note>—such as the studies and talents he promoted; the histories he commissioned and allowed Varchi <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), a historian whose *Florentine History* was commissioned by Cosimo</note> to write freely; the revival of commerce and industry; the opening of colleges; the endowment of universities; the vigorous observation of laws; the reclaiming of marshes; the aid given to agriculture; and other praiseworthy deeds, which were either kept silent or lightly glossed over by our academic.

The agrarian art, which draws something simple, noble, and poetic from the pure and majestic beauty of the fields, was cherished by elite minds in Tuscany no less than in Greece, where as many as fifty georgic writers are found cited. Tuscan are the fourteenth-century translations of Palladio and Crescenzi <note>Palladius (4th century) and Pietro de' Crescenzi (13th century) were foundational authors on agriculture</note>: Tuscan too are Vettori, Soderini, Alamanni, and Magazzini, who dressed the matters of the country villa in such elegance. But no one, in terms of evident propriety and nimble, lucid concision, goes before Davanzati, whose *Treatise on Tuscan Cultivation* is a precious and rare gem. This writing too...

# BIBLIOGRAPHY

## OF THE WORKS OF BERNARDO DAVANZATI.

---

**I. — The first book of the Annals of Gaius Cornelius Tacitus expressed in the Florentine vernacular by Bernardo Davanzati Bostichi, to demonstrate how brief and sharp this speech can be. In Florence, printed by Giorgio Marescotti, 1596. Small octavo.**

The first 8 leaves <note>In early printing, a "leaf" consists of two pages, front and back.</note>, which contain the title page and the letter to Baccio Valori, although included in the count, are not numbered. It has numbers marked in the margin referring to the <term>postille<gloss>marginal or explanatory notes provided by the author to clarify the text</gloss></term>, which begin on page 78 and number 60 in total. On pages 75-77 is the declaration of *Ancient names and how they are spoken modernly*. The final page notes six errors to be corrected.

> « Of this small edition, which gives us the first sample of the celebrated translation of Tacitus made by Bernardo Davanzati, the Academicians <note>The Academicians of the Crusca, the primary authority on the Italian language.</note> made use. See the entry for STRINGATO <note>meaning "concise" or "tightly wound"</note> which is taken from the author's dedication to Baccio Valori, and which is read in the last line of the fourth page. » (Gamba.)

> « The author's dedicatory letter to Baccio Valori is also found in *The Reign of Tiberius Caesar*, printed by the Giunti in 1600, but with notable changes made by the author. And as he revised it in that book, so it was afterwards reproduced by Nesti following the *Postille* in the *Works of Cornelius Tacitus translated by Davanzati* and printed in 1637, in folio; but because of the changes made there, the word *stringato* is no longer found in these reprints. And therefore, as it is read only in the edition of the *First Book of the Annals*, made by Marescotti in 1596, it is manifest that this edition was also used by the Academicians. » (Colombo, cited by Gamba.)

**II. — The Reign of Tiberius Caesar written by Cornelius Tacitus in the Annals, rendered in the proper Florentine language by Bernardo Davanzati Bostichi. In Florence, by Filippo Giunti, 1600, with permission of the superiors and privilege. Quarto.**

The first six unnumbered leaves contain, besides the title page, 1st: the dedication to Baccio Valori, altered and summarized, as mentioned above. 2nd: Another letter to the same man, in which he discusses the reasons for his translation, extended through the entirety of the sixth book of the Annals, so that the victory of the Florentine language might be more certain in the proof of brevity. 3rd: The description of the *Lineage of Augustus*, divided into two tables, and of the *Lineage of Livia, wife of Augustus* in a single table. The translation occupies 160 numbered pages, perfectly aligned with the Lyonese edition (1581) of the Latin text to facilitate the counting of Latin and Italian words and the comparison of their totals. It should be noted that the books of the Annals translated here appear to be five; but in the last one, the fragments of the fifth and the whole of the sixth are included. On page 161, the *Postille* begin, which go until page 203, marked by error as 603. Some of these notes are not read in later editions because the translator changed or corrected the passages to which they referred; others are read there either expanded or corrected in their phrasing. Finally, some important notes from the later editions are not read here. After a blank page follows the *Table of the most notable things*, compiled by the translator stes-

LII

# BIBLIOGRAPHY.

text, which occupies 10 unnumbered leaves. Finally, the last leaf has the table of Errors occurred by fault of the typographer on the front side, and some few *Changes* on the back. The last leaf features the Giunti coat of arms, the register, and the typographic notes, repeated as they appear on the title page. — The books are not divided into chapters. —

The first book is reproduced with many corrections and revisions, which are very useful to consider. The Academicians <note>The members of the Accademia della Crusca, the official guardians of the Italian language.</note> do not seem to have benefited much from this edition, although it could have provided them with vocabulary not found in later versions. Even modern editors have taken no account of either this or the previous one. And yet, since these were the only printings conducted under the translator's own eyes, they could have drawn much light from them to make their editions more exact and complete.

A copy formerly existing in the Rinuccini library, and now held by the distinguished Count Mortara, is entirely annotated in the translator’s own hand. Through the courtesy of the owner, we have been able to examine it and profit from it for our edition, as can be seen from the *Variants* recorded at the end of the volume. That these marginal notes are in the translator’s hand does not seem to me to be in doubt after comparing them with known autographs; and if a few seem at first glance to be by a different hand, this arises from the difference in the ink and the time at which they were written. There are some curiosities to note which give ever greater credit to the authenticity of these notes. The first is that at the end of the second book, where Tacitus, describing the character of Arminius, says <note>original: "proeliis ambiguus"</note> *uncertain in battle*, Davanzati translates: “*in battles dangerous*;” but in the right margin he pulls out <margin>ambiguus</margin>, and in the other notes: <margin>there was something to say.</margin> <note>original: "ci fu che dire"</note> This shows that Davanzati, reading his translation to some learned friend or in the Academy of the Alterati <note>A Florentine literary society where scholars critiqued each other's work.</note> itself, did not find approval for that passage. And indeed, in the Nesti edition, one sees it changed thus: “*in battles varied.*” The second is that, by a whim of portraying popular pronunciation even in writing, he truncates a great number of words, linking them together, almost as in the *Ciane* of Zannoni. Here are some examples: *megli' amavan'* <note>they loved better</note> the present: *'l debol aiuto* <note>the weak help</note>: *molto giovanett' al pontificato* <note>very young to the pontificate</note>: *ogni cos' a lui* <note>everything to him</note>: *mentr' Agusto* <note>while Augustus</note>: *voless' anzi* <note>wanted rather</note>: *d' anim' arrogant' e crudele* <note>of an arrogant and cruel soul</note>: *pér tem' o 'nvidia* <note>for fear or envy</note>: *la nott' o la ser' a contaminare* <note>the night or the evening to contaminate</note>: *i pe'* (peli) <note>the hairs</note> gray: *mettess' a ferr' e fuoc' e 'n terror il paese* <note>put the country to sword and fire and terror</note> etc.: then he always changes *poco* <note>little</note> into *po'*; *fece* <note>he did/made</note> into *fe'*; *cotali* <note>such</note> into *cota'*; *furono* <note>they were</note> into *fur'*; *sarebbe* <note>it would be</note> into *sar'*; *li, delli, alli, cappelli* into *gli, degli, agli, capegli*; and so on until the end.

The manuscript that served for this Giunti edition is preserved in the Magliabechiana <note>Now part of the National Central Library of Florence.</note> (cl. XXIII, 150) with the title “Marginal notes to the Annals of Cornelius Tacitus and books II, III, IV and V of the said Annals translated into the Florentine language by Bernardo Davanzati Bostichi. Original.” This codex belonged to Senator Carlo di Tommaso Strozzi, 1673. But it is not truly the original, as is written here and as Salvino Salvini also asserts (*Fasti consolari, page 228*): what are original are many corrections, the marginal notes, and some leaves at the beginning. That this copy then served for printing is seen from the approvals of the ecclesiastical censors, Carlo Rucellai, Florentine canon and academician, Alessandro Caccia, inquisitor, and Brother Matteo Sanmattei, chancellor (June 7 and 15, 1599). The first book is missing because the translator perhaps made the corrections for it directly upon the Marescotti edition.

### III. — Works of Gaius Tacitus with the translation into the Florentine vernacular by Mr. Bernardo Davanzati placed opposite the Latin text with the marginal notes of the same and the explanation of some less-understood words, with a most copious table. To the most serene Prince Leopold of Tuscany. In Florence, in the printing house of Pietro Nesti, 1637, with permission of the superiors.

Folio. Following the title page are 24 unnumbered leaves containing the Dedication, the Warning, the lineage of Augustus and Livia, and the Table of Contents. The text and the translation number 424 pages divided into columns. From page 425 to 461 are the Notes: from page 461 to 465 are the two letters to Baccio Valori and a third to the Academicians of the Alterati. There follows the *Declaration of some words commonly less understood* in eight unnumbered pages: and lastly a monstrous list of errata, which barely meets half the need, as Volpi says, not without exaggeration.

LIII

# BIBLIOGRAPHY.

This is the first edition of the complete vernacular translation, prepared by the members of the Crusca Academy <note>The Accademia della Crusca is the primary institution for the study and preservation of the Italian language.</note>, 31 years after the author's death. It was cited in their Dictionary, although it turned out to be quite full of errors. “Desired by many scholars, but for various reasons held back and delayed after the death of Davanzati, who did not have time to polish and correct it. But several worthy men, devoted to his memory and moved by zeal for the common good and for their own tongue, employed every effort and every means so that the work might be printed in the best possible way.” — Zeno, notes to Fontanini, vol. I, page 296. Gamba asserts that *The Empire of Tiberius Caesar* <note>original: "Imperio di Tiberio Cesare"</note> was reproduced in this edition. But this is not the case, because a comparison shows that the reading of the first book, and the five that follow, varies greatly—due to many corrections and revisions—from the Marescotti and Giunta editions. From this it is manifest that the Academicians (though they make no mention of it) based their edition on manuscripts, without taking into account the two aforementioned printings: perhaps because they saw that the translator had made many changes to them. But they should have at least provided an account of the manuscript: whether it was an original or a copy, and where and how they found it.

The letter to Baccio Valori, previously printed by Marescotti, is here entirely changed and summarized. Another letter, to the *Accademici Alterati* <note>The "Altered Academicians," a Florentine literary society founded in the 16th century.</note>, is newly added. As for the marginal notes, see what we said above when discussing *The Empire of Tiberius Caesar*.

I am aware of two notable copies of this edition. One is held by Marquis Gino Capponi; it is entirely corrected by hand by an anonymous writer of that time, who seems to have intended to use it as the basis for a new, more correct, and better-ordered printing. Nor would I be far from believing that he was one of the very editors assigned to the task. He is certainly a man of letters, for he does not limit himself only to correcting the errors listed at the end of the book, but makes other corrections of his own, and expands and corrects both the table of contents and the explanation of less common words. — G. Poggiali also possessed an elegant, wide-margined copy, furnished with ancient handwritten marginal notes regarding linguistic matters. (See *Series of Linguistic Texts* <note>original: "Serie de' testi di lingua"</note>. Livorno 1813, vol. I, page 373.)

The other copy is found in the Magliabechiana Library <note>Now part of the National Central Library of Florence, named after the bibliophile Antonio Magliabechi.</note>, and its margins are filled to overflowing with tiny handwritten notes, some philological <note>Relating to the study of language in historical literary texts.</note>, others scholarly, concerning both the Latin text and the translation. It contains this note on the flyleaf in Magliabechi's hand:

> “*The handwritten marginal notes in this Tacitus, with the translation by Davanzati, are by Mr. Pietro Pietri Danzicano, a great expert in our language and a member of the Crusca Academy, and they are written in his own hand. The said Pietro Pietri lived in Florence for a long time, and later retired to Padua, where he died.*”

(Regarding this man, see also the letter from Rosso Martini, here on page LXV.) He performed many other studies on the text of Tacitus and on Davanzati’s translation, which can be found in two Magliabechian codices, marked numbers 34 and 35, class XXIII. It appears the Academicians made significant use of them in the fourth printing of the Dictionary. In general, these marginal notes (many of which concern the Latin text) are not of great value. We have provided a sample of some of the more important ones in our edition.

The Florence edition by G. B. Landini, 1641, is a copy of the previous one both in its layout and its type; but it provides only the *Annals*, without an index or explanation of words.

### IV. — Works of Gaius Cornelius Tacitus with the translation into the Florentine vernacular by Mr. Bernardo Davanzati placed alongside the Latin text with his marginal notes and the explanation of certain less-understood words with a very copious table. New edition, purged of the innumerable errors of all previous ones, as is demonstrated in the preface. In Padua 1755 by Giuseppe Comino, with permission of the superiors.
->Large Quarto.<-
<note>A "Large Quarto" refers to a book format where each sheet is folded twice, creating four large leaves.</note>

This edition, upon which all subsequent ones have been based, was edited by Giovanni Antonio Volpi. Although he took the *Nesti* edition as his text, he nevertheless removed a great many of the errors that had occurred in it. I say a great many, not all; because he left some, even large ones, and added others of his own. See further on the notes to his *Preface*.

# BIBLIOGRAPHY.

Two Venetian editions barely deserve mention; *one by Fr. Storti, 1658, in quarto*; <note>A "quarto" is a book size where the printed sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note> where the editor says of Davanzati that he can make one doubtful in interpreting the meaning whether the vernacular or the Latin was the original: *the other by Pezzana, 1677, in quarto*; who, dedicating it to Pietro Morosini, claims—quite innocently—to win for Tacitus, through Morosini's name, that reputation for piety that he has lacked until now.

## V. — The same. <note>Referring to the previously mentioned translations of Tacitus.</note> Paris, Widow Quillau, 1760, 2 vols. in sextodecimo. <note>A small, pocket-sized book format.</note>

> "An elegant edition in Garamond type <note>original: "garamoncino," referring to a small size of the classic Garamond font</note>, overseen by G. Conti, professor of the Tuscan language at the Royal Military School of Paris. It contains only the translation into the vernacular, and has neither the tables nor the glossary of less common words. The notes are placed at the end of each of the six books; the three letters are at the beginning; and the family tree of the lineage of Augustus is at the end." (Gamba.) <note>Bartolommeo Gamba was a famous 19th-century Italian bibliographer.</note>

It is a pure reproduction of the Comino edition, except that the things indicated above by Gamba are omitted.

## VI. — The same. Bassano, Remondini printing house, 1803, 3 vols. in quarto.

This was prepared by the Abbot Raffaele Pastore, and is to be held in much higher regard than the one given by the same Remondini in 1790. It also contains the supplements by Brotier <note>Gabriel Brotier was a French scholar who wrote "supplements" to fill in the missing parts of Tacitus's histories</note>, translated by Pastore.

## VII. — The same. Milan, Andrea Mainardi, 9 vols. in octavo. <note>A standard book size, roughly 6 by 9 inches.</note>

*Like the previous ones, it has the Latin text and the supplements. This edition deserves to be remembered only for an unpublished draft of a first translation by Davanzati, accompanied by a letter of his taken from the original manuscript by Davanzati himself, which is preserved in the Ambrosian Library, with a preliminary discourse by the Abbot Don Cesare della Croce, custodian of the aforementioned Library.*

## VIII. — The same. Paris, Fayolle, 1804, 2 vols. in octavo, edited by G. Biagioli.

Gamba, in the addition to the biography of Davanzati written by Ginguené in the *Universal Biography* (Venezia, Missiaglia, 1829), cites this edition and Conti’s edition, calling them both elegant but very incorrect.

## IX. — Schism of England up to the death of Queen Mary, abridged in the proper Florentine tongue by Bernardo Davanzati Bostichi. In Rome at the request of Gio. Angelo Ruffinelli, with permission of the superiors, by Guglielmo Facciotto, 1602.

An edition in octavo, of 99 pages including the unnumbered title page and dedication. The last page contains the end of the work and the errata <note>A list of printing errors and their corrections.</note>: the title page is decorated with the Aldine anchor <note>The famous printer's mark of a dolphin wrapped around an anchor, originally used by Aldus Manutius.</note>. The date 1602 is only found in some copies. This is the first edition and the only one produced during the author's lifetime; he dedicated it to the *most illustrious lord, Mr. Gio. Bardi, Count of Vernio, Lieutenant General of both guards of His Holiness*, and the letter is dated Florence, April 1, 1600. This led Haym into error, as in his *Library* he gave this edition the date of 1600, rather than 1602 as he should have. Perhaps he had on hand one of those copies without a date on the title page and deduced it from the dedicatory letter.

In a copy of this edition kept in the Parma library <note>The "Parmense," or Palatine Library of Parma.</note>, one reads this note in the hand of Michele Colombo:
> "This printing initially bore another title page somewhat different from the present one: on the back there was no portrait, and in the catalog of the minor works contained in the book, *Tuscan Cultivation* was not mentioned. It was followed by the same dedication by Davanzati that is read in the edition of the *Schism of England* produced in Rome in 1602 in octavo <note>original: "in-8"; a book size where each printed sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves.</note>, and immediately following the dedication, the work began. But later the title page was changed, Davanzati’s dedication was replaced by the one currently read from the printers, and a summary of the author's life was added under the title of *Portrait*. The first title page the work had and the aforementioned dedication by Davanzati will be found inserted (and indeed they are there) at the end of this volume."

We owe this note, like others we will cite by Colombo, to the courtesy of the distinguished A. Pezzana, librarian of the Parma library.

### XI. — The same minor works. Padua, Comino, 1727, in octavo, with portrait.

It is a reprint of the Florentine edition. In a copy of this printing existing in the Parma library, M. Colombo wrote in different words the same warning he made for the Massi and Landi edition, referred to above, and at the end adds:
> "It must be said that Davanzati's letter (*dedication to the Bardi family*) was not known to the Volpi gentlemen; for just as they reprinted the said dedication by Massi and Landi (*to the Grand Duke*), they would not have failed to reprint that one as well: and it certainly would have been well worth the effort (*) <note>original: "ne valea ben la pena"</note> both for being a work by the author himself, and even more because he reveals within it the reason that moved him to compose his little work."

A reprint was made by Comino in 1754, in octavo.

### XII. — Minor works of Mr. Bernardo Davanzati Bostichi, Florentine gentleman, taken from the Padua edition of Giuseppe Comino, divided into two volumes. 3rd Edition with added notes. Livorno 1779, by Francesco Calderini and Lorenzo Faina at the sign of Pallas. In octavo.

It is dedicated to Canon D. Gio. De Silva. Here too, the ancient *dedication to the most serene Ferdinand II* is placed before the *Schism* and the author's letter to G. Bardi is omitted: the *Portrait by Rondinelli* follows; and after the *Schism* comes the *Eulogy of Bernardo Davanzati*, which is the same one read in volume III, pages 299-304 of the *Collection of eulogies of illustrious Tuscan men. Lucca, 1770*, signed G. P. (Giuseppe Pelli). At the end of the first volume are some historical notes on the *Schism of England*; and at the end of the second, the notes on the *Lecture on Money* and on the eulogy for Cosimo. For these embellishments, and not for its accuracy, this printing is to be held in some regard.

> (*) "Here Colombo did not notice that he had lapsed into a Gallicism <note>A phrase or idiom borrowed from French; in this case, "valere la pena."</note> without necessity. We have *Valere il pregio*, *Portare il pregio*, *Metter conto*, etc. <note>These are traditional Italian phrases meaning "to be worth it."</note>" — Note by Pezzana.

LVI

# BIBLIOGRAPHY.

## **XIII. — On the manner of planting and maintaining a bird-net grove and of fowling with a net.** <note>original: "Del modo di piantare e custodire una ragnaia e di uccellare a ragna"; a *ragnaia* is a grove of trees specifically planted and pruned to support large, fine vertical nets called *ragne* used for catching birds.</note> Florence, by Giuseppe Tofani and Company, 1790. Octavo. 34 pages, including the title page and notice to the readers.

This pamphlet was found by Doctor Targioni in the Rosso Martini library, and its style seemed to him to be that of Davanzati; he was confirmed in this judgment when he saw it joined to the *Cultivation* <note>Davanzati's *Tuscan Cultivation of Vines and Trees*.</note> in a codex that had belonged to the Palatine Library. But Colombo, recording this booklet in his *Catalog of some works pertaining to the sciences etc... which... deserve some consideration on account of their language* (See Works of M. Colombo, Parma 1827, vol. III, page 490 and following), demonstrated that Targioni had been too hasty in his judgment. He returned to this same subject in a note written by him in a copy of that booklet kept in the Parma library. Which note, being unpublished, we willingly report here.

> "I cannot find between this pamphlet and the works of Davanzati known to us that resemblance of style that Mr. Targioni finds there. I recognize in it neither that choppiness of the period, nor that pregnancy of concepts following one another in a certain manner, nor that extreme parsimony of words which are seen in all his writings. Wherefore I take the liberty of doubting if this little work is really his until more convincing proofs are brought to me. For if in the codex cited by Tofani it is placed after the treatise on *Tuscan Cultivation* almost in the manner of a final chapter, is it certain that the codex is in the hand of the author himself? And if not, could it not have been added by the copyist as a sort of supplement, even though it belongs to a different author? This is made quite likely if one considers that in the manuscript seen by Mr. Targioni it stands by itself; and it is not to be believed that this single part would have been written there without the others that precede it, had it been composed by Davanzati himself to be joined with the other articles of his *Cultivation*. To this consideration, let another of even greater weight be added. In the *Tuscan Cultivation*, both the *Bird-net Grove* and *Fowling* had already been treated in the two articles preceding those instructions of what must be done month by month, with which the author closes the work. Now, how can one ever suppose that a writer such as Davanzati—concise, sober, and a capital enemy of every redundancy—would wish to treat the same thing twice in the same work?" To all this it may be added, that the author of the *Ragnaia* clearly cites Davanzati in those words read at p. 229, v. 13 and following; which is enough in itself to make the matter clear. But there is more. In the former Rinuccini collection, there existed a miscellaneous codex where this pamphlet bears the name of Giovanni Antonio Popoleschi, a contemporary and friend of Davanzati, who should be regarded as the true author of that writing. In the dispersal of that rich library, it is not known where that codex went. Writing of it to the eminent Mr. *G. Aiazzi*, who for a long time was its active and intelligent director, he replied to me among other things: *"Not knowing the certain handwriting of Popoleschi to be able to make a comparison, I could not say if this copy is in his hand: it is certain that it is from that time, and was part of the manuscripts that passed from the Valori house into a branch of the Guicciardini and then into the Rinuccini. However, take it as most certain that the writing on the Bird-net Grove is not by Davanzati... Indeed, Professor Nesti, with whom I once held a discussion on this pamphlet, showed me a printed copy in which there was a long handwritten note by the celebrated Gio. Fabbroni, where he refuted with reasons derived from the pamphlet itself the error of having attributed it to Davanzati, reclaiming it for Popoleschi."*

## **XIV. — The Schism of England and the other minor works of Bernardo Davanzati Bostichi, Florentine gentleman, with a discourse by Francescantonio Mori on the life and writings of the author. First Sienese edition, more complete than all the preceding ones. Siena, from the presses of Pandolfo Rossi at the sign of the she-wolf, 1828. Octavo.**

Besides the minor works printed in previous editions, it contains ten letters to Baccio Valori; <note>A Florentine politician and patron of the arts (1535–1606).</note> two to Belisario Bulgarini with the replies, a sonnet for the Sabine by Giambologna, <note>Referring to the famous sculpture *The Rape of the Sabine Women* by Jean de Boulogne.</note> and the pamphlet

*On the manner of planting a bird-net grove.* <note>Referencing the work discussed on the previous page regarding fowling.</note> However, the *Oration* delivered upon taking the *Consolata* is missing here, as are the sonnets found among those of Varchi and others. It is preceded by a judicious Discourse by Francescantonio Mori on the Life and Works of the Author.

As for the pamphlet on the *Bird-net Grove*, the editor does not believe it to be by Davanzati, but he reproduces it with a much-improved reading, comparing it with a Riccardian codex (no. 2973), both because it is a valuable piece of writing and so that the reader may compare it for themselves with those of Davanzati, since the Tofani edition has now become rare.

### XV. — The Schism of England, abridged by Bernardo Davanzati and compared with the autograph existing in the Marciana Library of Venice, edited by Bartolommeo Gamba. To which is added The Schism under the reign of Elizabeth, abridged by the Venetian Giambatista Gaspari. Venice, from the Alvisopoli press, 1831.

->In-sixteen <note>A small book format where the sheet is folded to create 16 leaves.</note>, of pages XXXII-168, with an ugly portrait of the author made from thin air. <note>original: "fatto a aria"; likely meaning an imaginary or poorly reconstructed likeness rather than one drawn from life.</note><-

It contains: 1st, A long letter from Gamba to Angelo Sicca, in which he gives an account of the Marcian codex from which the edition is drawn, and of another codex, also a Marcian autograph (Class VI, 18), which contains the sketches of nearly three books of the translation of Tacitus into the vernacular with some unpublished marginal notes: 2nd, the discourse on the life of Davanzati written by Mori for the Siena edition: 3rd, the index of proper names used by Davanzati, restored to their original spelling: 4th, the letter from Davanzati to Giovanni Bardi: 5th, a short proem written by Davanzati, which in the Marcian codex is seen prefixed to the *Schism*: 6th, the *Schism of England*, divided into two books, of which the first comprises the reign of Henry and the second the reigns of Edward and Mary: 7th, a third book of continuation, which comprises the reign of Elizabeth, written by Edward Rishton <note>original: "Eduardo Ristono"</note> and abridged by the Venetian Giambatista Gaspari, who undertook this work at Gamba’s request and succeeded very well in imitating Davanzati’s style.

The reading of the Marcian codex offers an infinite number of variants, not a few of which greatly improve the text of the common editions. *But sometimes (even in Gamba’s opinion) it falls below the common version already printed, so that adopting it assiduously would only result in the loss of the most correct phrasing.*

Furthermore, Gamba did poorly to modernize the spelling, using the double "z" and ignoring the other orthographic idiosyncrasies peculiar to our author.

### XVI. — Tuscan Cultivation.

This minor work was printed for the first time in Florence by Filippo Giunti, 1600, in-quarto, along with the *Treatise on the cultivation of Vines* by Giovanvettorio Soderini and with the *Defense and praise of the melon* by Lionardo Giacomini. The book is dedicated to Luigi Alamanni the younger. Salvino Salvini (*Consular Annals*, page 228) informs us that Doctor Francesco del Teglia possessed a copy of this edition 

> wherein could be read, in the translator's own hand, not a few corrected passages and various readings in which his good taste and finest discernment appear throughout.

Giunti produced two other reprints; one in 1610, the other in 1622, and in the latter he also added the *Cultivation of Olives* by Pier Vettori. It was thereafter always reproduced with the other Minor Works, as seen in the editions cited above.

*We do not wish to remain silent regarding the elegant reprint made by L. Carrer in the Italian Classical Library of sciences, letters and arts, class VI, vol. III, which bears the title "Three treatises concerning agriculture." Venice, 1840.*

The original manuscript of this minor work is preserved in the Magliabechiana <note>The library of Antonio Magliabechi, now part of the National Central Library of Florence.</note>, Class XIV, no. 48, and formerly belonged to the library of Senator Carlo di Tommaso Strozzi, where it was marked as no. 290. It is in-quarto, of 21 leaves numbered on one side only, not including the flyleaf which bears the title "Tuscan Cultivation by Bernardo Davanzati in his own hand." *The summaries are not at their respective chapters, but at the end in the manner of an index with the title "Table to this treatise."* It has here and there quite a few cancellations and revisions <note>original: "pentimenti"; literally 'repentances,' referring to an author's changes during the writing process.</note>. We have collated it with every care.

LVIII
BIBLIOGRAPHY.

### XVII. — Oration on assuming the Consulate in the Florentine Academy.

This was published for the first time by Salvini in the *Consular Annals of the Florentine Academy*, <note>original: "Fasti consolari dell' Accad. Fior."</note> Florence, 1717, pages 222-231. Salvini states he transcribed it from the original manuscript obtained from Giuseppe Bianchini and published it with total accuracy. It was later reproduced in volume I, second part of the *Florentine Prose*; in volume V, page 115 of the *Little Works* printed in Livorno, 1779; and in volume IV, page 165 of the *Selected Italian Prose*, Milan, Fontana, 1826.

### XVIII. — Note on Exchange. <note>original: "Notizia de' Cambi"</note>

Two non-original manuscripts of this pamphlet are held in the Magliabechiana <note>The Magliabechiana is a core collection of the National Central Library of Florence.</note> in two miscellaneous codices, class VIII, 43; XXV, 339, which offer very notable variations. There is also a manuscript in the Riccardiana, no. 2312. In a Magliabechian codex, class VIII, 73, titled *Various excerpts and notes by Antonio Francesco Marmi*, this pamphlet is cited as existing in the library of Saint Mary New <note>Santa Maria Nuova</note> under the title "Note on Trade by Mr. Bernardo Davanzati." Nor could it be a different pamphlet, because he provides the opening line, which is this: "Trade is an art found by men for the common benefit and to supply what nature seems to have lacked, etc."

### XIX. — Lecture on Coinage. <note>original: "Lezione della moneta"</note>

This is found accurately printed (according to Gamba) in volume IV, part II of the *Florentine Prose*, 1729, and this version was the primary source used by the lexicographers. <note>original: "vocabolaristi," referring to the editors of the Accademia della Crusca dictionary.</note>

In the Marucelliana library, there exists a miscellaneous codex marked A. 156, which contains several different writings by Anton Maria Salvini. At the end, he inserted a small-format booklet containing an accurate copy of the *Lecture on Coins*. It is interleaved, and in these inserted sheets and the margins of the text, there are various annotations. Some are by Davanzati (at least according to the attribution), though not in his hand, and others were written by Salvini; they all consist of citations and authorities that support what is stated in the text.

### XX. — Oration on the death of Grand Duke Cosimo I.

This was reprinted in volume I, part I of the *Florentine Prose*, Florence, 1661, and in the *Selected Italian Prose*, vol. IV, Milan, 1826, page 149.

We have seen many manuscripts of this Oration throughout the Florentine libraries, but no autograph <note>A manuscript written in the author's own hand.</note> exists. We will list them here, distinguishing them by the letters of the alphabet for the convenience of citations that will occur when referring to the variant readings in the proper place.
A. Magliabechian Codex, class IX, 65.
B. Magliabechian Codex, class XXVII, 20.

In this codex, it is preceded by the following letter, though it is not clear to whom it is addressed:

> *My very magnificent lord.*
> *In our conversation a few days ago regarding the many orations given by various learned men in praise of the late Grand Duke Cosimo, I told you that among the beautiful ones, it seemed to me (if I am not mistaken) that the most beautiful was the one recited to the Alterati academics* <note>The "Alterati" (The Transformed) was a private Florentine literary academy to which Davanzati belonged.</note> *by Mr. Bernardo Davanzati. Since you approved of the same, I thought to make a copy for you and send it as I now do; for being such as it is, and not yet fully made public, it is worthy of your possession. And though I am late, I do this at least so as not to fail in the promise made to Your Lordship, whom I pray to offer and recommend me to Mr. Galeotto, your son, for I have no greater desire than to hear of his well-being. And I pray to God for your every contentment and just desire. From San Casciano, September 3, 1624.*

-> *From Your Lordship's most Magnificent* <-
-> *Servant* <-
-> *Michele della Rocca.* <-

C. Magliabechian Codex, class XXVII, 104: dates from 1575.
D. Magliabechian Codex, class XXVII, 114, formerly owned by Senator Carlo Tommaso Strozzi.
E. Magliabechian Codex, class XXVII, 52, beginning of the 17th century.
F. Magliabechian Codex, class XXVII, 5, 17th century.
G. Magliabechian Codex, class XXVII, 4, beginning of the 17th century.
H. Magliabechian Codex, class XXX, 162.
I. Magliabechian Codex, class XXXVIII, 115. The handwriting is contemporary to the period.
L. Magliabechian Codex, class VI, 155.

LIX
BIBLIOGRAPHY.

### XXI. — Accusation given by "the Silent One" to "the Troubled One" during his audit of the Regency of the *Alterati*.
<note>The "Silent One" (*Il Silente*) and the "Troubled One" (*Il Travagliato*) were academic pseudonyms used by members of the Academy of the *Alterati* (the "Altered" or "Transformed" ones), a prominent Florentine literary society.</note>

### XXII. — Oration in a deliberative style regarding the overseers of the Academy of the *Alterati*.

Of these two discourses, published by Massi and Landi and in the Livorno edition of the *Little Works* (*Operette*), a manuscript exists—though not the original—in a Riccardian codex, marked no. 2178.

### XXIII. Some civic and literary insights by Bernardo Davanzati the Florentine, taken from his marginal notes to Tacitus and from an autograph codex in the Marcian Library. Venice, from the Alvisopoli Press, 1831.

Bartolommeo Gamba published this small volume *For the noble wedding of Papadopoli and Mosconi*; <note>It was a common 19th-century custom to publish short, rare literary works as commemorative gifts for aristocratic weddings.</note> but he did so with little care, according to his habit: for he made no distinction between the unpublished marginalia and the printed ones, and provided no indication for the latter. At times, he confused the words of the text with those of the notes. Among the *Civic Insights*, the unpublished notes are the 5th, 6th, and 11th; and among the literary ones, the 2nd and the last, which will be reported by us in the *Appendix* to Volume III of this edition. To these *Insights*, he added a *Fragment of three different translations of Tacitus*, which you may see at the end of this volume.

### XXIV. — Letters.

Ten letters from Davanzati to Master Baccio Valori and two to Belisario Bulgarini, along with the latter’s replies, were printed with many gaps in Volume III, Part IV of the *Florentine Prose*, and reprinted exactly as they were among the *Little Works* in the Siena edition.

The Chevalier Giuseppe Manuzzi recently collected 52 of them, both published and unpublished, and published them with a few short notes for an illustrious wedding. Florence, 1852, in-octavo.

### XXV. — Rhymes.

There are a few printed sonnets and a madrigal, which have never, as far as we know, been collected together among Bernardo’s works.

a) *Sonnets of Benedetto Varchi.* Florence, 1555, Torrentino. — In the second part, there are three sonnets by Davanzati.

b) *Spiritual Sonnets of Master Benedetto Varchi.* Florence, Giunti, 1573. — On page 57, there is a sonnet by our author.

c) Another sonnet is among the poems published by Ser Martelli, Florence, 1583, in honor of Giambologna when he unveiled the group of the Sabine woman. <note>Referring to the famous marble sculpture *The Rape of the Sabine Women* in the Loggia dei Lanzi.</note> It was later reprinted in the Siena edition of the *Little Works*.

d) *Sample of Rhymes by various good authors who flourished from the 14th to the 18th century.* Florence, Ronchi, 1825. — On page 237, there is a madrigal extracted from a codex once belonging to Luigi Poirot, now held in the Magliabechiano collection.

e) Lupicini Antonio, *Military Architecture.* Florence, Marescotti, 1582. — After the dedication, there is a sonnet by Bernardo in praise of the author. It was reprinted by L. Carrer alongside Lupicini's work. Venice, 1840. See the editor’s preface, page VIII, in the notes.

f) Some unpublished sonnets are in the manuscripts that passed from the Rinuccini collection to the Magliabechiana, which will be printed by us in their proper place.

### XXVI. — *Unpublished Works.*

### 1. — Life of Master Giuliano Davanzati.

We have news of this from Antonio Benivieni, who, in the dedication of the *Life of Piero Vettori the Elder* (Florence, 1583), after recalling various *Lives* written by some of his contemporaries, continues:

> "I understand, furthermore, that others are being collected: that of Master Manno Donati by Filippo Sassetti, and that of Master Giuliano Davanzati by Bernardo, his descendant."

— Today, no trace of it remains.

BIBLIOGRAPHY.

## 2. — Two discourses or *Cicalate* in the manner of funeral orations recited in Pisa in 1592 upon the suppression of the Office of Decency for the Garrison.
<note>A *cicalata* (literally "chatter") was a lighthearted, often satirical or humorous academic speech. The *Ufizio dell'Onestà* (Office of Decency) was a Pisan magistrate that regulated public morals and prostitution, specifically regarding the military garrison.</note>

> « Small quarto autograph paper manuscript of 32 pages. It begins: *Great indeed was always the hope held by the ancient Egyptians etc.* <note>original: "Grandissima fu sempre la speranza che ebbero gli antichi Egizi ec."</note>; and ends: *Pincon Pinconi nine hundred and sixty-one* <note>original: "Pincon Pinconi novecentosessantuno"</note>. This charming little work is completely unknown; and if one could manage to penetrate the jargon and the true subject for which it was written, it would deserve to see the light of publication for the liveliness and the witticisms—at times too bold—to be found within. »

This report is taken from the *Catalogue of Manuscripts of the former Rinuccini Collection*, compiled by the illustrious Mr. G. Aiazzi.

## 3. — Hero of Alexandria.

From this Greek writer, Davanzati translated—or to put it better, condensed in his own manner—that part which concerns the method of making water rise through pipes; <note>Hero of Alexandria was an ancient mathematician and engineer; Davanzati was interested in his work on hydraulics.</note> and he dedicated his work to the celebrated architect Bernardo Buontalenti, at whose request he had performed it. The manuscript is in the Palatine Library, jealously guarded, and awaits publication by Mr. Palermo, the librarian. We provide this inexact report based on the accounts of some friends who were able to cast a glance upon it.

It is curious that Buontalenti also requested a translation of this same part of Hero from Oreste Vannocci, who sent it to him from Rome on December 28, 1582, with a letter which is contained in the *Unpublished Correspondence of Artists*, published by Dr. Giovanni Gaye. Volume III, pages 449-50.

## 4. — *Zibaldone*.
<note>A *Zibaldone* is a "commonplace book" or personal notebook where an author collects miscellaneous thoughts, excerpts from books, and drafts.</note>

This is a thick notebook with many loose sheets, entirely in Davanzati's hand. Besides many notes and jottings, the fruit of his reading, it contains various thoughts and fragments, of which we will provide a sample in the Appendix to the third volume. This *Zibaldone* was owned first by Manni; then by Moreni, and is now in the hands of our friend Pietro Bigazzi.

LXI
1. f

# DEDICATORY LETTER

## TO PRINCE LEOPOLDO OF TUSCANY

->Introduction by the deputies of the Accademia della Crusca<-
<note>The Accademia della Crusca is the preeminent linguistic society of Italy, founded in Florence to maintain the purity of the Italian language.</note>
->to the first edition of the complete translation into the vernacular made in Florence by Pietro Nesti<-
->in the year 1637.<-

---

Most Serene Prince.
*The translation of **Cornelius Tacitus** by Mr. **Bernardo Davanzati**, desired in vain for many years now by the majority of scholars, hindered or delayed for various reasons (as often happens with human affairs), was almost reduced to being prey to the voracity of time. Wherefore, some devoted to the memory of the author, who were saddened by the universal loss—and especially the loss to our language—if such a work were to perish; and considering how unjustly the desires of lovers of fine literature were being defrauded; they have endeavored with every effort that it be printed in the best manner possible for the time being: excusing the author if any imperfection should be found within it, because death*¹ *did not allow him to correct it. It lacks nothing else to sustain its purpose except a protector like your Serene Highness, to whom, therefore, with all affection, we recommend and dedicate it. And making the most humble reverence to you, we pray for your happiness.*

->Of Your Serene Highness<-

->Most humble and devoted servants<-
->**THE DEPUTIES.**<-

<note>1 The printed edition has *glie le* <note>original: "glie le"</note>. But in the copy of the Nesti edition corrected by hand, owned by Marquis G. Capponi, one reads *gliele*, nor have I hesitated to accept this correction.</note>

---

LXII

# NOTICE
## TO THE DISCERNING READER
### which follows the Dedicatory letter in the Nesti edition. ^1

---

Nothing else seemed to be missing to fully honor **Cornelius Tacitus** and his translations than to print them with the accompaniment of both the Latin and the vernacular <note>The "vernacular" (volgare) refers to the Italian language, specifically the Florentine dialect championed by the author.</note> text together. And this could not be done more suitably ^2 nor perhaps with any other translation than that of Mr. Davanzati: for he has surpassed all others in the similarity of style and the brevity of Tacitus, whereby he has deserved to be called a "Florentine Tacitus" rather than a simple translator. For from the vividness of his speech one can draw instruction and delight, in addition to the knowledge of history, leaving for now to the judgment of the learned whether he has in any place, if not surpassed (and let this be said with all modesty), at least equaled Tacitus himself. --- Regarding the Latin text, for the most part ^3 that of Mr. **Curzio Picchena** ^4 was used, although Davanzati in some places followed **Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a towering figure in Renaissance scholarship, famous for his editions of Tacitus.</note> or other variant readings that seemed more appropriate to him at the time. --- The same Davanzati made some learned and curious annotations to the first six books, which have been placed at the end. The numbers in the margin of the vernacular text indicate them; ^5 and the numbers in the Latin text show the notes of Mr. Picchena, which, being also found printed separately from the work, have been omitted for now. --- If any defect should be found in the explanation of the concepts, as sometimes happens (though it is not believed so), let the kind reader know that Mr. Davanzati, being overtaken by death, could not revise it, and we faithfully give it to you as we received it, ^6 leaving room for anyone who might wish to take the trouble to illustrate it more accurately. --- We pray the reader to correct the printing errors ^7 noted at the end beforehand, so as not to be forced to interrupt the reading and take the meaning in reverse, without fault of the author.

1 We have deemed it not useless to reproduce this Notice, so that the care (though unfortunate) used by the Academicians of the Crusca in the first edition of the complete translation, also cited in the *Vocabulary* <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca*, the first great dictionary of the Italian language.</note>, may be known.
2 The handwritten correction says *conveniently* <note>original: "comodamente"</note>. See note 1 to the Dedicatory letter.
3 *for the most part*: added in pen by the corrector.
4 I do not know what judgment led to choosing Picchena's text, while Davanzati translated from that of Lipsius.
5 Likewise in the two editions by Marescotti (1596) and Giunti (1600), overseen by Davanzati himself.
6 Why not tell us if they drew their edition from original manuscripts or from copies: and why did they not care for the previous editions in the first six books?
7 Volpi <note>Giannantonio Volpi, an 18th-century editor and publisher.</note> took the patience to count up to 700 of them. A pity that the care in showing off others' errors made him pay little attention to his own!

LXIII

<header>DEDICATION OF THE COMINIANA EDITION.</header>

# TO THE RENOWNED ACCADEMIA DELLA CRUSCA
## LADY AND MISTRESS OF BEAUTIFUL TUSCAN SPEECH
### GIOVANNI ANTONIO VOLPI. <gloss>1</gloss>

---

Bernardo Davanzati, a writer of great merit and renown, comes before you, most worthy Archconsul and noble Academicians, and presents to you his translation <note>The original term is *volgarizzamento*, referring to the process of translating classical Latin into the "vulgar" or common Italian tongue.</note> of Tacitus. Through my own diligence and that of my brother, <gloss>2</gloss> it has been restored (as I hope), as much as was possible for us in this new edition, to that fine polish which the author might perhaps have wished for from his printers. This work—one of the most select treasures of your wealthy *Vocabolario* <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca* was the first great dictionary of the Italian language; Davanzati's translation was used as a primary source for authoritative "pure" Tuscan usage.</note>—lay, so to speak, choked among the thorns and briers of shameful printing errors. Because of the audacity of those who, though afflicted by ignorance, dare to handle the gold and gems of good books with filthy hands, it was losing its luster; so much was the dust, or rather the rust, that was plastered upon it. It would be long and tedious to recount to you in detail the labor and annoyance we suffered in weeding out the noxious plants, clearing the fertile but poorly cultivated field, and restoring the tarnished jewel to its true brilliance. Likewise, we had to "sharpen our eyebrows" <note>An Italian idiom meaning to look very closely or exert intense mental focus.</note> to strip away every stain, proceeding slowly and with careful circumspection, in the manner of a traveler walking through a suspicious land full of snares. You yourselves, being the shrewd and expert men you are, and lovers of diligence, already understand this perfectly well without me spending many words to declare it. If the common...

---

<gloss>1 Volpi, in this work of his, truly gives himself much more credit than is his due: for in the end, he did nothing more than take the very extensive *errataccorrige* <note>A list of errors and their corrections.</note> placed by Nesti at the end of his edition, and, with that in hand, removed the printing errors—though not all of them—and added many of his own. For example, he wrote *paesi* (countries) instead of *pesi* (weights); *Nota* instead of *Mola*; *maneggiare* (to handle) instead of *mangiare* (to eat), and several others that completely change the meaning and have been perpetuated in all subsequent editions. Nevertheless, this distinguished man of letters was very deserving of praise in the field of good studies for his beautiful and correct editions of Latin and Italian classics, issued from the famous Paduan printing house of Giuseppe Comino, and for his elegant Latin verses. He was born in Padua in 1686 and died in 1766.</gloss>

<gloss>2 This is Gaetano Volpi (born 1689, died 1761), a priest of great learning and rare piety, who assisted his brother in the Comino printing house and published excellent devotional works. He also had two other brothers who were men of letters: Giuseppe Rocco (born 1690, died 1746), a Jesuit who wrote with much praise on ecclesiastical antiquities; and Giambatista (born 1687), who was a physician and professor of anatomy in Padua.</gloss>

LXIV DEDICATION OF THE COMINIANA EDITION.

...whether the learned will be grateful to us for what we have undertaken for their benefit, I cannot be entirely certain. Malevolence, talkativeness, listlessness, excessive fastidiousness and delicacy, and finally the diversity and extravagance of opinions—the common vices of men, ready to disparage the works of others even when they are of great value—leave me in doubt of a successful outcome. However, I feel I can live securely in the knowledge that our hard work will be dear and acceptable to you, most virtuous Academicians. I am promised this by that same kindness with which you deigned to approve what we did for other linguistic books, which, to our great honor and satisfaction, you chose to use in the latest printing of your distinguished dictionary <note>Referring to the *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca*, the foundational dictionary of the Italian language.</note>. This favor, so kindly granted by you, will have the power to console us and sustain our courage, even should an entire nation of detractors rise against us; for a thousand censures and sophistries are not worth your approval and your good grace alone.

The excellent city of Florence—more beautiful than any other in Italy, according to Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), author of the *Decameron* and a pillar of the Tuscan literary tradition.</note>—is a mother in every age fertile with rare geniuses who raised her to a high degree of glory with their immortal writings, a loving nurse of every fine art, and a refuge and asylum for celebrated men of letters fleeing their homelands due to unfortunate accidents. She was always, and still is, the target of envy for other nations, who look upon her with a squinted eye and grudgingly grant her the primacy of the pure Tuscan tongue <note>The "Tuscan tongue" (*toscana favella*) was the dialect of Florence, which the Accademia della Crusca championed as the gold standard for all of Italy.</note>. Their own rough speeches—poor in lively expressions, mostly tasteless and languid—have nothing to do with the vigor, efficacy, gentleness, and abundance of yours. Hence the resentment of foreign writers who, quite often unwilling or unable to separate the gold from the dross, and refusing to submit to the strict rules of the best authors, set themselves to blaming what they despair of achieving. 

I believe this is precisely one of the main reasons why Davanzati <note>Bernardo Davanzati (1529–1606), the Florentine merchant and scholar whose translation of Tacitus is the subject of this book.</note> is not equally praised by everyone. His translation—excellent and marvelous in my view—cannot be easily imitated; for who lives today who, besides deeply understanding the author being translated into the vernacular, can couple such brevity with such clarity? As for the objections made against him, even by learned and authoritative men, it seems to me that he sufficiently defended himself in his learned marginal notes <term>postille</term> <note>From the Italian *postille*, these are Davanzati's own scholarly annotations that accompany the text.</note>, and that he even anticipated and soundly resolved many of them. 

Therefore, I do not fear that I have been mistaken in my choice, or that I have labored over an ordinary author whose work will not repay the effort and expense. I believe that you, most noble Academicians, will share this sentiment, for I too have the rare fortune of being enrolled in your assembly. Meanwhile, with due submission, I pray each of you to accept with a joyful face and a courteous spirit this book, which I dedicate to you as a testimony of the esteem and gratitude I justly profess to you, wishing you every complete happiness from heaven.

<summary>Volpi defends Davanzati’s concise translation style against critics, arguing that the superiority of the Florentine dialect and the Academy’s approval outweigh the complaints of envious detractors. He concludes by formally presenting the edition to the Accademia della Crusca.</summary>

LXV

# RESPONSE OF THE ACCADEMIA DELLA CRUSCA

## TO GIOVANNI ANTONIO VOLPI. <note>original: "1"</note>

---

->*To the most illustrious Sir, my most worshipful patron, Mr. Giovanni Antonio Volpi,*<-
->*professor of humanities at the University of Padua.*<-

**Most illustrious Sir and most worshipful patron.**

Your most kind letter, most illustrious Sir, dated the 29th of September, reached me at a time when the Accademia della Crusca <note>The premier institution for the study and preservation of the Italian language, based in Florence.</note> was closed for the usual autumn holidays; therefore, it has not yet been possible to present to a full assembly the beautiful and most diligent reprint of the <term>vernacular translation</term> <note>original: "volgarizzamento" — the practice of translating classical Latin or Greek texts into the common Italian tongue.</note> of Cornelius Tacitus by Bernardo Davanzati, which your generous kindness was pleased not only to send as a gift, but also to honor with a dedication. Having nonetheless shared it for inspection with the Arch-consul <note>The head of the Academy.</note> and various other academicians currently in the city, I can assure you, most illustrious Sir, that it has pleased them immensely, from which I foresee a complete and universal appreciation from the entire Academy. For this institution has always been of the opinion that Davanzati, with his robust and pithy <note>original: "sugosa," literally "juicy" or full of substance.</note> manner of writing in the Tuscan idiom—which is otherwise quite copious—acquired a particular merit for having known how to marvelously pair a great brevity with a singular force of expression. Hence, the Academy has always held his writings in high esteem, and has always considered the examples drawn and cited from them in past compilations of our Dictionary <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca*, the first major dictionary of the Italian language.</note> to be of great strength and authority. Indeed, Pietro Pietri, a man of letters from Danzig <note>Modern-day Gdańsk, Poland.</note> and our illustrious academician, when he resided in Florence in the past century, learned the Tuscan language primarily from this translation, as reported in his Tuscan prose by our most clear and unnamed <note>original: "innominato," referring to a specific academic title or status within the group.</note> Abbot Anton Maria Salvini. Now, when the whole Academy sees and knows that it possesses this celebrated translation reprinted in such an adorned manner, and—through your inimitable accuracy, most illustrious Sir—purged of the many errors by which past impressions were foully spoiled, it is to be believed without any doubt that they shall feel a profound pleasure, seeing that through such illustrious labor they are placed in a position to make much better use of it in the future. To which pleasure will infallibly succeed...

---

LXVII

# PREFACE TO THE COMINIAN EDITION.

The *Schism of England* and the other minor works of Bernardo Davanzati, which we have reprinted twice here at the Cominian press, so pleased the lovers of the Tuscan tongue <note>The "Toscana favella" refers to the literary Italian language based on the Florentine dialect, highly prized for its purity.</note> that, seeing them well-received and universally approved, we could not resist the frequent encouragements of friends who exhorted us to publish anew the translation of Tacitus into the vernacular—the illustrious labor of the same Florentine author. To set about this none-too-easy undertaking, it was necessary to find the 1637 Florence edition in folio <note>A "folio" is a large book format where sheets are folded only once.</note>, published by Pier Nesti, which was the first complete edition and featured the original Latin alongside the text. This version had already become quite rare and costly; therefore, to obtain it, we turned to Sir Guglielmo Camposanpiero, a Paduan knight and member of the Accademia della Crusca. Being as courteous and accommodating to honorable requests as he is noble and learned, he, with his accustomed kindness toward us, drew the volume from his ample collection—or rather, his treasure-trove—of books cited in the Dictionary <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca*, the authoritative dictionary of the Italian language.</note>, and permitted us to use and compare it at our great leisure. 

Once we had it, we immediately observed, not without astonishment, about seven hundred printing errors listed and corrected at the end of the volume. Following such a long catalog was a sincere confession and a request for pardon for many other defects that occurred during printing. The labor required to correct all these mistakes in their proper places was enormous, so that they would not slip through once again in this new printing. This diligence was neglected by those who supervised the previous reprints, in which, in fact—as a "bonus" to the bargain—one finds the number of errors increased beyond measure. We also had to be careful not to blindly correct everything according to the aforementioned catalog; for not infrequently, the "correction" itself is a mistake. It sometimes ordered, for example, the spoiling of the text, which was previously immaculate and should not have been changed under any circumstances. <sup>1</sup> It is commonly believed that books containing an *errata corrige* <note>original: "errata corrige" — a list of corrected errors.</note> at the end are very accurate; but this should only be understood to apply to a small number of defects...

---

<sup>1</sup> This happened several times even to Volpi <note>Giovanni Antonio Volpi, the editor of this edition.</note> himself, spoiling passages where Nesti <note>The 1637 printer.</note> had written perfectly well. In fact, in the *Histories*, Book III, 21, he spoils *fondi* <note>foundations or depths</note> into *fonti* <note>fountains or sources</note> (see the note at that location); in the same book, chapter 29, *intronata* <note>stunned/deafened</note> into *intonata* <note>intoned/tuned</note> (see the note); in Book IV, 2, he adds a "but" that ruins everything (see the note); in the same book, chapter 5 (page 361 of the Florentine edition, line 12), Nesti has a printing error *dedicane* which he corrects in the *errata* to *dedicano* <note>they dedicate</note>. Volpi, in the *Saggio* <note>the "Essay" or "Specimen" edition</note>, corrects *dedicano* to *dicono* <note>they say</note>, which ruins everything, and prides himself on it, while later in the text he places Nesti’s correction. In marginal note 49 of Book I, Nesti printed *spicciare* <note>to gush or hurry</note> and in the *errata* corrected it to *spiccicare* <note>to detach or unstick</note>; here too, Volpi took the correction for an error and made a fuss, restoring *spicciare*. And what is even stranger, the Crusca Academy created a specific paragraph just to make room for Volpi’s blunder <note>original: "granchio" — literally "crab," a common Italian idiom for a mistake or oversight.</note>. See the note at that location.

LXVIII

### PREFACE TO THE COMINIAN EDITION.

—not that of an immoderate man. But what shall be said then, when we assert, without departing at all from the truth, that those seven hundred oversights mentioned above are but a small portion, and perhaps the least important, of countless others in the Florentine edition? These occur principally in the Latin text, which we had the great patience to collate with the very accurate edition of *Matthias Bernegger* <note>original: "Mattia Berneggero"; a noted German philologist (1582–1640) famous for his commentary on Tacitus.</note>. Nor was it a matter of variant readings or the opposing opinions of learned men, but of palpable and gross errors. So much so that, after printing several sheets, it seemed right to gather a few and put them before your eyes, discreet readers, as a brief sample of many others that deform and cover, so to speak, with a foul leprosy the edition by *Nesti*. That edition is shabby, poorly printed, and in it the attentive reader encounters every imaginable failure of the most negligent printers. It is a great pity, in truth, that such a famous work, worthy of respect and wonder, and now superior to contradictions, critiques, and envy, should have come out the first time so battered! Had destiny reserved it for the modern presses of the illustrious city of Florence, our labor would perhaps be superfluous; for the books printed there in our day are very polished and perfect regarding their correction.

We will refrain from using many words to describe the horrible reprints of this translation, one copy of which—namely the Venetian one by Francesco Storti from 1638 in quarto—was used and torn apart in the Comino workshop. We were thus forced to swallow the boredom and endure the trouble of purging this truly Augean stable <note>original: "stabulum Augiae"; a mythological reference to a massive, filthy task, as Hercules had to clean stables that had been neglected for thirty years.</note>. You will find the punctuation improved in countless places; this diligence, although (as Salvini <note>Anton Maria Salvini (1653–1729), a prominent Florentine scholar and member of the Accademia della Crusca.</note> notes in his Tuscan prose) it may seem at first glance a petty and minute business, is nonetheless the soul of good books. It eases the understanding for the reader, removes doubts, and demonstrates at the same time the knowledge of those presiding over the printing.

In those words usually written with two 'z's, we have used only one, conforming to the custom and opinion of *Davanzati*, expressed in one of his notes. We did not, however, follow this in the first sheets, not having noticed this singularity from the beginning—a rule which was not always observed with full rigor even in the Florentine edition. *Agusto* <note>An archaic Italian spelling of "Augusto" (Augustus).</note>, not *Augusto*, shall be read consistently in this edition of ours. In some other words, we chose to follow the instability of orthography, a thing both permissible and practiced. 

We have made use of italic type in some obscure places that are difficult to understand, or that we judge ought to be supplemented; for it appears *Davanzati* did not give the final hand to this fine work of his. Had a longer life, or a greater abundance of literary leisure, provided him the opportunity to revise and retouch it, it is believable that he would have further polished, emended, and improved it in more than one place. We have added, where necessity required it, numbers in the margin, and footnotes at the bottom of the pages. Indeed, for the convenience and satisfaction of those who handle the Crusca dictionary <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca*, the first great national dictionary of Italian.</note>, we have not failed to have printed in a somewhat...

<meta>This page concludes the editor’s preface to the Cominian edition of Tacitus, translated by Bernardo Davanzati. LXIX

### PREFACE TO THE COMINIAN EDITION.

...the number of pages in the Florentine edition is larger, as these are precisely the ones pointed out by the compilers of the aforementioned dictionary <note>This refers to the *Vocabolario della Crusca*, the authoritative dictionary of the Italian language, which used Davanzati’s translation as a linguistic model.</note>. We have also removed the frequent abbreviations that offended the eyes of readers and caused them annoyance and stumbling blocks, ensuring that every word from which obscurity might arise was printed in full. After such great labor, which we have willingly undertaken for the public utility, there will probably be those who, according to the current customs and "honesty" of this century, will want to snatch and seize the fruit of our work from us with some hasty reprint. Therefore, we protest from this moment on that we will never recognize as our own any edition except for this present Cominian impression supervised by us; we hold and declare this one alone to be sincere and legitimate. On the contrary, we declare all others that might spring up from anywhere else to be spurious, wild, and counterfeit. Indeed, we promise that in the event of a rival reprint, we will examine it—and have it examined by our friends—with the most severe and sharpest lens, subsequently publishing its errors:

->And let this be the seal that undeceives all men.<-
<note>original: "E questo sia suggel ch' ogni uomo sganni." A quotation from Dante Alighieri's *Paradiso* (Canto XIX, v. 129), here used to warn readers against inferior counterfeit editions.</note>

Nonetheless, we confess that due to human fragility, more than one error may have escaped even us, despite all our diligence; nor shall we ever foolishly claim the boast of being infallible in this regard. Let the buyers of books think well on their choices; for the Cominian prints have the privilege of a nearly inimitable accuracy that makes them singular and sought after everywhere. And we wish this to be understood not of this work alone, but of all others generally that have until now emerged from the presses of our Comino <note>Giuseppe Comino (died c. 1762) was a celebrated printer in Padua known for his elegant and scholarly editions.</note>. Let the tedious corrupters of corrected things reprint them as they please. Unless self-love blinds us, we flatter ourselves that we have some merit before the Republic of Letters <term>Republic of Letters: The international community of scholars and intellectuals from the late 17th to 18th centuries.</term> for this new publication of Davanzati's Tacitus, and we feel a particular delight in it; hoping at the same time that your favor and approval, learned and discerning readers, shall confirm us in this enjoyment and opinion of ours. Live happily.

LXX

# TO MESSER BACCIO VALORI
### FLORENTINE SENATOR
### KNIGHT AND JURIST

## BERNARDO DAVANZATI BOSTICHI
### GREETINGS. <gloss>1</gloss>

---

From the Latin language, corrupted by barbarians, there were born—as everyone knows—different corrupted tongues in different places, which were called "vulgar" <note>the common speech of the people, as opposed to formal Latin</note> by the common people who used them. Later, when nobles also applied themselves to these tongues, writing and composing poetry in them, they gave them the rules and forms of proper languages. The Florentine tongue was raised to such perfection by its three lights <note>the "Three Crowns" of Italian literature: Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio</note> that the whole world has fallen in love with it; and whoever most resembles them—much like the Venus of Apelles <note>a lost masterpiece of ancient Greek painting, considered the pinnacle of beauty</note>—is the most highly prized. Nevertheless, some do not want the most excellent vulgar tongue to be, or to be called, Florentine. Praise be to the knight Lionardo Salviati, who, with that novella translated into various dialects, provided that graceful proof of what was most similar to the best. <gloss>2</gloss> This has made me want to create another such proof against a worthy man <gloss>3</gloss> who crowns and miters <note>elevates to supreme status</note> his French language above all others; he shows it to be conforming to Greek and gives it the prize for brevity, while calling ours long and languid and—like Aesop’s crow <note>referring to the fable of the bird that dressed itself in the feathers of others to appear more beautiful</note>—embellished with French feathers. But those Greek similarities that he counts, we also have almost all of them, and many others left to us by the Greeks who inhabited Sicily, Magna Graecia <note>the coastal areas of Southern Italy colonized by the ancient Greeks</note>, and other parts of Italy much more than Marseilles <note>a Greek colony in southern France</note>: and the words common between us come from the common mother and Latin corruption. It would therefore suffice to say to him as Lucio di Valbona said to Messer Rinieri da Calvoli: "Sir, out of courtesy, attend to your own affairs, but do not spoil those of others, and do not speak ill of beautiful women whom you do not know." <note>A quotation from Boccaccio's *Decameron*, Day 1, Novella 9</note> But to show with ef-

LXXI

# TO MESSER BACCIO VALORI.

...perfectly and without dispute where this boast of brevity rests. I am invited to this by your proverb, *“Everyone says they are right, but the sight [of the evidence] reveals the fact”*;¹ <note>original: "Chacun dit j'ay bon droit, mais la veve descouvre le faict"</note> and by your having brought into the field Cornelius Tacitus, perhaps the briefest writer there is, whom I call the elixir of political wisdom. I have dictated the first book of his *Annals* using Florentine words and idioms; and even with all our disadvantages of articles and other things, it turns out to be measured at sixty-three thousand letters; the Latin, sixty-eight thousand; the French printed in Lyon, more than a hundred thousand. Thus, one hundred of our words are worth and yield as much as one hundred and eight of Cornelius’s Latin ones, and as much as one hundred and sixty French ones. It seems to me that I have matched Cornelius, if not in majesty, then in liveliness; and I have surpassed him in clarity and purity. Such is the power, the dexterity, and the excellence of the living Florentine speech. Anyone who pays the slightest attention can harvest from the sea of nature most effective words and manners of speaking that are not all found in dictionaries or in the preserves of dead authors; nor do non-native speakers fish them out. Their vernacular for the most part, though regulated and ornate, is like wine begged from door to door; it does not seem to sparkle or fizz like that harvested from one's own land, and—like a tree that lacks a taproot—it is not vigorous! You can see this in that Muzio <note>Girolamo Muzio (1496–1576), a writer who argued for a "courtly" Italian language rather than a strictly Florentine one</note> who came from Capodistria to teach us how to speak, and mocked our idioms, calling them "Florentinarisms" <note>original: "fiorentinarie"</note> with a judgment and a term as clumsy as himself. It does not seem necessary to translate all of Tacitus into the vulgar tongue, as Giorgio Dati has already done so in an ample and easy style—I believe to broaden and soften a text so pithy and harsh. One can recognize from this sample, as the lion is known by its claws, the fierceness of our vernacular, which is worthy of being used with more glory and freedom than fits this small and simple translation. For a translation is subject to following behind the Latin like a servant walking in steps not his own, and it retains most of the ancient names to avoid confusing the understanding of things that have changed or been lost with modern names that do not correspond well. Moreover, readers become accustomed to those ancient names and make them our own, and the language is enriched by them; however, they will be placed at the back with some notes to the text.² I send and give you this writing with the wish that, when you are less occupied, you might go about considering it a little and telling me your opinion, which I value as much as a hundred thousand others. Blame your natural courtesy and the affection you bear for this language, and our great friendship, if the trouble is too much; and blame the hatred I bear for modern, "empyreal" <note>Davanzati is mocking the overly grandiose and flowery titles common in the Baroque period</note> titles if I seem to you in this letter, as perhaps in the rest, too much a lover of ancient simplicity. Farewell.

->From Florence, the 15th day of September 1595.<-
