LXXII

<header>THE SAME LETTER</header>

# TO MESSER BACCIO VALORI

->AS READ IN THE FLORENTINE EDITIONS BY GIUNTI AND NESTI<-
->AND IN THE PADUAN EDITION BY COMINO.<-

---

From the language corrupted by the barbarians, as everyone knows, different corrupted languages were born in different places, and were called "vernaculars" by the common folk who used them. When nobles later began to write and compose poetry in them, they gave them the rules and forms of proper languages. The Florentine tongue was raised to such perfection by its three lights <note>The "three lights" (tre lumi) refer to the three pillars of Italian literature: Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.</note> that the whole world has turned to imitating them; and whoever most resembles them—much like the Venus of Apelles <note>A reference to the lost masterpiece of the ancient Greek painter Apelles, signifying a standard of absolute perfection.</note>—is most highly prized. Nonetheless, some do not want the best vernacular language to be called, or even considered, Florentine. Praised be the knight Lionardo Salviati <note>A founding member of the Accademia della Crusca, famous for his defense of the Florentine language.</note>, who, with that novella [translated] into several dialects, provided a charming proof of which was closest to the best.

This inspired me to perform another test for a worthy man who crowns and miters his French tongue above all others: he claims it originates from Greek; he grants it the boast of brevity; and he calls ours "long and languid," like Aesop’s crow dressed in French feathers. But as for the Grecisms <note>Words or idioms of Greek origin.</note> he counts, we have even more, left to us by the Greeks who inhabited Sicily, Magna Graecia <note>The coastal areas of Southern Italy colonized by ancient Greeks.</note>, and other parts of Italy more than they did Marseille. The words we share come from our common mother, which was the corruption of Latin. It would suffice, then, to say to him what Licio ¹ of Valbona said to Messer Rinieri da Calvoli: "Messer, by your courtesy, attend to your own affairs, but do not spoil those of others; praise your own language, but do not mock ours. ²"

But to clarify the matter of brevity with facts, I have set the Florentine tongue to race against Latin and French for the prize of brevity in this arena of the first book of Cornelius Tacitus, which I am sending to you. And despite all the disadvantages of articles, substituted cases, and auxiliary tenses that we must repeat so often, I find eight percent more writing in the Latin, and in the French printed in Paris

¹ This name varies across the different editions, appearing at times as Licio, Lisio, or Lucio.

LXXIII

<header>TO MESSER BACCIO VALORI.</header>
<sig>L. g</sig>

...in 1584, more than sixty. I have left no concept behind. I have departed from Latin words and phrases where our own expressed the meaning better, for every language has its own particular virtues. From this sample, one may recognize the brevity of our speech—as one knows the lion by its claw <note>The author uses the proverbial phrase "ex ungue leonem," suggesting that even a small specimen allows the reader to judge the power and character of the whole work.</note>—and there is no need to go further, as Giorgio Dati <note>A 16th-century translator known for his more verbose and explanatory version of Tacitus.</note> has already translated all of Tacitus in a full and expansive style, suited to his goal of making everything perfectly clear.

I retain many ancient terms for things now lost or altered, for which modern words do not provide a good match. Moreover, by accustoming ourselves to the ancients, we make them our own; this enriches the language, and there is no shortage of geographers, nomenclators <note>A "nomenclator" is a scholar who compiles specialized lists of names or technical terms.</note>, and dictionaries to explain them.

While writing, I found myself adding certain notes to the text <margin>marginal notes</margin> to correct, clarify, or compare it. In truth, these are hardly necessary thanks to the commentaries of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a towering Flemish scholar whose editions and commentaries on Tacitus were considered the gold standard of the Renaissance.</note>, a great genius and the light of letters in our age. When you are less occupied, may it please you—for the sake of my love and our great friendship—to consider this writing for a moment and tell me your opinion, which I value more than a hundred thousand others. Fare you well.

LXXIV

## TO THE SAME. ##

<note>Refers to Baccio Valori, the recipient of the dedication begun on the previous page.</note>

->— <-

They say that Demosthenes <note>The famous Greek orator of the 4th century BCE.</note> copied Thucydides **nine times** to saturate his mind with that author’s brevity. In my youth, to make Cornelius Tacitus easier for me, I translated several books into my own tongue for my own use, with no other study than that of clarity. Seeing later that a certain Frenchman mocked our language, I refined somewhat that first book I sent to you, to show how much he erred regarding our brevity. I understand that such a thing is not proven by so small a writing as a single book, which could be a singular effort, and that the book speaks in a manner that is "too Florentine." I am therefore sending it back accompanied by the other books that narrate the reign of Tiberius (perhaps the most useful because of the great wisdom of that prince); and they all are, as you see, 160 pages of this printing <gloss>1</gloss> knowingly made with 39 lines of 55 letters per page, just like the Plantin edition of 1581 <note>Christophe Plantin was a famous printer in Antwerp; his editions were renowned for their accuracy and beauty.</note>, of which the same Latin books take up 178 pages. This is so that the mocker may see with his own eyes that these Florentine books are contained within the Latin ones in a ratio of nine to ten; and within the French—which would take up 266 similar printed pages—they move as if in a ratio of fifteen. <gloss>2</gloss> Let it not cast a shadow that the first Latin sheet has one line fewer per page, and this last vernacular one has one more; for these small errors do not create a meaningful difference. I did not wish to abandon the "Florentine-ness" of the work, in order to make this further trial: whether in writing—which is "thought speech"—one can add the necessary artistry without cutting the nerves of the language, which are its natural properties. It seems to me we do exactly that when we write not in our own living language, but in that "common Italian" which is not spoken, but is learned like a dead language from the "three writers" <note>The "Tre Corone" or Three Crowns of Italian literature: Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.</note>, who could not say everything...

LXXV

# TO MESSER BACCIO VALORI. #

...thing; and whatever is not found in those generic styles, or has fallen out of use, is rejected. Thus, that language remains very poor and less effective and ready than this one which is commonly spoken in Florence. It is true that many great men have written admirably in that "Italian" style; but they would have surpassed themselves if they had written in this Florentine tongue like those three <note>Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio—the "Three Crowns" of Italian literature.</note>: in whom, as in the Greeks and Latins, one does not see such a fear of "lowness." This "lowness" is nothing other than a bit of froth <note>The author uses the word "stumia" (scum/froth) to describe the raw, vibrant quality of idiomatic speech.</note> generated by the distinctive character of the language, which, when it is spirited, like a generous wine, consumes it. From the lord of the loftiest song <note>Dante Alighieri.</note>, the members of the Accademia della Crusca <note>The prestigious institution founded in Florence in 1583 to oversee and "sift" the Italian language.</note> have drawn more pure Florentine language than from all the others. Let us not even speak of Boccaccio the storyteller; even Petrarch, so polished and grave, is full of it: *talk of the town* <note>original: "favola del popolo"</note> — *my troubles* <note>original: "i miei guai"</note> — *stubborn* <note>original: "restio"</note> — *stench* <note>original: "lezo"</note> — *he has filled the sack so full it bursts* <note>original: "ha colmo il sacco sì che scoppia"</note> — *to raise and break one's horns* <note>original: "alzare, e rompere le corna"; meaning to show pride and then be humbled.</note> — *to point out with a finger* <note>original: "mostrare a dito"</note> — *to double the barley for the steeds* <note>original: "raddoppiar l'orzo a' corsieri"; meaning to increase pace or effort.</note> — *to entwine with tails* <note>original: "avvinchiarsi colle code"</note> — *very quiet* <note>original: "queta queta"</note> — *gradually* <note>original: "a mano a mano"</note> — *very slowly* <note>original: "pian piano"</note> — *step by step* <note>original: "passo passo"</note> — *to pluck the wings of Love* <note>original: "spennacchiar l' ali ad Amore"</note> — *little chamber* <note>original: "cameretta"</note> — *little bed* <note>original: "letticciuolo"</note> — *the little old woman spinning* <note>original: "filare la vecchierella"</note> — *you well know* <note>original: "ben sai"</note> — *citizen of the woods* <note>original: "cittadin di boschi"</note> — *my salvation was gone* <note>original: "mia salute era ita"</note> — *to change one’s tune* <note>original: "mutar verso"; literally "to change the verse."</note> — *I don’t want a single one* <note>original: "nieno non ne voglio una"</note> — *to flee faster than a gallop* <note>original: "fuggir più che di galoppo"</note> — *keeps him in line* <note>original: "lo fa stare a segno"</note> — *so much noise is made* <note>original: "si fa tanto romore"</note> — *to swing the sword in a circle* <note>original: "menar la spada a cerchio"</note> — *to settle our accounts* <note>original: "saldare le nostre ragioni"</note> — *wandering* <note>original: "ramingo"</note> — *in the hands of dogs* <note>original: "in man di cani"; meaning to be in the power of cruel or unscrupulous people.</note> — *they go about dancing* <note>original: "vanno trescando"; "trescare" implies a rustic dance or a suspicious intrigue.</note> — *that intrigue* <note>original: "quella tresca"</note> — *whole and firm* <note>original: "interi e saldi"</note> — *recommend me to your son* <note>original: "raccomandami al tuo figliuolo"</note> — and a thousand other local idioms <term>idiotismi</term> <note>In this context, "idiotisms" refers to "idioms" or linguistic features unique to a specific place, not "idiocy."</note> are there, but they are wisely placed; **this is the task!** <note>original: "hoc opus!"</note> and not to banish them from writings. **All words are best in their own places; even low words are called proper when used correctly,** <note>original: "Omnia verba suis locis optima; etiam sordida dicuntur proprie."</note> says Quintilian <note>A celebrated Roman rhetorician of the 1st century CE.</note>; and he wants us to take bold risks to enrich languages.

I, therefore, out of zeal for my language, seeing how much wealth and glory we would add to it if we wrote down many of the unique expressions we speak—and lose them by not writing them—and how many lost ancient beauties we might recover; I have dared not to oppose "usage" (the master of languages), but to propose to it in these books that it might wish to receive some of them, as Horace says he is wont to do. <note>In his "Ars Poetica," Horace argues that a poet may use new or revived words if done with care.</note> These will not be many; they will force no one to use them. I would have known how, and been able, to do without them: nothing is easier than to exchange them for common words and manners. To many, perhaps, it will not be unpleasant to see them placed in this sort of "depository," until their cause is clarified. I will have put into use, and perhaps into example, a small particle of our speech that the aforementioned Academicians <note>The Accademia della Crusca.</note> note as being without a literary precedent. And having made this further trial of my dearest language, even if it does not succeed, what harm will it do? If no one had attempted to write those rough verses and that very ancient, material prose, where would this language be now? It was born coarse; time, which tames all things, has made it refined. And who knows if many of these today’s "lowly" words might not one day be stars? Finally, I believe that just as the Aeolians, the Ionians, the Dorians, and the common Greeks did not blame the Athenians for their Atticisms—

He likens his preservation of these expressions to the various dialects of Ancient Greece, suggesting that today's common speech may become tomorrow's literary standard.</summary>

LXXVI

# TO MESSER BACCIO VALORI. #

...[Florentin]isms, so too should foreigners not criticize us for our **Florentinisms** <note>original: "fiorentinismi"</note>; rather, they should learn about them from the Florentines in their own lands, wishing for that reason to come to Florence—as did Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547), an influential scholar who championed Petrarch and Boccaccio as linguistic models.</note>, Ariosto, Castiglione, Caro, and recently Chiabrera, and on occasion honoring Guarino and others—who were illustrious celebrators of this noble homeland (the foundation of the **vernacular language** <note>original: "volgar lingua"</note>), unlike Tassino, $^1$ who strove to disparage it. ->She is glorious, and hears it not.<- <note>original: "Ella s' è gloriosa, e ciò non ode."</note>

1 *Tassino.* Thus the Giunti edition, revised by the translator; that of Nesti in the Cominiana edition corrects this to *Trissino* <note>Gian Giorgio Trissino (1478–1550), a diplomat and grammarian who argued that the literary language should be "Italian" rather than strictly "Florentine."</note>. At first, I doubted whether the correction was appropriate, thinking that our author might have wanted to slight Tasso <note>Torquato Tasso, the famous poet.</note>, who was called by the diminutive precisely to distinguish him from his father <note>Bernardo Tasso.</note>. But then, finding no evidence that Tasso strove to disparage the Florentine language, and seeing that Trissino had sharp disagreements with the Florentines on this account, I have come to believe the correction is right; although, out of respect for the Giunti edition, I did not dare to place it in the main text.

LXXVII

# TO THE ALTERED ACADEMICIANS #
## BERNARDO DAVANZATI. ##

---

Writing simply, appropriately, and naturally, almost as one speaks, has always pleased me; for it seems to me that it expresses a concept more briefly, vividly, and clearly than that which is compiled with great art. But because this refined century and the majesty of Roman history seem to demand a high style, I send to you, most judicious Academicians <note>The *Accademici Alterati* (The Altered Academicians) was a Florentine literary society founded in 1569. Their name referred to being "altered" or transformed by their studies, often using wine-related metaphors for their intellectual pursuits.</note>, my Florentine Cornelius Tacitus, so that where my love for the work might have carried me away, you may correct it; for you are well able to do so. It turns out to be shorter than the Latin, not because that language <note>Latin.</note> is not—due to its lack of articles and other things—shorter than Greek and the common vernacular; but$^1$ because the native Florentine dialect that is spoken is rich in choices, terms, and witty ways of abbreviating which, like shortcuts in the streets or foreshortening in a painting <note>original: "scorci di pittura"</note>, express a meaning by merely hinting at it: of which you will find many instances here. It also proves clearer to my Florentines, for whom I have undertaken this labor, because of the accustomed natural properties of the speech. For me, it was easier to set down, and very pleasing to bring to life, some of those properties which are often lost because no one dares to write them for fear of appearing "low" or vulgar.

Regarding this "lowness," it occurs to me to say that every city takes its own linguistic properties, one or another, according to how they are spoken by the ingenious; the common people immediately gather them up, and if the nobility receives them, they pass into general use. They are then no longer "common," but proper to that city, and worthy of entering the palace of noble writings—just as great ministers enter the chambers of great lords, though born of humble status, because their virtue has made them most noble. Therefore, a city may well (since nature wills that each speaks in its own way) refuse the properties of another, even a neighboring one; but if she were to disparage them, it would be as if the African and the Ethiopian were to compete with the Englishman or the Frenchman over their complexions, which nature has made necessarily different. Therefore, properties approved by nobles and by usage are not "lownesses," but strengths and sinews; neither Homer nor Dante shunned them in their loftiest poems, in those places where they operate with great vigor.

---

1 I did not hesitate to add this *but* <note>original: "ma"</note>, even though it is not found in the printed editions, because without it the syntax does not flow.

<summary>Bernardo Davanzati dedicates his translation of Tacitus to the Altered Academicians, defending his use of concise, natural Florentine idioms which he argues are even more brief than Latin.</summary>

LXXVIII

# TO THE ALTERED ACADEMICIANS #

---

One must, therefore, have an eye for the setting: this is what Donatello did with the eyes of the famous **Zuccone** <note>Literally "The Big Gourd" or "Bald-head," referring to the statue of the Prophet Habakkuk (historically often called David) on the Florence Cathedral bell tower.</note> on our Cathedral’s bell tower. He carved them so deeply ¹ that from up there they seem dug out with a shovel; yet if he had sculpted them normally, the figure would appear blind from the ground, because distance eats up the detail. There is a magnanimous nonchalance <note>original: "sprezzatura magnanima." This refers to the art of making difficult tasks look effortless, a key Renaissance concept.</note> that brings a concept to life rather than diminishing it—as when one portrays great anger, dishonesty, sedition, or fury, not with measured words, but with words poured out. Nor does the roughness of the unpolished stone blocks <note>original: "bozi." Referring to the rustic, rugged stonework found on the exterior of Florentine palaces like the Palazzo Medici.</note> in great palaces diminish their majesty; rather, it increases it. 

I further consider that if the Florentine vernacular was once considered so low and vile that Dante had to apologize so much in his *Convivio* for offering "barley bread" <note>In his *Convivio* (The Banquet), Dante compares his use of the vernacular to coarse barley bread, rather than the "wheaten bread" of Latin, to feed the uneducated.</note>; and if Boccaccio says that to avoid envy ² he wanders through the deepest valleys, writing his *Novelle* in the Florentine vernacular and in a style as humble and submissive as possible; and yet, if their writings and those of Petrarch pleased so well that everyone has rushed to imitate them, why should I cast away all hope? Why should some of our present-day "Florentinisms," born under the same sky, not be worthy of good literature, even if they were not found in those three authors—either because the occasion did not arise for them, or because the words had not yet been born? It is not impossible for a living language to find things as good as those of the ancients. Every novelty seems harsh at the beginning, it is true; but then, those who grow used to it discover its virtue and embrace it. 

I hear that some signs of this are appearing even outside of our city; and you heard it said by a most grave and noble person, full of goodness and human and divine knowledge, that: "I have gathered among the brambles of the Arno the jewels of Florentine speech, and set them in the gold of Tacitus." Just as I have not abandoned any concept, I have not sworn an absolute oath to the specific words; rather, I have said the same thing in my own words when it worked better due to the differences between languages. I retain the ancient names of places and technical terms when modern ones do not correspond well, deferring to Ortelius <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), a famous Flemish cartographer.</note>, Junius <note>Hadrianus Junius (1511–1575), a Dutch physician and philologist.</note>, and others who explain them. There will be few new marginal notes, because I did not record them at first. Those ideas have flown away, and it would take the falcon of youth to recapture them. When I depart from the standard text, I choose from the corrections of many most talented men the one that pleases me most for now; and, rather than finding fault with any of them, I celebrate that charming saying of Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:

->Bakers’ wives are used<-
->To trading insults; not the sacred Muses.<-

---

¹ This is the statue of King David <note>Actually the Prophet Habakkuk, though Davanzati identifies it as David.</note>; bald, and therefore called the *Zuccone* by Donatello. "Which (*says Vasari*) being held as a thing most rare and beautiful as anything he ever made, Donato was used to say, when he wanted to swear an oath so that he would be believed: 'By the faith I bear to my Zuccone!' And while he was working on it, looking at it, he would continually say: 'Speak, speak, may a bloody plague take you!'" <note>original: "favella, favella, che ti venga il casasangue!"</note>
² *to avoid envy*. The annotator of Gino Capponi’s "Nestian" copy corrects this to "who, to avoid envy."

->BY<-

## GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.$^1$

### SUMMARY.

**I.** The state of Rome from its foundation to the death of Augustus. — **V.** Tiberius delays taking the empire, feigning reluctance. — Rome in servitude. — **XVI.** A serious mutiny of three Pannonian legions, barely quelled by Drusus, the son of Tiberius, who was sent there. — **XXXI.** A similar occurrence in Lower Germany <note>The Roman province of *Germania Inferior*, located in what is now the Netherlands and western Germany.</note>, settled with no small amount of blood and slaughter. — **L.** Germanicus Caesar attacks the enemy: by his hand the Marsi, Tubantes, Bructeri, and Usipetes are pillaged or cut to pieces. — **LIII.** Julia, the daughter of Augustus, dies at Reggio. — **LIV.** Priests established in honor of Augustus, and the Augustan festivals. — **LV.** Germanicus again crosses the Rhine against the Chatti: their fields, houses, and people are put to the sword and fire. He rescues Segestes from the siege of Arminius; then he is hailed as commander <note>original: "imperadore"</note>. — **LIX.** War against the Cherusci: the remains of Varus and his soldiers are gathered, and funeral rites are performed for them. — **LXIII.** Danger to the Romans during the return under Caecina: yet the enemy is broken and routed by a successful sally. — **LXXII.** The law of treason <term>crimenlese</term> <note>From the Latin *crimen laesae maiestatis*, or "the crime of injured majesty." It refers to crimes against the dignity of the state or the emperor.</note> is renewed and strictly observed. — **LXXVI.** The Tiber overflows. — **LXXVII.** Licentiousness in the theater; then express decrees of the Fathers <note>A common term for the Roman Senators (*Patres*).</note> to restrain the actors. — **LXXIX.** Finally, the matter of diverting the waters of the Tiber elsewhere is discussed: appeals are made against it, alongside embassies from the cities of Italy.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

I. Rome $^1$ was ruled by kings from the beginning: $^2$ from Lucius Brutus came liberty and the consulate: dictatorships were held for a limited time: $^3$ the power of the ten $^4$ <note>Referring to the Decemviri, a ten-man commission established to compile the first Roman law codes.</note> did not last beyond two years, nor did the consular authority of the military tribunes last long: neither Cinna nor Sulla held dominion for a great while: the power of Pompey and Crassus soon passed to Caesar, and the arms of Lepidus and Antony fell to Augustus, who, finding everyone exhausted by civil discord, took everything for himself under the title of Prince $^5$ <note>original: "principale"; referring to the Latin *Princeps*, meaning "First Citizen."</note>. Famous writers have recorded the successes and misfortunes of the ancient Roman people, nor were distinguished minds lacking to recount the times of Augustus, until growing flattery did not corrupt them. $^6$ The affairs of Tibe-

---

$^1$ **Rome.** This summary of the changes in the Roman state seems taken wholesale from a speech by the Emperor Claudius, recorded by Lipsius in the eleventh book of these Annals as his own. It is beautiful to compare it with the one composed by Tacitus in that same book, to recognize from the difference the vigor and greatness of this writer.

$^2$ **was ruled by kings.** <note>original: "ebbe i re"</note> The softness of the vernacular <note>The Italian language of the translator</note> did not allow for the Latin hardness of "Rome the kings had" <note>original: *Roma i re ebbero*</note>. Therefore, I turned the active voice into the passive, which conveys the same meaning, in the manner of those cloths and fabrics that are the same on the right and wrong sides; nor do I see that it is an improper phrase to say that a city and nation "had" kings. "We have no king but Caesar" <note>original: *Non habemus regem, nisi Cæsarem*</note>; so translated Saint Jerome from the Greek text of Saint John.

$^3$ **for a limited time.** <note>original: "a tempo"</note> Not perpetual, as Sulla and Caesar took for themselves, but only in urgent cases. He was anciently called the "master of the people," says Seneca to Lucilius, for six months at most; and not outside of Italy. See Dio in book 36, in the speech of Catulus.

$^4$ **of the ten.** <note>original: "de' dieci"</note> Perhaps it is better to say "of the <term>decemviri</term>," and to leave such names, both proper titles and technical terms, in their original forms. See Aelian at the beginning of the *Greek Tactics*.

$^5$ **under the title of Prince.** <note>original: "con titolo di principale"</note> That is, of emperor <note>original: *imperatore*</note>, a title given to the general or chief commander of the army when, for some outstanding deed or success, the soldiers shouted "Io! Io!" <note>A Latin exclamation of triumph</note>; which today we would say "Long live our Emperor," meaning commander. Augustus, having made himself master of Rome, took this modest title to avoid envy, and used to say that he was the master of slaves, the emperor of soldiers, and the prince <note>original: *principale*</note> of all; and this caused these adjective titles of rank—*emperor* <note>original: *imperator*</note>, *leader* <note>original: *dux*</note>, *prince* <note>original: *princeps*</note>—to become nouns of lordship and absolute power. Tacitus a little further down says that Augustus was hailed as emperor twenty-one times, and in the third book he says: "The leaders, having conducted affairs well, hailed them as emperors in the joy and impetus of victory; and there were several emperors at the same time, nor did Augustus grant this title to certain individuals beyond the equality of the others; but then Tiberius granted it to Blaesus for the last time." <note>original Latin: *Duces, re bene gesta, gaudio et impetu victoriæ imperatores salutabant; erantque plures simul imperatores, nec super cæterorum æqualitatem concessit quibusdam et Augustus id vocabulum; at tunc Tiberius Blæso postremum.*</note> Livy in the first book: "The princes on both sides stirred up the fight, Mettius Curtius for the Sabines, Hostus Hostilius for the Romans." <note>original Latin: *Principes utrinque pugnam ciebant, ab Sahinis Metius Curius, ab Romanis Hostus Hostilius.*</note> See Dio at the end of book 51.

$^6$ **did not corrupt them**, reading *detererentur*: if one reads *deterrerentur*, it translates as **did not frighten them.** (*) — Thus Horace, to whom the history of Augustus was entrusted, in place of that history, wrote odes, so that he could praise him.

(*) The Medicean-Laurentian manuscript has *deterrerentur*. With the other reading, Orelli observes, this inept sentence would result: "distinguished minds existed, until they became worse" <note>original Latin: *extiterunt ingenia decora, donec fierent deteriora*</note>.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ANNALS.
<meta>catchword: Mar-</meta>

[Tibe]rius, of Gaius, of Claudius, and of Nero were compiled falsely; while they lived, out of fear; and afterwards, because of fresh resentments. Therefore, I intend to relate some of the final deeds of Augustus, then the reign of Tiberius and what followed, without anger or bias <note>original: "senza tenere ira nè parte"; a translation of the famous Latin phrase *sine ira et studio*.</note>, as I am far removed from the causes. $^1$

II. Once all public arms were laid down $^2$—Brutus and Cassius being dead, $^3$ Pompey defeated in Sicily, Lepidus stripped of power, and Antony killed $^4$—no leader remained for the Julian faction but Caesar [Augustus]. He, no longer calling himself "triumvir" but "consul," and contenting himself with the "tribunician power" <note>An office originally created to protect the common people, which Augustus used to give his rule a legal, populist veneer.</note> to defend the common people, won over the soldiers with gifts, the people with grain, and everyone with the sweetness of peace. He began to rise up bit by bit, taking on the functions of the senate, the magistrates, and the laws, with no one to oppose him. The most defiant had died in battle or through proscription, and the rest of the nobles—who were enriched and honored the more they were ready to serve, and who grew in status under the new regime $^5$—preferred the safety of the present to the dangers of the past. Nor did this state of affairs displease the provinces, $^6$ who were suspicious of the rule of the senate and the people because of the rivalries of the powerful, the greed of the magistrates, and the exhausted protection of the laws, which were subverted by force, intrigue, and bribery.

III. To strengthen his position in the state, Augustus elevated Claudius Marcellus, his sister's son, $^7$ a mere youth, to the priesthood and the curule aedileship; and Marcus Agrippa—a man of humble birth but a good soldier and companion in victory—to two successive consulates; $^8$ and, after Mar[cellus] died...

---

$^1$ *as I am far removed from the causes.* Because Augustus and the other four emperors had died long before the author's time.

$^2$ * **Once all public arms were laid down, etc.** In the *Translation Essay* addressed to Pinelli (found at the end of this volume), the translator Davanzati wrote *mancate* (ceased/vanished); this is better and more faithful to the original Latin text, which says: " *nulla iam publica arma* " [now no public arms remain]. This means that the armies were no longer, as before, at the service of the republic, but belonged to a few ambitious citizens. *Posate* (laid down) might imply a different meaning.

$^3$ * **Brutus and Cassius dead:** this occurred at the Battle of Philippi in the year of Rome 712 [42 BCE].

$^4$ * **and Antony killed.** The scholar Dati more accurately translates this as: "and Antony killed himself."

$^5$ * **and for the new state.** This follows the common reading *ac novis* [and by new things]. However, the scholar Horkel, followed by Orelli, reads *ut novis* [as by new things], etc., and the concept gains much from this, revealing the practiced art of ruling: namely, throwing a "sop to Cerberus" <note>A mythological reference to throwing a piece of food to the three-headed dog of Hades to distract it; here, it means Augustus distracted the nobility with wealth to keep them from noticing their lost liberty.</note>.

$^6$ * **Latin: " *provinciæ*."** [The provinces/subject territories].

$^7$ * **of Octavia.** He died while serving as aedile in the year of Rome 731 at the age of 20. (See Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 860; Propertius III, 18.)

$^8$ * **The years of Rome 726 and 727.** [28 and 27 BCE].

<sig>1*</sig>

[coar]se and furious,¹ but innocent of crime. He appointed Germanicus (the son of Drusus) as general of the eight legions on the Rhine, and ordered Tiberius to adopt him, even though Tiberius already had a grown son of his own; this was undoubtedly done so that Augustus might strengthen his position from several sides. <insert>ink stroke</insert>² At that time, no war remained except for the one against the Germans, which was pursued more to erase the shame of the army lost under Quinctilius Varus³ than to expand the empire or for any other worthy gain. At home, the city was quiet; the titles of the magistrates remained the same; the young men had been born after the victory at Actium,⁴ and most of the old men during the civil wars; who was left, then, who had ever seen the Republic?

¹ *furious*. In the beginning of the seventh book, Livy says exactly the same of the son of Manlius: <note>original Latin: "Nullius probri compertum, et stolide ferocem"</note> "Found guilty of no disgrace, yet stolidly fierce." Aristotle says in the second book of the *Rhetoric* that the children of courageous fathers often degenerate into the reckless, and those of quiet fathers into the cold. Similarly, in a worn-out field, the grain grows into wild oats or tares—grasses that are not entirely different. And Dante writes:

->Seldom does human virtue rise through<-
->The branches; and this He wills<-
->Who gives it, so that it may be called His.<-
<note>Reference to Purgatorio VII, 121-123, suggesting that noble character is not always inherited by offspring.</note>

² <note>original Latin: « sed quo pluribus munimentis insisteret. »</note> "but so that he might stand upon more fortifications."
³ The year 762 [9 AD]. See Velleius II, 117; and Tacitus himself later in chapters 55, 65, 71, and Book II, 45. <note>This refers to the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, a catastrophic Roman defeat.</note>
⁴ *after the victory at Actium: which occurred in the year of Rome 723.* — **Actium**. Our ancestors, less concerned with "correct" spelling than we are, would have written *Actio* in the Latin style; a few moderns write *Attio*; many write *Azzio*. It seems to me that just as the Latin language does not double the letters in *gaza*, *oxymel* and others, so our vernacular should never double either of our two "Z" sounds (*); because they are naturally double, composed either of "TS" like *zazera* [mop of hair], or "DS" like *sizania* [discord]. Each has its own double sound, which, if doubled again, would result in four consonant sounds joined together—something our sweet pronunciation cannot tolerate. In these two words, the second "Z" has no greater or more forced sound than the first, even when between two vowels, unless one wants to deceive the ear into hearing what is not there. The reason is that the tongue positions itself between the teeth and the palate, acting as an organ for the escaping breath.

(*) In his *Cominiana* edition, Volpi adds the following note at this point: "Throughout the translation of Tacitus in the Florentine edition (that of Nesti in '37), this rule is often violated. In the *Cominiana*, it is only violated in the first few pages; this was because it was not noticed before printing." Volpi did well not to stray, when possible, from our author’s own spelling system, whatever it may have been. However, R. Pastore, in the *Remondiniana* edition, felt he should act otherwise, shielding himself with the following note: "This note was not omitted so as not to detract from the integrity of the work. However, the reasons provided by Davanzati [the translator] carry little weight in themselves, and even less against common usage, to which even laws must yield: <note>original Latin: "consuetudo optima legum interpres"</note> 'custom is the best interpreter of laws.' Therefore, in this new edition, we have followed an orthography that does not oppose the grammatical laws of correct writing, does not offend the eye, and does not disgust the reader for the trivial goal of following antiquity." — In the editions printed under the author's own eyes, such as the *Marescottiana* and the *Giuntina*, the rule is observed, except in a few places through inadvertence. And we, too, have not allowed ourselves to change it for the reasons stated in the *Foreword*. As for its actual merit, that is another matter. See what Salvini says about it in the 230th of his *Academic Discourses*.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

## IV. [Year of Rome 767, Year of Christ 14.] 

Everything thus being overturned, no ancient good custom was to be seen: everyone, brought low, waited for the prince's command without taking any thought for themselves, while Augustus, of a robust age, sustained himself, his house, and the peace—

<note>The sentence above breaks off as the translator begins a long linguistic digression in the commentary section below.</note>

in the same manner when pronouncing the first Z before the second. Now, if writing *follows* pronunciation, *as the student follows the master*, or the dance follows the sound, and the song follows the notes; then to read correctly the words *zazzera* <note>shaggy hair</note> or *zizzania* <note>discord or "tares"</note>, one would need to expend four times the breath, burst a vein in the chest, and explode—or else read them incorrectly. 

Lodovico Martelli, in his letter to Cardinal Ridolfi—where he poorly mocks Trissino regarding the addition of letters to the Italian language—does not allow this letter to ever be doubled, for the reasons cited there. <note>Gian Giorgio Trissino (1478–1550) attempted to reform Italian spelling by introducing Greek letters like Ɛ and Ω to distinguish open and closed vowels; Martelli was a fierce critic of this "Grecizing" of the alphabet.</note> Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian of the 6th century.</note> blames the Romans for similar things; since their consonant J was double, they doubled it when it fell between two vowels, such as *Majus* or *Pompejus*, and were forced in the genitive case to write *Majii* or *Pompejii*. This error pleased Caesar and others, as often happens to those who delight in opposing nature to maintain a certain subtlety. 

But without doubt, just as words ought to be portraits and not blotches of the soul's concepts, so should letters be portraits of words. If the portrait does not resemble the subject, what is it worth? The French speak in one way and write in another, because that language (says Perionio <note>Joachim Périon, a 16th-century scholar who argued that French was derived directly from Greek.</note>) has its origin in Greek, being preserved more in their writing than in their speech. Thus, our ancestors retained much Latin spelling, such as *Philosophia*, *actione*, *letitia*, *optimo*, *pecto*, *annuntio*. We now write more correctly according to pronunciation: *filosofia* <note>philosophy</note>, *azione* <note>action</note>, *letizia* <note>joy</note>, *ottimo* <note>excellent</note>, *petto* <note>chest</note>, *annunzio* <note>announcement</note>. This is because our language, though born from Latin, is today grown up; it governs itself and walks without the "walker" or the support of those letters which, no longer being pronounced, are an embarrassment to be cleared away—like the centering and the scaffolding once the stone vault has set. 

Ultimately, the vulgar <note>meaning the common or vernacular Italian</note> tongue is "incorrect Latin." Its past incorrectness, having passed into common use, has converted into its natural essence. Against this essence, the "semi-learned" man—who wishes to over-orthographize—actually "cacographizes" <note>writes poorly or incorrectly</note>. For example, placing an H where it is not pronounced serves no purpose, and we can do without it. Similarly, when writing *a lo*, *de lo*, *fa mi*, *de la bella*, *de la casa*, *d' Avanzati* (*), instead of *allo*, *dello*, *fammi*, *della bella*, *della casa*, *Davanzati* and the like, one divides what usage—which is a manufactured nature—has composed into a single body. 

Nor is it good to break one's teeth (as some do) to utter the Greek language in a "learned" fashion; rather, follow the usage of the fatherland. One could represent the two sounds of our Z with two different characters, Z and z. But since Trissino and others, with excellent reasons, tried in vain to complete our lacking alphabet, what can we say? Except that:

->Against custom, reason has short wings?<-

But those brave men can take comfort, since the Emperor Claudius did not succeed in helping the Roman alphabet with his three letters; indeed, they were so thoroughly rejected that no memory remains of them, except for the Aeolic digamma <note>The "inverted F" used by Claudius to represent the 'V' sound.</note> on certain tablets. It is a great marvel that Custom—this master of speaking and writing—has accepted many letters from writing-masters that are strangely varied for the sake of whimsical flourishes, yet has not accepted the necessities discovered or added to our lacking script by great and learned men. For my part, I would add Greek-style accents to help the pronunciation of the reader. But <note>original Latin: "quis ausit feli alligare tintinnabulum"</note> "who would dare to bell the cat," since those brave men were mocked for it?

---

(*) *d' Avanzati*. This is found in some manuscripts of that time and also in some prints, such as in the *Coltivazione* by Magazzini, Florence, 1634.

**VII.** In Rome, everyone rushed headlong into servitude: consuls, senators, and knights. The most illustrious among them were the most eager; they wore false expressions, taking care not to appear too joyful at the death of one prince nor too sorrowful at the entry of the next. They mingled tears with joy and laments with flattery. Sextus Pompeius and Sextus Appuleius, the consuls, were the first to swear allegiance to Tiberius Caesar; after them came Seius Strabo, commander of the guard, and Gaius Turranius, the grain official <term>abbondanziere: the official in charge of the *annona*, or the city's food supply</term>. The Senate, the military, and the people followed suit. Tiberius made the consuls the head of every matter, as if the Republic still stood and he himself were hesitant to rule. For this reason, in a brief and very modest proclamation—where he used only the title of Tribune granted to him by Augustus—he asked the senators to come and advise him on the honors for his father, whose body he wished to accompany <margin>The historian Dio Cassius writes that Tiberius was granted a religious pardon for touching the corpse, an act normally forbidden to those holding high public office.</margin>, and claimed no other public concern. It could be a word, a sound (like a trumpet), or a visual signal.</margin> to the guards in his capacity as Emperor; he kept sentries, carried arms, and maintained a formal court. ...to the guardsmen <note>The Praetorian Guard</note> twenty-five per head, and to the Roman legionaries seven and a half. They proceeded to the honors. The most notable men proposed them;¹ Asinius Gallus proposed that the funeral procession should pass through the Triumphal Gate; Lucius Arruntius proposed that the titles of the laws enacted and the names of the nations conquered by him [Augustus] should be carried in the lead. <column-break/>

<note>The following is a detailed commentary on ancient currency values compared to 16th-century Florence.</note>

...a silver drachma, that is an eighth of an ounce; it was worth four **HS** <term>HS: the symbol for the sestertius, a small silver Roman coin</term> coins, or if you prefer, ten *asses* or ten *libellae*. A gold coin weighed a drachma of fine gold, like our lily florin; it was worth ten denarii, forty **HS**, 100 *asses*, or 100 *libellae*. They kept their accounts in sesterce coins and counted up to a hundred thousand. Then they would say: "Two times a hundred thousand, three times, 4, 10, 20, 100, 1000, 2000, and up to a hundred thousand times a hundred thousand"; and they understood that many **HS** coins. Such a sum of **HS** amounts to 250 million in gold, which in human commerce can perhaps not even be contained. Although Suetonius claims in chapter 16 that Vespasian said the republic needed a thousand million; perhaps that text is corrupted and should mean *quadragies* [forty times], that is one hundred million, and not *quadringenties* [four hundred times]. Vespasian said it to aggrandize the Roman State with hyperbole. Therefore, the 435 times were **HS** 43,500,000; which at four to the denarius equals 10,875,000 denarii; which at ten to the florin equals 1,087,500 florins, as was stated. And the thousand **HS** per head to the guardsmen equals 25 florins; and the 300 to the legionaries, seven and a half florins. 

Now, since that gold coin is the same as our florin—that is, a drachma, or truly an eighth of an ounce of pure gold <note>original: 'oro obrizo'—refined gold without impurities</note>—which in this present year of 1599 in Florence is worth ten lire; that Roman denarius is worth one lira today; that sesterce coin, five *soldi piccioli*; that *asse* or *libella*, two *soldi*. 

I will add two corollaries. One is that Florence began to strike the florin in the year 1252 at the value of one lira of currency; so good was it! In the year 1530, it was worth seven lire; so much had they worsened! Today it is worth ten. At this rate (*), currency will soon be reduced to those "iron spikes" <note>original: 'cappelli d' aguti'—likely referring to the primitive iron spits or bars used as currency in ancient Sparta</note> which must have been the iron money of the Spartans. This is a great error of princes who so greatly diminish their own revenues and the ancient levels of legacies, taxes, and private credits. They disturb trade no less by failing to keep currency steady—which is the measure of value for all tradable things—than if they were to change the scales, the bushel, the barrel, or the yard-stick, which are the measures of quantity. 

The other corollary is that just as the Lighthouse [Pharos] built by Ptolemy Philadelphus upon four glass bases, through the skill of the architect Sostratos of Cnidus, moved every city (out of its utility and wonder) to build a lighthouse in its own port for the safety of sailors; similarly, our florin, for its beauty and goodness, was received with such applause that every power wanted to strike and name "florins." Today, with sequins, crowns, piastres, and ducatoons, the glory of such a beautiful name has vanished (**).

¹ * They proposed the most notable, that is, as the most notable honors. Latin: "*ex quis (honoribus) maxime insignes visi ec.*" <note>original Latin: "from which [honors] the most distinguished seemed [to be], etc."</note>

(*) At this rate, at this reckoning, proceeding at this pace.
(**) See the *Lecture on Money*, where he repeats these same observations.

"Only the mind of the divine Augustus had been capable of such a massive burden; having been entrusted with a portion of those responsibilities, he <note>Tiberius</note> had learned how arduous and risky <margin>risky: derived from *zara*, a game of chance.</margin> it is to rule the whole. They should not give all the cares of a city founded by so many illustrious men to one man alone; several companions helping one another would accomplish public affairs more easily." In this speech of Tiberius, one could perceive more pomp than sincerity; his words, by nature and habit, were ambiguous <margin>Ancient captains used the Minotaur as their emblem, showing they must keep secrets in the impenetrable depths of their souls, like the center of the labyrinth. Tiberius used to say: "When the prince has not let himself be understood, it is time to do much good and avoid much evil." But he wished to do evil without being discovered; therefore, he did not command clearly, but hinted darkly, and punished both those who misunderstood him out of dullness and those who, through sharp penetration, had uncovered and offended him. By keeping his claws in and his eyes closed, he wished not to be recognized as a "sly old cat." Thus, it behooved the poor senators to walk a very straight line.</margin> and dark when he spoke openly; now, as he hid himself with all his might, they were entangled in even greater doubt and shadows. <insert><image-desc>A small horizontal pen flourish follows the end of the paragraph.</image-desc></insert>

But the fathers <note>the Senators</note>, for fear of appearing to understand him (which was their great dread), gave themselves to weeping, lamenting, and commending themselves with outstretched arms to the gods, to the image of Augustus, and to Tiberius's own knees. <margin>+</margin> XIII. After him, Lucius Arruntius spoke in almost the same manner <gloss>1 *</gloss> and offended Tiberius, although he had no previous grievance with him <gloss>2 *</gloss>; but as he was wealthy, <gloss>3 *</gloss> learned, and renowned, Tiberius suspected him. This was especially because Augustus, in his final discussions about his successors, <note>original: succe[ssori]</note> had said <gloss>4 *</gloss> "that Manius Lepidus would be capable, but indifferent; Asinius Gallus greedy, but not up to the task; and Lucius Arruntius [suitable] <gloss>5 *</gloss> and bold, seeing the opportunity." Of the first two, all agree; instead of Arruntius, some name Gnaeus Piso; and all, except for Lepidus, eventually fell into the snares of various crimes that Tiberius laid for them. That suspicious mind was further stung by Quintus Haterius, who asked: "How long do you wish, O Caesar, for the republic to remain without a head?" and by Mamercus Scaurus saying: "The Senate hopes, since you have not vetoed the consuls as a tribune would, that you will grant them this favor." He lashed out <gloss>6 *</gloss> immediately against Haterius; but to Scaurus, against whom he was more venomous, he gave no reply. Finally, as everyone was shouting and lamenting, he relented—not to say he accepted, but to say: "Come now, let there be an end to so much refusing and so much pleading. <gloss>7 *</gloss>" Haterius went to the palace to apologize...

---

<gloss>1 * "spoke in almost the same manner": he spoke with nearly the same sentiment as Asinius.</gloss>
<gloss>2 * "had no previous grievance": although Tiberius did not hold any old grudge against him.</gloss>
<gloss>3 * "wealthy": add "courageous," following the Latin text which says: "divitem et promptum" <note>original: "wealthy and ready/bold"</note>.</gloss>
<gloss>4 * "having... said": I have followed the reading of the Marescotti and Giuntina editions, instead of the common version which reads: "and for Augustus having, in his final discussions of successors, discoursed etc." But note that here Davanzati <note>Bernardo Davanzati (1529–1606), a famous Florentine translator of Tacitus.</note> has omitted many words of the text, which we will translate with Politi: "Treating of those... who, being able, would not aspire to the empire, or who, being unfit, would dare to, or of those who could and would, he had said etc."</gloss>
<gloss>5 * "the case" <note>original: "il caso"</note>: understand this as "was." And "to be the case" means to be suitable or fit. In the *Lepidezze* published by Moreni, "to be the most suitable case" is also used.</gloss>
<gloss>6 * "he lashed out": Latin: "invectus est." Politi: "he unburdened himself."</gloss>
<gloss>7 * "so much refusing and so much pleading": Others say that he finally accepted.</gloss>

...for having nearly died at the hands of the guards, because in embracing the knees of Tiberius while he was walking, he had—either by chance or because he tripped over those feet—fallen; nor did the danger of such a man <note>Quintus Haterius, a senator known for his oratory, who had offended Tiberius with a blunt question about the division of power.</note> appease him, until he was finally <gloss>1 *</gloss> defended by the persistent pleas of Augusta <note>Livia, the widow of Augustus and mother of Tiberius.</note>, to whom he had turned for help.

XIV. The senators <note>original: "i padri" - literally 'the fathers,' referring to the Conscript Fathers of the Senate.</note> were even more nauseating in their flattery of Augusta: some wanted to call her "Parent," others "Mother of the Country"; many suggested that "after the name of Caesar, there should be written *Son of Julia*." <note>By the will of Augustus, Livia was adopted into the Julian family and took the name Julia Augusta.</note> He [Tiberius], claiming that honors for women must be tempered (and that he would do the same for those granted to himself) <gloss>2 *</gloss>, but envying her high status as if it overshadowed his own, did not even grant her a lictor <term>Lictor: an official attendant who carried the fasces, symbolizing the power to punish.</term>, and he took from her the altar of adoption <gloss>3 *</gloss> and other such things. He appointed Germanicus to the rank of proconsul; ambassadors were sent to confer the rank upon him and to console him for the death of Augustus. For Drusus, who was already consul-elect and present in Rome, this was not necessary. When it came time to appoint the praetors, he nominated twelve, the number established by Augustus. The Senate urged him to increase the number, but he swore not to exceed it.

<margin>+</margin>
XV. The elections <term>original: "squittini" - the process of balloting or voting for officials.</term> were then moved from the Campus Martius <note>The traditional outdoor field where the Roman people met to vote.</note> to the Senate: because up until that day, offices had been granted through the favors of the tribes, though the best candidates were chosen by the Prince. The people, having this privilege taken from them, did little more than make a bit of noise; to the Senate, this change was welcome, as it freed them from the need to give bribes or humble themselves with indignity to the commoners. Tiberius limited himself to proposing only four candidates, who were to be elected without the usual campaigning or bribery. The tribunes of the plebs requested permission to hold a festival every year at their own expense, to be named...

...truly so that the senators would be satisfied to soon take them back, to give his old age some rest.

² * *and he would do the same for his own.* Great things are read regarding the genuine modesty and good works of Tiberius, especially while Germanicus lived; he refused temples, the title of "Augustus," "Father of the Country," and the annual oath of loyalty. He did not maintain a stable or a splendid life; he revered the magistrates and sought justice in his own legal cases; he gave to impoverished nobles. Many buildings and temples belonging to private citizens that were either unfinished or ruined, he completed and repaired, while keeping their original names on them. This was a courtesy also used by the Grand Duke Cosimo [de' Medici], who, having bought the Pitti Palace and made it a royal residence, did not wish to change its name nor display his own coat of arms there.

</note>

...from the name of Augustus, the games became known as the Augustalia, and were added to the calendar. <note>original: "IV. eid. Octob. AUGUST." — The 12th of October. These games were held previously, but the tribunes asked to continue them after Augustus's death as if to a god. They were not permitted to fund them themselves, so they wouldn't gain too much popularity with the people.</note> They were granted at public expense: the officials were to process through the Circus in triumphal robes, but not in a chariot; the praetor <term>Praetor: a high-ranking magistrate who served as a judge.</term> who oversaw cases for citizens and foreigners was to have the annual care of them. <note>The original text here is corrupted. The translator Davanzati was uncertain; scholars suggest Tiberius gave this task to a secondary magistrate rather than a primary one out of a sense of petty jealousy.</note>

**XVI.** Such was the state of affairs in the city when the legions in Pannonia <note>A Roman province in modern-day Central Europe, including parts of Hungary, Austria, and Croatia.</note> broke out in mutiny. This happened for no other reason than that the change in emperors seemed to offer a license for disorder, <note>original: "licentiam turbarum...... ostendebat."</note> and the prospect of civil war offered a hope for profit. Three legions were stationed together in their summer quarters under the command of Junius Blaesus, <note>The uncle of Sejanus, who would later become Tiberius's powerful and feared commander of the Guard.</note> who, upon hearing of the death of Augustus and the accession of Tiberius, had suspended military duties—partly out of grief and partly for celebration. From this, the soldiers began to grow idle, to argue, and to listen to malicious gossip; eventually, they sought only pleasure and ease, while fleeing from obedience and hard work. There was a man named Percennius, formerly a leader of stage actors and then a loud-mouthed common soldier, who was skilled at stirring up trouble; having been accustomed to the partisan bickering of theater fans, he was quite effective. In the evenings and at night, he began to incite <note>The Italian word used here is *contaminare*, which the translator uses to mean "to tempt or push others to do something."</note> the weak-minded, who were doubtful about how they would be treated now that Augustus was gone. Once the honorable men had retired, he gathered the dregs of the camp, and having prepared other wicked tools, he questioned them as if in a formal assembly:

**XVII.** "Why obey like slaves to four barefoot centurions <term>Centurion: a professional officer of the Roman army who commanded about 80 to 100 men.</term> and even fewer tribunes? When will we have the heart..."

...to redeem ourselves,¹ unless we confront the prince with prayers or arms now that he is new and wavering? Weak we have been to tolerate thirty and forty years of service; to find ourselves old and mangled by wounds; and even being discharged brings no relief, since we are kept under the standards <note>original: "sub vexillis" — refers to veterans who were technically discharged but kept in a reserve unit, often suffering the same hardships as active soldiers</note>, and suffer the same hardships under another name. And if any survive so many misfortunes, they drag us to distant lands and give us, in the name of estates, swamps and "cricket-fields."² Truly, this trade of ours is troubled and meager! Ten *asses* <term>As: a bronze Roman coin. At this time, it took 10 or 16 asses to make one silver denarius.</term> a day is what our souls and bodies are worth! With these we must buy food, clothing, arms, tents, and pay for mercy from the centurions and a bit of respite.³ Eternal are the beatings, the wounds, the harsh winters, the distressing⁴ summers, atrocious war, and wretched peace. We must unburden ourselves with clear terms: that every day we receive a full denarius;⁵ that service last sixteen years; that this limit not be exceeded; that we are not kept under the standards; and that the discharge bonus be counted out in cash⁶ right there on the field.⁷ Do the guardsmen <note>The Praetorian Guard stationed in Rome, who enjoyed higher pay and shorter service.</note>, who get two denarii and return home after sixteen years, face more danger than we? We do not mock the city garrisons; yet we live among fierce peoples, and from our tents, we see the enemy face to face."

**XVIII.** The soldiers were muttering and grew heated, showing their bruises,⁸ their gray hair, their worn clothes, and their naked bodies. And they fell into such a fury that they wanted to make one legion out of the three; but the pride of the name, as each man wanted to give his own legion's name to the new unit, ruined the plan.

---

¹ *rimedirci*: to redeem or rescue ourselves. The Nestiana edition reads *rimediarci* (to remedy): an error that passed into the Cominiana and all others, although the Nestiana corrected it in its extensive *Errata*.

² *grillaie*: a word still used in the Tuscan countryside to signify arid, stony, and infertile lands <note>Literally "cricket-fields," places where only crickets could live.</note>.

³ *risquitto*: rest, a breathing spell from toil, a holiday. The Latin text has "vacationes munerum" (exemptions from duties). On the origin and meaning of this word, see Salvini, *Academic Discourses*, vol. VIII, discourse 8, Venice edition 1834.

⁴ *rangolose*: troublesome, distressing, or full of toil. Latin: "exercitas" (laborious).

⁵ *un denaio intero* (a full denarius). The value of a denarius for military pay was raised from ten *asses* to sixteen. Yet the soldiers were still receiving the usual ten *asses* as if it were a full denarius; they were essentially receiving only five-eighths of a denarius for buying goods that had risen in price proportionally.

⁶ *ci si snoccioli di contanti* (be counted out in cash). Such proverbial and idiomatic phrases, placed in the mouths of agitated, lower-class people, are very fitting and expressive: they put the matter before the eyes and make the scene present. <meta>· i.</meta>

⁷ *in su’ l bello del campo*. From the Marescottiana edition. Others say *in sul bel*, which means "in the middle of the field" or "right there on the spot."

⁸ *i lividi* (the bruises). The Latin: "verberum notas" (the marks of lashes).

...punishment, how did those beastly burdens <note>original: *pesi*</note> and long marches appear to him? For Rufus, having been for a long time a common soldier <note>original: *fantaccino*; Latin: *manipularis*</note>, then a centurion, and later camp prefect, renewed the harsh military discipline of old: he never ceased from labors and toils and, having endured them himself, he was all the more cruel.

**XXI.** Upon their return, the sedition flourished again; breaking ranks, they plundered the surrounding countryside. Blaesus, still obeyed by the captains and the more disciplined soldiers, in order to strike terror into the others, ordered that some who were most heavily laden with loot be whipped and imprisoned. They allowed themselves to be dragged away, embracing the knees of those standing by, calling them by name, crying out: "I am so-and-so, of such-and-such century, cohort, or legion: the same will be done to you!" They cast every insult at the legate <note>The commanding officer, Blaesus.</note>, invoked heaven and the gods, and did everything possible to provoke hatred, mercy, anger, and fear. Everyone rushed forward; they broke open the prisons, unshackling and mingling among themselves the swindlers and those sentenced to death. This rekindled the rage of the mob and brought many new leaders to light.

**XXII.** A certain Vibulenus, a common soldier <note>literally "a soldier of the dozen," meaning one of no special rank</note>, stood before the tribunal of Blaesus. Lifted upon the shoulders of several others, he drew a crowd and said: "You have done well to restore life to these innocent wretches; but who will restore it to my brother? Who restores my brother to me? The army of Germany sent him to you for our common benefit, and this man has had him slaughtered tonight..."

<note>³ *fantaccino* (infantryman). The Latin is: "*manipularis*."</note>

From this, Secretary Curzio Picchena, an excellent scholar of Tacitus, drew an ingenious correction: *vetus operis* <note>Latin: practiced or experienced in work</note> (later noted by Lipsius in his *second thoughts*), a phrasing typical of this author, such as *vetus regnandi* <note>old hand at ruling</note>, *scientiae* <note>experienced in knowledge</note>, *ceremoniarum* <note>practiced in ceremonies</note>, and others; for it is much easier for a scribe to have erred by writing *intus* instead of *vetus* than for *invictus*. (*) It seems to me that I have expressed the essence of both words: because *vetus operis* means practical, veteran, or accustomed—"A mind accustomed to profound questions" <note>A reference to Dante, *Inferno* X, 18</note>—and *invictus* means one who was never seen to be weary.</note>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the mutiny in Pannonia following the death of Augustus. The agitator Vibulenus is in the middle of a fabricated, highly emotional speech accusing the commander Blaesus of murdering his brother to suppress the soldiers' demands.</meta>

<page-num>22</page-num>

...slaughtered by his henchmen, whom he keeps and arms to kill soldiers. Answer me, Blaesus, where have you thrown the body? Even enemies do not deny burial. Let me kiss it, bathe it with tears, vent my grief, and then slaughter me as well, provided these men bury us after we are killed—not for any crime, but for seeking the benefit of the legions."

**XXIII.** He helped his words with weeping, striking his face and chest with his hands. Having pushed aside those who were supporting him, he fell; and, rolling at the people's feet, he stirred up <gloss>1</gloss> so much fury and hatred that the soldiers rushed off—some to bind the henchmen and the rest of Blaesus' household, others to search for the body. If it had not soon been revealed that no dead body could be found, that the prisoners did not confess to any killing, and that the man had never even had a brother, they were moments away from killing the legate <note>The commanding officer, Blaesus.</note>. They drove away the tribunes and the camp prefect, whose baggage they seized during the flight; and there died Lucilius the centurion, nicknamed in soldierly jest "Bring-another" <note>Original: *Quallaltra*; Latin: *Cedo Alteram*</note>, because when he had broken one vine-staff <gloss>2</gloss> over a soldier's back, he would shout, "Bring another!" and then, "Bring another!" The other officers were hidden away, with only Clementius Julius being held back, because he was considered an effective messenger for the soldiers' demands due to his quick wit. The eighth and fifteenth legions were even on the verge of a skirmish—the former demanding the centurion Sirpicus so they might kill him, the latter protecting him—had the ninth legion not intervened with pleas and, when those failed to work, with threats.

**XXIV.** These reports moved Tiberius who, though hiding his great displeasure and feigning indifference, sent his son Drusus there with the leading men of the city and two reinforced cohorts of the guard <note>The Praetorian Guard, the elite unit protecting the Emperor and Rome.</note>, with no other instructions than to act as he saw <gloss>3</gloss> necessary for the situation. He added a large part of the cavalry <gloss>4</gloss> of the guard, along with the core of the Germans <gloss>5</gloss>, who at that time served as the personal bodyguard.

<note>The following notes were restored based on the Florentine printing by Marescotti and the Latin text which reads "he [Blaesus] throttled him last night."</note>

1 * *stirred up.* Thus in the Marescotti edition; others say *put.*
2 * *one vine-staff.* Grave crimes were punished by the hand of the lictor with the axe and the rods; lighter offenses were punished with a vine-staff <note>The *vitis*, a staff made of grapevine, was the symbol of the centurion's authority.</note> by the hand of the centurion. As Pliny says: "The vine honors the punishments." Book XIV, chapter I, at the end.
3 * *saw.* The Marescotti edition reads *wanted.*
4 * *cava'*, cavalry.
5 * *Germans.* After the defeat of Varus <note>The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, where three Roman legions were destroyed.</note>, Augustus became suspicious of this nation, which had been a very faithful bodyguard; Tiberius reinstated them.

**XXV.** When he was within the ramparts, they placed guards at the gates and armed men at the posts, while the rest surrounded the tribunal in great numbers. Drusus stood upright and with his hand requested silence <note>The translator notes a parallel here to Dante's *Purgatorio*, Canto VIII: "...who asked for listening with his hand."</note>. When the soldiers turned their eyes toward their own multitude, they raised a savage roar; but when they looked at Caesar <note>Referring here to Drusus, who held the title of Caesar.</note>, they turned pale <note>original: *allibbivano*, meaning they were stunned or paralyzed with fear.</note>. An unintelligible whispering, a harsh screeching, and then a sudden silence—these conflicting movements of the soul showed them to be either trembling with fear or terrifying to behold. Once the tumult subsided, Drusus read his father’s letter, which stated: "Those strongest legions, with whom he had endured so many wars, were closest to his heart; once his mind had rested from its grief <note>Tiberius was officially in mourning for the late Emperor Augustus.</note>, he would discuss their demands with the Fathers <note>The Senate.</note>. In the meantime, he was sending his son to console them as much as was then possible. The rest was reserved for the Senate, as the right to grant favors or dispense punishments could not be taken from them."

**XXVI.** The crowd replied that Clemens the centurion would set forth their mind. He spoke of discharge after sixteen years of service; of the retirement bonus; of the pay being one denarius a day; and of not being held under the banners as veterans <note>Soldiers were often kept in service as "reserves" even after their official discharge date, a major point of contention.</note>. Anyone is permitted to scourge and kill us! Tiberius used to make the legions' desires vanish into smoke by citing Augustus; now Drusus comes with the same trickery <note>original: *ragia*, literally "resin," but used here idiomatically to mean a sticky trap, fraud, or deceit.</note>. **XXVII.** They leave the assembly: every soldier on guard or friend of Caesar [Drusus] whom they encounter, they strike in the face with their fists to provoke quarrels, seeking an excuse to take up arms. They were most hostile <note>original: *niquitissimi*, meaning extremely wicked or spiteful.</note> toward Gnaeus Lentulus, who was believed more than the others—owing to his age and military glory—to be advising Drusus and to abhor such military disorder. To ruin the benefits of the legions even there! » They attack him with stones, and he was already bloodied and near death, if Drusus's men had not come to his rescue.

**XXVIII.** That night threatened great evil, which fate then softened. The moon—the sky becoming almost brighter than she was—seemed to fade. <note>original: *Nam luna clariore paene caelo visa languescere* ("For the moon, in a sky that was almost brighter, seemed to grow faint"). This follows the common text without alteration. When the sky becomes luminous for some reason, everyone knows that the stars lose their brilliance. It sometimes happens at night that terrestrial exhalations or similar matter, rising above the cone of the earth's shadow and being illuminated by the sun, create a sort of nocturnal dawn, especially in northern regions. For this reason, some have called them "aurora borealis," which, by whitening the sky, causes the moon to lose its beautiful color. Pliny the Elder also attests to this in his second book, chapter 33: "Light from the sky was seen at night during the consulship of C. Caecilius and Gn. Papirius, and often at other times, so that a likeness of day shone at night." The demonstration of this phenomenon was observed and taught in modern times by Mr. Galileo Galilei, who reports having happened upon a night in Venice where, two hours after sunset, the entire sky brightened—particularly toward the North and Northeast—to such an extent that all the stars vanished. Even though the brightness was great, the shadows of the buildings were so washed out that they were hardly distinguishable. This derived from the immensity of the space from which the light came. The Orelli text reads: "for the moon, in a suddenly clear sky, seemed to grow faint."</note> The soldiers, who did not know the scientific reason for it, took it as an omen for themselves, believing the planet was failing because of their current hardships, and that their rebellion would turn out well if the goddess <note>The Moon, often associated with the goddess Diana or Luna.</note> shone bright again. They therefore took up trumpets, cymbals, and horns; according as she became clearer or darker, they were joyful or sad—

Stung by these words and becoming suspicious of one another, they separated the veterans from the recruits, and one legion from another. The desire to obey returned; they left the gates and carried the ill-assembled standards back to their proper places.

**XXIX.** The following morning, Drusus called an assembly. With a natural generosity and without calculated art, he blamed their former actions and praised their present ones, declaring that threats had no power over him. If they would be wise and ask for mercy, he would write to his father to be appeased and to hear the prayers of his legions. At their request, they sent to Tiberius the same Blaesus as before, along with Lucius Apronius, a Roman knight of Drusus’s cohort, and Justus Catonius, a centurion of the first rank. It began with the twenty-first <gloss>1</gloss> and fifth legions, who drew the first and twentieth along with them; they were all stationed together at the borders of the Ubii <note>A Germanic tribe allied with Rome, located near modern-day Cologne</note>, and had been little or not at all burdened by labor. **XXXVI.** There, a council was held, it being understood¹ "that they were sending messengers to the army further up the river to draw them to their side; they intended to raze the land of the Ubii <note>A Germanic tribe allied with Rome, living near modern-day Cologne.</note> and, enriched by the spoils, break into the Gallic provinces to plunder." May I be forgiven here. That man Muzio <note>Girolamo Muzio (1496–1576), a scholar who criticized the Florentine dialect in favor of a more courtly Italian.</note> who came from Capodistria to Florence to speak and write of this homeland villainously, and to teach us to speak with the whip of his pedantic *Battaglie* in hand, would scoff at this "Florentinism" (for so he calls our linguistic properties with his clumsy barbarism), and would criticize it thus: *They urged him to wound himself*. We already knew that: but that act of placing the scene before one's eyes is a great virtue of speech; for which Dante, who was more than the *lamp of the world*, used it with reason in his poem, which is not merely grave but sacred. And let those speak who, amidst so many eternal beauties, call it unworthy. Of what sort and what are the low points of Homer? To call Juno *Ox-eyed*, or Minerva *Owl-eyed*, is nothing. Our Tacitus, so severe, let himself go to depict the imprudence of Cotta Messalinus with that *My little Tiberius* <note>original: *Tiberiolus meus*</note>. To others, it did not seem an indignity of history to recount that the Emperor Domitian used to impale flies on pins; or that Commodus gulped down wine in the theater while the people shouted *Bravo, Bravo!* <note>original: *Pro', pro'*</note> and he shot arrows at them as if he were Hercules against the Stymphalian birds. And he held an ostrich head raised in his left hand, and the bloody sword in his right, and shaking his fierce head, he wanted everyone to be terrified: wherefore some who could not hold back their laughter ate leaves from their laurel wreaths to induce vomiting and appear to be laughing from the sickness: or that the army of Severus in Arabia, with parched mouths, could not utter <note>original: *spiccicare*</note> any other word than *water, water*: or that Geta threw himself at Julia’s neck crying *Mama, mama*. If, therefore, such men, to powerfully represent reality, descend to such "low" things, I may well err with them, and here say *Thrust, thrust* <note>original: *Ficca, ficca*</note>: which responds to that act of thrusting the dagger into the breast, mentioned just above. (**)

**XXXVII.** The soldiers realized this was merely a meal to keep them occupied <note>A stalling tactic</note> and demanded immediate fulfillment. She had been reluctant, reminding him that she was the granddaughter of Augustus and did not shrink from danger, but he eventually convinced her. A miserable procession of women moved away: the wife of the general fleeing with her little son in her arms, surrounded by the weeping wives of his dear friends who followed her, and no less grief among those who remained behind <margin>A dispute over the text</margin> <note>The translator follows a suggestion by the scholar Lipsius ("quæ manebant"), interpreting this as the women staying behind; however, the Medicean Codex suggests it refers to Germanicus and his friends who remained, now separated from their families</note>.
