<meta>This page consists of scholarly annotations and philological notes regarding the previous passage of Tacitus's *Annals*, specifically focusing on the mutiny of the Rhine legions and Germanicus’s intervention. These notes compare various Italian translations and explain the linguistic choices made by the translator.</meta>

1 * **dismembered**. <note>original: "smembrato"</note> The Germans still use the practice today of making soldiers deserving of death "pass through the pikes." <note>This refers to the "running the gauntlet" punishment, where a soldier ran between two rows of comrades who struck him with weapons.</note>

2 * **the rage remained among the dogs**. <note>original: "la rabbia rimaneva tra' cani"</note> The Latin has: "*penes eosdem saevitia et invidia erat.*" <note>Latin: "the cruelty and the hatred remained with those same men."</note> "The cruelty of this act and all the burden that would follow... remained among them." —Dati. <note>Carlo Dati (1619–1676), an Italian philologist and scientist.</note> "The cruel act and the hatred were theirs." —Politi. <note>Adriano Politi (1542–1625), known for his 1604 translation of Tacitus.</note> "Upon themselves the atrocity of the act and the burden fell." —Valeriani. <note>A referance to another contemporary translator.</note> "With them remained the cruelty and hatred of the [act]." —Unpublished 16th-century translation; a manuscript in my possession. While all these are more "noble" in style, none have more effectiveness than Our Author. <note>“Our Author” likely refers to Bernardo Davanzati (1529–1606), whose translation is celebrated for its concise, idiomatic, and vigorous Italian.</note>

3 * **bull-enraged**. <note>original: "intorati"</note> Just as from "serpent" one forms *serpent-like* and *to serpentize*, used several times by Our Author; and from "viper," *envenomed*; from "dog," *dogged* <note>original: "accanito"</note>; from "hawk," *to become hawk-like*; and (as in Dante, *Paradiso* XV, 115) from "dragon," *to become dragon-like* <note>original: "indracarsi"; to have the spirit of a dragon</note>; so from "bull" Our Author forms <term>intorato: to be burning with a grim and deep anger, such as is usually imagined of a bull.</term> The Crusca <note>The Accademia della Crusca, the primary authority on the Italian language.</note> includes this word using this very example. The Latin says: "*trucibus adhuc.*" <note>Latin: "still grim-looking."</note>

4 * **at the Old Places**. <note>original: "alle Vecchie"</note> Latin: "*Vetera,*" meaning *castra* <note>Latin: "camp."</note>, which Valeriani calls Old Camp; today it is Vettera, or rather, according to others, Xanten in the Duchy of Cleves. <note>Castra Vetera was a major Roman legionary base on the Rhine frontier.</note>

5 * **to rise up**. <note>original: "levare in capo"</note> See note 7 on page 31 above.

6 * **to regret, to repent, repentance**. <note>original: "pentere, pentire, pentimento"</note>

## XLVI. 
All of Rome, hearing of the movement in Germany before the unrest in Illyria had even settled, was thrown into a state of turmoil. They began to "tear Tiberius to pieces,"<note>An Italian idiom meaning to criticize someone harshly or tear their reputation apart; see note 2.</note> complaining that while he mocked the weak senators<note>The "fathers" refers to the Roman Senators.</note> and the unarmed commoners with his "song" of refusing the throne, the armies were meanwhile in open rebellion. They believed he was trying to correct them with "two tender whips of two boys."<note>Referring to his sons, Drusus and Germanicus, whose authority was not yet mature; see note 3.</note>

> “He should have gone in person,” they said, “and shown himself with imperial majesty; they would have yielded at the sight of a prince who is supremely experienced, strict, and generous with rewards. Augustus, even when old and exhausted, was able to go to Germany so many times; this man, fresh and capable, sits in the senate nitpicking the words of the fathers. The city is already so bridled that he could well go and 'give food'<note>To "give food" here means to stall or appease with empty words; see note 5.</note> to the military spirits, to keep them in check at the first sign of movement.”

## XLVII. 
Against such talk, Tiberius became even more obstinate in his refusal, unwilling to leave the head of the empire and risk both himself and the state. Many conflicting concerns troubled him: 

> “The army in Germany is more powerful, but the one in Pannonia is closer; the former is strengthened by the Gauls, the latter sits over Italy. To which one should I go? ¹ *unwilling; that is, in the event they were not willing, etc.*

It is exactly the Latin "aliquem proscindere" <note>Latin: to cut someone down/criticize publicly</note>. However, the text of Tacitus says: "incusare Tiberium" <note>Latin: to blame or accuse Tiberius</note>. See also Annals III, 59; XIV, 186.*

³ *with two tender whips of two boys; that is, with the not yet mature authority of two youths. Latin: "duorum adolescentium nondum adulta auctoritate" <note>Latin: by the not-yet-adult authority of two youths</note>. Just as a staff is taken as a sign of authority and command, so Davanzati <note>Bernardo Davanzati (1529–1606), the translator known for his concise style</note>, needing to express a childish authority here, takes the metaphor not from a staff, but from a "scuriscio" <note>a small leather whip</note> which is a thing for children.*

## XLVIII.
Germanicus was with the army, ready to punish the rebels: nonetheless, to give them more time to come to their senses through a recent example, he wrote to Caecina, who was coming [with a powerful force]: "Unless they have punished the scoundrels, the sword will turn in a circle."³ <note>original: "girerà la spada a tondo"; an idiom meaning he would order an indiscriminate massacre of the entire camp.</note> Caecina showed the letter secretly to the standard-bearers and the most loyal men, begging them to free everyone from infamy and themselves from death, which in peace is given to those who deserve it, but in war, both the good and the guilty die [together]. > "...what is unusual is wonderful to the multitude. Pennyroyal <note>A common Mediterranean herb.</note> among the Indians is more expensive than pepper. Everything common becomes cheap through [abundance]. Even the best things are despised when they are not rare; [and when they are] very familiar, because they are always ready, they lose reverence. For [this] reason, the best prophet is not accepted in his own country. And the host's wine pleases more, though diluted and expensive, than the pure [wine] from home." (*)

¹ *as if he were about to depart.* Tiberius never wanted to leave [Rome], and every year he made a show of wanting to visit the armies and provinces. Putting things in order, he would move, stop, and turn back quickly as a rooster does; hence they called him "Chicken-foot." <note>original: "Gallopiè"; a mocking nickname combining "Gallo" (rooster) and "piè" (foot).</note>

## XLIX.
In all the civil wars that were ever seen, no such thing was ever witnessed; to emerge not for battle, not from an enemy host, but from the same beds where they had eaten together by day and slept by night; to divide into factions and strike blows at one another. Here were screams, wounds, and visible blood, but the cause was hidden; chance played its part, and even some good men perished. Once it was seen who was being targeted,³ even the worst men took up arms. Neither legate nor tribune said, "No more," but left them to punish and sate one another. Germanicus entered the camp, and calling it not a cure but a slaughter with many tears, ordered the bodies to be burned. In those still-frenzied minds, a mania grew to attack the enemy—a true purgation, they said, of their madness; they believed the souls of their dead companions could not be appeased unless they received glorious wounds in their own impious breasts. Caesar <note>Germanicus</note>, favoring their zeal, built a bridge and crossed twelve thousand of our native infantry, twenty-six cohorts of auxiliaries, and eight squadrons of cavalry, who had remained most disciplined during those disturbances.

## L.
Not far off, the Germans were jubilant, seeing us first entangled in the mourning for Augustus,⁴ then in our own discords. But the Romans, crossing the Caesian forest <note>likely the modern-day Arnsberger Wald</note> with long strides, camped on the frontier⁵ started by Tiberius. They fortified the front and rear with a palisade and the flanks with felled trees. From there they passed through the dark forest and debated which of two paths to take: the short and common one, or the obstructed...

...into a proverb. Moreover, I may well use such an anachronism since even Titus Livius <note>Livy</note> used it, having someone in his second book complain of being held for debt in a harsh prison called an *Ergastulum* <note>a Roman work-house or private prison for slaves</note>, a term used in Livy's time but not in the time of that prisoner. See Lipsius in *Eletti*, Book 2, Chapter 15. (*)

**1 \*** *why.* This "why" does not truly capture Tacitus's full meaning, which says: <note>original: "nullo... noscente quod cædis initium, quis finis"</note> "no one knowing what the beginning of the slaughter was, or what the end."

**2 \*** *beds, where... eaten.* Regarding how the Romans ate on couches and the arrangement of their dining rooms <note>triclini</note>, see Agostini, Messer Fulvio, Lipsius, and other modern scholars.

**3 \*** *seen who was being targeted;* that is, when the wicked saw that they themselves were the ones marked for death, they too took up arms, and thus even some of the good men were killed in the chaos.

**4 \*** *the holidays of Augustus;* that is, during the mourning period for the death of Augustus.

**5 \*** *frontier* <note>original: "termine"</note> was an embankment that, in the absence of other natural limits, marked the border of the empire and served to face the barbarians. It was not only started but completed by Tiberius; since the "begun" <note>original: "cæptum"</note> in the text is equivalent to "made" <note>original: "factum"</note>.

**(*)** A *Sicilian Vespers*, <note>original: "un vespro siciliano"</note> meaning a general massacre, such as the one against the French in Sicily on March 30, 1282. Although Davanzati <note>the 16th-century translator</note> in the above note, and after him Cesari, strive to justify such anachronisms in translating the ancients, they can never save themselves from being seen as ridiculous.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

...and neglected and therefore not watched by the enemies. They took the long way by hastening through the remaining distance, for the scouts reported that the Germans were celebrating a solemn festival that night with banquets and games. Caecina was sent ahead with light-armed troops to clear the forest path; the legions followed close behind, aided by the clear night sky. Reaching the villages of the Marsi <note>a Germanic tribe located between the Rhine and Lippe rivers</note>, they surrounded the outposts, finding the people scattered in their beds or at their tables, carefree, without sentinels or military order—idling in a drunken, foolish peace.

## LI.
Caesar <note>Germanicus Caesar</note>, so that the greedy legions could plunder more land, divided them into four columns;¹ they put everything within fifty miles to sword and fire. No regard was shown for sex, age, sacred or profane things, and Tanfana, their most famous temple, was desolated. None of our men were wounded, having cut the enemy down like sheep while they were drowsy, unarmed, and disorganized. At such a slaughter, the Bructeri, Tubanti, and Usipeti <note>neighboring Germanic tribes</note> rose up and took to the woods through which the army had to return. Having been informed of this, the commander marched in battle formation: part of the cavalry with the auxiliary infantry in front; the First Legion followed; on the left, with the baggage in the middle, the Twenty-First; on the right, the Fifth; and the Twentieth at the rear; the rest of the allies at the tail. The enemies stayed still and let them enter the woods; then, having harassed the front and flanks, they ran with all their force to the tail, and with tight groups, they began to break the light infantry. Then Caesar spurred toward the men of the Twentieth and cried: "Now is the time to wipe out the memory of the mutiny: come on, turn your guilt into glory!" They threw themselves fiercely at the enemy, who was immediately broken, pushed into the open, and slaughtered. The vanguard suddenly emerged from the wood and fortified itself. The journey then became quiet, and the soldiers, confident in these last actions and having forgotten the first <note>referring to their recent mutiny</note>, were returned to their winter quarters.

## LII.
These reports gave Tiberius both joy and anxiety. He rejoiced that the mutiny was extinguished, but the fact that Germanicus, by squandering² money and granting furloughs, had procured the favor of the soldiers—and his great military glory—pierced him. Yet, in his heart...

### LIII.
In that same year, Julia died. She had been confined for her indecencies by her father Augustus on the island of Pandateria, and then at Reggio on the strait of the Sicilian sea. She had been the wife of Tiberius while Gaius and Lucius Caesar were living, and she looked down on him² as beneath her: this was the most intimate reason for his retreat to Rhodes. Once he became emperor, he saw her banished and shamed; and after Agrippa Postumus was killed, she fell into utter despair. He let her rot in long suffering, for it seemed to him³ that he could hide⁴ her murder by keeping her alive for so long⁵.

He used similar cruelty for the same reason against Sempronius Gracchus, a man of a great house, a dexterous mind, and a harmful eloquence. He had slept with the said Julia when she was the wife of Agrippa; and after she became Tiberius's wife, this persistent adulterer incited her to disobey and rage against her husband. It was believed that the venomous letters she wrote to her father Augustus against Tiberius were dictated by him. Having been held in Cercina,⁶ an island in the African sea, for fourteen years, he was then found by assassins at a sea lookout, where he was expecting dire news. Having obtained time to write his final wishes to his wife Alliaria, he offered his head: in his constant manner of dying, he was not unworthy of the name Sempronius, a name he had stained in living. <meta>This page continues the military narrative of Germanicus’s campaign against the Germanic tribes, following the civil and political updates in Rome. Having established a fort upon the ruins <gloss>1</gloss> of a stronghold built by his father on Mount **Taunus**, he led his light-armed army swiftly into the territory of the **Chatti** via dry paths and low riverbeds; for that year (a miracle in that country) it did not rain. And because he expected the weather to turn on the return journey, he left **L. Apronius** to repair roads and bridges. He reached the **Chatti** so suddenly that he captured or killed all those who were weak due to age or sex. The young men swam across the **Adrana** <note>the modern Eder River</note> and prevented the **Romani** from building a bridge. Driven back by siege engines and arrows, they sought a peace treaty in vain. Some fled to **Germanico**; the others, abandoning their hamlets and villages, scattered through the forests. **Caesar** <note>Germanicus is often referred to by the title Caesar</note> burned **Mattium**, their capital, plundered the countryside, and withdrew toward the **Rhine**, without the enemy harrying his rear—as they usually do when they retreat out of cunning rather than fear. The **Cherusci** wished to help the **Chatti**, but **Caecina** terrified them with sudden raids here and there; and he defeated and drove back the **Marsi**, who had dared to attack.

**LVII.** Ambassadors soon arrived from **Segestes** to ask for help against his own people, <gloss>2</gloss> who were besieging him. They valued **Arminius**—who counseled war—more highly, for those barbarians consider the boldest to be the most noble and the most reliable leaders in times of trouble. With these ambassadors came **Segimundus**, son of **Segestes**, though with a heavy heart; for in the year the **Germanies** revolted, having been made a priest at the altar of the **Ubii**, he tore off his sacred fillets and fled to the rebels. But because his father told him to hope in Roman clemency, he obeyed; he was received kindly and sent with a guard to the bank of **Gaul**. It was advantageous for **Germanico** to turn back; he broke the siege and rescued **Segestes** along with many relatives, followers, and noblewomen. Among them was the wife of **Arminius**, the daughter of **Segestes**,<gloss>3</gloss> who sided not with her father but with her husband; though defeated, she did not weep nor beg for mercy, but with her hands clasped to her chest, she stared down at her pregnant womb. They carried the spoils from the defeat of **Varus**, which had already been given as plunder to many of—

### LVIII.
“This is not the first day that I have shown firm faith toward the Roman people. Since the divine Augustus <note>Emperor Augustus, who had granted Segestes Roman citizenship</note> made me a citizen, I have chosen neither friend nor enemy except for your benefit; I do this not out of hatred for my homeland—for traitors are displeasing even to those they serve <gloss>1</gloss>—but because I believe peace to be useful for both you and us, and I have always loved peace more than war. For this reason, I accused Arminius—who stole my daughter from me and broke his treaty with you—before **Varus**, your late commander. Delayed by his slowness, <gloss>2</gloss> and hoping for little from the legal path, I urged him to seize Arminius, the other conspirators, and myself. That night passed <gloss>3</gloss>—would that it had been my last! What followed I can only mourn rather than defend: I put Arminius in chains, but I have also suffered them from his faction. Now, since you have finally given me the opportunity, I resume my ancient loyalty and desire a state of quiet—not for my own profit, but to clear myself of the charge of treachery <gloss>4</gloss>; and also because I might be a good mediator to reconcile you with the Germanic people, should they choose to repent rather than face destruction. For the youthful error of my son, I beg your pardon; as for my daughter, she is here by force, I confess. But consider which carries more weight: her being pregnant <gloss>5</gloss> by Arminius, or being born of me.” **Caesar** [Germanicus]...

<gloss>5</gloss> **Pregnant.** *Incientes*, from *cieo cies* [to stir or move], was the term ancient Romans used for women when they were in labor. Our writers generally used *incinte* for pregnant women. *Rincinga*, says Master Aldobrandino, refers to a pregnant woman [loosening her belt] when the child is killed. Joachim Perionius derives this word from the Greek <unclear>κύειν</unclear> <note>kyein, meaning "to conceive"</note>. This is a noble and generous word, one of those that have been overwhelmed and almost choked out, like fine herbs, by the many new or foreign words brought in by trade and the court.

LIX. The news of Segestes surrendering and being welcomed with kindness brought either hope or grief to those who fled from or hungered for war. Arminius, violent by nature, now seeing his wife taken from him and his child a slave even before being born, ran distracted here and there through the lands of the Cherusci <note>A Germanic tribe located in the northern plains of Germany</note>, calling for arms against Caesar <note>Referring to Germanicus</note>, and arms against Segestes. > “A brave father, a great emperor, a powerful army—what a conquest they have made with so many men over one meager woman! I myself struck down three legions and three commanders; I do not wage war with treachery nor against pregnant women, but face-to-face with horsemen and armed men. One can still see the Roman standards in the Germanic woods, which I hung there as offerings to our gods. Let Segestes remain on that conquered shore of his; let him restore the priestly bands to his son <note>Segestes’ son, Segimundus, had been a priest at the Roman altar at Cologne before joining the rebellion</note>. There is no German who will forgive him for allowing the rods, the axes, and the toga to be seen between the Elbe and the Rhine. <note>original: "verghe, scuri e toga" — These were symbols of Roman legal authority and the lictors who carried out punishments.</note> Other nations that do not know the Roman Empire have not experienced their tortures and know nothing of taxes. Now that we have shaken them off, and sent back that deified Augustus <note>original: "indiato Agusto"</note> and that chosen Tiberius in shame, let us not fear a mere fledgling youth or a scavenged army. If your homeland, your blood, and your ancient rites are dearer to you than masters and new colonies, then follow Arminius to glory and liberty, rather than Segestes to foul servitude.”

LX. Such goading stirred not only the Cherusci but the neighboring tribes as well, drawing in Inguiomerus, Arminius’s paternal uncle, who had long held great authority among the Romans. Because of this, Caesar became more apprehensive. To avoid the brunt of the entire war falling on one point, he sent Caecina with forty Roman cohorts through the territory of the Bructeri to the river Ems <note>original: "Amisia"</note> to keep the enemy forces divided. Therefore, a desire came upon Caesar <note>Referring to Germanicus, who had been adopted into the Caesarian line</note> to bury them: the entire army there mourned their relatives, their friends, the disasters of war, and the human lot. He sent Caecina to scout deep into the woods and to build bridges and embankments <note>original: "ghiaiate." The Latin source uses "aggeres," referring to earthworks or causeways built to provide passage through marshes</note> over the swamps and mires. They moved through those sorrowful places, a grim sight and a bitter memory. Varus's first camp was recognizable by its wide circumference and the layout of the <term>principia</term> <note>The administrative and religious heart of a Roman military camp</note> designed for three legions. Furthermore, from the ruined rampart and the shallow ditch, it was evident where the broken remnants of the army had taken shelter. Across the field, bones lay whitening, either piled in heaps or scattered, depending on whether the men had fled or stood their ground. On the ground lay pieces of weapons and the limbs of horses, while human heads were nailed to the trunks of trees. In the nearby groves were horrific altars where the Germanic tribes had sacrificed the tribunes and the senior centurions. The survivors of the defeat or of captivity recounted:

> “Here the legates fell, here the eagles were seized, there Varus received his first wound, and over there he ended his life by his own unlucky right hand. From that platform Arminius harangued his men; look at how many crosses and pits were prepared for the prisoners—and how the proud man mocked our eagles and standards!”

LXII. And so, in the sixth year after the defeat <note>The defeat occurred in September of 762 AUC (9 AD); this burial took place in the spring of 768 AUC (15 AD)</note>, the Roman army buried the bones of the three legions. No one could tell whose remains they were; they covered them all as if they were relatives and kin, their hearts filled with increasing anger and grief. Caesar threw the first sod of earth for the...

...tomb, a most grateful act of piety toward the dead, and a bond of brotherhood in sorrow for the living. **LXIII.** As Arminius <note>The leader of the Germanic tribes</note> retreated through difficult paths, Germanicus followed him and, as soon as he could, pushed his cavalry to drive him from a plain where he had positioned himself. Arminius, having ordered his men to close ranks and draw near the woods, suddenly turned his face and, giving the signal, his hidden ambush jumped out. This new battle broke the cavalry; infantry were sent to help them but, swept away by the fleeing men, they only increased the panic: and they were being pushed¹ into a swamp familiar to the victors but treacherous for our men, if Caesar <note>Referring to Germanicus</note> had not presented himself with the legions. This struck terror into the enemy and gave courage to our men, and both sides withdrew with equal standing. Then, having led the army back to the Amisia <note>The Ems River</note>, he took the legions back by water as they had come, and part of the cavalry went to the Rhine along the ocean shore. Caecina, who was returning with his men by the usual route, was ordered to clear the path via the *Long Bridges* <note>original: "Pontilunghi," referring to the *Pontes Longi*, a narrow causeway built through the marshes</note>. This is a path that Lucius Domitius built over wide marshes and mires, through thick, clinging mud or bottomless streams, surrounded by gentle wooded hills. Arminius filled these hills with his people, having hurried ahead by shortcuts to reach the place before our men, who were burdened with arms and baggage. In order to repair the bridges broken by time and to keep the enemy at a distance, Caecina set up camp there, with some men fighting and some working.

**LXIV.** The barbarians, to force the guards and reach those working on the bridges, harassed² them, encircled them, and confronted them. The air was filled with the shouting of both the workers and the combatants,³ and everything was stacked against the Romans: deep mud, soft or slippery ground, and bodies heavy with breastplates; nor could they throw their spears while standing in the water. In contrast, the Cherusci <note>A Germanic tribe</note> were practiced in fighting in swamps, having tall statures and long spears to strike from a distance. Night finally drew back...

...bucked or lashed out with their heels, unhorsing men, scattering those nearby, and trampling those who had fallen. There was great toil around the eagles <note>The sacred golden eagle standards of the Roman legions, which were considered holy</note>, which could neither be carried forward against the shower of spears nor planted in the water-soaked ground. While sustaining the battle, Caecina had his horse killed beneath him; he fell and was nearly taken prisoner,$^1$* had the first legion not come to his aid. The greed of the enemies, who stopped killing to start looting, helped the Romans: for in the meantime the legions exerted themselves so much$^2$* that by evening they reached open and solid ground. Nor did their troubles end there: it was necessary to build palisades and embankments, to dig and to cut wood, yet a great part of their tools were lost; there was no medicine to treat the wounded, and no tents for the soldiers. They shared food fouled by mud or blood, lamenting that fateful night and fearing that so many thousands of people had only one day left to live.

**LXVI.** A horse, having broken its halter and frightened by the shouting, ran off and knocked some people down. This caused such a panic—the men thinking the Germani <note>The various Germanic tribes fighting the Romans</note> had entered the camp—that everyone ran to the gates, and especially to the decuman gate, which was opposite the enemy$^3$* and therefore safer for fleeing. Once Caecina found the fear to be groundless, but being unable to hold them back by his authority, nor by prayers, nor by force, he threw himself down across the threshold; thus, out of piety and a refusal to trample the body of their commander, the way was blocked. Soon, the tribunes and centurions clarified that the fear was false.

**LXVII.** Then, having gathered them in the *principia* <term>the central square or headquarters of a Roman camp</term> and commanded silence, he showed them the extreme danger they were in:
> "Only arms can save you, if used with wisdom; that means staying inside the trenches to give the enemy the courage to approach and storm—"

---

$^1$* **was a prisoner**, meaning he was on the verge of being made a prisoner.
$^2$* **so exerted themselves**, they worked and struggled to such a degree.
$^3$* **opposite the enemy**. Adriano Politi, in a letter to N. Sacchetti (*Letters, Venice, 1624, page 364*), accuses our author [Davanzati] of having misunderstood the Latin *aversa* [the rear gate] for *adversa* [the front gate facing the enemy]. But certainly Davanzati, by using "opposite the enemy," did not mean "across from" or "facing" the enemy (which would have been an error, because the gate facing the enemy was the *praetoria*), but rather on the side opposite to that which looks toward the enemy. And "opposite" in this sense is also recorded in the *Crusca* dictionary of Manuzzi <note>A famous dictionary of the Italian language</note>. Politi, to avoid the ambiguity, had to expand it like this: "at the main gate and most sheltered from the enemy." And even more so Dati: "which... is placed at the rear part of the fortification and further away from the enemies." Valeriani, rather than dragging himself through so many words, translated it just like our author: "opposite the enemy."

**LXX.** So that the fleet might sail more lightly through those shallow seas and rest more easily during the ebb tide, Germanicus disembarked the Second and Fourteenth legions, entrusting them to Publius Vitellius to lead them back by land. At first, the journey was dry or only lightly sprayed by the tide; but then the ocean swelled, forced by a northern wind and the equinox—as is its custom—and it scattered the ranks and swept them about. The ground vanished: sea, shore, and fields were all water; whether it was shallow or deep, firm ground or a pit, could not be discerned. Waves capsized them, whirlpools swallowed beasts and baggage; they stumbled over and collided with drowned bodies. The companies became mixed together, with water now at their chests, now at their throats; losing their footing, they were scattered and drowned. It did no good to shout or offer encouragement, because when the surge struck, whether one was weak or brave, novice or experienced, luck or wisdom were worth the same,² as that great violence turned everything into a chaotic mess. Vitellius, exerting all his strength, pulled the army to high ground. They froze all night, without clothes to dry themselves, without fire, naked, broken, and in a worse state than if they were in the midst of enemies; for there, one can at least die with some glory, but here there was none. Daylight revealed the land, and they passed to the river Visurgis <note>The modern Weser River in Germany</note>, where there was...

...Germanicus having arrived with the fleet, he embarked those legions to rescue <note>The original Italian suggests "to make them [safe]"</note> those who had been considered drowned and never expected to be saved, until he was seen <note>The Italian translator notes that "sì" is used here to mean "until."</note> and the army was led back.

**LXXI.** Meanwhile, Stertinius, who had been sent to receive the surrender of Segimerus, the brother of Segestes, had led him and his son into the city of the Ubii <note>Modern-day Cologne.</note>. He pardoned Segimerus easily, but showed more restraint <note>The translator notes this means "with greater difficulty."</note> toward the young man, because he was said to have mocked the corpse of Varus <note>Publius Quinctilius Varus, the Roman general who lost three legions in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD.</note>. Gaul, Spain, and Italy competed to repair the damages suffered by the army, each offering weapons, horses, and gold, whichever was most ready at hand. Germanicus, having praised their readiness, accepted only the weapons and horses for the war; he aided the soldiers with his own money. To soothe the grim memory of the defeat with kindness, he visited the wounded, praised their prowess, and looked upon their wounds—winning them all over to himself and to the war, some with hope and others with glory, but all with his words and deeds.

**LXXII.** This year, the Senate honored Aulus Caecina, Lucius Apronius, and Gaius Silius with triumphal insignia <note>These were honorary decorations granted when a full military triumph—a massive parade—was not possible or permitted.</note> for their actions under Germanicus. Tiberius refused the title of "Father of the Country," which the people had pressed upon him several times; nor would he allow the Senate to swear an oath to uphold his acts, declaring that mortal affairs were uncertain, and the higher one climbed, the more precarious the fall. Yet, he was not believed to possess a truly civic spirit <note>Meaning a modest, Republican-style leadership.</note>, for he had revived the law of "injured majesty" <term>maiestas: a high treason law originally meant to protect the state, but later used to punish perceived insults against the Emperor</term>. This law was well known to the ancients, but it was applied to different matters: if someone had betrayed an army, stirred up the common people, or mismanaged public affairs—thereby diminishing the "majesty" of the Roman people—he was accused for the deed; words were not yet punished. Augustus...

$^2$ * *more restraint*, meaning with more hesitation or greater difficulty.
$^3$ * *each offering what was most ready*, whatever they had close at hand. Latin: <note>original: "quod cuique promptum"</note> "whatever was ready for each."
$^4$ * *kindness*, or gracious deeds.
$^5$ * *nor would he allow... an oath to uphold his acts*. Latin: <note>original: "neque in acta sua iurari... permisit"</note>. To swear by the acts of the prince meant, as Cassius Dio explains (47.18): <note>original Greek: "βεβαια νομιειν παντα τα υπ' εκεινου γινομενα"</note> "to consider all things done by him to be legally binding." This was a type of flattery invented by the Triumvirs for Julius Caesar in the year 712 <note>42 BC</note>.

...the first who made a matter of state and <term>majesty: treason against the dignity of the state or the Emperor</term> out of libels <note>original: "cartelli"—libelous posters or pamphlets</note>, moved by the malice of Cassius Severus, who had defamed noble men and women with them. Tiberius, later asked by the praetor Pompeius Macer whether he should accept cases regarding "majesty," replied: "The laws must be observed." He too had been embittered by certain anonymous poems that exposed <note>See footnote 1</note> his cruelties, his arrogance, and his conflicts <note>See footnote 2</note> with his mother.

**LXXIII.** I shall also recount the offenses for which complaints were brought against Falanius and Rubrius, Roman knights of modest rank, so that it may be known from what beginnings, and with what art on Tiberius's part, a most cruel fire was sparked, then dampened, and finally burst into a flame that consumed everyone. The accuser stated that Falanius had included a certain Cassius, a mime of ill-repute, among the priests of Augustus (who were organized like a college in every noble household), and that he had sold a statue of Augustus along with his garden. Rubrius was accused of perjury sworn by the name of Augustus. When Tiberius learned of this, he wrote to the consuls:

> "His father was not declared celestial to be used for the ruin of citizens. Cassius is a performer like any other at the games that my mother holds in memory of Augustus; nor is religion harmed if his statues, like those of other gods, are included in the sale of houses and gardens. As for that perjury, it is to be treated as if it were sworn against Jupiter; the gods themselves take care of injuries against the gods."

**LXXIV.** Not long after, Granius Marcellus, the praetor in Bithynia, was accused of treason by his own quaestor, Caepio Crispinus, a charge reinforced by Romanus Hispo. This Hispo was a man who took up a profession <note>The profession of the professional informer, or *delator*.</note> that later gained great influence through the miseries of the times and the local's shamelessness. Poor, unknown, and restless, by acting as a secret spy, he crept into the favor of the cruel prince, laying traps for those of higher rank.

1 * *svertavano*. A *verta* is the bottom of a fishing net, from which the verb *svertare* is formed, meaning to turn inside out, and figuratively to reveal hidden things. Varchi, in *Ercolano*: 
> "Of those who confess the catch, that is, say everything they have said and done... they use these verbs, *svertare*, *sborrare* [to blurt out], etc."

2 * *traversie*: used here for "cross purposes," adversities, or discords. In this specific sense, it is missing from the Dictionary.

...and having become powerful under one man, while being hateful to all, he raised the standard¹ <note>original: "lo stendardo alzò." The Latin source uses *dedit exemplum*, meaning he "set an example" or "provided a precedent" for others.</note> for those who, by following him, went from poor to rich and from lowly to terrifying, bringing about the ruin of others and, in the end, their own. The complaint alleged that Marcello had spoken ill of Tiberius; and there was no defense, because the "gallant man" <note>Used sarcastically to describe the accuser, Caepio Crispinus.</note> chose the most shameful facts about the Emperor which, because they were true, were believed to have actually been said. Hispo added that Marcello had placed his own statue higher than those of the Caesars, and that on another statue of Augustus, he had removed the head and replaced it with that of Tiberius. At this, Tiberius flew into such a rage that, unable to remain silent any longer, he cried out that in this case he too wished to give his opinion openly and under oath, so that the others would not dare to contradict him. Yet, some spirit still remained in their gasping liberty. Thus Gnaeus Piso said: "And when will you speak, O Caesar? If you speak first, I will be able to follow you; if you speak last, I might, without wishing to, speak against you." Realizing his outburst, Tiberius humbled himself to acquit the accused of the treason charge, though he still faced the audit of the <term>pretura: the office of the praetor, involving judicial and administrative oversight</term>.

**LXXV.** He did not mind, in addition to the Senate, sitting also during trials at the corner of the tribunal, so as not to displace the praetor from his seat. This presence brought about good order against the schemes and favors of the powerful; but in repairing justice, liberty was spoiled.² <note>The author means that while Tiberius’s presence ensured that justice was administered strictly, it restricted the freedom of the judges, who felt compelled to follow the prince’s lead.</note> Among other matters, the senator Aurelio Pio, whose house had been ruined to build a road and an aqueduct, petitioned the <term>fathers: the Senators</term> to be compensated. When the treasury officials opposed it, Tiberius paid him out of his own pocket, as he was fond of making "honorable expenses"; this virtue, and no other, he maintained. To Propertius Celer, a former praetor who petitioned to leave his rank due to poverty,³ Tiberius, finding his inheritance meager, gave him a gift of...

---

¹ \* *raised the standard. Latin: "dedit exemplum" (set an example).*
² \* *but in repairing etc. This means that while Tiberius wanted to ensure through his presence that justice was strictly administered, he bound the liberty of the judges, who had to take their lead from the prince's judgment.*
³ *leave his rank due to poverty: to avoid demeaning the senatorial rank, it was considered modest for someone who could not maintain it with the customary magnificence to step down. This author says in the twelfth book: "Then those were praised in the prince's speech who, due to family hardships, voluntarily withdrew from the senatorial order; and those were removed who, by remaining, added impudence to their poverty" <note>original Latin: "Laudati dehinc oratione principis qui ob angustias familiares ordine senatorio sponte cederent: motique qui remanendo, impudentiam paupertati adiicerent."</note>. Asinius Gallus explains for what reason greater magnificence and expense are necessary for the higher ranks.*

twenty-five thousand gold florins.^1 To others who attempted the same, he wrote back: "Let them prove their poverty to the senate," as he was a man who, to maintain his severity, even bestowed favors^2 with bitterness. And those men chose to suffer rather than expose their shame to the people.

**LXXVI.** In that same year, the Tiber, due to prolonged rains, flooded the level parts of the city, and as it receded, it caused great destruction of houses and people. Asinius Gallus advised that they consult what the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Books were a collection of oracular utterances consulted by the Roman state in times of crisis.</note> had to say of it. Tiberius refused, wishing to keep men in the dark^3 concerning divine matters just as he did with human ones; instead, Ateius Capito and L. Arruntius were appointed to oversee the repairs of the river. As Achaia and Macedonia <note>Provinces in modern-day Greece and the Balkans.</note> were complaining of excessive tax burdens, it was decided to lighten them for the time being by removing them from the jurisdiction of the proconsul and placing them among the governments of Caesar <note>This moved them from "senatorial" to "imperial" provinces, usually resulting in more direct and efficient administration.</note>. Drusus celebrated the spectacle of the gladiators <note>original: "accoltellatori," literally knife-wielders.</note>, which had been previously promised in his own name and that of Germanicus, and he took too much pleasure in that blood, base though it was. Because of this, the people grew fearful of him, and his father scolded him for it. Tiberius himself did not wish to attend the celebration; some said it was because he found gatherings loathsome,^4 others because of his own moody nature and for fear of being noticed.

---

**1** *bestowed twenty-five thousand florins*. This amount is ten times one hundred thousand, that is, a million <term>sesterces: the standard silver coin of ancient Rome</term>. This is the amount Augustus gave to Hortalus, the grandson of Hortensius the Orator, so that he could take a wife and rebuild that illustrious family; and the senate proposed giving twenty thousand more to his four sons; and it was proposed to give 125 thousand to the son of Piso before sending him away. Such was the regard held for the nobility; with such liberality were they aided; such was the greatness and the necessary expense of a Roman citizen.

**2** *bestowed favors*. A favor should be done with a happy face, not a rude or spiteful one. For an insult does not mix with courtesy; rather, it spoils it and drives it from the memory, while the insult remains. Thus, he who has forgiven a spiteful favor has already repaid it.

**3** *to keep men in the dark*. Tiberius wanted to extinguish all knowledge; he hated and feared scientists or talented men. In this, he was mistaken according to Aristotle, who says that the learned and the wise conspire against princes less than others do, because they see the dangers and the ruin of the city more clearly. They are few, and few follow or help them; whereas the ignorant are many and reckless, they look at few things, and have more impulse than counsel. In times of danger, thinking is cowardice to them; to strike blindly is a royal act, as is said of the Parthians <note>An empire in the ancient Near East, famous for their horse archers.</note>. Today, the Uskoks <note>A group of Balkan soldiers and pirates active in the 16th and 17th centuries, known for their fierce resistance against the Ottomans and Venetians.</note> are known to get crazily drunk on brandy <note>original: "acqua vite," water of life.</note> when they go to fight, so as to go in warmed by recklessness and fury, without thinking of danger. Ignorance truly is the mother of injustice; this is the root of all evil in the city. But because fish flee the net in clear water because they can see it, murky water suits those who wish to catch and eat them.

**4** *because he found gatherings loathsome*. When Tiberius wished to feed a serpent that he kept for his pleasure, he found it had been eaten by ants. The soothsayers told him to beware of the multitude; therefore he fled from it.

...to show the contrast between his own saturnine face $^1$ and the jovial one that Augustus used to bring there. Others believed (though I cannot credit it) that he did so to allow the people to see and hate his son's inherent cruelty. $^2$

**LXXVII.** The theater riots, which had begun the previous year, grew worse. There were deaths not only among the common people but also among the soldiers and a centurion; even a guard tribune was wounded while trying to hold back the crowd from brawling and insulting the magistrates. This scandal was discussed in the Senate. The prevailing opinions were that the praetors <note>High-ranking Roman magistrates responsible for the administration of justice and public games.</note> should be granted the power to whip the actors <term>strioni</term> <note>From the Latin *histriones*; stage performers who were often viewed with social stigma in Rome.</note>. Haterius Agrippa, a tribune of the plebs, spoke against this. Asinius Gallo argued with him, while Tiberius remained silent, wishing to give the Senate a semblance of liberty in such trivial matters. The "no" prevailed because the Divine Augustus (whose decrees Tiberius would not dare to alter) had previously exempted actors from corporal punishment. Their pay was regulated, and measures were taken against the excessive behavior of their fans $^3$: it was decreed that no senator should enter a comedian's $^4$ house; Roman knights were not to surround or follow them in public; no performances were to be given outside the theater; and the praetor was empowered to punish disruptive spectators with exile.

**LXXVIII.** The Spaniards were granted permission to build a temple to Augustus in the colony of Tarraco <note>Modern-day Tarragona, Spain; this was the first such temple in the provinces dedicated to the deified Augustus.</note>, providing an example for other provinces. When the people requested that the one-percent sales tax, established at the end of the civil wars, be abolished, Tiberius declared that this tax was the primary funding for the military treasury and that the Republic could not afford to pay honorable discharge bonuses $^5$ before twenty years of service. Consequently, he revoked the ill-advised concession of sixteen years of service made during the recent mutiny. $^6$

---

$^1$ *saturnine face*, surly and dark. Machiavelli, *Commentary in Verse on A. I, s. 4, 2:*

->But who is he who comes looking so saturnine?<-

The common people also use the term *saturnine* <note>original: "saturno"</note> for a gloomy person, and I find it in a manuscript Necrology from the late 16th century in my possession: "This man was a good son, but of few words; rather *saturnine* than anything else."

$^2$ *as cruel*. Because of this reputation, people called well-sharpened and cruelly cutting blades "drusian" <term>drusiane</term> after Drusus.

$^3$ *against their excessive popularity, etc.* Latin: "against the insolence of their supporters, many things were decreed." <note>original Latin: "adversus lasciviam fautorum multa decernuntur"</note>

$^4$ *in the house of comedians*, meaning belonging to comedians.

$^5$ *to give the honorable discharges*. When a soldier died before twenty years of service, he had not earned the retirement bonus from the Republic. — *honorable discharges*, the discharge papers and bonuses <note>original: "i ben serviti," literally "the well-served."</note>.

$^6$ *See chapter XVI and following.*

**LXXIX.** The deputies of the Tiber proposed in the senate whether, to prevent floods, the rivers and lakes that cause it to swell should be diverted elsewhere. The embassies of the lands and colonies were heard: the Florentines begged that the Chiana <note>The Clanis river; a major tributary of the Tiber.</note> should not be diverted from its bed into the Arno, for that would be their ruin. Similar things were said by those from Terni, arguing that the most fertile land in Italy would be spoiled if the Nera <note>The Nar river; its waters are high in sulfur.</note> were divided, as was planned, into several small streams and allowed to stagnate there. The people of Rieti cried out against blocking the mouth of Lake Velinus, which flows into the Nera, because it would overflow into those plains:
> “Nature has provided <gloss>1</gloss> for the affairs of mortals most excellently, giving to rivers their appropriate sources, courses, beds, and mouths. One must also respect the religious rites of the allies, who have consecrated their woods, altars, and shrines to the rivers of their homelands. The Tiber himself would not wish to flow with less pride, deprived of the company of his tributary rivers.”
Whether it was the pleas of the colonies, the difficulty of the work, or religious considerations, the opinion of Piso prevailed: that nothing should be changed.

**LXXX.** Moesia was confirmed for Poppaeus Sabinus, and Achaia and Macedonia were added to his command. It was Tiberius's habit not to change his ministers; <gloss>2</gloss> many he kept for life in a single army or a single administrative post. Some say he did this because, once he was satisfied with someone, he wanted to keep them forever to relieve himself of further thought; others say it was out of envy, <gloss>3</gloss> so that

---

<gloss>1</gloss> *Nature has provided.* Just as veins spread through the bodies of animals and through the leaves of plants, so the rivers spread through the earth with turns and twists according to the needs well known by Nature—the true master-builder and engineer. They cannot be altered without violence, error, damage, and heavy burdens upon the people, or without creating opportunities for corrupt officials.

<gloss>2</gloss> *Tiberius’s habit not to change ministers.* Josephus says (in Chapter 18 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*) that he did this so as not to drive away the flies already full and satiated from the sores of the poor citizens, only to replace them with empty, hungry ones. Such charity could not have moved Tiberius, who, as writers say, used his ministers like sponges to draw blood (by selling favors and justice, and through iniquity) from the people, and then, by punishing them, he squeezed them. (*) Thus he grew rich, and the people blessed him for it, as he otherwise would have ruined his own craft. Cornelius <note>Referring to the author, Cornelius Tacitus.</note> provides more solid reasons here.

<gloss>3</gloss> *out of envy.* Great things are found regarding Tiberius’s envious nature. It is notable that when a great portico in Rome had leaned to one side, an architect straightened it. Tiberius admired the skill and rewarded him generously; but out of spite, he would not allow the man’s name to be written in the account books and drove him out of Rome. The man returned to him to regain favor with another feat; and

(*) *squeezed them*, that is, the sponges.

Out of these hesitations, he went so far as to grant provinces to men whom he had no intention of allowing to leave Rome.

**LXXXI.** The manner of appointing the consuls held first by this prince, and followed thereafter, I can hardly say: it is found to be so varied not only among historians but in his own speeches. Sometimes he described the candidates by their lineage, life, and military service, yet without names, so that it might be understood of whom he spoke; at other times, without such descriptions, he urged the seekers not to overwhelm the <term>ballot|squittino: An old Florentine term for a secret vote, used here to translate the Roman electoral process</term> with their pleas, but promised to assist them. <gloss>1</gloss> He often stated that, besides those he himself had nominated for the consulship, no one else had applied: if anyone wished to test their own influence or merits, they should step forward. These were grand but empty words intended to deceive with false displays of great liberty, only to result in a servitude that was all the more cruel.

---

*Achaia* in the Peloponnese, where Nafplio <note>original: "Napoli di Romania," the Venetian name for the Greek city of Nafplio</note> is located.
*Actium*, Preveza, a promontory in Albania, where Nicopolis is, near the Echinades, called the Curzolari, where the Turk was defeated in the year 1571 <note>A reference to the Battle of Lepanto, where the Holy League naval forces defeated the Ottoman Empire</note>.

*Batavi*, the Dutch, on the Ocean between the Meuse and the Rhine.
*Cercinna*, an island in the African sea. Kerkenna <note>original: "Carcana"</note>.
*Chatti*, the people of Hesse in Germany.
*Chauci*, part of Saxony and Brunswick.
*Cherusci*, perhaps the Zealanders.
*Curule Aediles*, officials in Rome in charge of buildings, rivers, festivals, etc.
*Cereal Aediles*, in charge of the food supply and provisions <note>original: "abbondanza e grascie"</note>.
*Germani*, Germans, Teutons, Alemanni.
*Gallia Togata* <note>meaning "Gallic land wearing the toga"</note> between the Alps and the Rubicon, because it was peaceful and used the Roman toga.
*Gallia Bracata* <note>meaning "Gallic land wearing trousers"</note>, because they used certain furs <note>The term *bracata* actually refers to *bracae*, or breeches/trousers, which the Romans considered barbaric compared to the toga</note>: Narbonensis, Languedoc.
*Gallia Comata* <note>meaning "Long-haired Gaul"</note> from their blond hair, beyond the Alps; divided by Caesar into Celtica, Belgica, and Aquitaine; today France, Flanders, and Gascony.
*Legates in the army*, Commissioners sent by the republic or by the prince.
*Luppia*, a river: it flows into the Rhine along Wesel in Cleves.
*Legion*, a choice selection of Roman people, containing—excluding the auxiliary troops—according to Vegetius <note>A 4th-century Roman writer on military matters</note>, ten cohorts, namely: The first of 1,105 infantry and 130 cavalry; the other nine, each of 555 infantry and 66 cavalry.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ANNALS

->BY<-

## GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

---

### SUMMARY.

I. The East is in some turmoil. — III. Vonones, King of the Parthians, driven out by Artabanus, takes refuge with the Armenians; he is accepted by them as king, but rejected shortly after due to fear and threats from Artabanus. — V. Tiberius, using the rumors of the East as a pretext, removes Germanicus from the Germanic legions; Germanicus obeys with a heavy heart <note>original: "a piè zoppo," literally "with a lame foot," meaning reluctantly or with difficulty</note>. Once he enters Germany, he defeats the Cherusci and Arminius in a great battle. He suffers a storm at sea, but compensates for everything with a successful expedition against the Marsi. — XXVII. Libo Drusus is accused of revolutionary activities <note>original: "novità," referring to political conspiracy or subversion of the state</note>. The pleas of M. Hortalus are struck down. — XXXIV. Clemens, under the false name of Agrippa Postumus, stirs up a rebellion. Sallustius Crispus captures him by craft and brings him to Rome. — XLI. Germanicus triumphs over the Chatti, Cherusci, and other nations as far as the Elbe <note>original: "Albi"</note>. — XLII. Archelaus, King of the Cappadocians, lured to Rome by a trap and mistreated, dies. His kingdom is made into a province. — XLIII. The East is given to Germanicus; Syria to Piso with secret instructions against Germanicus, as it is believed. — XLIV. Drusus is sent to Illyricum against the Germans who, because of their own discords, allow the Romans to remain safe and idle. — XLV. The Cherusci under Arminius defeat the powerful and ancient King Maroboduus in a great and bloody battle. — XLVII. Twelve cities of Asia are overturned by an earthquake. The generosity of Tiberius. — L. The law of the state <note>the *Lex Maiestatis*, or treason law</note> stretches out its hands <note>meaning its reach and severity are increasing</note>. — LII. Tacfarinas takes up arms in Africa; he is immediately repressed by Furius Camillus. — LIII. Germanicus, consul again, passes into Armenia: by their own will he appoints Zeno as king, having removed Vonones: then he travels to Egypt. — LXII. Drusus sows discord among the Germans. Maroboduus, driven from his kingdom by Catualda, comes to Italy and is held for 18 years in Ravenna. Catualda, having met a similar fate, is sent to Frejus <note>original: "Fregius"</note>. — LXIV. Rhescuporis, King of Thrace, is put in irons through the work of Pomponius Flacco and brought to Rome. — LXVIII. Vonones is killed. — LXIX. Germanicus returns from Egypt; he finds his orders abolished or reversed by Piso, sowing seeds of discord between them. Not long after, having fallen ill, he dies in Antioch to the great mourning of the people. — LXXIV. Piso, suspected of having given him poison, is forbidden from returning to Syria. — LXXXIII. Great honors are paid to the deceased Germanicus by Rome. — LXXXV. Laws are passed against female unchastity. — LXXXVI. The selection of a Vestal Virgin; a fixed price is set for grain. — LXXXVIII. Arminius is killed in Germany by the treachery of his own people.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

---

### I. [Year of Rome 769, Year of Christ 16.] 
The realms of the East and the Roman provinces were thrown into turmoil, a movement begun by the Parthians. They had requested and received a king from Rome, but despite him being of the Arsacid blood, <note>The Arsacids were the descendants of that Arsaces who liberated the country of the Parthians from the rule of Alexander the Great's successors, turning it into a vast and powerful kingdom.</note> they soon loathed him as a foreigner. This king was Vonones, who had been given to Augustus as a hostage by Phraates. Phraates, although he had once driven away Roman armies and their generals, <note>Referring to the Roman commanders Oppius Statianus and Mark Antony in the year 36 BC. See Plutarch's *Life of Antony*, 38.</note> had later turned to venerating Augustus; he sent a portion of his sons to him as a pledge of friendship, fearing not so much us as the loyalty of his own people.

### II. 
After the death of Phraates and the subsequent kings who murdered one another, the Parthian nobles sent ambassadors to Rome to bring back Vonones, the eldest son. Caesar, regarding this as a great honor, sent him back with rich gifts. The barbarians welcomed him with the celebration traditionally reserved for new kings. Soon, however, they felt a sense of shame, believing that as "bastardized" Parthians, they had called for a king from another world who was infected by the customs of their enemies.

> “Already the Arsacid throne is regarded and given away as if it were a Roman vassalage; <note>original: "per vassallaggio di Roma," meaning as if it were a Roman province.</note> where are those glorious men who cut Crassus to pieces and drove out Antony, if someone who endured so many years of being Caesar’s slave is now to command them?”

Vonones himself also disgusted them with his ways, which differed from their ancient customs. He rarely hunted; he took no delight in horses; he traveled through cities in a litter; and he held the foods of his homeland in contempt. <note>original: "fargli afa," meaning to be disgusted by. Tacitus's Latin reads: "fastuque erga patrias epulas" (disdain toward the national feasts).</note> They mocked his Greek-style retinue and his habit of keeping even the most trivial household items under seal. <note>original: "bollare ogni cencio." Tacitus's Latin: "vilissima utensilium anulo clausa" (even the cheapest utensils were locked away with his signet ring).</note> His willingness to grant audiences and his friendly welcomes—virtues new to the Parthians—were seen as new vices; and because these things were not traditional, they hated them, whether they were good or bad.

### III. 
Therefore, they called into the field Artabanus, an Arsacid who had been raised among the Dahae. <note>A tribe located near the Caspian Sea; today known as Dahistan.</note> In the first battle, Artabanus was defeated; however, he regrouped and seized the kingdom. The defeated Vonones fled to Armenia, which was then "vacant" <note>meaning "without a master." Being situated between the domains of the Parthians and the Romans, the Armenians were often loyal to neither side.</note> and caught between...

...the Roman and Parthian forces, an intermediary <note>original: "tramezo." The translator remarks that the "tra-" prefix here is a redundancy, unappealing to a writer who weighs every word.</note> land, not faithful to us due to the capture of Antony, <note>original: "cattività d' Antonio." Artavasdes, though a friend and aid to the Romans, had allowed the Roman commander Oppius Statianus to be cut to pieces. Antony later punished him with this betrayal. Today, we might not call this "capture," but rather military strategy or "reason of state," which permits whatever is useful. Common folk would call it "scoundrelry."</note> whom Artavasdes, the king of that land, invited as a friend, then enchained and killed. For this reason, his son Artaxias, <note>The translator adds: "who became our enemy in memory of his father," following the original Latin text: "filius Artaxias, memoria patris nobis infensus."</note> defended himself and the kingdom against us with the strength of the Arsacids. After he was betrayed and killed by his own people, Caesar invested Tigranes with that kingdom, and Tiberius Nero led him there. He and his children held a brief rule, though they were joined in kingship and marriage with their own sisters, according to the barbarian custom. Augustus then placed Artavasdes on the throne; he was driven out, though not without a defeat for our forces.

### IV. 
Gaius Caesar <note>Gaius Caesar, the grandson of Agrippa and adopted son of Augustus; he died during his return journey in the year 757 [4 AD]. See Book I, Chapter 3.</note> was sent to settle the affairs of Armenia and gave them Ariobarzanes the Mede. He was handsome and fierce, and they held him dear. When he died by misfortune, the people were dissatisfied with his children and tried the rule of a woman named Erato. She was soon driven out; the people were confused and disorganized, being without a master rather than truly free, until they made the refugee Vonones their king. But because Artabanus was threatening him, and the Armenians could offer little help—and because if we defended him, we would be forced into a war with the Parthians—Creticus Silano, the governor in Syria, summoned him and made him a prisoner, though he allowed him to maintain his royal finery and title. How Vonones attempted to flee this indignity, I shall tell in the proper place.

### V. 
This turmoil in the East did not displease Tiberius, as it provided an excuse to pull Germanicus away from the legions that were too devoted to him, and to send him under the pretext of new governorships, perhaps to be disposed of <note>original: "a smaltire," meaning to die. The Latin reads: "and set him over new provinces to expose him to both fraud and chance."</note> through treachery or misfortune. But the eagerness of the soldiers and the malice of his uncle were spurs to Germanicus to hasten his victory; he pondered the methods of combat and the successes and failures he had seen in three years of...

VI. Having committed to this plan, he sent Publius Vitellius and Cantio <note>original: "Canzio," used here for Caius Antius, similar to how Agellio is used for Aulus Gellius.</note> to collect the tithes <note>original: "le decime," referring to tax or tribute mentioned in Annals Book I, Chapter 31.</note> of the Gauls; and to Silius, Anteius, and Caecina he gave the task of building the ships. <note>Tacitus describes their form, name, and use in the third book of his *Histories* during the war of Anicetus.</note> One thousand ships seemed sufficient and were quickly made ready. Some were short and narrow at the prow and stern and wide in the belly to better withstand the waves. Others were flat-bottomed so they could settle safely <note>original: "per ben posare." This translates the Latin "ut sine noxa siderent," meaning that in shallow waters or during the ebb of the tide, they could ground themselves without damage.</note>. Most had rudders at both ends <note>original: "a ogni punta," translating the Latin "utrinque," meaning from both prow and stern.</note> so as to land from any side with a turn of the oars. Many were decked <note>original: "acconce," translating the Latin "pontibus stratae," meaning fitted with decks or bridges.</note> to carry siege engines, horses, and provisions; they were nimble and swift as hawks <note>original: "sparvierate," translating the Latin "citae remis," meaning fast-moving by oar.</note> under oar; and the confidence of the soldiers made them appear even more numerous and terrifying. It was ordered that they should assemble <note>original: "facessero massa," translating the Latin "convenirent."</note> at the Island of the Batavians, which provided an easy landing and was convenient for sending the necessities of war via the Rhine <note>The Latin "transmittendum ad bellum opportuna" is translated here to mean sending supplies through the river.</note>, which, flowing through a single bed, forms several small islands upon reaching the Batavians and then divides like two rivers: one continues with its own name and rapid course through the...

...many branches into the ocean; the other branch, which flows wider and more gently along the border of Gaul, changes its name and is called the Vaal <note>original: "Vaale," the southern distributary of the Rhine.</note> by the locals, and shortly after, the Meuse <note>original: "Mosa."</note> which empties into the same ocean through a very wide mouth.

### VII.

While the fleet is being assembled, Caesar <note>Referencing Germanicus Caesar, the commander of the Roman forces.</note> sends Silius, his lieutenant, with light-armed troops to raid the Chatti <note>A powerful Germanic tribe.</note>: he himself, hearing that a fortress on the Lippe <note>original: "Luppia," a river in modern-day Germany.</note> was being besieged, marched there with six legions. Silius, hampered by sudden rains, accomplished little more than capturing the wife and daughter of Arpus, the leader of the Chatti. Nor did Caesar engage the besiegers, because they scattered at the news of his arrival. Nevertheless, he restored the new tomb of Varus’s legions <note>Varus was the Roman general who lost three legions in the disastrous Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD.</note> and the old altar of Drusus.^1 He rebuilt the altar, and with the legions behind him, he performed a ceremonial military procession <note>original: "torneò." See footnote 2.</note> in honor of his father.^2 The tomb was not judged to be in need of restoration; and between the fortress and Aliso^3 and the Rhine, he fortified the entire area with new boundaries and ramparts.

### VIII.

Once the fleet had arrived, he sent the provisions ahead; he distributed the legions and the auxiliary troops among the ships; and having entered the trench known as the Drusian Canal <note>A canal built by Germanicus's father, Drusus the Elder, to connect the Rhine to the North Sea.</note>, he prayed to his father Drusus, asking that he might look favorably upon his daring in this same enterprise, and that he might show him the deeds and remind him of his own methods. He sailed through the lakes and the ocean successfully as far as the mouth of the Ems <note>original: "Amisia."</note>. There he left the ships on the left bank of the river, which was an error in not disembarking the troops further upstream; for as they had to travel through those lands to the right, he was forced to lose several days building bridges over those tidal flats, which were crossed boldly by the legions and horses before the tide returned: but the rear auxiliaries, wanting to challenge the waters^4 and show courage...

---

1 * *of Drusus*; that is, erected where Drusus died in the year 745 <note>745 Ab Urbe Condita, or 9 BC.</note>.
2 *with the legions... he performed a military procession*. Regarding this ancient custom called *decursio* <note>A ritualized military parade or "run" around a funeral pyre or monument.</note>, see Xenophon in the sixth book of *Cyropaedia*; Dio, 55; Suetonius, in *Nero*. Lipsius cites Homer, Virgil, Livy, Lucan, and Statius. See note 55 of this book. (*) — *with the legions... he performed a military procession*; that is, he was the leader, and the legions followed behind him. The Latin has: <note>original: "princeps ipse cum legionibus decucurrit." / "The leader himself ran [the ritual] with the legions."</note>
3 * *between the fortress and Aliso*. The text reads: "castellum, Alisonem ac Rhenum." But the best editions read: "castellum Alisonem ac Rhenum," meaning: between the fortress of Aliso and the Rhine. — Aliso is the name of the fortress, located at the confluence of the Lippe and the Aliso river, as attested by Dio 54, 33. See Orelli’s edition of Tacitus on this passage.
4 * *wanting to challenge the waters*; that is, wanting in that river, with a certain boldness, to win the trial against the force of the waters: or rather, wanting to show that the waters did not frighten them, etc. The Latin has: <note>original: "dum insultant aquis." / "while they leap into/defy the waters."</note>
(*) From this edition, page 109, note 3.

...slow to disembark, they fell into disorder, and some drowned. While Caesar <note>Referencing Germanicus Caesar, the Roman commander.</note> was setting up camp, he learned that the Angrivari <note>A Germanic tribe living along the middle Weser.</note> behind him had rebelled. Stertinius was quickly sent there with cavalry and light infantry, and he punished them with fire and sword.

### IX.
The Weser <note>original: "Visurgo," a major river in north-western Germany.</note> flowed between the Romans and the Cherusci. Arminius, standing on the bank with his chieftains, asked if Caesar was there. Having heard that he was, he asked to speak with his brother Flavus. This man was highly esteemed in our army for his loyalty and for having lost an eye in a battle under Tiberius. Stepping forward, Arminius greeted him; then, having moved his archers away from the bank, he requested that our men also withdraw. This being done, he said to his brother: "What happened to that eye?" — "I lost it in such-and-such a place, in such-and-such a battle." — "What did you gain from it?" Flavus recounted his increased pay, a neck-chain, a crown, and other military gifts. Arminius mocked him for serving for such a small price.

### X.
Then, one man spoke of Roman greatness, the power of Caesar, the harsh punishments for the defeated, the ready mercy for those who surrender, and the kind treatment shown to Arminius's wife and son. The other reminded him of his duty to his homeland, their ancient liberty, their ancestral religion,¹ and the tears of their mother; he urged him not to abandon and betray his own blood, relatives, and countrymen by serving the enemy, but rather to lead them. One word led to another until they reached insults; nor would the river have kept them apart had Stertinius not run to restrain the furious Flavus, who was demanding his weapons and his horse. On the other side, Arminius could be seen threatening and challenging him to battle, speaking half in Latin, because he had previously commanded companies of Germans in the Roman camp.

### XI.
The next day, the Germans presented themselves in formation beyond the Weser. Caesar, not thinking it wise for a commander to risk the infantry without bridges and guards, sent the cavalry across at a ford. Stertinius and Aemilius, a <term>primipilus</term> <note>A senior centurion of the first rank; original: "capo di prima fila."</note>, led them from points far apart to divide the enemy's attention. Chariovalda, leader of the Batavians <note>A Germanic tribe allied with Rome, known for their swimming and fording abilities.</note>, crossed where the current was strongest. The Cherusci feigned flight, drawing him into a plain surrounded by woods, from which they poured down upon them from every side. They pushed back those who fought and pursued those who fled, throwing the ranks into disorder with hand-to-hand combat or missiles...

...attacked from all sides. Cariovalda, after long enduring the enemy’s fury, said to his men: "Close ranks and break them apart!" <note>The Italian translator uses "sdruciteli," meaning to unrip or tear through. The original Latin is *catervas frangerent*, meaning to break the enemy troops.</note> Having charged into the thickest part of the fray, weighed down by spears and with his horse killed under him, he fell along with many nobles around him. The rest were saved by their own courage or by the aid of the cavalry led by Stertinius and Aemilius.

XII. Caesar <note>Referring to Germanicus Julius Caesar, the Roman general.</note>, having crossed the Weser <note>original: "Visurgo," a river in modern-day Germany.</note>, learned from a deserter where Arminius intended to give battle: that other tribes were gathered in the Forest of Hercules and intended to attack the Roman camp at night. He believed the report, as fires were visible; furthermore, scouts sent to investigate reported hearing the neighing of horses and the murmuring of a vast crowd nearby. Therefore, with the decisive moment fast approaching <note>The Italian text uses the idiom "la cocca in su la corda," meaning the nock of the arrow is on the string—a metaphor for being at the point of action. Vegetius, in his work on military matters, suggests that a leader must carefully judge the spirit of his soldiers before battle by observing their faces and gestures.</note>, he felt he should test the soldiers’ spirit. He sought a reliable method to do this, because tribunes and centurions often report pleasing things rather than the truth; freedmen still have the heart of a slave; friends are prone to flattery; and in a formal council, what a few voices start, the others merely echo. He resolved to overhear his men when they were eating and, thinking themselves unheard <note>The original text implies they were in private and unguarded.</note>, would speak their minds freely <note>original: "si discredono." To speak confidently and freely, unburdening one's heart or venting one's true feelings.</note> among themselves.

XIII. At nightfall, he left through the augural gate <note>The *porta agurale* was located to the right of the general's tent; it was here that the commander would take omens from the sacred chickens.</note> with a single companion. Wearing a fur cloak <note>original: "impellicciato." He wore this to look like one of the Germanic auxiliary soldiers who typically wore animal skins, serving as a disguise.</note> to avoid being recognized, he walked through the paths of the camp. He approached the tents and was pleased to hear various men talking about him: "Oh, what a noble commander! What a fine man!" They praised his patience and pleasant manner, and how in every action, whether serious or lighthearted, he was full of kindness. They said they should surely show their gratitude <note>original: "riconoscere," here meaning to be grateful or to repay his leadership with loyalty.</note> in this battle, and sa—
