...sacrifice these dogs, who broke the peace, to his vengeance and glory." A horseman from the enemy side approached the barricades and, in a loud voice and speaking in Latin <note>original: "lingua latina"</note>, offered on behalf of Arminius wives, lands, and two and a half gold coins <note>The Italian translator uses "fioríni" (florins), an anachronism for the Roman *sestertii* mentioned in the original Latin text.</note> a day for the duration of the war to whoever would defect to his camp. This insult reignited the soldiers' anger: 

> "Let the day come; let us engage; a good omen! <note>The soldiers take the enemy’s offer of land and wives as a sign that they will soon possess these things as spoils of war.</note> We shall seize the lands, the wives, and the money of the Germans." 

At the third watch <note>The period of the night from midnight to approximately 3:00 AM.</note> they approached the enemy camp without firing a shot, finding that the enemy was not asleep.

**XIV.** That night, Germanicus dreamed of making a sacrifice; he dreamt that the sacrificial blood splattered onto his robe, <note>The original Italian "vestone" refers to the *praetexta*, the purple-bordered toga worn by Roman priests and magistrates.</note> and that his grandmother Augusta <note>Livia, the widow of Emperor Augustus and grandmother of Germanicus.</note> offered him another, more beautiful one. Encouraged by this and by favorable omens, he addressed his troops, highlighting the wise provisions made and what they must do in the upcoming battle: 

> "The Roman soldier can fight not only on the plains, but in forests and ravines if need be. Those clumsy shields and long poles of the barbarians are worthless among thickets and trees compared to our javelins, swords, and well-fitted armor. <note>The Italian "assettata armadura" describes armor that fits the body closely, unlike the bulky equipment of the Germanic tribes.</note> Strike often with the point at their faces! They have no breastplates, no helmets, nor shields made of iron or leather, but only of wicker or thin painted boards. Their spears—such as they are—are found only in the first ranks; for the rest, they carry only charred stakes. They are terrifying to look at and ruinous in their first fury, but they cannot endure wounds. They turn and flee, knowing neither shame nor obedience. In defeat, they are cowards; in times of peace, they remember neither man nor God. If you desire to end the weariness of travel and the sea, it all rests on this day. You are closer now to the Elbe than to the Rhine; the war will be over if you conquer here."

---

1 * *let us engage, let the battle join.* — *a good omen;* that is, let us take it as a good sign that the enemy has offered us the very lands, wives, and money we intend to take.
2 * *At the third watch,* the vigil: near daybreak. Vegetius, Book III, Chapter 8; translated by B. Giamboni: "And because it seemed impossible for all those on guard to watch the entire night, the watches (*vigiliae*) are divided into four parts, so that one need not watch for more than three hours of the night."
3 * *robe.* The Latin: "*praetexta*."
4 * *well-fitted armor.* Latin: "*haerentia corpori tegmina*." Dati: "armor fitted to their backs."
5 * *spears;* that is, the barbarians use spears, etc. — *such as,* of what kind.
6 * *If you desire to end,* etc. More clearly in the Giuntina edition: "if they desired the end of the travels and the sea, etc." — *rests:* understand this as the conclusion of the journeys, etc.
7 * *will be over,* it shall be finished.

...following the footsteps of your father and your uncle, you will stand victorious in these lands." The commander’s words set the soldiers on fire, and the signal for battle was given.

**XV.** Nor did Arminius and the other leaders fail to encourage the Germans:
> "These are merely the paltry remains <note>The original Italian "Romanastri" is a derogatory term suggesting they are "pseudo-Romans" or "little Romans."</note> of Varus’s army, who huddled together only to avoid fighting. Desperate men, they return to their own ruin to feed the German swords with limbs already riddled with holes from behind, or crushed by the storms. They have come slinking back by way of the sea so that no one might confront them face to face, or pursue and press them. But when we come to hand-to-hand combat, their winds and oars will be of no use to them. With a people so greedy, cruel, and arrogant, what else is there to do but defend our liberty or die?"

**XVI.** Thus inflamed and demanding battle, they were led into the plain of Idistaviso <note>A plain on the right bank of the Weser River; the name likely means "Plain of the Nymphs."</note>, which winds between the Weser <note>original: "Visurgo"</note> and the hills, following the path carved by the slopes or the erosion of the water. Behind them rose a forest with high branches and a clear floor. The barbarians occupied the plain and the outskirts of the woods; the Cherusci alone took the hilltops, intending to swoop down upon the Romans once the fray had begun. Our army advanced with the Gallic and German auxiliaries in the front, followed by the foot-archers. Then came four legions with Caesar <note>Germanicus</note> in the middle, flanked by two praetorian cohorts and select cavalry; after them came another four legions, the light infantry, the horse-archers, and the remaining auxiliaries. All stood ready and intent on the fight.

**XVII.** Seeing the swarms of Cherusci descend with ferocity to strike the best of the cavalry on the flank, Caesar sent Stertinius with the remaining horsemen to circle around and strike them from behind; he himself would move to help at the right moment. Then, at a most beautiful omen <note>original: "agùro"</note> of eight eagles seen flying into the forest, the commander turned and cried:
> "Go! Follow the Roman birds, your very own gods! <note>1</note>"

The infantry charged, and the cavalry already sent forward broke through—

$^1$ *thrusting against the archers.* "He put all his effort where the archers were: he gathered almost all the strength of his body into one point to pass through the squadrons of archers. — Dante, *Purgatorio* 20: *And that lance thrusts so that it makes Florence's belly burst.* 'To brace one's feet against the wall' or 'to thrust with the head against the lid,' says Boccaccio in novella 28. $^2$ *climbed high*, went up into the trees.

$^3$ *From the fifth hour of the day.* Germanicus had fought with the Germans for three years to avenge the defeat of Varus <note>The "Varian Disaster" of 9 AD, where three Roman legions were destroyed in the Teutoburg Forest.</note>. Just as he was on the verge of subjugating them, Tiberius, jealous of his greatness, recalled him. Not wishing to lose such glory, he hurried to take the field and fought two major battles this year, 769 <note>Years counted from the founding of Rome; this corresponds to 16 AD.</note>. This first battle was at the start of spring; since the days are twelve hours long everywhere then, the fifth hour of the day—counting from sunrise in that country—was at 5:00 PM according to our modern way of counting from sunset. The second battle, mentioned later when the summer was "full-grown" <note>original: *adulta*</note>, occurred in midsummer; in Latin, the seasons are called "new" [spring], "adult" [summer], and "headlong" [autumn].

There they stationed their infantry, hiding their cavalry in the nearby woods to fall upon the rear of our troops once they entered.

**XX.** Caesar <note>Referring to Germanicus Caesar, the Roman commander.</note> knew all their plans, their locations, their secrets and public movements, and he turned the enemy's own cunning against them. He assigned the cavalry and the plain to his lieutenant Seius Tubero. He ordered the infantry to divide: some were to enter the woods through the plain, while others were to capture the embankment. The most difficult <note>original: "Il più forte," meaning the hardest part of the assault.</note> task he reserved for himself, leaving the rest to his lieutenants. Those on the plain entered easily, but those scaling the embankment were struck heavily from above, as if they were beneath a city wall. Seeing that the close-quarters combat was unequal, the commander drew the legions back a little and ordered the slingers and skirmishers to clear the embankment with stones and bolts from the catapults and engines. Anyone who showed themselves to defend it fell. Caesar, with his Praetorians, was the first to take the palisade and force his way into the woods. There, it came to hand-to-hand combat. <note>original: "si venne alle mani," corresponding to the Latin "conlato gradu certatum," meaning a close-quarters struggle at sword's length.</note> The enemy was trapped from behind by the swamp, and our men by the river and mountains. For both sides, the terrain left no choice but necessity, their courage gave them hope, and victory was their only salvation.

**XXI.** The Germans were not inferior in courage, but they were disadvantaged by their way of fighting and their weapons. In such a narrow space, these massive people could not manage their long spears, nor were they able to leap or run with agility; instead, they fought rooted to the spot. Our men, meanwhile, with shields held close to their chests and swords in hand, thrust at those giant limbs and exposed faces, carving their way through with slaughter. Nor was Arminius <note>The leader of the Germanic tribes and former Roman ally who famously defeated Varus.</note> as fierce as before, worn down by continuous perils or perhaps by a fresh wound. Inguiomero <note>Arminius's uncle and a fellow Germanic leader.</note> flew everywhere, lacking luck rather than valor. Germanicus, bareheaded,<gloss>1</gloss> so as to be better recognized, cried out: "Kill, kill! Take no prisoners; only the total destruction of them all will end this war." Toward evening, he withdrew one legion from the battle to begin building the camp; the others satiated themselves with the blood of the enemy until nightfall. The cavalries fought to a draw.

**XXII.** Caesar <note>Referring to Germanicus Caesar.</note> called forth and praised the victors, and raised a trophy of arms with a proud title: **THAT THE ARMY<gloss>2</gloss> OF TIBERIUS CAESAR HAD CONSECRATED TO MARS, JUPITER, AND AUGUSTUS THIS MONUMENT OF THE SUBJUGATED NATIONS BETWEEN THE RHINE AND THE ELBE.** He said nothing of himself, either fearing envy or being satisfied with the deed itself. He immediately sent Stertinius to fight the Angrivarii, but they were quick to surrender on any terms and were granted mercy.

**XXIII.** It being now mid-summer, he sent some legions back to their winter quarters by land, and the others he embarked and led down the Ems <note>original: "Amisia."</note> to the ocean. The soldiers, terrified and unaccustomed to the hazards of the sea, caused trouble or gave poor help to the skilled efforts of the sailors. "He had done and risked enough: many great and successful battles; but he should also remember the losses, which, though not his fault, were terrible, suffered at the sea. Nine times Augustus had sent him to Germany, and he had accomplished more through counsel than through force: thus the Sicambri and the Suevi were brought to terms, and King Maroboduus was bound by peace. Now that the Cherusci and the other rebels have been punished, the Romans could leave them to quarrel among themselves." Germanicus asked for one more year to finish everything, but Tiberius countered his modesty with even greater force, saying, "that he had reappointed him consul; he should come to take his office, and leave, if anything remained to be done, some matter of glory for his brother Drusus; for, there being no other war outside of Germany, Drusus could not otherwise earn the title of Commander or the laurel crown." Germanicus did not wait any longer, although he knew these were excuses born of envy to strip him of the glory <note>original: "isbarbarlo dal già acquistato splendore," literally "to uproot him from his splendor"</note> he had already earned.

<meta>This page concludes the episode of Marcus Hortalus, whose plea for financial assistance was coldly rejected by the Emperor Tiberius. ### THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

...he never again took pity on them,¹ even though the house of Hortalus² fell into a shameful state of poverty.

XXXIX. In that same year, the audacity of a lowly man³ <note>The Italian translator uses the word "verme" (worm), suggesting a base or contemptible person, though Tacitus's original Latin simply refers to the "audacity of a single slave."</note> would have plunged the republic into civil discord and arms, had it not been swiftly countered. Upon hearing of Augustus’s death, Clemens, a slave of Agrippa Postumus, conceived a plan far beyond a slave’s station: to travel to the island of Pianosa and, by force or trickery, rescue Agrippa and present him to the armies in Germany. A merchant ship was so delayed that by the time he arrived, he found Agrippa had already been killed. From this, he moved to an even greater gamble: he stole the funeral ashes and crossed over to Cosa,⁴ a coastal promontory in Tuscany, where he remained hidden until his beard and hair had grown out. Resembling his master in both age and features, he spread word through suitable accomplices that Agrippa was alive. At first, this was done in secret,⁵ as is the way with dangerous things; then, the rumor filled the ears of all people, especially the ignorant, the curious, and the troublemakers who thrive on upheaval. He traveled through the countryside in the twilight, never showing himself in public. As soon as he arrived in a place, he would vanish, leaving fame behind him or appearing just before it arrived; for the eyes and a long stay help reveal the truth, while haste and uncertainty aid a falsehood.

XL. It was already being spread throughout Italy that Agrippa had been saved by the grace of the gods; in Rome, it was widely believed. At times, shame and fear dictated his thoughts—warning him that nothing should be ignored, yet not everything should be feared. # XLI.
At the end of the year, an arch was consecrated near the Temple of Saturn to commemorate the recovery of the standards lost by Varus <note>Referring to the disastrous defeat at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, where three Roman legions were lost</note>, which Germanicus had reclaimed for Tiberius. [Year of Rome 770, Year of Christ 17.] In the consulship of Gaius Caecilius⁴ and Lucius Pomponio, on the 26th of May, Germanicus Caesar triumphed over the Cherusci, Chatti, Angrivarii, and other nations as far as the Elbe. Carried in the procession were the spoils of war, the prisoners, and representations of the mountains, rivers, and battles. That war was considered finished, though it had not been allowed to reach a true conclusion. People could not see enough of his great beauty and his five children riding upon the chariot; yet there was a secret heartache, considering that for his father Drusus, the favor of the people had been unlucky; and his uncle Marcellus, for whom the common people were once wild with passion,⁵ had been snatched away before his time: these loves of the Roman people are always brief and ill-fated.

Leaving the Latin aside, I observe that the Tuscan people often use the phrase *far giuoco* to mean being convenient or opportune; for example, *"This thing is of use [fa giuoco] to me."* One could believe that here too *giuoco* stands for something convenient, *good, or opportune*, and it would fit Tacitus's sentiment perfectly: "To kings it does not seem good to suffer, etc." If I have hit upon the truth, this meaning could be added to the Dictionary.

XLIII. Tiberius then reported all these matters, along with the previously mentioned affairs of Armenia,³ to the Senate. Beyond his father’s proud spirit, the nobility and wealth of his wife Plancina further inflated his ego. **XLV.** To him <note>Arminius</note> fled from the kingdom of Maroboduus the Suebi, the Semnones, and the Langobards <note>The Lombards; a Germanic tribe that would centuries later settle in Northern Italy</note>. This occurred solely because Inguiomerus, being an elder and an uncle, disdained to obey his young nephew. The battle lines were drawn with equal hopes. No longer were the Germans divided into scattered bands rushing here and there, as was their custom; through long warfare with the Romans, they had learned to follow their standards, support one another, and obey their commanders. Arminius, riding through the whole army, reminded each man of "their recovered liberty and the slaughtered <note>literally: 'torn to pieces'</note> legions." An honorable agreement was made, nor is there cause for regret <note>original: "ripitìo"—a cause for repentance or grievance</note>, since it rests with us whether we wish to fight anew or live in peace without bloodshed." Both armies were driven by these words and by their own particular reasons: the Cherusci and the Longobards fought for their glory and their newfound liberty, while the others fought to increase their dominion. The clash was never so powerful or the outcome so doubtful, because both right wings were broken; they would have rejoined the fray had Maroboduus not retreated to the hills. This was a sign that he was afraid, and so those who had fled in disarray abandoned him. He went among the Marcomanni and sent ambassadors to Tiberius to ask for help. Tiberius replied that Maroboduus could not ask the Romans for help against the Cherusci, since he had previously denied the Romans help against those very same people. Nonetheless, Drusus was sent, as we have said, to act as a peacemaker between them.

**XLVII.** In that same year, twelve noble cities of Asia were ruined by earthquakes that occurred at night, making the destruction more sudden and severe <note>original: "sprovveduto e grave scempio"—the disaster was particularly deadly because it caught people by surprise while they slept</note>. It was of no use, as is common in such cases, to flee into the open, because the earth opened up and swallowed people. There are accounts of mountains sinking, of plains being raised high, and of lightning flashes appearing amidst the crashing noise. The darkness was greatest among the Sardians, and for this reason Caesar <note>Referring here to the Emperor Tiberius</note> promised them two hundred and fifty thousand florins <note>The Italian translator uses "fiorini" as a contemporary equivalent for the massive sum of ten million sesterces recorded in Roman history</note> and exempted them for five years from everything they paid to the public treasury and the imperial coffers. The people of Magnesia-by-Sipylus received the second-greatest amount of relief and suffered the second-greatest damage. It was decided to relieve the inhabitants of Temnus, Philadelphia, Aegeae, Apollonia, Mostene, and the Macedonians <note>original: "Macedoni detti Ircani"—referring to the Hyrcanian Macedonians, descendants of colonists in the Hyrcanian plain of Lydia</note>, as well as Hierocaesarea, Myrina, Cyme, and Tmolus, from their tributes for the same period of time. It was also decided to send a senator of praetorian rank, rather than a consular one, to visit and provide for them. This was done so that he would not clash as an equal with the governor of Asia <note>who would typically be of consular rank</note> and cause delays; thus, **Marcus Aletus** was chosen.

...the rich inheritance of Emilia Musa, who died without a will <note>original: "senza testare"—intestate</note>, which would have gone to the imperial treasury, to Aemilius Lepidus, who seemed to belong to that family; and that of Patuleius, a rich Roman knight (although he left a part of it to Tiberius), to M. ---

1 $^*$ *burnt-out, very poor. With the same metaphor, our common people use the term "burnt" to mean having no money.*

2 $^*$ *rejected. In the Giuntina edition <note>A famous 16th-century edition of Tacitus printed by the Giunti family in Florence.</note>: "threw away."*

3 $^*$ *deprived... or permitted them to leave it. The Giuntina: "unseated or made them step down."*

4 $^*$ *impoverished by profligate living.* It is in the public interest that no one squanders their means, but rather preserves them for their descendants to maintain noble families and good men, as these make the republic happy. For when one who is rich and noble falls into necessity, he fears no law; he does not wish to stoop to ignoble tasks to survive, but gives himself over to robbery, gambling, betrayal, spying, and bearing false witness—*Pander, graft, and similar filth*; and these make the republic unhappy. This is the reason for the many sumptuary laws <note>Laws intended to restrain luxury and extravagance.</note> that are made every day and none of which are observed. And guardians are assigned to spendthrifts no less than to those who are insane. This was done in Rome by the magistrate with these most beautiful words:

> <note>original Latin: "QVANDO TVA BONA PATERNA AVITAQVE NEQVITIA TVA DISPERDIS, LIBEROSQVE TVOS AD EGESTATEM PERDVCIS; OB EAM REM TIBI EA RE COMMERCIOQVE INTERDICO."</note> SINCE YOU ARE SQUANDERING YOUR PATERNAL AND ANCESTRAL PROPERTY THROUGH YOUR OWN WICKEDNESS, AND BRINGING YOUR CHILDREN TO POVERTY; FOR THAT REASON, I FORBID YOU FROM THE ADMINISTRATION OF THAT PROPERTY AND FROM LEGAL COMMERCE.

Thus was the son of Fabius Maximus placed (as we say) under guardianship; for Rome could not endure that the property which was meant to maintain the great splendor of the Fabii should be gambled away. And the son of Sophocles tried to place him there, claiming he neglected his assets to attend to his tragedies: but Sophocles, reading to the judges the *Oedipus at Colonus* which he was then composing, showed them how much he was still in his right mind. Holy also was the ordinance of Solon, taken, says Herodotus, from the Egyptians—and I understand it is observed in China—that every person must give an account each year of their income and expenditure. For this reason Cleanthes, Menedemus, and Asclepiades were summoned to <unclear>give</unclear> an account of how it was that, possessing nothing and attending all day to philosophy, they remained so cheerful and <unclear>prosperous</unclear>. But when the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens.</note> heard from a miller and a gardener that every night they earned two silver drachmas each by turning the wheel and drawing water, the court gifted them two hundred. In Corinth, anyone who spent more than they earned was ordered to reduce their spending; and he who had no income and lived a lavish life was executed without further process, as it was assumed he must live by criminal acts. But Tiberius only took the senatorial dignity from these four "disheveled ones"—to use a new term our city has found for the "melters" of their assets—due to the new and excessive luxury flowing in— <meta>The text breaks at "entra-", likely continuing as "entrata" (income/influx).</meta>

**XLIX.** He dedicated to Bacchus, Proserpina, and Ceres the temple¹ vowed by the dictator Aulus Postumius; it had been begun by Augustus and damaged by time or fire, and was located beside the Great Circus. In the same place, he also dedicated the temple of Flora, commissioned by the ediles <note>Roman officials responsible for public buildings and festivals.</note> Lucius and Marcus Publicius; and the temple of Janus at the herb market, which Gaius Duillius built to commemorate the first Roman naval victory and the triumph over the Carthaginians. **L.** The law of the state was "growing its teeth,"² and Apuleia Varilia—the granddaughter of a sister of Augustus—was accused of having mocked him, Tiberius, and his mother, and of having committed adultery³ despite being so closely related to Caesar.⁴ Regarding the latter, she was referred to the Julian law.⁵

...all: pure poison to her life, which was founded on parsimony and industry; these are more necessary for her now than ever, as no more than a quarter of real estate remains in the hands of private laypeople, as shown by the census <note>original: "catasto"—a public registry of property for tax purposes</note>, and things continue this way while beggars are fed; which Pope Saint Sylvester provided should fall to the wealthy convents. 1 * *the temple:* it was not just one. The Latin: "*ædes*" <note>A building or sanctuary.</note>. 2 * *growing its teeth.* The Latin: "*adolescebat*" <note>To grow up or reach maturity.</note>; it was becoming stronger and making itself felt.

3 * *committed adultery.* To the ancient punishments for adultery collected by Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous 16th-century humanist scholar.</note> in his commentary on the 4th book regarding Aquilia and Varius Ligure, add this one told by Vopiscus regarding the Emperor Aurelian. He had the tops of two neighboring trees bent down, tied a foot of the culprit to each, and let them go. The body was torn into two pieces and remained there as a display, an example of the strict union of husband and wife being violently sundered.

**LIX.** [Year of Rome 772, Year of Christ 19]. During the consulship of Marcus Silanus and Lucius Norbanus, Germanicus traveled to Egypt to view its ancient wonders, though his stated purpose was to visit the province. He opened the public granaries and lowered the price of grain, performing many acts of kindness for the people: he walked without a guard, with bare feet,¹ and dressed in the Greek style, just as Scipio once did in Sicily, even during the heat of the Carthaginian war. Tiberius scolded him slightly² regarding his attire, but very harshly for entering Alexandria without his permission, contrary to the state secrets left by Augustus. Among these rules was that no senator or notable knight should enter Egypt without a permit; for a person with only a small force could hold that key to land and sea against great armies and starve Italy <note>Egypt was the "breadbasket" of Rome; controlling its grain supply was a powerful weapon of rebellion.</note>.

**LXI.** He also wished to see the other principal wonders: the stone statue of Memnon, which gives a vocal sound when struck by the sun's rays; the pyramids, like mountains reaching toward the sky, built by the wealth of rival princes amidst nearly impassable sands; the vast lakes dug as reservoirs for the overflowing waters of the Nile; and elsewhere, narrow, bottomless abysses. Then he came to Elephantine and Syene, which were then the limits of the Roman Empire, though today it extends to the Red Sea.

**LXII.** While Germanicus spent that summer sightseeing, <gloss>2</gloss> Drusus gained no small glory by sowing discord among the Germans and bringing about the downfall of the already weakened Maroboduus. Among the Gotones was a noble youth named Catualda, who had previously been driven out by the power of Maroboduus and now, in his rival’s moment of crisis, dared to take his revenge. He entered the lands of the Marcomanni with a strong force and, with the collusion of their leaders, stormed the royal city and its neighboring citadel. There they found the old spoils of the Suebi, as well as sutlers and merchants of our own country <note>Referring to Romans.</note> who, drawn by the freedom of trade and the lure of profit, had forgotten their homeland and settled among the enemy.

**LXIII.** Maroboduus, abandoned by everyone, had no other refuge but the mercy of Caesar <note>Referring here to Emperor Tiberius.</note>. He crossed the Danube into Bavaria and wrote to Tiberius—not as a fugitive or a suppliant, but with the tone of the man he used to be: <gloss>1</gloss>

> “Not Philip to the Athenians, nor Pyrrhus nor Antiochus to the Roman people, were ever so much to be feared.”

Maroboduus was kept in Ravenna, as if to show he was available to be restored to his kingdom if the Suebi <note>A large group of Germanic tribes.</note> should take up arms. Vibilius, leader of the Hermunduri, drove him out not long after; he was received at Forum Julii, a colony of Narbonesse Gaul. Those barbarians who accompanied both leaders were settled beyond the Danube, between the rivers Marus and Cuso, so as not to introduce such a breed of people into the peaceful provinces; Vannius, of the Quadi nation, was given to them as their ruler.

<gloss>1</gloss> *as the man he used to be*; that is, with the dignity suited to his former fortune.
<gloss>2</gloss> *and the freedom to depart whenever he wished, with his arrival etc.* The text carries this sense: “if his own interests later required otherwise, he could depart with the same guarantee of safety under which he had come.”
<gloss>3</gloss> *enter Rome in ovation*. In the greater triumph, the victorious general entered Rome crowned with laurel, in a chariot drawn by four horses, and sacrificed bulls. In the second kind <note>The ovation.</note>, he wore a crown of myrtle <note>original: *mortine*</note>, which is more associated with Venus than with Mars; he entered on foot with the people following behind, shouting for joy *ou, ou*. <meta>This page continues the transition from the military exploits of Germanicus to the diplomatic and administrative maneuvers of Tiberius. Having neutralized Maroboduus through diplomacy (as detailed on the previous page), the narrative now moves to the Roman Senate's response and the brewing conflict in Thrace between the rival kings Rhescuporis and Cotys.</meta>

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

->...the temple of Mars the Avenger with the portraits of the Caesars.<- And Tiberius rejoiced at having secured peace through wisdom, rather than having won a war through battles. Thus, he also thought to entrap Rhescuporis, the King of Thrace, through cunning. Previously, Rhemetalces had held that entire country; upon his death, Augustus divided Thrace between Rhescuporis, the brother of the deceased, and Cotys, the son. The cities, the cultivated lands, and the areas neighboring Greece fell to Cotys; the sterile, harsh lands bordering the enemy fell to Rhescuporis. This was in accordance with their natures: the former was kind and cheerful, while the latter was fierce, greedy, and could not suffer a partner. At first, Rhescuporis feigned contentment <gloss>1</gloss>, but then he began to encroach upon the lands of Cotys, making them his own; and if he was resisted, he used force. He maneuvered cautiously <gloss>3</gloss> while Augustus lived, fearing him because it was he who had granted the lands; but once Augustus was dead, Rhescuporis sent bandits to plunder and ruined fortresses to stir up war.

LXV. Tiberius, whose greatest concern was that settled affairs should not be disturbed, sent a centurion to tell them not to settle their disputes with arms. Cotys immediately dismissed his people; Rhescuporis, with an air of total modesty, said, "Let us meet, for we might come to an agreement." There was no dispute over the time, place, or manner, as the gentle one conceded and accepted everything, while the treacherous one <gloss>4</gloss> planned his move. To solemnize the accord (so he said), Rhescuporis held a grand banquet where, at midnight, amid the joy of the food and wine, he threw Cotys into chains. When Cotys realized the deception, he invoked the sacred rights of kingship, the gods they both shared, and the safety of the dinner table. Having seized all of Thrace, Rhescuporis wrote to Tiberius, claiming he had merely struck first against a plotter. Meanwhile, he strengthened himself with new cavalry and infantry, saying he was preparing for war against the Bastarnae and the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic and tribal peoples of the regions north of the Black Sea.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the account of Roman diplomacy and intrigue in the frontier kingdoms of Thrace and the East. We follow the aftermath of the conflict between the Thracian kings Rhescuporis and Cotys, and the failed escape attempt of the deposed Parthian king, Vonones. The narrative highlights Tiberius's preference for achieving his ends through deception and "craftiness" rather than open warfare.</meta>

LXVI. **Tiberius** wrote back gently: "If there were no treachery, you should be of good heart; however, neither the Emperor nor the Senate can distinguish right from wrong without knowing the facts of the case. Deliver the prisoner and come to clear your name." **Latinius Pandus**, the vice-governor of **Moesia**, sent this letter along with soldiers to take custody of **Cotys**. **Rhescuporis**, caught for a time between fear and anger, chose to be guilty of a completed crime rather than one merely begun: he murdered **Cotys** and falsely claimed that the man had killed himself. Caesar [Tiberius] did not abandon his craftiness; when **Pandus** died—whom **Rhescuporis** alleged was his personal enemy—the Emperor purposefully sent **Pomponius Flaccus** to that government. Flaccus was a veteran soldier and a close friend of the king, and was therefore better suited to trap him. <note>original: "a giugnerlo." The Latin source text uses "ad fallendum," meaning "to deceive."</note>

LXVII. **Flaccus** traveled to **Thrace** and, through skillful use of grand promises, cajoled <note>original: "carrucolò." The Latin source is "perpulit," meaning urged or drove.</note> the king into the Roman lines, even though the king felt his own guilt. <note>meaning: he was aware he had committed a crime.</note> A strong band of men surrounded him under the guise of an honor guard; tribunes and centurions kept urging him to come forward and not to doubt. As they progressed, the guard became more obvious, and eventually, under open force which he finally understood, they brought him to **Rome**. The wife of **Cotys** accused him before the Senate; he was condemned to imprisonment outside his kingdom. **Thrace** was then divided between **Rhemetalces**, his son (who was known to have opposed his father), and the young children of **Cotys**. Since they were still minors, **Trebellienus Rufus**, a former praetor, was appointed as their guardian and governor of the kingdom—following the historical precedent of **Marcus Lepidus**, who was sent to **Egypt** to act as guardian for the children of **Ptolemy**. **Rhescuporis** was sent to **Alexandria**, where he was eventually killed, either during a genuine escape attempt or one that was staged to justify his death.

LXVIII. At the same time, **Vonones**, who had been waylaid (as I previously mentioned) in **Cilicia**, corrupted his guards in order to flee. Under the pretext of going on a hunt, he intended to escape through the lands of the **Armenians** to the **Albanians** and **Heniochi**, and finally to his relative, the King of **Scythia**. Leaving the coastal areas, he took to the woods and rode at full gallop toward the **Pyramus** river. However, the locals, having heard of the king's flight, had broken the bridge. Since he could not ford the river, **Vibius Frontone**, a cavalry captain, recaptured him on the riverbank. Then **Remmius**, an *evocatus* <note>An "evocatus" was a veteran soldier who, having completed his years of service, was invited to serve again with special status and pay.</note> who had been his primary guard, immediately [struck him] with a dag— <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("stoc-"), likely referring to a "stocco" or rapier/dagger.</note>

**LXXXII.** Where the news of Germanicus’s illness, being renewed and growing as it traveled from afar, caused grief, anger, and loose tongues to burst forth.
> “Behold why they banished him to the ends of the earth; ⁴* this is why Piso was given the province; this is what the whispers of the Augusta with Plancina ⁵* were plotting. Our elders spoke truly of Drusus: that princes do not want sons who are citizens. They were planning to restore liberty and make themselves equal ⁶* to the Roman people; for this reason, they have been taken away.”

The report of his death so inflamed these voices of the people that, without any decree or proclamation, a public holiday was observed: doors, shops, and windows were closed. All was horror, silence, and weeping, coming from deep within the heart, beyond all the usual demonstrations used in funerals. Certain merchants, who had left Syria when Germanicus was improving, brought this news: immediately it was believed and spread. Some told others, and those to many more; though not well understood, it was always magnified, and people joyfully reported it. They ran through the streets and beat upon the doors of the temples; the night helped the belief, and the darkness helped the affirmation. Tiberius did not oppose the error, but let it vanish with time. The people later mourned him even more desperately, as if he had been taken from them a second time.

Let his name be sung by the Salii <note>The Salii were an ancient college of priests who sang sacred hymns during processions</note>: let curule chairs crowned with oak be placed for him in the theaters: in the places of the priests of Augustus, and in the games of the circus, let his ivory image be carried at the head of the procession: let no augur or flamen be appointed in his place unless they are of the Julian house. Arches were built in Rome, on the banks of the Rhine, and in Syria <term>Soria: the historical Italian name for Syria</term> on Mount Amanus, with epitaphs of his deeds and how he died for the republic: a sepulcher in Antioch where he was cremated: a tribunal in Epidaphne where he breathed his last. Tiberius granted it as he had for others,¹ saying that greater fortune does not make for greater eloquence: it was enough to place him among the ancient writers. The order of the knights renamed the "wedge" of horses, previously called the "Juniors,"² after Germanicus, and established that in the mid-July cavalry review³ his image should be carried as a banner. Of these honors, many are still observed; some were abandoned immediately or over time.

**LXXXIV.** In the midst of this grief, Livia <note>Also known as Livilla</note>, the sister of Germanicus and wife of Drusus, gave birth to twin boys. This event, rare and joyful even to men of modest means, caused Tiberius such great joy that he broke out in a boast before the Senate, saying that no other Roman of his high rank had ever had two grandsons from a single birth: turning even matters of fortune into personal glory. But the people were saddened even by this in such a circumstance, seeing that the opening house⁴ of Drusus seemed to close off that of Germanicus.

Retranslate this whole passage as follows: “the order of the knights named the ‘wedge of Germanicus’ that which was previously called the ‘wedge of the young’.” By “wedges” (*cunei*), understand the sections formed by the stairs that intersect the rows of seats in the theater and amphitheater. These sections were shaped like wedges. (See Maffei, *Verona Illustrata*, part IV, book II, chap. 8.) In the fourteen rows near the orchestra reserved for the knights, one of these sections was called *of the young*, because those knights who had not yet reached the age of 45 sat there. Germanicus, having died at the age of 34, belonged to this order. Hence that honorary title.

**LXXXV.** In that same year, the senate issued severe decrees against female immorality, establishing that no woman whose father, grandfather, or husband was a Roman knight¹ should ever make herself available for profit <note>This refers to registering as a prostitute</note>. This followed the case of Vestilia, a woman of a praetorian family, who had registered herself with the aediles <term>Aediles: Roman officials responsible for public order and morals</term>. The ancients allowed this practice, believing that for a high-born woman, the mere act of publicly declaring her own lack of chastity was punishment enough. Her husband, Titidio Labeone, was summoned to explain why he had not sought the legal punishment for his guilty² and publicly disgraced wife. When he made the excuse that the sixty days granted for deliberation had not yet passed, it was decided to judge her case alone (as she was the primary offender); she was subsequently confined to the island of Seriphos³. A proposal was also discussed to expel Egyptian and Jewish religious rites from the city. The fathers <note>The Senators</note> decreed that four thousand freedmen of these faiths, who were of military age, should be transported to Sardinia to suppress banditry there; if they should perish from the foul air of that place, it would be little loss. The rest were given a set time to either renounce their beliefs or depart from Italy.

**LXXXVI.** Caesar <note>Tiberius</note> then suggested that a new virgin should be elected to replace Occia, who had governed the sacred orders of Vesta with the highest sanctity for fifty-seven years. Fonteius Agrippa and Domitius Pollio offered their daughters, and Caesar thanked them for their willingness to compete in service to the republic. Pollio’s daughter was preferred, solely because her mother still lived with her first husband, whereas Agrippa had diminished the standing of his household through a divorce. However, Caesar consoled the other girl with a dowry of twenty-five thousand florins <note>original: "fiorini"; the translator uses contemporary currency to represent the Roman sesterces</note>.

**LXXXVII.** As the common people were complaining about the high cost of living, he fixed a price for grain and promised to give twenty soldi <note>original: "venzoldi"; a contemporary Italian coin</note> per bushel⁴ to those who...

¹ *Roman knight.* The first rank of dignity was held by the senators; the second by the Roman knights. ² *for his guilty wife.* When a husband did not see to the punishment of a dishonorable wife, the magistrate would intervene.

A sestertius was a quarter of a denarius; a denarius was a tenth of a fine gold drachma; a drachma is our florin, which is worth ten lire today. Tiberius therefore gave two sestertii per *modius*, which is four per bushel, which equals one denarius, which is a tenth of a florin, which is one lira, or rather twenty small soldi. ...nor did he accept the name of "Father of the Country," which had been offered to him on other occasions, and he rebuked those who called his duties "divine" and referred to him as "Lord" <note>original: *Signore*, translating the Latin *Dominus*, a title Tiberius famously rejected as implying a master-slave relationship</note>: so much so that it was difficult and dangerous to speak under a prince who held free speech in suspicion and flattery in hatred.

**LXXXVIII.** The elders and writers of those times say that letters were read in the senate from Adgandestrius, prince of the Chatti <term>Chatti: A powerful Germanic tribe located in modern-day Hesse</term>, who promised the death of Arminius if poison were sent to him. The reply was that the Roman people took revenge on their enemies with open arms, and not with trickery; in this glory, Tiberius equaled those ancients who discovered the plot of the poisoner against Pyrrhus <note>King Pyrrhus of Epirus, a famous enemy of early Rome</note> and sent him away. Arminius, after the Romans departed and Maroboduus <note>A rival Germanic king</note> was driven out, sought to reign as king; but those tribes fought him for their liberty with varying fortune, and he died by the treachery of his own relatives. He was, without doubt, the liberator of Germany; a challenger not of the early Roman people, as other warriors and kings had been, but of the Empire at its most powerful. In individual battles he had mixed results, but in the overall war he was undefeated. He lived thirty-seven years and commanded for twelve. The barbarians still sing of him; the Greeks do not count him in their annals, because they only boast of their own history. Nor is he celebrated by us Romans as much as he deserves; for we magnify ancient things and care little for the present.

# THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ANNALS
### BY
# GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

### SUMMARY.

I. Agrippina travels with the ashes of Germanicus to Brindisi, then to Rome. These are entombed in the tomb of Augustus: the funeral rites. — VII. Drusus returns to Illyricum. — VIII. Gnaeus Piso, having returned to Rome, is accused of poisoning and treason. After delivering a speech and seeing everything go poorly for him, he takes his own life. — XX. Tacfarinas rekindles the war in Africa, which is suppressed by Proconsul L. Apronius. — XXII. Aemilia Lepida is accused of adultery and poisoning and is condemned. — XXV. The Papian-Poppaean law <note>A law intended to encourage marriage and child-bearing</note>, which had been strictly enforced until then, is softened by Tiberius; its complexities are untangled: the origin and history of the laws. — XXX. The distinguished L. Volusius and Sallustius Crispus die. — XXXI. Tiberius in Campania. — XXXII. Tacfarinas attacks Africa once more. Junius Blaesus is chosen to guard it. — XXXVII. Certain equestrians <term>equestrians: Members of the Roman knightly class, second in rank only to senators</term> are condemned for treason <note>original: "maestà," referring to *maiestas*, or crimes against the dignity of the state</note>. — XXXVIII. Discord among the Thracians. — XL. The Gallic cities rebel to no avail under the leaders Julius Sacrovir and Julius Florus: their army, beaten by the Germanic legions, returns to the yoke. — XLIX. C. Lutorius, a knight condemned for treason, dies in prison. — LII. An attempt is made to moderate luxury, but it is abandoned. — LVI. Drusus receives tribunician power. — LVIII. The Priest of Jupiter <term>flamine di Giove: The Flamen Dialis, a high priest bound by ancient and restrictive rituals</term> is forbidden from requesting a province. — LX. Greek sanctuaries are visited and cleared of abuses. — LXVI. C. Silanus is condemned for extortion and treason. — LXXIII. Junius Blaesus brings trouble to Tacfarinas and captures his brother. — LXXV. Illustrious deaths and funerals.

**I.** She stayed for a few days to compose herself. <note>original: "a moderarsi," to regain a little calm. Latin: *componendo animo*. The manuscript originally had "to temper herself," but it was erased and rewritten as above.</note> When her arrival was heard of, her intimates, the soldiers who had served under Germanicus, and even those unknown to her from neighboring lands—some feeling a duty toward the prince, others simply following the crowd—poured into the port of Brindisi, as it was the nearest and safest harbor. At the sight of the fleet, the port, the shore, the walls, the roofs, and the highest lookout points were filled by a sad crowd, asking one another whether they should receive her with silence, or with words, or with some specific action as she disembarked. The fleet approached with the rowers appearing stunned, without the usual celebratory cheers. She stepped off the ship with her two children and with the tearful vessel <note>The funerary urn.</note> in her hands, upon which she cast her eyes down. <note>original: "ove affisò." She did not stare at the urn; rather, *defixit oculos in terram* (she cast her eyes to the ground), as is typical of the sorrowful.</note> A cry of lamentation rose from the women and men, both her own attendants and others, indistinguishable from one another; except that the grief of her own court was more exhausted from the long-endured tribulation. <note>original: "più stanco." The manuscript originally read "more languid," but was later corrected. Latin for tribulation: *maeror* (sorrow).</note>

**II.** [Year of Rome 773, Year of Christ 20.] Caesar <note>Referring here to the Emperor Tiberius.</note> sent two cohorts as a guard, with orders that in Calabria, Puglia, and Campania, the magistrates should perform the funeral rites for his son. Tribunes and captains, therefore, carried the ashes upon their shoulders, with unadorned <note>"Soiled" is perhaps too strong; the Latin *incompta* means unadorned or disheveled.</note> banners before them and the fasces <term>fasces: A bundle of rods with an axe, symbolizing a magistrate's power; here, they were held upside down as a sign of mourning</term> reversed. The common people of the colonies through which they passed wore black, and the knights wore mourning robes; according to their means, they burned garments and perfumes, along with other solemnities for the dead. From towns even off the path of the journey, people came to meet them, to offer sacrifices to that soul, and to show their sorrow with tears and cries. Drusus came as far as Terracina with his brother Claudio and the children of Germanicus who had remained in Rome. Marco Valerio and Marco Aurelio, the new consuls, the senate, and a great part of the people all crowded the road in a great throng, <term>bulimà: A crowd or a great flock of people</term> and they wept despite the joy of Tiberius, which was poorly hidden and known to all; he was happy at the death of Germanicus but could not openly flatter that feeling.

**IV.** The day the ashes were placed in the tomb of Augustus, Rome seemed at times like a cavern for its silence, and at other times like an inferno for its weeping. ...scarcely a day [of mourning]; his uncle <note>The Emperor Tiberius.</note> did not even appear at the door. Where are the ancient customs? The effigy placed atop the bier? The translator notes that in the Kingdom of Naples, women called *triboli*—hired mourners—still perform these rituals, screaming, scratching their faces, and recounting the virtues of the deceased. **VI.** Tiberius was aware of these public outcries, and to suppress them, he issued a formal proclamation to the people: "Many illustrious Romans have died for the republic, but no death has ever been celebrated with such fervor. This is honorable to the deceased and to all of us, provided it is kept within limits; for the same behaviors do not suit princes and a ruling people that suit private households and small cities. <note>original: "non convenendo a' principi... le cose medesime." This refers to the displays of grief mentioned above. The scholar Curzio Picchena, a diligent secretary and student of Tacitus, suggested the Latin text should read: "For the same honors are not fitting for leading men and a ruling people as they are for modest households or cities." He argues Tiberius meant that such indignities of public weeping were beneath the dignity of his own rank.</note> Grief and tears were owed to the fresh wound of loss, but now the mind must be steadied and melancholy cast away. This is how the divine Julius and Augustus acted when the former lost his only daughter and the latter his grandsons. One need only remember how many times the Roman people bravely endured defeated armies, the death of generals, and the total extinction of noble families. Princes are mortal; the republic is eternal. Therefore, return to your business and—since the Megalesian Games <note>A festival held in April in honor of Cybele, the "Great Mother" of the gods.</note> are approaching—return also to your pleasures."

**VII.** At that point, the public holiday ended. Drusus departed for the armies in Illyricum. <note>original: "Schiavonia," a historical name for the Balkan regions of the eastern Adriatic.</note> Everyone waited with bated breath for the punishment of Piso; they could not find peace knowing that he remained in the gardens of Asia and Achaia enjoying himself, using such an arrogant and malicious delay to destroy the evidence of his crimes. It had become common knowledge that Martina, the notorious sorceress whom Gnaeus Sentius was sending to Rome, had—as I mentioned—died suddenly in Brindisi.

**VIII.** Piso sent his son ahead to Rome, well-instructed on how to appease the prince <note>Emperor Tiberius</note>, while he himself went to see Drusus. He hoped to find Drusus not so much embittered by the death of his brother <note>Germanicus</note> as he was softened by the removal of such a powerful rival. Tiberius, to show that the legal proceedings would be handled properly, received the young man and granted him the favors usually given to the sons of noble families. In public, Drusus said to Piso: "If what they say were true, it would grieve me more than anyone; but I pray to the gods that these are merely fables, and that the death of Germanicus does not bring ruin upon anyone at all. <gloss>1</gloss>" It was recognized that these words were the "grass of Tiberius," <gloss>2</gloss> by whose ancient arts this gentle and un-cunning youth was being guided.

**IX.** Piso sailed to Dalmatia and then to Ancona, where he left his ships. Traveling through the Marches and then along the Flaminian Way, he caught up with a legion that was marching from Hungary <note>original: "Ungheria." The translator uses the contemporary name for the Roman province of Pannonia.</note> to Rome, to then be sent to Africa <gloss>3</gloss> as a guard; it was said that during the journey, he often presented himself to the soldiers among the ranks. To avoid further suspicion, or perhaps because fear makes one dazed, he had himself carried from Narni down the Nera River into the Tiber. This only reignited the people's anger, as the banks were crowded on that solemn day. They saw him disembark at the Tomb of the Caesars <note>The Mausoleum of Augustus.</note> with a great retinue—he with his followers and his wife Plancina with her ladies—all with their heads held high. What disgusted people most of all was seeing his house on the square decorated for a feast, the lavish banquet prepared, the doors wide open, and the festivities in full swing.

**X.** The following day, Fulcinius Trio summoned Piso before the consuls. Vitellius, Veranius, and the others who had been with Germanicus argued that Trio had no business in this matter; they did not wish to act as accusers, but as witnesses to carry out the dying wishes of Germanicus. Trio obtained permission to accuse him at least of his other past misdeeds. The prince <note>Tiberius</note> was petitioned to be the judge of this case; and neither...

---

<gloss>1</gloss> The translator chose to omit: <note>original: "Hæc palam et vitato omni secreto"</note> "These things were said openly and avoiding all secrecy," feeling it was enough to have said above "Drusus said to Piso in public," where the original Latin text simply has <note>original: "Drusus Pisoni"</note> "Drusus to Piso."

<gloss>2</gloss> These words were recognized as "the grass of Tiberius"; that is, they were whispered or suggested to Drusus by Tiberius. The Latin has: <note>original: "neque dubitabantur præscripta ei a Tiberio"</note> "nor was it doubted that these things were prescribed to him by Tiberius."

<gloss>3</gloss> *a legion that was going...* to Rome, to pass into *Africa*; for the war against Tacfarinas <note>A Numidian deserter who led a long-running insurrection against Rome.</note>, where one legion usually remained (though another, the Ninth, was later recalled).

...the accused was displeased; fearing that love the people and the senators <note>original: "padri" (fathers), a standard term for the Roman Senate</note> held for Germanicus. Meanwhile, Tiberius made a great mockery of the people’s talk, saying: "He and his mother were personally interested in this: a single judge distinguishes the facts from what is believed better than a crowd; hatred and envy blind the many." Tiberius, knowing how important this judgment was and the weight it removed from him; <gloss>1</gloss> heard the threats and defenses of the parties in the presence of some of his court, and then referred the matter to the senate.

**XI.** During this time, Drusus returned from Illyria. The senators <note>original: "padri"</note> wished that, because he had received Maroboduus and for other deeds of that summer, he should enter Rome with the lesser triumph <term>ovation: a minor victory procession where the general entered on foot or horseback rather than in a chariot</term>, shouting "Ou, où;" <gloss>2</gloss> but this honor was postponed. Piso sought out Lucius Arruntius, Fulcinius, Asinius Gallus, Aeserninus, Marcellus, and Sextus Pompeius to be his advocates; but as they all offered various excuses, Marcus Lepidus, Lucius Piso, and Livineius Regulus accepted. The whole city was on edge, watching to see how faithful Germanicus’s friends would be; what the accused would rely upon; and whether Tiberius would reveal his true feelings or not. <gloss>3</gloss> Never was the people so curious, nor did they whisper so much against the prince, or suspect him in their silence.

**XII.** Therefore, Caesar <note>Emperor Tiberius</note> gave the senators this carefully composed <gloss>4</gloss> and balanced speech: "Piso was a lieutenant and friend of my father: by your order, I gave him as an aid to Germanicus to rule <gloss>5</gloss> the East. Whether he embittered the young man there through disobedience or contention, and rejoiced at his death, or truly caused him to die criminally; this must now be judged without animosity. If it is proven <gloss>6</gloss> that he stepped outside the obedience a lieutenant owes to his commander...

<gloss>1 * "and the weight it removed from him." See the note to chapter 46, book I.</gloss>
<gloss>2 * "shouting 'Ou ou'." In the Giuntina edition, it is written "Ou où." The Latin text says: "ut ovans iniret;" that is, that he should enter with the honor of a triumph <note>specifically an ovation</note>.</gloss>
<gloss>3 "Whether Tiberius revealed himself or not." It is better to read as the Medici text does: *Satin' cohiberet ac promeret sensus suos Tiberius, is haud alias intentior: Populus plus sibi, etc.* And to say: "Whether Tiberius knew how to hide what he had done (*), for he never labored harder at it: nor did the people whisper more against the prince, or suspect him in silence;" that is, suspecting him of having commissioned Piso to poison Germanicus. That word *promeret* was contrary, superfluous, not typical of Tacitus, and lacked grace.</gloss>
<gloss>4 "carefully composed speech": of stupendous prudence, highly noteworthy.</gloss>
<gloss>5 * "rule." The Manuscript says: "govern;" later corrected as above.</gloss>
<gloss>6 * "If it is proven, etc."; that is, when it is proven that he disobeyed, etc., and that he rejoiced, etc. — The Nestiana edition, instead of "a suo," reads "al suo."</gloss>

<gloss>(*) "what he had done." The Giuntina copy with autograph notes owned by Count Mortara corrects this to: "what he had in his heart."</gloss>

...if he has rejoiced in his death and my grief, I shall hate him and banish him from my house, punishing a private enmity of mine, and not as a prince with the force of the state. <note>1</note> But if a capital crime is found in anyone, provide just comfort to Germanicus’s children and to us, his father and grandmother. Clarify as well if Piso has stirred up and troubled the army; if he has gained the soldiers through trickery; if he has attempted to retake the province by arms; or if these are merely falsehoods spread and amplified by the accusers out of excessive affection, for which I have cause to complain. What an indignity it was to strip that body naked and expose it to the eyes of the people to be almost mistreated? To fill the world with the claim that he was poisoned, if it is still unknown and under investigation? I mourn my son and shall mourn him forever: yet I do not forbid the accused from producing every proof of his innocence or any wrong received from Germanicus. And I pray you that my grief does not make you take the accusations given as proven facts. If there are relatives or confidants to defend him, help him with all eloquence and diligence; and likewise <note>2</note> on the contrary, let the accusers sharpen their arguments. Let it be enough of a privilege for Germanicus that his death is investigated in the Senate council, and not in a regular court by a judge: in all else, let the process be equal. Let no one look to the tears of Druso, nor to my grief, nor to anything that might be falsely said about us."

XIII. Two days were given as a limit to speak against him; six to prepare; <note>3</note> and three to defend himself. Fulcinius said that he had ruled Spain with ambition and greed; these were old and trivial sins which, even if proven, did not harm him (if the new charges were cleared <note>4</note>), nor, if defended against, did they release him from the more serious ones. After him, Servaeus and Veranius and Vitellius, with equal heat—but Vitellius with more eloquence—accused Piso of having, in order to ruin Germanicus...

<note>1 **"punishing a private enmity of mine, and not as a prince with the force of the state."** Previously read as *novi principis* (new prince), which was incorrect; it was corrected to *non principis* (not as prince), which was not bad; now I see *non vi principis* (not with the force of a prince), which is excellent; and I correct myself: *not as a prince with force.* The Latin text says: <note>original: "et privatas inimicitias non vi principis ulciscar"</note>; which Orelli interprets as: "I will not use the power that a prince has; but I will avenge the harms done to me as a private citizen."</note>

<note>2 **"likewise"**; the original word *alsì* is an archaic form of *altresì*. Also used in Book I, chapter 26; Book II, chapter 64.</note>

<note>3 **"to prepare;"** that is, six days were granted to the accused to study and organize his defense, and three to deliver it before the judges. Whereas the accusers were given, in total, only two days. From this one can see which way Tiberius was leaning.</note>

<note>4 **"cleared"**, if he had succeeded in clearing himself.</note>

...Germanicus and to overturn the state, the dregs of the soldiers with license and insolence toward the allies, <gloss>1</gloss> corrupted in such a way that the worst of them called him the "father of the legions"; used, on the contrary, every cruelty toward the best men and especially toward the friends and followers of Germanicus; and finally, that he had poisoned, bewitched, and sacrificed him—both he and Plancina—to demons: that he had attacked the republic with arms, and that to be able to bring him to trial, it had been necessary to fight and defeat him in battle.

**XIV.** There was no defense against the charges of having bribed the soldiers, of giving the province into the hands of the most wicked men, and of slandering his general: only the charge of poisoning seemed refuted. This was because the accusers claimed that while Piso was dining with Germanicus and reclining above him, <gloss>2</gloss> he poisoned the food with his own hands. It did not seem plausible that among another man's servants, with so many eyes upon him and in the presence of Germanicus himself, he would dare such a thing; Piso even requested that his own servants and those of Germanicus be put to the torture to prove his innocence. But the judges were hostile to him for various reasons: Caesar <note>Referring here to the Emperor Tiberius.</note> because Piso had waged war against a Roman province; the Senate, because they could never believe that Germanicus died without foul play <gloss>3</gloss>.... Which both Tiberius and Piso denied. Outside, the people were shouting, "If the fathers <note>The Senators.</note> acquit him, he shall not escape our hands," and they began breaking his statues and dragging them toward the Gemonian Stairs, <note>The Gemonian Stairs were a flight of steps leading to the Forum where the bodies of executed criminals were displayed before being thrown into the Tiber.</note> had the prince not ordered them to be saved and restored. Piso was placed in a litter and escorted home by a tribune of a praetorian cohort; some said this was to protect him, while others whispered it was to ensure his end.

**XV.** Plancina was no less hated, but she was more favored by the court: thus it was unknown how much Caesar might be able to decide regarding her. As long as there was some hope for Piso, she promised to share his fortune and, if necessary, to die with him. But once she obtained a pardon through the secret prayers of Augusta, <note>Livia, the mother of Tiberius and grandmother of Germanicus.</note> she distanced herself from her husband and divided her cause from his.

There were three people, and Germanicus was in the middle, says Lipsius. <note>Justus Lipsius was a famous 16th-century scholar known for his editions of Tacitus.</note> He does not prove it, and it does not satisfy me.

**3** *never being able to believe.* Without the words "they had written, demanding an explanation," <note>original Latin: "scripsissent expostulantes"</note> the meaning follows very well. ...his own cause. **XVII.** Tiberius excused the young man for the civil war commanded by his father, as he was forced to obey him, and he expressed sorrow for the noble family and the heavy misfortune of the deceased <note>Piso, who has committed suicide.</note>, whatever he might have deserved. **XVIII.** Regarding this sentence, the prince <note>The Emperor Tiberius</note> moderated many things: he ruled that Piso’s name should not be erased from the records, since the names of Mark Antony, who made war against his country, and Iullus Antonius, who violated the house of Augustus, still remained. He also ruled that Marcus <note>Piso’s son</note> should not receive that mark of disgrace <note>original: *frego*</note> and should enjoy his inheritance; for Tiberius, as I have stated, was not greedy, and the shame of having acquitted Plancina made him less harsh. Nor would he allow a golden statue to be consecrated in the temple of Mars the Avenger, as Valerius Messalinus wished; nor another to Vengeance, as Caecina Severus proposed. He argued that such monuments are for foreign victories, whereas domestic misfortunes should be buried in grief.² When Messalinus added that thanks should be given to Tiberius, Augusta <note>Livia</note>, Antonia, Agrippina, and Drusus for the avenging of Germanicus, Lucius Asprenas asked him in the presence of the Senate: "And Claudius? Did you leave him out on purpose?³" Then the name "and Claudius"⁴ was added to the record. The more I reflect upon both ancient and recent history, the more I find reason to laugh at the affairs of mortals. For everyone else was rumored,⁵ hoped for, or venerated as a future prince except for this man, whom fortune held in reserve.

**XIX.** A few days later, Caesar <note>Tiberius</note> had the Senate grant certain priesthoods to Vitellius, Veranius, and Servaeus. To Fulcinius he promised his support should he seek⁶ honors, but warned him not to "break the neck" of his rhetoric through excessive zeal.⁷ Here ended the vengeance

<gloss>
¹ *frego*: a scar, mark, or disgrace.
² *domestic misfortunes should be buried in grief*. Augustus made such matters public (*) and was criticized for it. Domitian, Amyntas, Philip, and others kept them hidden and were praised. Lorenzo de' Medici reminded a man who wanted to resort to bloodshed that in Florence, the latrines <note>original: *agiamenti*</note> are emptied at night <note>A metaphor for handling dirty affairs privately</note>.
³ *on purpose?* <note>original: *a sciente?*</note>. Implicitly, "with a conscious mind"; the ancients spoke this way with refinement; we say "intentionally" or "on purpose" more crudely.
⁴ *Claudius*, the brother of Germanicus, was a man considered so inept that he was easily forgotten even by flatterers; yet he was the only member of the family who eventually reached the imperial throne.
⁵ *was rumored*. See Book II, 56.
⁶ *should he seek*, meaning "whenever he might ask."
⁷ *not to break the neck of his rhetoric*. This man, by pressing so hard against Piso and Plancina (**), as mentioned a little above, moved the listeners to pity and thus secured their release. — *through excessive zeal*. The Manuscript reads: "and warned him not to do to rhetoric, for..."

(*) *made them public, and below, kept them hidden*, referring to the "evils"! All the best printings read this way, and I have not dared to correct "them" (*le*) to the masculine form, having seen other times that our author <note>the translator Davanzati</note> uses the feminine pronoun instead of the masculine as a certain stylistic quirk.
(**) The Giuntina edition: "by too much attacking Plancina... he placed her;" and the phrase "and secured their release" is missing.

# THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ANNALS #

...his rhetoric by pushing too hard <note>The Italian translator is refining a phrase here about not "breaking the neck" of one's own eloquence by over-exerting it; the original Latin implies a "violent headlong rush" of speech</note>;" then he spoke of the death of Germanicus as narrated by those who were living, which differs from later accounts:¹ so poorly are the greatest events understood. Some hold what they hear as certain truth; others distort the facts; and both errors are magnified by those who come after. Drusus, in order to reclaim his military rank, left Rome and then re-entered ² in ovation. A few days later, his mother Vipsania died—the only child of Agrippa to die a natural death; as for the others, it was known they died by the sword, or it was believed they died by poison or hunger.

**XX.** In that same year, Tacfarinate—who the previous summer had been defeated by Camillus, as has been mentioned ³—renewed the war in Africa. At first, he raided much of the countryside with impunity due to his speed; he destroyed villages and took great spoils. Later, he besieged a Roman cohort near the Pagida river in a fort held by Decrio, a brave and experienced soldier. To Decrio, it seemed a disgrace to endure a siege; having encouraged his men, he led them outside to fight. They gave way at the first assault. He threw himself into the thick of the weapons; he blocked those who fled; he shouted at the standard-bearers, asking if Roman soldiers would turn their backs to swindlers and rabble. Covered in wounds, having lost an eye, he threw himself forward against the enemy blades and, though abandoned by his own men, continued to fight until he fell. ⁴

**XXI.** At such news, Lucius Apronius—who had succeeded Camillus—being more moved by the shame of his own men than by the glory of the enemy, took one in ten of the disgraced cohort by lot (a punishment rare in those times) and had them beaten to death. ⁵ This severity was so effective that a commander of no more than five hundred veteran infantrymen defeated those same forces of Tacfarinate at the fortress of Thala...

...our fortress, they beat upon it. There, Helvius Rufus, a common soldier, earned the **civic crown** <note>original: "corona di cittadino salvato" — a prestigious military honor awarded to a soldier who saved the life of a fellow Roman citizen in battle.</note>. Caesar <note>The Emperor Tiberius.</note> granted it to him, and complained to Apronius—though without true displeasure—that as proconsul he had not also given him this honor, along with the decorative collars and the spear. <note>original: "le collane e l'asta" — standard military decorations for bravery.</note> Tacfarinas, as the Numidians were frightened and no longer willing to endure sieges, spread his forces through the countryside; when confronted, he would slip away and then circle back to the rear. As long as the barbarian maintained this strategy, he mocked and exhausted the Romans. But when he descended to the coastal marshlands and remained in camp to guard his plunder, Apronius Caesianus was sent by his father with cavalry and auxiliary infantry, along with the swiftest of the legions; he fought them successfully and drove them into the deserts.

**XXII.** In Rome, Aemilia Lepida—who, besides the splendor of her noble house, could count Lucius Sulla and Gnaeus Pompey as great-grandfathers—was accused of faking a childbirth to Publius Quirinius, a rich and childless man. She was also accused of adultery, poisoning, and seeking <term>prophecies<note>original: "pronostichi" — specifically, consulting astrologers about the fate of the Imperial family, which was considered a form of treason.</note></term> from <term>Chaldeans<note>The term "Chaldeans" was used to describe astrologers and diviners, so called because their art was believed to have originated in ancient Chaldea (Mesopotamia).</note></term> regarding the house of Caesar. Her brother, Manius Lepidus, defended her. Quirinius had already divorced her, yet his continued pursuit of her caused people to feel pity for her, despite her being guilty and infamous. It was hard to see how the Prince <note>Tiberius.</note> intended the matter to go, as he so frequently shifted and mixed anger with mercy. First, he asked the Senate not to treat the case as a matter of treason <note>original: "maestà" — the crime of *laesa maiestas* or diminished majesty against the state.</note>; then he urged Marcus Servilius, a former consul, and other witnesses to testify about things he had previously suggested should be kept quiet. On the other hand, he transferred Lepida's slaves from the custody of the soldiers to that of the consuls <note>This was considered a "looser" or less severe form of imprisonment.</note> and refused to let them be tortured regarding matters involving his own household. Furthermore, he requested that Drusus, the consul-elect, let someone else voice their opinion first. Some attributed this to his civility, not wanting to compel others to follow his lead; others said he was so cruel that he would only have yielded his turn to ensure she was condemned.

**XXIV.** Having lost Piso of the Calpurnian house and Lepida of the Aemilian house in a short time, the return of Decimus Silanus to the Junian house brought some comfort to the misfortunes of these three great families. <note>The translator follows a correction by Mercerus: "Decimus Silanus, restored to the Junii, repaired the hateful losses suffered in a short time by the Calpurnii (Piso) and the Aemilii (Lepida)."</note> I will briefly recount his case. He drove them from Rome and had their lovers killed or exiled. He turned these common offenses into "crimes of state" and "sacrilege" <note>original: "resía" — The commentator Dati notes that when such offenses were made public, Augustus claimed they offended religion and violated the laws of majesty (treason), departing from the mercy of ancient laws and even his own statutes.</note>, exceeding the leniency of older laws and his own previous rules. 

But I shall weave the end of these people’s stories, along with the other events of that age, if I live long enough to complete the works I have begun. Decimus Silanus, having slept with the granddaughter of Augustus, understood the danger when the Emperor merely withdrew his friendship from him; he took this as a sign and went into exile. He did not dare to ask for pardon until the reign of Tiberius, aided by the influence <note>original: "col caldo" — literally "with the warmth," referring to the political pressure or "potency" mentioned in the Latin text.</note> of his brother Marcus Silanus, who was powerful due to his great eloquence and nobility. When Tiberius was thanked for this in the Senate, he replied that he also rejoiced that Marcus's brother had returned from his "long pilgrimage." This was a reasonable thing to say, since neither the Senate nor any law had officially banished him; nevertheless, he would still hold firm...

**XXV.** It was proposed to moderate the Papia-Poppaean Law, which Augustus, already an old man, enacted after the Julian laws to spur the unmarried into marriage through penalties $^2$ and to fatten the treasury; $^3$ yet despite this, neither marriages nor the raising of children increased (as being single was more profitable), but rather the number of ruined men grew. The quibbles of the informers $^4$ subverted every household. And where once we suffered for our sins, we then suffered for our laws. This invites me to speak from a higher perspective on the origin of justice and how laws reached this state of infinite variety.

**1** *safe but odious.* Both instances of the *s* are pronounced softly <note>The translator Davanzati is providing a phonetic guide for the Italian word "esoso"</note>; "odious" most accurately signifies a citizen who is disliked and in disgrace with the state that rules him, which has no cause to punish him but cannot stand the sight of him and grants him no honors.

**2** *to spur the unmarried into marriage through penalties:* — > "By stimulating the penalties of the unmarried" <note>original Latin: "Incitandis caelibum poenis"</note> — is a "Tacitism" <note>A stylistic quirk unique to Tacitus</note>; according to which one can say: to increase the penalties for those who are single. And perhaps there is a corruption in the text. Eighty thousand men of military age died in the civil war. Julius Caesar made strong laws so that people would marry. Augustus reduced them all to one and had it named not after himself, but called it the *Papia Poppaea*, from the names of the consuls of that year, 762 <note>9 AD</note>, because of the many snares and hooks added to the assets of private citizens; such that the Emperor Severus and the subsequent legal experts annulled all these and similar iniquitous Papian laws.

**3** *and to fatten the treasury.* This was the primary intention and the soul of the law. Little "law-twisting" doctors <note>original: "storcileggi"</note> were sent out, promised a third or a half of the gain, to search houses and seize documents to find those enjoying legacies or inheritances against the law. By twisting the law in most iniquitous ways, they were—with their legal assassin's weapons—the killers of everyone’s estates.

**4** *of the informers. The Latin:* > "of the informers." <note>original: "delatorum"</note>

**5** *The first mortals lived.* The writers of the *New World* $^ \text{(**)} $ tell how on the southern coast of the island of Hispaniola <note>The island containing modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note> men lived in this true Golden Age. There was no "mine" or "thine," the cause of all evils; no ditches, walls, or hedges divided them; the earth was common like the water and the sun, and everything (since they were content with so little) was more than enough for them. Loving justice by nature and hating the injurious like the cannibals, they knew neither laws nor judges nor lordships. From this, one can argue—seeing crude and savage countries lose their blessed simplicity upon the arrival of foreigners and acquire the light and splendor of new arts, sciences, and customs—that they also acquire miserable servitude, wars, and desolation, only to return to their primary savagery after a long time.

...any filth or wickedness, and therefore existed without restraints or punishments.
