...peius, taking this opportunity¹ to make an enemy of Marcus Lepidus, called him a worthless man, a beggar, and a disgrace to his house; he argued that Lepidus should not be sent to Asia, even though it was his turn by lot. The Senate, on the contrary, declared him to be kind and capable: they argued that poverty which does not stain nobility is a merit, not a shame. Thus, he was sent to Asia, and the decision of who should be given Africa was referred back to Caesar <note>A title used here for the Emperor Tiberius.</note>.

**XXXIII.** Then Severus Caecina gave his opinion that in a provincial command, one should not travel with a train of wives. He repeatedly stated that he had observed this rule himself for the sake of the public good; though he had gone out to war forty times, he had always kept his wife—a peaceful woman and mother of six children—in Italy.

> "It was not by chance that the entanglement² of women in friendly or foreign lands was once forbidden; for it brings expense in peace and fear in war; and on the march, it makes a Roman camp resemble a barbarian one. Women are troublesome,³ weak in the face of hardship, and, if you let them, cruel, ambitious, and domineering: they march among the soldiers and lord it over the centurions. Just recently, a certain woman⁴ had the companies drilling and the legions performing maneuvers. When it comes to official investigations into corruption, five out of every six crimes⁵ stem from the wives. The worst characters in the provinces flock to them: they take up the business, they conclude the deals. Two entourages are courted; two courts of justice are held. The hands of women—proud and treacherous in their command—were once bound by the Oppian and other laws; now that they have broken free, they rule our homes, our courts, and by now, even our armies."

**XXXIV.** Few were pleased by this speech, and many interrupted him, saying that this matter had not been formally proposed for debate, and that Caecina was not a reformer worthy of such a great business. To whom Valerius...

Messalinus, who had inherited the eloquence of his father Messala, replied: "Many of the harsh ways of the ancients have been softened and improved; for as we no longer have a Rome besieged by war, nor enemy provinces, we can afford some personal expenses for our wives, who do not burden the households of their husbands, let alone their subjects. As for the other objections raised, these matters are shared with the husband and are not such as to disturb the public peace.<note>The original phrase "e non da sollevare" implies these issues are not serious enough to ruin public order.</note> To go out to battle, one certainly wants to be unencumbered, but upon returning from labors, what comfort is more honorable than a wife? Some have indeed been ambitious and greedy, but are all the governors themselves like Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus was a Roman consul renowned for his extreme integrity and refusal of bribes.</note>? And yet we still send men to rule provinces. Many wives have corrupted their husbands; but are all bachelors therefore saints? The Oppian laws <note>Sumptuary laws passed during the Second Punic War to limit the luxury and mourning of women; they were highly controversial.</note> were enacted because those times required them; they were later broadened and softened because it was practical. If a woman oversteps her bounds, this is (let us call it by its true name) the husband’s weakness. We should not, for the sake of a few soldiers, take away from husbands their companions <note>The original Latin reads "consortia rerum secundarum adversarumque," meaning partners in both prosperity and adversity.</note> in good and bad times, and leave this fragile sex alone, a prey to its own vanities and the desires of others. They are barely kept safe even when we are watching them; what would happen if they were forgotten for years <note>The original "sdimenticate gli anni" refers to being left alone for a long duration of time.</note> and essentially cast aside? Remedy the minor disorders abroad, but consider also the greater ones within the city. <note>These two speeches by Caecina and Valerius Messalinus mirror the debate between Cato the Elder and Lucius Valerius regarding women's rights in Livy’s history (Book 34). In both instances, the outcome was the same: the side favoring the women won.</note>"

Drusus, who was also a husband, added: "It is fitting for a prince to often visit the distant parts of the empire. How many times did the divine Augustus travel with Livia to the East and West? And he himself went to Illyria; and he will go elsewhere if necessary, but not with a willing heart if he must be torn away each time from his sweetest wife, from whom he has so many children." Thus, Caecina’s proposal was discarded.

**XXXV.** At the next session of the Senate, Tiberius sent a letter in which—having reproached the fathers <note>original: "fiancheggiati li padri." A metaphorical expression meaning he "poked them in the flanks" or rebuked them obliquely for their indecision.</note> for always referring every matter back to him <note>original: "rimettere," referring to the practice of senators avoiding responsibility by asking the Emperor to decide all business.</note>—he nominated either Marcus Lepidus or Junius Blaesus for the office of proconsul in Africa. They were then heard. Lepidus made great excuses, claiming he was of poor health, had young children, and a daughter to marry off; it was also understood, though left unsaid, that Blaesus (who was the uncle of Sejanus) had the upper hand <note>original: "lo scavallava," literally "unhorsed him," meaning Blaesus had more influence and would inevitably be chosen.</note>. Blaesus made a show of refusing the position, but everyone knew this was merely a formal courtesy, and his words were met with flattery.

**XXXVI.** A long-repressed grievance held by many then broke out. Every scoundrel, by retreating to an image of Caesar, could hurl any foul insult at an honorable man; even slaves and freedmen used their voices and hands to terrorize their masters. Gaius Cestius the senator said: "Princes are like gods, but even the gods do not listen to unjust prayers, and no one flees to the Capitol or any other temple for help in order to commit a crime. The laws are being nullified and dragged down, since in the forum, at the very door of the Senate, Annia Ruffilla—whom I had convicted by a judge for forgery—insults me with threats; and yet I do not dare seek justice, because she stands under the protection of the Emperor's statue." Others grumbled about similar and even more atrocious things around Drusus, begging him to make an example of her. Eventually, he had her seized and, once convicted, imprisoned.

**XXXVII.** Considius Equus and Caelius Cursor, knights, were punished by order of the prince and a decree of the Senate for bringing a false charge of treason <term>maestà: the crime of "maiestas" or "diminishing the majesty of the Roman people," often used for political trials</term> against the praetor Magius Caecilianus. Drusus received praise for both of these judgments. By mingling and conversing with the people, he mitigated his father’s extreme isolation; it was more pleasing to the public to see him spend his day at the spectacles <note>original: "ispettacoli." The translator notes he follows the reading of Lipsius, referring to the public games.</note> and his nights at banquets than to see him shut away, brooding over troublesome matters <note>original: "cose rematiche." An archaic term derived from "rheum," referring to difficult or annoying business that weighs on the mind like an illness.</note>.

1 * *fiancheggiati li padri*: To strike the fathers [senators] in the flanks; that is, stinging them obliquely. The Latin: "*castigatis oblique patribus.*"
2 * *rimettere*: Understand this as "referring business."
3 * *lo scavallava*: Threw him from his horse; that is, he had more power than him, and therefore it would have been useless to compete against him.
4 *in ispettacoli*: I read this, following Lipsius, as *editionibus*, meaning the public games.
5 *cose rematiche*: Our ancestors used the Greek word *rema* to describe the "catarrh" or fluid that falls from the brain. See Master Aldobrandino. This derived word remains with us, and we call "rheumatic" those things which are difficult and annoying.

## XXXVIII.
Ancharius Priscus accused Caesius Cordus, the proconsul of Crete <note>original: "Candia," the name for Crete commonly used in the Renaissance.</note>, of extortion and treason—which was then the final seal on every accusation. Tiberius also insisted that Antistius Vetus, a nobleman of Macedonia who had been acquitted of adultery (for which Tiberius rebuked the judges), should return to defend himself against a charge of treason. He was accused of being a rebel and an advisor to Rhescuporis when the latter killed Cotys and intended to wage war against us. Consequently, Vetus was condemned to "interdiction from fire and water" <note>A Roman legal formula for exile, meaning the person was stripped of citizenship and basic necessities.</note>, confined to an island far from Thrace and Macedonia. This was because Thrace, divided between Rhoemetalces and the young sons of Cotys, was kicking against <note>original: "calcitrava," meaning to resist or rebel like a horse kicking back.</note> our new government and their tutor, Trebellienus Rufus. They were just as angry with Rhoemetalces for allowing his people to be devoured in such a way. The Coelaletae, Odrysae, and other tribes took up arms; they were strong nations but led by discordant chiefs, and equally inexperienced, so they did not know how to unite or wage a real war. Some devastated the countryside, others crossed Mount Haemus to bring in distant reinforcements; the most numerous and best-organized among them besieged the king and the city of Philippopolis, which had been founded by Philip of Macedon.

## XXXIX.
When Publius Velleius, the general of the nearby army, heard of these events, he dispatched the swiftest cavalry and light infantry against those scattered groups who were looting or seeking <note>original: "caendo." See note 2 below.</note> reinforcements. He himself led the main body of the infantry to lift the siege, and everything went well. The looters were killed, discord broke out among the besiegers, and the king made a sally just as the legion arrived. It resulted not in a battle (for it does not deserve to be called such) but in a slaughter of poorly armed, disorganized men, without any loss of our own blood.

<meta>This page concludes the Roman suppression of the Gallic rebellion led by Sacrovir and details Emperor Tiberius’s calculated response to the victory, as well as the death of the soldier-senator Sulpicius Quirinius.</meta>

### THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

...enemies. Of this army, a single cohort recently routed the rebellious Turonians; a band defeated the Treviri; a few horsemen the Sequani. Now these Aedui, the wealthier and softer they are, the less fit they are for war. What war? Bind them, and throw yourselves upon those who flee.¹" A great cry arose. The cavalry surrounded them; the infantry attacked from the front; there was no need to worry about the flanks, but rather the iron-clad <term>crupellarii</term> <note>original: *ferrati*; heavy gladiators encased in armor</note>. Our men, since their swords and spears could not pierce those plates, took up axes and pickaxes as if they were tearing down towers; they hacked through the armor and the limbs within, or used poles and forks to topple those heavy masses. Once they fell, being so stiffened by their armor that they could not rise again, they were left for dead. Sacrovir retreated, first to Autun and then—fearing he would be surrendered—to a nearby villa with his most faithful followers. There he killed himself by his own hand, and the others killed one another; they set fire to the villa, and every one of them burned.

XLVII. Then, and not before, Tiberius wrote to the senate regarding the beginning and end of this war truthfully,² explaining how the legates had conducted it with loyalty and courage, and he with his counsel. He added that neither he nor Druso had gone in person for the sake of majesty; for it was unbecoming of a prince, if one city or another turned wayward, to leave the center of the entire government. Now that he no longer acted out of fear, he would go to see everything with his own eyes and establish order. The fathers <note>The Senators</note> decreed vows, processions, and other honors for his return. Cornelius Dolabella, a flatterer more clever than the rest, proposed that the Emperor should enter Rome from Capua with an ovation <term>ovante</term> <note>original: *ovante*; a minor triumph where the general entered the city on foot or horseback rather than in a chariot</note>.³ Here is a letter from Caesar, who was not so beggarly for glory that, after conquering so many ferocious nations and having received and refused so many triumphs in his youth, he would now in his old age peacock about over a pilgrimage around the gates of Rome.

### THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

**XLIX.** Toward the end of the year, Gaius Lutorius Priscus, a Roman knight—who had previously been rewarded by the Emperor for a celebrated poem mourning the death of Germanicus—was accused of having composed another poem during the illness of Drusus. It was said that, while striking his thigh, he remarked: "May the gods make that Drusus suffer; he didn't die, or I would have earned another reward." Out of vanity, he read the poem at the house of Petronius to Vitellia, his mother-in-law, and other noblewomen, who later confessed out of fear. Vitellia alone maintained that she had heard nothing;¹ but the others were more readily believed. Haterius Agrippa, the consul-elect, condemned the accused to the ultimate penalty.² <note>the death penalty</note>

**L.** Marcus Lepidus argued against the sentence as follows:

> "If we look only, Conscript Fathers <note>A formal title for Roman Senators</note>, at the foul words with which Lutorius Priscus has stained his own mind and the ears of men, neither prison, nor the noose, nor the tortures of a slave would be enough for him. But if our moderate Prince, if our ancestors, and if you yourselves apply moderate punishments or remedies to even immoderate sins; and since there is a great difference between vanity and malice, between words and deeds; a sentence can be rendered by which he is punished and we maintain fairness. I have often heard our Prince lament that he was unable to pardon those who killed themselves too soon.³ Lutorius is alive; there is no danger in keeping him so, nor is there any useful example in killing him. He occupies himself with trifles and follies that fade away; a man who incriminates himself and targets the minds not of men but of women intends little harm. Let him nonetheless be expelled from Rome, lose his property, and be barred from water and fire <note>original: *acqua e fuoco*; a legal formula for exile</note>, as if it were a crime against the state."

**LII.** [Year 775 of Rome, 22 AD] The consulship of Gaius Sulpicius and Decius Haterius followed. Abroad, the year was quiet; in Rome, there was a sense of suspicion regarding a severe reform of the luxury and squandering of money that had reached excessive levels. Many expenses, though vast, were often hidden by falsifying prices; but the rich banquets and the preparations of the gluttons were the talk of everyone, and there was a miserable fear that the prince—frugal in the ancient fashion—might harshly curtail them. First Gaius Bibulus, and then the other Aediles <note>magistrates in charge of public order and markets</note> cried out: "The law on spending is held in contempt; prohibited luxury items increase every day; moderate remedies do not serve: what is to be done?" The Fathers referred the matter entirely to Tiberius. For a time, he weighed whether it would be possible to restrain such unbridled desires, or if it would be more harmful to the Republic—thinking it an indignity to lay hands on a problem that might not be solved, or if solved, might bring dishonor to the Great. Finally, he composed this letter to the Senate.

What a trivial thing the aediles <note>Roman magistrates responsible for public order and markets.</note> remind me of compared to everything else! No one remembers that Italy requires help from abroad; that the life of the Roman people is at the mercy of the sea and the storms. Without provisions from the provinces, who would feed us, our slaves, and our rural estates? Perhaps our beautiful groves and villas? These, Conscript Fathers <note>The formal title used to address Roman Senators.</note>, are the burdens of the prince; if these are neglected, they would sink the Republic to the bottom. For other matters, every man carries the medicine in his own heart. Let modesty reform us; let necessity reform the poor; and let satiety <gloss>1</gloss> reform the rich. If any magistrate has the heart to remedy this with sufficient skill or severity, I praise him and confess that he will take a great burden off me. But if they only wish to make themselves look good by scolding vices and then stir up hatred to dump it on me—believe me, Conscript Fathers, I too do not enjoy making enemies. And if I take them on for the sake of the Republic in major matters (often suffering disgrace wrongly), do not seek to burden me with minor things that have no effect or benefit for you or for me."

LV. Once Caesar’s letter was read, this concern was referred back to the aediles. Formerly, the noble, wealthy, and famous families were prone to excessive magnificence. At that time, it was still possible to court the common people, <gloss>3</gloss> the allies, and foreign kingdoms, and be courted in return. Whoever was most ostentatious in wealth, palaces, and furnishings achieved the greatest renown and following. But once the era of bloodshed began <gloss>4</gloss> and having a great name led to ruin, people turned to wiser ways. ### LVI.

Tiberius, having gained a reputation for moderation <gloss>4</gloss> by taking away this "grazing ground" <note>original: "pasciona", a metaphor for the profit spies and accusers made from enforcing laws.</note> from the emerging spies, wrote to the Fathers <note>The Roman Senators.</note>, asking for the **tribunician power** <gloss>5</gloss> for Drusus. Augustus devised this title of sovereignty so as not to call himself "king" or "dictator," and yet show himself superior through some name. He made Marcus Agrippa his companion in this power, and after his death, Tiberius Nero, so that there would be a successor; he felt this would take away the wicked hopes of others, trusting in Nero’s modesty and his own greatness. Following this example, Tiberius invested Drusus with the highest rank—a rank he had not declared for either son while Germanicus was still alive. The letter, after first invoking the gods to bless his designs for the Republic, listed the young man's good qualities, moderately and without exaggeration:

> "He is married with three children, and is the same age I was when I was adopted by Augustus. I ask for this companion for my labors—not a novice <note>original: "non soro"</note>, but one who has spent eight years quieting seditions, finishing wars, triumphing, and governing through two consulships."

1. * **savings**, or thrift.
2. * Here the text is damaged: <note>original Latin: "verum hac nobis....... maiores certamina ex honesto maneant."</note> Our author [Davanzati] has followed the conjecture of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous 16th-century scholar.</note>, who easily filled the gap with a simple *in*. Others, however, think much more is missing.
3. * **pasture**, or grazing: this refers to the profit made by the spies.
4. * **gained a reputation for moderation.** He chose the time to ask this great favor of the Fathers when he had sweetened them by not enacting the sumptuary law; for every law is a power for the prince and a "grazing ground" for spies.
5. * **tribunician power.** This was given to the elected emperor. Choosing a successor in advance and giving them a role in government is a very prudent counsel. One is secured and unburdened; the other learns and governs with respect, succeeding without disturbance.
6. * **not a novice**, or not inexperienced.

LVII. The Fathers <note>The Senators</note> had already prepared their speeches;¹ thus, their adulation was all the more refined. However, they devised nothing new beyond the usual images, altars, temples, arches, and similar honors. The exception was **Marcus Silanus**, who sought to dishonor the office of consul to flatter the princes; he proposed, without a prior motion, that on public and private records, to mark the era, the names of those holding the **sacred tribunician power** <term>Tribunicia potestas: A key power of the Roman Emperor, granting him the veto and personal sanctity, originally held by the protectors of the common people.</term> should be written rather than those of the serving consuls. **Quintus Haterius**, by suggesting that the decrees passed that day in the Senate be engraved in large gold letters, made himself a laughingstock; that a man so old would seek nothing but infamy from such foul flattery.

LVIII. **Junius Blaesus** was reconfirmed in his command in **Africa**, and **Servius Maluginensis** requested the governorship of **Asia**, even though he was the **Flamen of Jupiter** <term>Flamen Dialis: The high priest of Jupiter, subject to many ancient religious taboos.</term>. He argued: "The common saying that a Flamen cannot leave Italy is not true; nor is his priesthood different from those of Mars or Quirinus. If those priests can hold provinces, why forbid it to the priests of Jupiter? There is no law of the people regarding this, nor can it be found in the ceremonial books. In the absence of the Jovian priests due to illness or public duties, the pontiffs have performed their rites. After **Cornelius Merula** was killed, this priesthood remained vacant for seventy-two years, yet the rites never ceased. If the rituals can be performed for so many years without a replacement, surely a priest can stay away for a year as a proconsul. The right to go to provincial governments was taken from them in the past by the pontiffs due to private grudges; now, by the grace of the gods, the Supreme Pontiff is the greatest of men <note>A reference to Tiberius, who held the title of Pontifex Maximus.</note>: he has no rivalries, no hatreds, and no passions."

LIX. **Lentulus** the Augur and others disagreed on various points, and they turned to the Pontiff **Tiberius** to give a ruling. He deferred the decision² and proceeded to moderate the ceremonies ordained for the elevation of **Drusus** to the tribunician power; he specifically rejected the arrogant proposal and those novel large gold letters.³ A letter from **Drusus** to the Senate was read, which appeared modest in tone; but it was perceived as extremely arrogant. "Woe to us!"⁴ he has not even dried <note>This likely refers to an idiom for being "wet behind the ears" or perhaps not even having "dried his feet" from a journey before assuming such power.</note>

LX. But Tiberius, having thus fortified his position in the state, to give the Senate a shadow of its ancient power,⁶ referred to it the petitions from the provinces regarding the maintenance of sanctuary privileges <term>franchigie: Specifically 'Right of Asylum,' where temples protected individuals from legal prosecution</term>, which had grown into excessive license among the cities of Greece. These temples allowed the worst slaves, debtors, and fugitives from justice to seek refuge. Not even chains would have held the people back⁷ from rising up to defend human wickedness as if it were divine religion. It was ordered, therefore, that the cities should send ambassadors with all their legal arguments. Some cities gave up the privileges they had usurped. Many relied on ancient devotion or services rendered to the Roman people. It was a magnificent day for the Senate, when it reviewed the benefits granted by our ancestors, the treaties, the decrees of great kings from before Roman power, and the religions of the gods, with its original freedom to confirm or reform them.

Boccaccio writes: "Do you think you know more than I, you whose eyes are not yet dry?"

<meta>This page continues the Senate's investigation into the rights of asylum (sanctuary) claimed by various Greek cities. Previously, Tiberius had referred these claims to the Senate to maintain a semblance of their ancient authority. The following text details the historical and mythological justifications presented by various embassies to defend their temple privileges.</meta>

-># THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ANNALS.<-

**LXI.** First, the Ephesians stated that Apollo and Diana were not born on the island of Delos, as is commonly believed, but that Latona gave birth to them at the foot of an olive tree which still stands by the river Cenchrius, within their grove called Ortygia <note>A sacred forest near Ephesus</note>, consecrated by divine command. It was there that Apollo, having slain the Cyclopes, fled to escape the wrath of Jove; and there Bacchus pardoned the defeated Amazons who had sought refuge by embracing that altar. Later, the devotion to that temple—with the permission of Hercules when he was ruler of Lydia—was increased and maintained by the Persians, the Macedonians, and finally by us Romans.

**LXII.** The Magnesians <note>Residents of Magnesia on the Maeander</note> followed, stating that after Lucius Scipio had defeated Antiochus, and Lucius Sulla had defeated Mithridates, they granted an inviolable right of asylum <term>franchigia: The legal right for a temple to protect fugitives from arrest</term> to the temple of Diana Leucophryne for the city’s loyalty and bravery. Next, others defended their own temples: the Aphrodisians for the temple of Venus, and the people of Stratonicea for those of Jove and Diana. They produced a recent grant from Augustus and an even older one from Caesar the Dictator, awarded for having supported their factions in war. They were also praised for maintaining their loyalty to the Roman people during the raids of the Parthians. The Hierocaesareans showed even greater antiquity, claiming that their temple of the Persian Diana was dedicated by Cyrus; they also cited Perpenna, Isauricus, and many other commanders who granted the sanctuary a sacred boundary of two miles^1. The Cypriots recommended three of their temples: the most ancient, that of Venus at Paphos, founded by Aeria;^2 that of Venus at Amathus, founded by her son Amathus; and that of Jove at Salamis, founded by Teucer when he fled the anger of his father Telamon.

**LXIII.** The Fathers <note>The Senators</note> heard so many other embassies that, being exhausted and divided by their personal favorites, they delegated the matter to the consuls. They were tasked with examining the justifications of each claim and, if any deception was found, reporting back to the Senate. The consuls reported that the stated rights of asylum were—

These privileges were confirmed with great honor; however, a rule was established, and it was commanded that a sacred record of them be affixed in bronze within those temples, so that religious devotion would not lapse into personal ambition.

**LXVII.** Silanus was further accused by Gellius Publicola, his former quaestor <note>A quaestor was a junior official responsible for financial administration.</note>, and Marcus Paconius, his lieutenant. He was indeed a cruel and greedy man; but many things were stacked against him—dangers that could threaten even an innocent man. He was hated by so many senators and accused by the greatest orators of all of Asia. He stood alone to answer them, lacking any training in rhetoric and defending his own cause—a situation enough to make even the most eloquent man lose his speech. Furthermore, Tiberius pinned him down with harsh glares, strange outbursts of voice, and frequent questions from which he could neither hide nor defend himself <note>The manuscript originally read: "from which he could neither push back nor mock."</note>. Indeed, Silanus was often forced to confess to avoid the Emperor's questioning being in vain. To allow for his own slaves to be <term>tortured</term> <note>original: "collare." It was against the law to torture slaves to provide evidence against their own masters; this legal trick of "selling" them to the state agent was used to bypass that protection.</note> for evidence against him, a public agent purchased them. And so that no relative might help him, they framed the charges as crimes against the state—matters so grave that one is not even permitted to speak of them. Silanus, therefore, requested a few days' time, then abandoned his defense and dared to write to Tiberius, stinging him with his words while simultaneously commending himself to his mercy.

**LXVIII.** To show by example that he intended to do his duty regarding Silanus, Tiberius had a record read of a trial from the time of Augustus, including the Senate's sentence against Volesus Messala, who had also been a proconsul of Asia. Then, turning to Lucius Piso, he said, "Speak your mind." Piso, after a long preamble about the great clemency of Caesar, said: "I would banish Silanus, stripped of fire and water, to the island of Gyaros <note>original: "Giara." A desolate, barren island in the Aegean Sea used as a place of exile.</note>." The others agreed, except for Gnaeus Lentulus, who noted that since Silanus had been born of a different mother, the maternal property should be set aside for his son. Tiberius was pleased with this suggestion.

**LXIX.** Cornelius Dolabella, with even more long-winded flattery, spoke very ill of Silanus and proposed: "That no one of ill-repute or who has lived a bad life should govern a province, and the Prince should be the one to declare it; for laws punish sins after they are committed, but how much better is it for the provinces to provide that no sins be committed at all?" Tiberius spoke against this, saying, "That while he knew what the people were saying about Silanus, laws should not be made based on rumors. Some have turned out better in governing, and some worse, than what was expected of them. In great affairs, some are awakened to duty while others become sluggish. The Prince cannot know everything, nor should he let himself be led by the whims of others. Laws punish sins—"

Cornelius Scipio, the lieutenant, went with one to prevent him from taking plunder in the region of the Leptis <note>referring to the coastal cities of Leptis Magna or Leptis Minor in modern Libya</note> and to block his retreat to the Garamantes <note>An ancient Saharan people who controlled caravan routes.</note>. With his own division, the younger Blaesus went to defend the villages of Cirta <note>A major city in Numidia, modern-day Constantine, Algeria.</note> on the other side. In the center was Blaesus himself with the best troops; by placing forts and guards where necessary, he brought exhaustion and damage to the enemy at every turn. Wherever they moved, they found Romans in front, to their side, and at their rear. Thus, many having been killed and captured, he further divided the three columns into smaller bands under centurions of proven valor <note>original: "di prova," translating the Latin "virtutis expertae."</note>. When the summer ended, he did not withdraw his troops to their usual winter quarters in the province, but as if at the start of a war, having secured the strongholds with light cavalry and men familiar with those deserts, he hunted Tacfarinas, who was expected here or there. Finally, he captured the rebel's brother and returned—sooner than was necessary for our allies—leaving behind those who might restart the war. But Tiberius, considering it finished, even wished that the legions...

...they should acclaim Blaesus as emperor <note>At this time, "Imperator" was still a military title of honor given to a victorious general by his troops, rather than solely the title of the head of state.</note>; an ancient honor that the army bestowed upon their commanding general for some outstanding feat in a burst of joy. Indeed, multiple "emperors" could exist at once, remaining private citizens in other respects. Augustus granted this title to a few, and then Tiberius granted it to Blaesus for the last time. ¹

**LXXV.** In that year, two great men died: Asinius Saloninus, grandson of Marcus Agrippa and Asinius Pollio, and brother of Drusus, who had been intended as the husband for one of Caesar’s granddaughters; and Ateius Capito, the leading jurist of Rome, as I mentioned previously. Sulla, his grandfather, had been a centurion, and his father a praetor. Augustus had quickly elevated him to the consulship so that, through such dignity, he might surpass Antistius Labeo, who was no less excellent—that age having produced these two "lights of peace." However, Labeo was straightforward and outspoken, ² and was therefore more celebrated by the people; Capito was a courtier, and found more favor with the masters of the state. Because Labeo never rose beyond the rank of praetor, he was more highly esteemed for the injustice he suffered; Capito, who became consul, was hated out of envy.

**LXXVI.** This year, sixty-four years after the defeat at Philippi <note>The battle in 42 BCE where the forces of Brutus and Cassius were defeated by Mark Antony and Octavian (Augustus).</note>, Junia also died. She was the daughter of Cato’s sister, the wife of Gaius Cassius, and the sister of Brutus. Her will caused much talk, for having great wealth, she honored almost all the leading men of Rome with legacies, but left out Caesar [Tiberius]. He took this with a citizen's restraint, allowing her to be praised from the rostrum <note>The *rostra*, the public speaking platform in the Roman Forum.</note> and her funeral to be honored with every solemnity. The ancestral wax images <note>original: "immagini." It was a Roman custom to carry wax masks of famous ancestors during the funeral processions of the nobility.</note> of twenty most illustrious families were carried there—the Manlii, the Quinctii, and other such sublime names. But the images of Brutus and Cassius outshined ³ all the others by the very fact of their absence <note>Because they were the assassins of Julius Caesar, their images were legally prohibited from being shown, yet their absence reminded everyone of their cause.</note>.

### SUMMARY.

**I.** Origin and character of Aelius Sejanus. — **II.** He wins over soldiers and senators, with his eye on the throne. — **III.** In what state he finds the troops and the republic. — **VIII.** In league with Livia <note>This refers to Livilla, the sister of Germanicus and wife of Drusus.</note>, wife of Drusus, he poisons him—the first step in his hope to rule. **I.** It was the year of the consulship of **Gaius Asinius** and **Gaius Antistius** <note>AD 23</note>, the ninth year that the republic remained peaceful in the hands of **Tiberius** and his house flourished—for he even counted the death of **Germanicus** among his strokes of good fortune—when fortune suddenly began to turn. Tiberius began to grow cruel, or at least to give others the encouragement to be so; and it all began with **Aelius Sejanus**, commander of the guard soldiers, whose power I touched upon above: <note>original: "di sopra toccai"; see Books I, 24; III, 29, 72.</note> I will now describe his origins, his character, and the audacity with which he sought the lordship. <note>The translator reads the Latin as *captaverit* (aimed for), not *captaverit* (attained). He did not achieve it, because **Tiberius** destroyed him, but he began the attempt and reached such heights that he was already called "Emperor," while **Tiberius** was called the magistrate of those islands.</note> He was born in **Bolsena**, the son of **Seius Strabo**, a Roman knight. In his youth, he was a page to **Gaius Caesar**, the grandson of **Augustus**, and he was not without a reputation for having sold his virtue to the wealthy and extravagant **Apicius** <note>A famous Roman gourmet known for his immense spending on luxury.</note>. Later, through various arts, he won over **Tiberius** so completely that the Emperor, who was dark and reserved with everyone else, became open and trusting with him alone. This happened not so much through his own wisdom <note>The manuscript originally read "craftiness" (*scaltrimiento*), but was corrected to "wisdom" or "subtlety."</note> (for in this he was ultimately defeated), but through the wrath of the gods: thus, he rose and fell with equal damage to **Rome**. <note>The manuscript originally used the word "ruined" (*rovinò*) before settling on "fell" (*cadde*).</note> He was tireless in body and daring in spirit: <note>The manuscript originally read "his body was tireless, his spirit daring."</note> he masked his own vices while defaming others. He was both a sycophant and arrogant; outwardly he appeared dignified, but inwardly he was most greedy. To achieve his ends, he was lavish with gifts and spending, employing a level of industry and vigilance that cost too much <note>The manuscript originally added: "no less harmful."</note> when they are used for the purpose of reigning.

**II.** The command of the guard was not originally a position of great consequence. He made it so by gathering the soldiers—who had previously been scattered in various lodgings throughout **Rome**—into a single camp, claiming that, once united, they could better obey orders: and—

...seeing themselves face to face in such numbers and strength, they would gain more confidence while terrifying others. In the event of a sudden crisis, they would be more ready to help one another; he argued that when separated, they were more easily corrupted, but they would live more strictly if their camp were established far from the luxuries of the city. Once this was done, he gradually won over the minds of the soldiers by visiting them, calling them by name, and personally appointing the centurions and the tribunes. III. However, the presence of so many Caesars in that house—a son and several grown grandsons—delayed his plans. It was impossible to murder so many at once, and treachery requires time. He chose this path: to start <note>original: "farsi"</note> with **Drusus**, motivated by a fresh anger. For Drusus, who would not tolerate a rival and was of a volatile temper, had happened into an argument with **Sejanus**; he struck him in the face, and when Sejanus tried to resist, Drusus beat him. Therefore, having considered everything <note>A manuscript note shows the translator originally wrote: "Therefore, having thought of every way, it seemed most effective to make use of Livia."</note>, it seemed best to make use of **Livia**, the wife of Drusus and sister of **Germanicus**; though an ugly girl in her youth, she had become a very beautiful woman. He feigned a deep love for her, and having successfully seduced her—since there is nothing a woman will not do once she has cast off her modesty—he induced her to give poison to her husband, promising to marry her and rule the Empire alongside him. Thus she, whose uncle was **Augustus**, whose father-in-law was **Tiberius**, and who had children by Drusus, disgraced herself, her ancestors, and her descendants by lying with a provincial <note>original: "castellano," here meaning someone from the provinces, a "rustic" compared to the old Roman nobility.</note>, all to wait for uncertain and wicked prospects in place of her present honorable life. They brought into the conspiracy **Eudemus**, a physician and friend of Livia, meeting with him often under the pretext of his medical profession. Sejanus even sent away his own wife, **Apicata**, by whom he had three children, to remove any cause for suspicion from his mistress.

...Egypt: and four more guarded the entire circle of land from Syria to the Euphrates, bordered by the Iberians, the Albanians, and other kings whom our greatness protects from other powers. Rhoemetalces and the sons of Cotys held Thrace; on the banks of the Danube were two legions in Hungary <note>The translator uses "Ungheria" for the Roman province of Pannonia.</note>, two in Moesia; and two were positioned in Dalmatia at the rear of those, convenient for any sudden need for assistance in Italy: even though the city itself held within its body for its own guard three urban cohorts <note>Original: "Romaneschi." These were the *cohortes urbanae*, responsible for maintaining order in the city of Rome.</note>, and nine Praetorian cohorts chosen from almost all of Tuscany <note>Etruria.</note>, Umbria, Latium, and the ancient Roman colonies. And in the appropriate places of our provinces, there were armed forces of allies, infantry and cavalry reinforcements, of slightly smaller strength: the exact number cannot be said, being placed here and there, more or less,<gloss>1</gloss> according to the times.

VI. It also seems right for me to give an account <gloss>2</gloss> of how the other members of the republic stood until then: since in that year Tiberius began to worsen his rule. Firstly, public matters and the most important private ones were handled by the fathers <note>The Senators, often called the "Conscript Fathers."</note>. The leading men spoke their opinions: he himself would rebuke those who fell too much into flattery. He granted honors, without doubt, to the best men based on ancient nobility, civic virtue, and glory in arms. The consuls and pretors maintained their prestige; the minor magistrates exercised their own authority. The laws, except for cases of high treason <note>The laws of *majestas*, which later became a tool for political persecution.</note>, were used well. Grain, tributes, and other public revenues were managed by companies of Roman knights <note>The Equestrian order, who acted as tax farmers and financial administrators.</note>. Caesar had his own affairs administered by the finest of men, of proven character or famous name: he kept them in their posts so long that many grew old in a single office. The common people suffered from high prices: but what fault of the prince was that? Rather, he increased cultivation and seafaring with every possible expense and industry.<gloss>3</gloss> He imposed no new burdens: he ensured the old ones were tolerated without the greed or cruelty of the officials. He did not allow persons to be afflicted, nor their goods to be seized.

VII. He held few estates throughout Italy: no throngs of slaves: few freedmen in his household. If he litigated with private citizens, he sought a judge and the rule of law. And all these kindnesses...

<meta>This page continues from the description of the Roman military and administrative order under Tiberius, transitioning to the point where the Emperor’s governance began to deteriorate due to the influence of Sejanus and the internal conflicts within the imperial family.</meta>

[Tiberius] maintained [his governance] with methods that were not kind, but rather coarse or frightening <gloss>1</gloss>, until the death of Drusus. For Sejanus, just as he was beginning to rise in power, wanted a reputation for giving good advice, and he feared Drusus, a rival already openly hostile and seething <gloss>2</gloss>—chafing that while the Emperor’s son was still alive, another man should be summoned as an assistant to the empire. "What is he missing to become a partner?" [Drusus would say]. "It is a hard thing to grasp at sovereignty: once you gain a foothold, supporters and ministers come running. He has set up the camp in his own way; the military has been placed in his hands; his own fine statue is seen in the buildings of Pompey; this lineage will be mixed with the blood of the Drusi. Let us pray to Modesty that he stops here! <gloss>3</gloss>" He would say such things often and in public, and his wicked wife <note>Livia Julia, also known as Livilla, who was Drusus's wife but Sejanus's lover.</note> would repeat his secret words [to Sejanus].

### VIII.

Sejanus, therefore, thinking he should act quickly, chose a slow poison that would mimic some other illness, and gave it to Drusus via the eunuch Lygdus; this fact was only discovered eight years later. While the sickness lasted, Tiberius maintained—or pretended to maintain—a firm heart. Even when his son was dead but not yet buried, he entered the Senate. To the consuls, who were sitting on lowly benches <gloss>4</gloss> to show their grief, he reminded them of their honor and the dignity of the place; with dry eyes and an unbroken voice, he comforted the Senate, which was weeping bitterly, <gloss>5</gloss> saying, "That I should come here...

---

1 *coarse or frightening*. *We might say, he drew his bread with a crossbow.* <note>An archaic Italian idiom for living under extreme tension or "pulling one's weight" through force.</note> See Note 69 of the first book. (*) — * "by methods that were not kind, etc." The manuscript strikes out: "with a harsh face and mostly frightening."

2 *and seething, etc.* He lamented that Tiberius had preferred Sejanus over himself as an assistant to the empire.

3 *let us pray to Modesty that he stops here.* Latin: <note>original: "precandum post haec modestiam, ut contentus esset"</note> "After all this, nothing remained but to pray for his modesty, that he might be content and not strive to climb any higher."

4 *to show grief, they were, etc.* The manuscript strikes out: "out of grief they sat on lowly benches;" and rewrites: "they sat low;" then strikes it out again and returns to the first way: "on lowly benches."

5 *the Senate, which was weeping bitterly.* He had written: "who wept bitterly;" then he struck it out and rewrote: "the bitter weeping of the Senate," and this reading is found in the Giuntina <note>The Giuntina refers to a famous 16th-century printing house in Florence.</note> edition. But in later revisions, he corrected it as seen above. Likewise, in the following passage, several changes are seen. The first draft is this: "saying he knew that by coming here in such great sorrow to be seen in the Senate he might be blamed: the grieving are barely able to speak to their relatives, barely able to look at the light, and this is not counted as weakness." Then he corrected: "saying that by coming here in such great sorrow to be seen he knew he might be blamed: the afflicted are barely able to hear their kin and usually flee the light without appearing weak." Finally, he corrected it as it appears in the main text.

(*) From this edition, note 1, page 53.

->THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.<-

[Tiberius, standing before the Senate] knew he might be blamed for showing himself while in such grief, as it is the habit of those in mourning to avoid the comforts of relatives and the light of day—usually without being noted for weakness. But he, in embracing the Republic, had sought the only true comforts. He lamented the decrepit age of Augusta <note>Livia, the widow of Augustus and mother of Tiberius.</note>, his own failing years, and his two grandsons <note>original: *nipotini*. These were the twin sons of Drusus, then about four years old.</note> who were still like chicks with their shells on their heads. <note>original: *col guscio in capo*. This is a colorful Italian metaphor for being extremely young or "just hatched." The translator notes that this captures the vulnerability of the four-year-old twins better than the drier Latin phrase *rudem adhuc nepotum*, which means "grandsons still unpracticed in ruling."</note> He then asked that the sons of Germanicus <note>Nero and Drusus Caesar, the Emperor's grand-nephews, who were next in the line of succession.</note> be brought in, as they were the only comforts for their present misfortunes. The consuls went for the youths and, having encouraged them with kind words <note>original: *firmant alloquio adolescentulos*</note>, presented them. He embraced them <note>The translator adds a passionate note here: "He embraced them. Oh, you old fox! <gloss>original: gattone</gloss> Do you hate the house of Germanicus so much, and yet put on these shows for me?"</note> and said: “Conscript Fathers, I entrusted these orphans to their uncle; and I prayed him that, even if he had children of his own, he would cherish them and raise them as his own blood for his own support and for the sake of those to come. Now that Drusus is taken from us, I pray and—in the presence of the gods and the fatherland—I conjure you: take these great-grandsons of Augustus, born of the most illustrious blood; guide them, and fulfill both your duty and mine. These boys, Nero and Drusus, are your parents: you were born such that your good and your ill are the concern of the Republic.”

### IX.

He brought everyone to tears and prayers for their future happiness. And had he ended his speech here, he would have left everyone filled with compassion and respect for him. But when he returned to those old stories of his—so often mocked—about wanting to leave the Republic, or having the consuls or someone else take over the government, he was not believed even when he spoke with truth and honesty. To the memory of Drusus...

---

<note>Translator's Note on "two grandsons": Here in the manuscript, there are many "repentances" (corrections) that we will note for the benefit of those who love to discover the secrets of art in great writers. The text originally read: "without grandsons of age (corrected to: with two infant grandsons : corrected to: not able) he asked for the sons of Germanicus to be brought, the only relief for present evils."</note>

<note>Translator's Note on "shells on their heads": Metaphors in speech are like twinkling stars. Our common tongue is full of them and fortunate for it. Why shut the door to them in noble writings just because the "establishment" has not found them in other writers? Let us open the door to this one about chicks; it places before our eyes the age—unfit for reigning—of those four-year-old twins. This is different from the Latin *rudem adhuc nepotum*, which is one of those "Tacitisms" that Alciato, in his letter on Giovio’s history, calls *senticeta* <gloss>thickets or bramble patches</gloss>. Truly, they are like thornbushes that catch on one's clothes, holding back and tiring the reader. With this metaphor, the speech is more affectionate, brief, and clear. I do not believe metaphor creates baseness; rather, it shows the dexterity of the mind in finding the similar in the dissimilar.</note>

<note>(*) The text following this point does not appear in the Giunta edition <gloss>a famous early 16th-century Florentine printing</gloss>.</note>

The honors for Germanicus were decreed, along with many others, as is the way with subsequent flattery. The funeral procession was most magnificent <gloss>1</gloss> with its display of ancestral images. Aeneas, the origin of the Julian line, all the Alban kings and Romulus, the founder of Rome, the nobility of the Sabines, Appius, and the other members of the Claudian house followed in a long line.

**X.** I have drawn the account of Drusus' death from many of the most faithful writers. But I will not keep silent on a rumor that arose in those times and still persists: that Sejanus <note>Lucius Aelius Sejanus, the ambitious commander of the Praetorian Guard.</note>, having corrupted Livia <note>This refers to Livilla, Drusus’ wife and Tiberius’ niece, who was seduced by Sejanus.</note>, also gained the mind of the eunuch Lygdus through the same dishonesty—a pageboy <gloss>2</gloss> who was attractive and dear to his master, and one of his primary ministers. And once it was agreed among the conspirators where and when <gloss>3</gloss> the poison should be given, Sejanus dared to change the plan. He whispered to Tiberius, as he was dining with Drusus: "Drusus is poisoning you in the first cup; do not drink it." The old man, deceived by this trick, took the cup and handed it to his son, who, being young, drained it. This made it even more believable that he had, out of fear and shame, swallowed the death he had intended for his father.

**XI.** This is a popular rumor, but historians do not confirm it, nor is it to be believed. For what man of even moderate prudence, let alone Tiberius with his great wisdom, would have blindly handed death to his own son with his own hand, in a way that could not be retracted? <gloss>4</gloss> Would he not have tortured the cupbearer first <gloss>5</gloss> and sought out who ordered it, proceeding with the deliberation that nature demands toward strangers, let alone toward an only son who had always been good? But because Sejanus was seen as a vessel for every enormity, and was so excessively loved by Caesar <note>Tiberius</note> while both were deeply hated, every outrageous tale was believed. And when it comes to the deaths of masters, <gloss>6</gloss> tongues will wag. The true order of this event was revealed by Sejanus' wife, Apicata, and clarified through the torture of Eu...

1 * *The funeral procession was most magnificent*. The Manuscript shows a deleted version: "In the carrying out there was very great pomp etc."

2 * *pageboy*. The Manuscript cancels: "valet."

3 * *and where and when*. The Manuscript cancels: "then fixed among the conspirators the time and place to give the poison."

4 * *in a way that could not be retracted* etc. The text means: how could he have given death to his son without hearing his defense, and by his own hand, without being able to turn back?

5 * *tortured the cupbearer first*, that is: how could he not have instead tortured the cupbearer etc.?

6 * *and when it comes to the deaths of masters* etc. The Latin reads: "rumors regarding the deaths of rulers are always particularly atrocious." <note>original: *atrociore semper famâ erga dominantium exitus*</note>

**XII.** While Tiberius praised his son from the rostrum <note>The "ringhiera" or speaker's platform in the Roman Forum.</note>, the senate and the people adopted the clothing and voices of mourning <gloss>3</gloss>, but inwardly they felt joy that the house of Germanicus was being revived. **XV.** In this year, Caesar [Tiberius] suffered a new grief from the death of one of Drusus’s twins; and no less from that of Lucilius Longus, his friend, who shared in all his sorrows and joys, and was the only senator to keep him company during his retreat to Rhodes. Therefore, the fathers decreed for him a censor’s funeral—though he was a "new man" <note>A term for the first man in a family to reach the Senate.</note>—and a statue in the Forum of Augustus at public expense. For at that time, Caesar still conducted all business through the hands of the Senate. Thus, they summoned Lucilius Capito, the procurator of Asia, to defend himself and then condemned him; he had been accused by the province of acting as a governor and employing soldiers, with Caesar greatly asserting <note>original: "magna cum asseveratione"</note> that he had granted him no authority beyond his slaves and his finances. If he had usurped such power, the province should be granted justice. For this reason, and because of the judgment made the previous year against Gaius Silanus, the cities of Asia decided to build a temple to Tiberius, his mother [Livia], and the Senate. It was granted and built. In the youth, there was a modesty and a beauty befitting a prince, which were made even more graceful by the known hatred and danger he faced from Sejanus.

**XVI.** At the same time, Caesar spoke of appointing a new Flamen of Jupiter <note>Also known as the *Flamen Dialis*, the high priest of Jupiter.</note> in place of the deceased Servius Maluginese, and of reforming the office. **XVII.** [Year of Rome 777; 24 AD] When the consuls Cornelius Cethegus and Visellius Varrone took office, the pontiffs, and with them the other priests, prayed to the gods for the life of the Prince, and also for Nero and Drusus <note>The sons of the late Germanicus.</note>. This was not done out of love for those young men, but out of flattery—a vice where a corrupted people errs as much through excess as through neglect. Consequently, Tiberius—who was never kind to the house of Germanicus—was so offended <note>original: "qui si versò"; meaning he took great offense that these youths were being treated as equals to his own old age.</note> that prayers were offered for those children alongside his own. He summoned the pontiffs and asked them if they did this because of the pleas or threats of Agrippina. Although they denied it <note>original: "e negando"; even though they insisted she was not involved.</note>, he rebuked them skillfully, as they were his relatives or the leading men of the cities. However, in the Senate, he warned that in the future they should not stir the flighty minds of the youths with such arrogant and premature honors. For Sejanus never ceased saying: "The city is split into factions, as if in a civil war; some call themselves followers of Agrippina, and they will grow if allowed to. There is no other remedy for this growing discord than to strike off <note>original: "scapezare"; literally to decapitate or cut down.</note> one or two of these fierce partisans <note>The most ardent supporters of Agrippina.</note>."

**XVIII.** The first to be struck down <gloss>1</gloss> were Gaius Silius and Titius Sabinus. For both, their friendship with Germanicus proved to be their ruin. Silius suffered more; having commanded a large army for seven years, earned triumphal honors <note>original: "le trionfali"; refers to the *ornamenta triumphalia*, the highest military honor available to those outside the imperial family.</note> in Germany, and defeated Sacrovir, the greater his stature was, the more his fall terrified others. He offended Tiberius even more by boasting that his soldiers had always remained obedient while others were mutinous; he claimed that Tiberius <gloss>2</gloss> would not be emperor if his own legions had wavered <gloss>3</gloss> even slightly. "Therefore," Tiberius thought, "I am nothing; I can never repay him." For benefits give pleasure only as long as they can be repaid; once they become excessive, they are repaid with ingratitude and hatred. <gloss>4</gloss>

**XIX.** Silius's wife was Sosia Galla, who was hated by the Prince because Agrippina loved her. Tiberius decided to attack these two first and to delay the move against Sabinus. The consul Varro was not ashamed to obey Sejanus <note>The ambitious and ruthless commander of the Praetorian Guard.</note> by bringing the accusation, using the pretext that their fathers had been enemies. When the accused asked for a short delay until the accuser’s term as consul ended, Caesar <note>Tiberius.</note> refused, saying, "That the summoning of parties <gloss>5</gloss> belonged to the magistrates, and the power <term>balia</term> <note>A term for legal authority or jurisdiction.</note> of the consul could not be diminished, for it is his vigilance that ensures the Republic suffers no harm." <note>original: "che la republica non riceva dannaggio"; this mirrors the famous Roman decree *caveant consules ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet*.</note> It was typical of Tiberius to use such ancient words to cloak his modern villainies. He therefore made a great show of summoning the Senators <note>referred to as "the fathers" (*i padri*).</note> as if to judge whether Silius was being tried by the laws, or if this was merely a case brought by the consul Varro, <gloss>6</gloss> or a matter of public interest. That he had known of or aided the war...

1 * **The first to be struck down etc.** The first of those partisans upon whom hands were laid were G. Silius and Titius Sabinus.
2 * **and that he**, Tiberius.
3 * **had wavered**, had wished to stir up trouble or revolution.
4 **benefits... excessive are paid with ingratitude and hatred.** For this reason, the bankrupt man, even if a settlement is reached, avoids the face of his creditor; and the man saved from drowning cannot bear to see his rescuer, by a first instinct and impulse of nature. (*) Nor can the minister of one's own crime endure to be seen, because he serves as a reminder and a reproach, just as Anicetus reminded Nero of his mother's death. <note>Anicetus was the freedman who carried out the murder of Nero's mother, Agrippina the Younger.</note>

Davanzati has used the word "aggiornare" <note>To adjourn or set a date.</note> here to mean assigning a day for someone to appear in court (the Latin *diem dicere*).
6 * **or if this was merely the consul Varro**, and not rather a henchman of Tiberius.
(*) What follows is not found in the Giuntina edition.

"Caesar’s anger is my crime," Silius said constantly, and nothing else in his defense. They could not find fault with his governance; but there was no answering charges of treason against the state. Silius did not wait for the sentence, and took his own life.

XX. Nevertheless, there was a rush for his assets,<sup>2</sup> not to restore taxes that had been poorly collected, as they claimed; for no one was asking for them back: but to seize the gift given to him by Augustus, which was deducted from his debt: the treasury <note>The *fiscus*, the emperor's private treasury.</note> recovered it down to the last penny. This was the first instance of Tiberius's diligence in seizing the property of others.<sup>3</sup> Sosia was banished by the opinion of Asinius Gallus, who proposed giving part of the assets to the children and the rest to the treasury. Manius Lepidus said, "A fourth should go to the accusers by force of law, the rest to the children." I find that this Lepidus was a grave and wise man of those times, because he tempered many cruelties devised by the flatterers, and was able to do so...

<sup>1</sup> **to the rebellion of Sacrovir.** Used as in Book III, 43-47, regarding which Tiberius, when asked for his opinion, took no account and fueled the war.

<sup>2</sup> **\* there was a rush for his assets:** which by law should have been respected as belonging to an accused man who had taken his own life.

<sup>3</sup> **the first instance of Tiberius's diligence against the property of others.** The second must have been when he had the Spaniard Sextus Marius accused of incest with his daughter, eyeing his boundless wealth and those gold mines, as in Book VI, 19. The third was a bit <term>bigerognola</term> <note>This archaic Italian term suggests something "mean-spirited" or "rather wicked."</note> (*) when he scraped the will of his mother <note>Livia, also known as Augusta.</note> which left to Sergius Galba (who later became emperor) *quingenties H-S* <note>original: "quingenties H-S"; roughly 50 million sesterces.</note> which meant one and a quarter million in gold. The man who drew up the document did not write it out in full, but wrote in their shorthand, D; and Tiberius scraped the body of the letter and turned it into an L, which then read *quinquagies* <note>original: "quinquagies"; roughly 5 million sesterces.</note>: he removed, in our way of thinking, a zero (*Suetonius in the Life of Galba, chapter five*). Others say that the writing was *quin. H-S*; which could be read as *quinquagies* just as easily as *quingenties*. Tiberius interpreted it to his own advantage as *quinquagies*, that is, one hundred twenty-five thousand florins; a measly legacy for the greatness of Augusta and Galba; and even that he did not receive. The fourth instance of diligence was perhaps (**) letting his ministers fill up like sponges so he could squeeze them, as Note 76 of the first book says. (***)

(*) **bigerognola, mean-spirited:** this is a figure of speech used for understatement, and actually means "the worst."
(**) **The Giuntina edition says:** "it was perhaps letting the ministers sell favors and justice, in order to punish them when they were full and squeeze them; hence he called them his sponges. Thus he grew rich, and the people blessed him." Here in the Magliabechiano Manuscript <note>A famous collection of manuscripts in the National Library of Florence.</note> there follows another section, which is crossed out, and says: "But Tiberius was a prince and could do these things easily. The real 'beauty' of it was using the property of others, like certain neighbors of mine, who took a notable sum of ducats from a friend to trade in partnership, and at the end of eleven months, without any accidents or losses in trade, they fled with 41,000; and they have found help, favors, friends, and ways; hence they walk with their heads held high and spend cheerfully. And they 'restore' that friend by rumoring that they satisfied his debt before the others, contrary to all truth.

...camped beneath the ruined fort of Auzea, which they had previously burned, trusting in a location surrounded by vast forests. Remembering the hardships endured to reach this long-desired and so often evaded¹ battle, our soldiers satiated themselves with vengeance and blood. Through the ranks went the cry: "Everyone head straight for Tacfarinas! Everyone knows him from so many battles; the war will not end unless this head is cut off." He, after his entire guard was killed,² seeing his son a prisoner and himself surrounded on all sides by Romans, rushed into the thick of the weapons and, through a well-avenged death, escaped imprisonment; and so the war was ended.

**XXVI.** Dolabella requested triumphal insignia. Tiberius denied them to him so as not to darken the glory of Blaesus, the uncle of Sejanus. But Blaesus gained no honor from this; instead, Dolabella earned greater renown for having, with a smaller army, taken distinguished prisoners, killed the general, and finished the war. One could see in Rome³ the ambassadors of the Garamantes (a rare sight) who, after the death of Tacfarinas, were so cowed that they came to clear themselves before the Roman people. To Ptolemy, in recognition of his merits in this war, the fathers <note>The Roman Senators.</note>, reviving an ancient custom, sent a senator to present him with an ivory staff⁴ and an embroidered toga, and to address him as king, companion, and friend.

**XXIX.** Then the accuser named Gnaeus Lentulus and Seius Tubero, to the great shame of Caesar <note>The Emperor Tiberius</note>, that two of his dearest friends, the foremost men of the city—Lentulus, now decrepit with age, and Tubero, sickly <gloss>2</gloss>—should be accused of causing riots, war, and a conspiracy against him. Tiberius showed such great bitterness against the elder Serenus because Serenus had written to him back when Libo was condemned, saying that he alone had served him without reward, adding other sharp words not meant for proud and disdainful ears. The Emperor nursed this grudge for eight years, during which time he laid several traps for him; yet the slaves withstood the tortures.

**XXX.** The opinions of the Senate favored the ancient punishment <note>Death by being beaten to death or strangled in prison</note>. Tiberius, however, to lessen the odium of the act, opposed this. Asinius Gallus proposed exiling him to the islands of Gyaros or Donusa. This did not please the Emperor, who said that there was no water on either island. He remarked that whoever wishes for another to live must allow them the means to do so. Thus, Serenus was taken back to Amorgos. And because Cornutus had killed himself, it was proposed that when a person accused of treason <note>The crime of *maiestas*</note> killed themselves before the judgment, the informants should not receive their reward. This motion would have passed, had Caesar not openly opposed it—contrary to his usual secretive custom—complaining that "the established orders were being ruined and the republic was falling; they might as well abolish the laws rather than the guardians of them." Thus the spies <note>The *delatores*, or professional informers</note>—a class of people created to ruin everyone, and who are never sufficiently restrained by penalties—were instead enticed with rewards.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Emperor Tiberius’s judicial decisions and the historian's reflections on the nature of his records. The previous page detailed the trial of Vibius Serenus and the Emperor's insistence on exile over execution.</meta>

...convicted of having defamed him with infamous verses, he was pardoned at the request of his brother, a senator. It is a matter of even greater wonder that, seeing the better path and how much clemency was celebrated,¹ he chose the worse. It should not be said² that he sinned out of ignorance. For it is well known when someone exalts a prince's deed with true praise, and when with gilded <note>Original: *orpellata*, meaning fake or showy like tinsel</note> praise. Tiberius himself was a speaker in bits and pieces; when it was helpful, he was expansive and quick. But in the case of Publius Suillius—formerly the treasurer of Germanicus, who had been driven out of Italy for taking money to provide a specific verdict—the Emperor banished him to an island with such great resolve that he swore it was for the good of the republic. This seemed harsh at the time, but the following age blessed him for it, seeing that once Suillius returned to power, he used the favor of Claudius for a long time as a venal man with great success, and always without goodness. The same penalty was given to the senator Cato Firmius for a false accusation of treason <term>maestà</term> <note>Latin: *maiestas*; a broad category of crimes against the dignity or safety of the state and the Emperor</note> brought against his sister. This man, as has been said, had entrapped³ and then accused Libo. Tiberius, mindful of this "good" service, spared him from exile under another pretext, though he still allowed him to be removed from the Senate.

...compare these annals of ours to the ancient histories of Rome. The writers of those times narrated great wars, cities taken by force, kings captured and defeated; and domestically, the discords of consuls with tribunes, laws regarding land and grain, and the brawls of the common people with the nobility—these were very broad fields. Our work is narrow and yields little praise: a firm peace, or one only slightly disturbed; a Rome paralyzed by dread; and a prince indifferent to expanding the empire. But it will not be useless to dissect such small fragments of history, which at first seem like nothing, but provide us with the greatest lessons for life.¹

### XXXIII.

It happens that nations and cities are ruled either by the people, or by the nobility, or by a single man. A form of republic drawn from all these² is easier to praise than to actually find, or if found, to maintain. Therefore, just as when the plebeians or when the senators held power, it was necessary to know the nature of the masses and how to manage them; and just as whoever understood the inner workings of the Senate and the nobility was called a wise and clever navigator of those winds; so now that the state has been overturned and one man commands, we must examine and note these minutiae. We do this because few are the prudent men who can discern useful and honest things from their opposites through reason alone; most learn them only from the experiences of others. These accounts, though useful, bring little pleasure. Descriptions of far-off lands, various battles, and the deaths of great captains entice and hold the readers' attention; but we must deal with atrocious condemnations, continual accusations, the downfall of innocents, and deceitful friendships and their causes—outcomes that are often the same and become tedious. Furthermore, ancient writers are not criticized;³ it matters to no one whether you favor the Roman or the Carthaginian ranks. But during the reign of Tiberius, men were punished or...

## XXXIV. [Year of Rome 778, Year of Christ 25]

When Cornelius Cossus and Asinius Agrippa were consuls, Cremutius Cordus faced a novel accusation: that in his published annals he had praised Marcus Brutus and called Gaius Cassius "the last of the Romans." His accusers were Satrius Secundus and Pinario Natta, the lackeys <note>original: "lance"; the Latin source uses "clientes"</note> of Sejanus. This was his undoing <note>original: "Questo gli dava lo scacco"; Latin: "id perniciabile reo," meaning it was fatal to the accused</note>, as was the stern expression the Emperor <note>Augustus/Tiberius are often referred to as "Cesare"</note> wore during the defense. Cremutius, certain of his death, began his speech in this way:

"I am, Conscript Fathers, so innocent in my deeds that I am only being charged for my words. These were not even spoken against the Prince or his mother, who are covered by the law of majesty <term>maiestas: a law concerning treason or any act that diminished the dignity and 'majesty' of the Roman state and its ruler</term>; rather, I am accused of praising Brutus and Cassius. Many have written of their deeds, and no one has ever mentioned them without honor. Titus Livy, supreme in eloquence and truth, praised Gnaeus Pompey so highly that Augustus called him a 'Pompeian,' yet he remained his friend. He calls Scipio, Afranius, this Cassius, and this Brutus distinguished men; he never calls them 'thieves' or 'traitors to the fatherland,' as I hear them called today. The writings of Asinius Pollio make noble memory of them. Messala Corvinus used to call Cassius his general; and yet both Pollio and Corvinus enjoyed great power and honors. When Marcus Cicero wrote a book that raised Cato to the heavens, what else did Caesar the Dictator do but write a rebuttal, as if he were arguing before a jury? <note>original: "quasi... alle civili"; Latin: "velut apud iudices," referring to Caesar's written response to Cicero's "Cato"</note> The letters of Antony and the speeches of Brutus contain false but venomous slanders against Augustus. The verses of Bibaculus and Catullus lash out <note>original: "trafiggono"; Davanzati considered the word "sferzano" (whip) in his manuscript</note> at the Emperors. And yet, the late Julius and Augustus themselves..."

**XXXV.** "I pass over the fact that the Greeks could speak not just freely, but without restraint. <sup>2</sup> At most, they repaid words with words. But writing about the dead, who are no longer hated or loved, has never been forbidden or blamed. Do I perhaps go with Cassius and Brutus in arms to the fields of Philippi to inflame the people to civil war? They died seventy years ago, and yet their likenesses are still recognized in statues that were saved—even by the victor—and part of their deeds live on in the memories of writers. The age that follows renders to each their own honor. Nor, if I am condemned, will there be a lack of those who remember Brutus, Cassius, and even me." He left the Senate and died by starvation <note>Cremutius Cordus chose suicide by fasting to maintain his dignity</note>. The Senators <term>padri: literally 'fathers,' the traditional title for Roman senators</term> ordered that the aediles <term>edili: city officials in charge of public order and archives</term> burn his books. But they were saved, hidden, and later published. Therefore, I laugh at the lack of foresight <sup>3</sup> of those who believe that princes can strip the memory of posterity by punishing genius; on the contrary, they grant such writers more credit. Nor have foreign kings or others who used such severity achieved anything but shame for themselves and glory for their victims.

**XXXVI.** So many legal cases rained down in this year that when Drusus, the governor of Rome, came to the tribunal during the Latin Festival to make a good start to his term, Calpurnius Salviano came before him against Sextus Marius. However, having been publicly rebuked for this by Caesar <note>Tiberius</note>, Salviano was sent into exile. The citizens of Cyzicus, accused of having neglected the worship of the Divine Augustus and of mistreating Roman citizens, lost the freedom they had earned during the siege by Mithridates, whom they drove back as much through their own steadfastness <sup>4</sup> as by the help of Lucullus. It is true that Augustus had the idea of giving his daughter to a knight; because he thought of everything: and seeing how much anyone who took her would be elevated, he considered Proculeius and others who were quiet and uninvolved in matters of state. <margin>They were never involved in the state affairs.</margin> But look at what he actually did: he gave her to Marcus Agrippa, and then to me. ...fearing the suspicions, the public outcry, and envy, he looked to his own interests. **XLII.** Around those days, the trial of Votieno Montano occurred—a man of great talent. This convinced Tiberius, who was already leaning that way, to no longer wish to see the Senators <note>original: "padri," literally "fathers," the formal term for Roman Senators</note>, nor hear his own shames and true insults thrown in his face. Votieno was accused of writing a satire against Caesar. A soldier named Aemilius testified to all those foul things with great eagerness. Though people tried to silence him <note>original: "eragli dato in su la voce," meaning they tried to shout him down</note>, he persisted to the end. Thus Tiberius heard his own disgraces with such scandal that he shouted he wanted to clear himself then and there in judgment;² and only with his friends' pleas and the flattery of everyone else did they calm him. Votieno was punished for treason <term>lesa maestà: the crime of "injured majesty," or treason against the state or the Emperor's person</term>. And hearing himself described as too cruel in his punishments, Caesar became even more enraged. And after Lentulus Gaetulicus, the consul-elect, had condemned Aquilia for adultery with Vario Ligure under the Julian Law;³ Tiberius condemned her to exile. He also struck Apidio Merula from the Senate because he had not taken an oath to the late Emperor Augustus.

**XLIV.** Two illustrious citizens died in this year: Gnaeus Lentulus, known for his well-endured poverty and later for his loyally acquired and sparingly used wealth, in addition to his consulship and the triumphal honors earned against the Getae; and Lucius Domitius, whose father was powerful at sea during the civil wars, later siding with Antony and then with Caesar. His grandfather died fighting for the aristocrats at Pharsalus; he himself was chosen as the husband for Antonia the Younger, daughter of Octavia; later, leading an army, he crossed the Elbe and penetrated further into Germany than any before him, earning triumphal honors. Lucius Antonius also died, a man of great but unfortunate noble blood; for Augustus had punished his father, Iullus Antonius, with death for committing adultery with Julia, and had sent Lucius, the grandson of Octavia, to Marseille while still a youth, where he lived in exile under the pretext of study. Nevertheless, the Senate decreed him a funeral and placed his remains among the Octavii.

...atrocious death. A peasant from the city of Termeste <note>Located in Hither Spain, modern-day Tiermes.</note> jumped out from the side of the road at Lucius Piso, the governor, who was traveling without a guard because the province was at peace, and gave him a mortal wound.
