However, this did him little good, for his horse was caught and led through the nearby villages, where it was recognized as his. The man was captured <margin>He was caught in much the same way as Poltrot, who killed the Duke of Guise. <note>Jean de Poltrot was a 16th-century assassin; the translator Davanzati adds this contemporary comparison for his readers.</note></margin> and terribly tortured <note>original: "collato," referring to the "colla" or strappado, where a prisoner is hoisted by their arms tied behind their back.</note> to force him to name his accomplices. With a loud voice, he shouted in his own language that they were wasting their time: even if his companions were right there <margin>Meaning: even if they did not flee, but stood right here watching the torture, he still would not betray them.</margin>, he would not speak, no matter how great the agony. <margin>Many wise and learned men believe that extracting truth through torment is neither humane nor reliable, and is harmful to the state: for we tear apart living bodies like wild beasts, and very often we free the guilty who can endure the pain and deny the truth, while we condemn the innocent who lie because of the suffering. Ulpian says that torture is a fallacious and dangerous proof <note>original: "prova fallace e pericolosa." Ulpian was a famous Roman jurist.</note>. And Cicero says in his speech *For Sulla* that in such agony truth has no place <note>original: "la verità non ha luogo."</note>. For this reason, the Romans did not examine free persons with torments, but only their slaves, because the laws considered slaves as nothing, like corpses. Yet we Christians inflict this slaughter upon ourselves, even for minor reasons, and sometimes for cases that are not even criminal but merely financial. Boccaccio rightly had his character Tedaldo degli Elisei consider the blind severity of laws and rulers who, acting as if they were diligent investigators of the truth, use cruelty to make people testify to falsehoods; they call themselves ministers of justice and of God, while they are actually executors of iniquity and the devil. See Anne Robert, Book I, Chapter 4 of the *Decisions of Paris*; see also the constancy of the maidservant examined against the false accusation of Octavia in the fourteenth book of these *Annals*. <note>This note, where Davanzati anticipates the ideas of the famous Cesare Beccaria regarding the abolition of torture, does not appear in the Giuntina edition.</note></margin> The next day, when brought back for further interrogation, he shook himself free from the guards with such great strength and smashed his head against a stone post that he died on the spot. It is believed the Termestinians had Piso killed because he was bleeding them dry with heavy taxes.

### XLVI. [Year of Rome 779, Year of Christ 26.]

In the following year, during the consulship of Lentulus Gaetulicus and Gaius Calvisius, triumphal honors were granted to Poppaeus Sabinus for having crushed the Thracian tribes of those high and rugged mountains, who were naturally fierce. They had rebelled <note>original: "Levaro in capo," literally "raised their heads," an idiom for starting an insurrection.</note> because of their wild nature and because they refused to give the flower of their youth to serve in our military. They were accustomed to disobeying even their own kings, or at most, only sending aid to...

**XLVII.** Sabinus gave them soothing words until Pomponius Labeo could arrive with the legion from Moesia <note>A Roman province located in the modern-day Balkans, along the Danube.</note>, and Rhoemetalces <note>A Thracian king loyal to Rome.</note> arrived with those Thracians who had remained faithful. The Roman commander ascended these slopes and easily drove them off with little bloodshed, as the enemy had a retreat nearby. There he established his camp and, with his best troops, occupied the ridge of a mountain which was level until it reached a fortress defended by a large, disorganized multitude of armed men. Against the fiercest among them, who were dancing in front of their trenches with songs and chants according to their custom, he sent skilled archers. From a distance, these archers inflicted many wounds with ease. When the Romans drew closer, they were momentarily thrown into disorder by a sudden charge from the fortress, but they were rescued by the Sugambrian cohort <note>A Germanic tribe serving as auxiliary troops in the Roman army.</note> which the commander brought forward—a unit no less ready for battle and, with their own clashing arms and songs, no less terrifying.

**XLVIII.** The camp was then placed next to the enemy, while those Thracians who were our allies were left in the old fortifications with permission to lay waste, burn, and plunder until evening; however, they were ordered to stay awake and on guard through the night. At first, they followed these orders. Later, having given themselves over to pleasures² and becoming enriched by their plunder, they abandoned their posts and immersed themselves in food, wine, and sleep. The enemies, noticing their negligence, formed two columns: one to attack the plunderers and the other to assault the Roman camp. This was not done with the hope of capturing it, but so that each Roman, distracted by the shouts and the danger to his own life, would not hear the noise of the other struggle. They moved under the cover of night...

# LI.
Suddenly, hordes of barbarians came running with large stones, scorched stakes, and oak trunks, striking at the wooden fence; they filled the ditches with bundles of brushwood, vines, and corpses; they set up bridges and ladders <gloss>1</gloss>, leaning them against the defenses. They tried to seize the ramparts, pull them down, and climb up, pushing back the defenders. The Romans, in turn, pushed them back, killed them, and cast them down with shields, spears, stones, and masonry. The Romans were emboldened by the victory already in their grasp and the shame that would follow a defeat; the barbarians were driven by their last hope of safety <gloss>2</gloss> and the presence and weeping of their mothers and wives. The night gave courage to some and fear to others. Unforeseen blows came and went, without the soldiers knowing from where or toward what they were aimed, nor could they distinguish friend from foe. The mountains echoed the shouts of the enemies opposite, who seemed to have appeared at the Romans' backs, frightening them so much that some Romans abandoned the trenches, believing them to have been breached. Only a few of the enemy actually entered; the others were killed, or their best men wounded. At dawn, they were driven back up to the fortress <gloss>3</gloss> which was taken by force; and the surrounding people surrendered. The sudden and cruel frost of Mount Haemus <note>The original Italian refers to "monte Emo," known today as the Balkan Mountains.</note> defended the rest from further force or siege.

# LII.
In Rome, with the Emperor's household in turmoil as they plotted the death of Agrippina <note>Agrippina the Elder, granddaughter of Augustus and a major rival to the Emperor Tiberius's confidant, Sejanus.</note>, her cousin Claudia Pulcra was accused by Domitius Afer. Afer had recently been praetor <gloss>4</gloss>, was little known, and was eager to make a name for himself by any means <gloss>5</gloss>. Pulcra was charged with adultery with Furnius, of using poison against the Emperor, and of sorcery. ...the Milesians were too preoccupied with the religious rites of Apollo, and the Ephesians with those of Diana. <margin>1</margin> The final judgment came down to the people of Sardis and the people of Smyrna. The Sardians read aloud a decree from Etruria <note>modern-day Tuscany</note> which they claimed proved they shared our blood. They recounted how Tyrrhenus and Lydus, sons of King Atys, had divided their burgeoning population: Lydus remained in his own land, while it fell to Tyrrhenus to seek out a new country. Each gave his own name to his people: the former in Asia, the latter in Italy. They claimed that as the Lydians grew in number once more, they sent a colony into Greece, which was named after Pelops. They further displayed letters from Roman commanders and treaties made with us during the Macedonian wars, while boasting of their fertile rivers, excellent climate, and the richness of the surrounding lands.

**LVI.** The Smyrnaeans, having recalled their own ancient origins—whether from Tantalus, the son of Jupiter, or from Theseus, also of divine lineage, or from an Amazon—moved on to the more significant weight of their merits toward the Roman people. they had sent fleets to assist not only in wars fought abroad, but even those suffered within Italy itself. They were the first to build a temple to the City of Rome, during the consulship of Marcus Porcius <note>Cato the Elder, in 195 BCE</note>, at a time when the Roman people were indeed great, but had not yet reached their current peak, as Carthage still stood and powerful kings ruled in Asia. They also recalled aiding the army of Lucius Sulla when it was in great peril; in the heart of winter, when the army was left destitute of clothing, the news reached the council of Smyrna, and every citizen stripped off his own garments to send them to the shivering legions. Consequently, when asked for their verdict, the Senators preferred the Smyrnaeans. Vibio Marso proposed that Marcus Lepidus, who had been assigned that province, should choose <margin>2</margin> a deputy to oversee the construction of that temple. When Lepidus declined the honor out of modesty, Valerius Naso, a man of praetorian rank, was chosen by lot.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding Tiberius's departure from Rome. On the preceding page, the historian concluded the debate over city temples and transitioned to the Emperor's fateful decision to leave the capital for the countryside of Campania.</meta>

...outside of Rome. I have mentioned, as many authors do, that this move was a scheme of Sejanus; but considering that Tiberius remained in that solitude for six years even after Sejanus was executed, I am led to wonder if it was actually his own plan to hide, in those secluded places, the cruelties and filth that he was making public by his very actions. Others believed he did so because he was ashamed, even in his old age, of his unsightly body: long, thin, stooped, and bald; his face was blotched with sores and often covered in medicinal plasters. Even during his time in Rhodes, he used to avoid crowds and hide his pleasures. Others say he did it to escape his unbearable mother, whom he did not want as a partner in power but could not drive away, as he held the Empire because of her. Indeed, Augustus had wanted to give the Empire to Germanicus <note>original: "nipote di sua sorella." Germanicus was the son of Antonia the Younger, daughter of Octavia the Elder, who was Augustus's sister.</note>, his sister’s grandson, who was well-liked by everyone; but, won over by his wife’s entreaties, Augustus adopted Tiberius, and Tiberius in turn adopted Germanicus. The Empress <note>Livia Augusta</note> would often throw this in his face and use it to her advantage.

**LVIII.** He departed with only a small retinue. Of the senators, there was only Cocceius Nerva, a former consul and a man learned in the law. Among the Roman knights of high standing were Sejanus and Curtius Atticus, along with several men of letters, mostly Greeks, to keep him entertained with their conversation. The astrologers <note>original: "strolaghi." An archaic Italian term for astrologi.</note> claimed he had departed at such a moment that he would never return to Rome. This proved to be the ruin of many who listened and gossiped, predicting he would die soon; they could not foresee the unbelievable circumstance that he would remain away for eleven years by his own choice. One can see from this how much "the art" <note>Referring to the art of astrology.</note> grazes the edge of error and how obscured the truth can be. That he would not return to Rome was correctly predicted; but they failed to see that he would grow so old in nearby villas, or along the coast, and often just outside the very walls <note>The translator notes that the Giuntina edition uses "mure" while others use "mura."</note> of the city.

**LIX.** During those days, he encountered a danger that gave the people much to talk about and gave Tiberius reason to trust in the great and steadfast love of Sejanus. While they were dining at "The Cave" <note>Spelonca</note>, a villa situated between the sea of Amyclae and the mountains of Fondi, in a natural cavern, the entrance collapsed, sending many stones down upon some of the servants <note>The manuscript shows the author struggled with this term, crossing out "ministers" and "stewards" before settling on "servants."</note>. Everyone fled in terror. Sejanus, however, braced himself on his knees, head, and hands, and...

**LXI.** At the end of the year, two distinguished men died: Asinius Agrippa, of a lineage more illustrious than it was ancient <note>Referring to a family that has achieved greatness recently rather than having a long, ancient pedigree.</note>, and of a life that did not stray from his rank; and Quintus Haterius, a senator and an orator celebrated in his lifetime. <margin>¹ *liable to making a greater blunder.* Latin: « *insidiis magis opportunum* » <note>original: "more vulnerable to snares."</note> — To "make a bag" (far sacco) or "the bag" is the same as committing some error. See History, II, 34.</margin>
<margin>² *that resounding river of his.* Similarly, at the end of the first book of the *Histories*, he mentions Galerius Trachalus, who, to fill the ears of the people, was worth a fortress. Cymbals without music could not have greatly pleased Cornelius <note>The author Tacitus.</note>, who so condensed his writings to give them life. One may wonder which is worth more, nature <note>Natural talent.</note> or doctrine <note>Learned skill and art.</note>. If they were entirely separated, nature on its own would be worth something; doctrine, nothing. A fertile field, if uncultivated, produces wild things; a stone (*) produces nothing and cannot be cultivated. Nature provides the raw material; doctrine, or art, gives it form. But if nothing is provided to it, art has nothing to shape. And if nature does not appear on the field, art cannot overcome it. When joined together, the more excellent one prevails. Both being perfect, they make the work perfect. But in the perfect speaker, which has the greater part? In the voice, nature; on paper, doctrine. The voice, with open reasons heated by the delivery, moves the people, for whom learned and subtle things would be lost or suspected; just as the greatest diligence in finishing statues or paintings that must be seen from afar results in strain and dryness. Writing that is held in the hand and examined subtly by scholars becomes common and does not live unless it possesses exquisite doctrine, made to shine like burnished gold through diligence and labor. I find these qualities were great in the great writers and noble artists, who were greedy for and never satisfied with excellence and glory. Lodovico Cardi, called Cigoli <note>A famous Italian painter and architect (1559–1613) active at the time this translation was being refined.</note>, a young man most enamored with painting, seems to me to be imitating them very well. — *that resounding river of his died with him.* The Manuscript cancels: "that fierce overabundance of his went with him to the grave;" and again: "that slippery resonance of his died with him;" and also: "that slipping and rumbling of his died with him."</margin>

**LXV.** That hill (since it is relevant <note>original: "a proposito." The manuscript cancels the phrase "in taglio," which meant "opportune."</note> to our subject) was called *Quercetolanus* in ancient times because it was fertile and full of oaks. From that foreign word, that district was called "Tuscan."

**LXVI.** If the kindness of the great and the liberality of the Prince gave comfort in those cases, the plague of accusations grew more numerous and cruel every day without relief. **LXVII.** After Caesar <note>Emperor Tiberius.</note> had dedicated the temples in Campania and decreed that no one should disturb his peace—posting guards to prevent any visitors from passing, as he now hated the cities, the colonies, and everything on the mainland—he retreated to the island of Capri, three miles beyond the Cape of Sorrento. He must have found it pleasing for being solitary and lacking harbors; small vessels could barely approach it, and no one could land there in secret. The winter air is mild, protected by the mountain from harsh winds; in summer it faces the west, with a pleasant view of the open sea and the beautiful coast, not yet disfigured by the fires of Vesuvius <note>A significant historical detail: Tacitus describes the landscape as it appeared before the catastrophic eruption of 79 AD.</note>. It is said that the Greeks once held it, and specifically the Teleboans. Tiberius was then occupied <gloss>1</gloss> with the buildings and the names of twelve villas; <gloss>2</gloss> and as much as he had previously been intent on public cares, so much there did he surrender himself to wretched idleness and secret lusts. In his foolish belief in the suspicions that Sejanus <note>Tiberius's powerful and treacherous prefect.</note> stirred up in Rome, fanning the flames and raising alarms here through traps already set against Nero and Agrippina <note>The son and widow of the beloved general Germanicus, whom Sejanus viewed as obstacles to his power.</note>. He kept soldiers to record, as if in annals, every one of their movements, deeds, and words—both public and private. False advisors were sent to urge them to flee to the armies in Germany, or to the statue of Augustus in a crowded forum, to embrace it and cry out:

> "Come, good people! Come, Senate! Help us!"

And though they [Nero and Agrippina] abhorred such suggestions, these acts were reported as if they had been planned by them.

<gloss>1</gloss> *Tiberius was then occupied, etc.* With all due respect to our author, this is a thorny expression <note>original: "senticeto," literally a thicket of thorns.</note>, made worse in the Postilla. Valeriani translates: "But Tiberius then occupied the depth and vastness of twelve villas." The island of Capri was famous for twelve large villas, which were believed to be named after twelve Gods. Tiberius occupied their space with new buildings, even destroying their original names. This is what Tacitus means with the words: "he had settled upon the names and masses of twelve villas" <note>original Latin: "duodecim villarum nominibus et molibus insederat."</note>.

<gloss>2</gloss> *with the buildings and the names of twelve villas.* Perhaps it is better to say: "He set himself around twelve villas of beautiful names and palaces." This phrasing—"he had settled upon the names and masses of villas"—means villas having names and masses, just as this author uses: "the moisture of the swamps and the roughness of the mountains" <note>original Latin: "humida paludum et aspera montium"</note> instead of "swamps having moisture and mountains having roughness," and many other similar thorny expressions, as Alciato calls them. See note 6. (*)

(*) Note from the Giuntina edition, omitted in later editions. Note 6 is note 2 on page 161 of this edition.

This unburdening <gloss>3</gloss> of such dangerous matters seemed to him a sign of true friendship. Consequently, Sabinus now sought out Latiaris of his own accord, visiting him at home and opening his heart to him, sharing all his woes.

**LXX.** Caesar, on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st, New Year's Day</note>, sent a letter to the fathers <term>Patres: the Senators</term>. And so it was done immediately. As he was led to his death,³ he cried out with all his might, though he was gagged: "This is how New Year’s Day is celebrated: these are the victims sacrificed to Sejanus." Wherever he turned his eye or directed a word, he made people scatter,⁴ vanish, and empty the streets and squares: and some would even return to show themselves again, for fear of having appeared afraid. "Tiberius did not intend to bring so much hatred upon himself,⁵ but there were those who wanted to show that the new magistrates can begin their terms in the prisons, just as they do in temples and at altars. **LXXI.** Had I not resolved to recount each event in its proper year, I would gladly tell here of the end of Latinius and Opsio, and those other scoundrels—not only during the reign of Gaius Caesar <note>the Emperor Caligula</note>, but under Tiberius himself. For Tiberius never wished for anyone to strike at the ministers of his crimes; rather, whenever he grew weary of them, he employed new ones and cast the tiresome old ones aside. We shall speak, therefore, in their proper places of their punishments. At that time, Asinius Gallus, although he was Agrippina’s brother-in-law,¹ declared that they should ask Tiberius to clarify whom he feared, and then let the Senate deal with them. Tiberius possessed no virtue (in his own view) so dear as dissimulation; thus, it tasted bitter to him that what he tried to hide was being uncovered. But Sejanus calmed him: not to benefit Gallus, but so the prince would never again² name those people, knowing with what thunder and lightning of words and deeds his simmering anger would burst from that clouded breast. At this time Julia died, the granddaughter of Augustus, who had been condemned by him for adultery³ to the island of Tremiti near the coast of Puglia. She lived there for twenty years at the mercy of Augusta <note>Livia, wife of Augustus</note>, who secretly extinguished her fortunate stepchildren while displaying mercy to the miserable in public.

**LXXII.** In the same year the Frisians, a people beyond the Rhine, broke the peace, more due to our greed than their own arrogance. Drusus <note>Drusus the Elder</note> had imposed a small tribute on them, suited to their poverty, consisting of cowhides for the needs of the soldiers. No attention was paid to the thickness or size. Olennius, a senior centurion <term>primipilus: the highest-ranking centurion of a legion</term> who served as their governor, chose certain skins of the Aurochs⁴ <note>extinct wild oxen</note>, and wanted them at that rate— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "ragione," meaning "rate" or "proportion."</note>

...tax assessment. He <note>The Roman official Olennius</note> was harsh toward all nations, but even more so toward the Germans, who have great beasts in their forests but few domestic herds at their homes. At first, they gave oxen; then their fields; then their wives and children were taken into service. From this came complaints and outcries, and when these did no good, war broke out. The tax collectors were seized and crucified. Olennius fled to the fortress of Flevum, where a significant number of our people <note>Roman soldiers</note> guarded those shores.

**LXXIII.** At this news, Lucius Apronius, the propraetor <term>Propraetor: a governor of a Roman province acting with the authority of a praetor</term> of Lower Germany, called up several companies of legions from Upper Germany, along with a choice selection of auxiliary infantry and cavalry. He moved both armies down the Rhine into Frisia. Abandoning the siege, the rebels went to defend their own territory. Over the first marshes, Apronius built dikes and bridges to move the troops; and having found a ford, he sent a troop of Caninefate cavalry <note>The Caninefates were a Germanic tribe living in the Rhine delta, allied with Rome</note> and all the German infantry serving us to the rear of the enemies. They, already in formation, broke those horsemen and the Roman troops sent to aid them. Then he sent in three light cohorts <term>Cohort: a standard Roman military unit of about 480 men</term>, then two more, and shortly after, more cavalry. All together, they might have won; but being sent a few at a time, they could not help those who were fleeing and were swept away by them. The rest of the auxiliaries were under Cethegus Labeo, a legate <term>Legate: a high-ranking officer in the Roman army, often a deputy to a governor</term> of the Fifth Legion. Seeing them in a desperate state and fearing the worst, he sent for help from the legions. The men of the Fifth Legion rushed forward first and, in a fierce battle, broke the enemy, rescuing the cohorts and cavalry units who were covered in wounds. The Roman commander did not take revenge or bury the dead, although many tribunes, lieutenants, and distinguished captains were among them. Later, it was learned from fugitives that nine hundred Romans had died in the Baduhenna wood, fighting until the next day; and four hundred had retreated to the villa of Cruptorix—once a soldier of ours—and killed one another for fear of betrayal.

**LXXIV.** The Frisians rose to great fame among the Germans for this victory. Tiberius concealed <note>original: *frodava*, meaning he dissimulated or hid the truth to avoid acknowledging a defeat</note> the disaster so as not to entrust this war to anyone; and the Senate did not care that the edges of the empire suffered shame. Internal fear troubled them, for which they sought a remedy through flattery. For every matter they discussed, they decreed altars to Clemency and altars to Friendship, along with images of Caesar <note>Tiberius</note> and Sejanus, begging them that they would let themselves be se—

...see. It was too much for them to come into Rome or its vicinity; it sufficed for them to leave the island <note>Tiberius and Sejanus were residing on the island of Capri</note> and show themselves near Capua. There, senators <note>original: "padri" (fathers), the traditional title for members of the Roman Senate</note>, equestrians <term>Equestrians: the 'knights' or the secondary social rank of the Roman elite, below the senators</term>, and many of the common people rushed breathlessly to see Sejanus. This was a difficult task, sought after through favors and by becoming a companion to his villainies. His arrogance was undoubtedly increased by that ugly servitude which appeared much more clearly there; for in Rome, the streets are busy, the City is large, and people’s private dealings are not always known. Here, throughout the fields and along the shore, everyone lay about in the same way day and night, waiting at the whim of the doorkeepers. When even this was eventually forbidden, those whom he did not deign to hear or see returned to Rome disheartened; others remained with an unhappy boldness in that friendship, over which ruin already loomed.

**LXXV.** Tiberius, in his presence, had Agrippina <note>Agrippina the Younger, daughter of the celebrated general Germanicus</note>, his granddaughter, marry Gnaeus Domitius, and ordered the wedding to be held in Rome. In Domitius, besides the antiquity of his family, the Emperor favored the fact that he was a relative of the Caesars, since Octavia <note>The sister of the first Emperor, Augustus</note> was his grandmother, and through her, Augustus was his great-uncle.

# THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

...Through the blood of Augustus, she shared common great-grandchildren with Germanicus. She managed her household with the sacred morals of antiquity. She was more affable than the women of old used to praise: a compliant wife, a proud mother, adapting herself to her husband's wishes and her son's <term>dissimulation: the art of hiding one's true feelings, a trait for which Tiberius was famous</term>. Her funeral rites were modest; her will was not carried out until much later. Gaius Caesar <note>The future emperor Caligula.</note>, her great-grandson, delivered her funeral oration from the <term>Rostra: the speaker’s platform in the Roman Forum</term>.

**II.** Tiberius did not set aside even one of his pleasures; he excused himself by letter to the <term>Conscript Fathers: the formal title for the Roman Senators</term> for not attending his mother’s honors, citing the pressures of business. Of the many honors the Senate offered her, he accepted only a few, claiming modesty, and noted that she herself had forbidden divine honors.¹ In one part of the letter, he criticized those "womanizers," specifically striking at the consul Fufius, who had been a great favorite of Augusta. Fufius was charming to women but possessed a sharp tongue; he was accustomed to mocking Tiberius with the kind of bitter jokes that rulers never forget.

**III.** From this point forward, the government became more violent and cruel. While Augusta lived, there was still a place of refuge, for Tiberius had always shown her respect, and Sejanus <note>The powerful and ambitious commander of the Praetorian Guard.</note> did not dare to challenge her authority. Now, as if unleashed, they hurried to send a hostile letter from Tiberius to the Senate against Agrippina <note>Agrippina the Elder, the widow of Germanicus and granddaughter of Augustus.</note> and her son Nero. It was believed the letter had been sent some time ago but held back by Augusta, as it was read immediately after her death. It contained very harsh words: he did not charge his grandson with taking up arms or a desire for revolution, but instead rebuked him for youthful lusts and indecency.

VIII. The cases of P. Vitellius and Pomponius Secundus <gloss>1</gloss> were then dealt with. **2** *offered the key... of the treasury*. A similar offer was made by Bertoldo Corsini in 1537.

Pietro Pietri in the cited manuscript notes observes: « *Lunghiere*, vain entertainments. One says *To give the long one to someone*, which is the same. One also says *lungherie*. **4** *to begin writing. With a literary knife <note>a tool for sharpening reed pens</note> he cut his veins*, <note>original Latin: « Scalpro librario venas sibi incidit »</note> says Suetonius. The ancients wrote on the leaves of papyrus, a plant that grows in Egypt, and on thin skins taken from the bark of trees, called *libri* <note>books</note> by the Latins. Perhaps they folded them into rolls; like our ancient public papers. One of these, completely written, they called a *libro* <note>book</note>: several books joined together, a *codice* <note>codex</note>. They also wrote like us on skins, and the writing that was not pleasing or no longer useful, they scraped away to write something else; and the scraped skin they called a *palimpsest*. Cicero, with Trebatius, who had written to him on a *palimpsest*, jokingly wondered what there could have been to scrape away, rather than write those trifles. On waxed tablets, called *pugillares*, they also wrote with reeds (that is, sharpened reed stems) or styluses; from which the manner of dictating was called *style <note>original Italian: "stilo"</note>*. But Pomponius, a man of most refined character and illustrious talent, adapted himself to his cruel fortune and survived Tiberius.

### IX.
It then seemed necessary to proceed against the other children of Sejanus, although the fury of the common people had subsided, and almost everyone was satiated by the first executions. Therefore, the young son, who did not yet understand his own misfortune, and the young daughter, so innocent that she kept asking, "What have I done? Where are you dragging me? I will never do it again: give me the switch instead," were carried to prison. Writers of those times say that because it was unheard of for a virgin to suffer the punishment of the *triumviri* <note>The "triumviri capitales" were the officials in charge of executions and prisons in ancient Rome.</note>, the executioner, with the noose at his belt, deflowered her:¹ and having strangled them, he threw their tender bodies onto the Gemonian Stairs <note>The Gemonian Stairs were a flight of steps in Rome where the bodies of executed criminals were displayed to the public as a sign of disgrace.</note>.

### X.
Asia and Achaia at this time experienced a great fright <note>The original Italian uses the word "battisoffia," a colloquial Florentine term for a sudden panic or "beating of the heart."</note>. He <note>Referring to an impostor pretending to be Drusus, a relative of the Emperor, who appeared in the East.</note> acted so as to carry away, if not full hands, at least wax tablets full of notes. Upon this wax, says Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman rhetorician.</note>, it was easy to erase; but it required better eyesight to read; yet it did not break the flow of writing and the impetus of one’s concepts, as the dipping of the pen does. And he desires that whoever composes should leave large spaces to add and change without confusing the written things, and to be able to note to the side—almost placing them in a deposit for future use—certain beautiful concepts that often occur to the writer outside of the current purpose, and which might otherwise escape them.

<note>¹ he deflowered her. A grim legality observed to make her a woman and eligible (*) for strangulation. Thus the *triumviri* (according to Dio Cassius in book 47), to make a boy eligible for execution, dressed him in the adult toga. Of another whom I know of, it was said: *Let him be of the age of hope*. Rhadamistus, having assured his uncle and sister against poison, threw them to the ground and smothered them with many clothes. Augustus and Tiberius, to torture slaves against their masters, would sell them to the public treasury <note>Roman law forbade slaves from testifying against their masters, so the emperors bypassed this by having the state "buy" them first.</note>. Malice is never lacking for those who wish to defraud the laws.</note>
<note>² experienced a great fright. *«They were terrified by a sharp, rather than a long-lasting, fear.»* <note>original Latin: "Exterritæ sunt acri magis, quam diuturno timore."</note> This popular term is used perfectly by Franco Sacchetti <note>A 14th-century Florentine storyteller.</note> in his 48th novella. That we should avoid it because the common language of Italy does not use it—since it is not found in Dante, Petrarch, or Boccaccio—does not seem right to me. I do not believe that a living language is obliged in writing to collect only the words of a few dead writers, like drops from a gutter; but it should draw from the perennial fountain of the city the most effective and vivid natural properties that shoot forth with force, striking the soul by the straightest and shortest path. Oftentimes they signify more than they say, like the fierce strokes and foreshortenings in painting. Since we speak to be understood and to move; the more proper and brief the speech is, the sooner and better it is understood and moves. And I believe that apart from the impious, the dishonest, and the sordid, whatever noble people say can also be written nobly in its proper place and time by a person of judgment, moderately learned and careful. Writing in this manner, and with these four conditions, the three authorities cited by the great critic in the "Response to Caro" on page 23 will not apply: one being from Bembo <note>Cardinal Pietro Bembo, who argued that writers should only imitate the style of Petrarch and Boccaccio.</note>, who claims that we Florentines, because of the excessive abundance of this language of ours, do not value it, and go along with the common people without a king—</note>
<note>(*) eligible: capable. Likewise below, "to make eligible," meaning to render suitable or legally qualified.</note>

->## THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.<-

...because Drusus, son of Germanicus,¹ had been seen in the Cyclades and then on the mainland. He was a young man of that stature, whom certain freedmen of Caesar, as if they had recognized him, followed with deceptive intent. Those Greeks, ever eager for news and marvels, were drawn by the fame of that name: they found him and believed their own eyes; rumors spread that he had escaped from prison and was heading to his father's armies to seize Egypt and Syria. He already had a gathering of youth and a public following, rejoicing in his current success and filled with vain hope for the rest.

When Poppaeus Sabinus—who was then in Macedonia and also governing Achaia—heard this news (whether true or false), he acted quickly to get ahead of the situation. He crossed the gulfs of Torone and Therma,² passed the island of Euboea in the Aegean Sea, the Piraeus of Athens, the coasts of Corinth, and that narrow strip of land [the Isthmus]; having entered the Roman colony of Nicopolis from the other sea, he finally learned that the youth, when questioned more closely about his identity, had claimed to be the "Son of Marcus Silanus." Having lost many of his followers, the pretender had embarked as if intending to go to Italy. Sabinus wrote everything to Tiberius; I have found no other account of the origin or end of this case.

### XI.
At the end of the year, the discord between the consuls, which had been held back, finally broke out.³ Trio, who as a litigious man picked quarrels over the slightest thing, gave a side-swipe <note>The original Italian term "fiancata" refers to an indirect reproach or an oblique attack.</note> to Regulus, accusing him of moving too slowly in crushing the ministers of Sejanus. Regulus, who was modest when not provoked, struck back at his colleague and attempted to accuse him of being part of that very conspiracy. However, they were begged by many of the fathers <note>The "fathers" refers to the Roman Senators.</note> to set aside such hatreds, which threatened to ruin them both; thus, they ended their term of office with lingering resentment and threats.

...one view to observe: and the other by Giulio Camillo, who denies that one should depart, when writing, from the voices of Petrarch and Boccaccio, from the time when the language rose—like the sun at midday—to its highest point of perfection. And he leaves out Dante! Oh, what a judgment! The third view is that of Aristides, who in his orations does not admit the words of simple speech, but only that of books.

I. Secret debaucheries of Tiberius. — II. Many accusations. — VIII. The noble and free defense of Marcus Terentius. — X. Death and funeral of Lucius Piso, prefect of Rome. — XI. Origin and progress of that Prefecture. — XII. Various accusations and deaths. — XXXI. Parthian envoys in Rome to ask for a new king. Tiberius sends one, then another. Lucius Vitellius made prefect of the East. — XXXIII. Battle between Armenians and Parthians. Artabanus driven from the throne, and a wanderer in Scythia. By the counsel and forces of Vitellius, Tiridates succeeds him. — XXXVIII. The cruelty of the informants <note>Professional accusers known as *delatores*.</note> increases: many accused die. Tigranes the king succumbs to execution by citizens. A fierce fire in Rome. — XLVI. Tiberius designates a successor. — L. Illness, death, and character of Tiberius.

I. [Year 785 of Rome, 32 AD.] Once the consuls Gnaeus Domitius and Camillus Scribonianus had entered office, <note>original: "Entrati consoli." Justus Lipsius, with good judgment, believes that with the three years that are missing, the fifth Book is completed here and the sixth begins.</note> Caesar, having sailed through the sea that lies between Capri and Sorrento, skirted the coast of Campania, either undecided or feigning <note>The manuscript cancels: "not knowing if he wanted to enter Rome, or feigning to want to etc."</note> a desire to enter Rome. He frequently disembarked nearby at those gardens along the Tiber, but always returned to his cliffs and solitary sea out of shame for his crimes and lusts. There, he became so bestial that, in the manner of barbarian kings, he defiled noble youths. It was not only lovely and provocative bodies that incited him, but in some a boyish modesty, and in others the splendor of their lineage. At that time, never-before-heard-of stewards of his nefarious chambers were found, along with designers of all that can be done within them. <note>The translator uses a Dantesque phrase: "To show what can be done in the chamber."</note> Slaves would go out to hunt for victims and bring them in, offering gifts to the compliant <note>The manuscript reads: "giving to the yielding, threatening the abominating: and if fathers or relatives had resisted; kidnappings, force etc." He changes "abominating" to "shunning," then cancels it all.</note> and threatening those who were repulsed. And if fathers or relatives resisted, kidnapping, force, and the venting of lust were used against them as if they were slaves.

II. ...of whom twenty at a time, drawn by lot and with weapons at their side, should serve as his guard whenever he entered the Senate. This proposal arose because it was believed that Tiberius had truly, in a letter, requested that one of the consuls escort him safely from Capri to Rome. Tiberius, who occasionally used to joke even amidst grave matters, thanked the fathers <note>The "fathers" refers to the Senators.</note> for their kindness:

> « But who should be left behind? Who should be chosen? Should they always be the same men, or should they rotate? Those who have finished their magistracy, or novices? Officials or private citizens? And how would they appear, girding their knives at the door of the Senate? I would not value life itself if it had to be defended with arms. »

With such words he corrected Togonius,¹ and yet he did not formally dissuade the underlying sentiment.

III. He struck home well² against Junius Gallio, who proposed that the Praetorian soldiers, once their service was complete, should be allowed to sit in the fourteen rows³ of the theater. Tiberius asked him as if he were standing right there:

> « What have you to do with the soldiers? It is the Emperor’s duty alone to command them and reward them. Have you perhaps discovered something that the Divine Augustus did not know? Or are you perhaps a spear⁴ <note>A "spear" or "instrument"—someone acting on behalf of another.</note> of Sejanus, wishing to light a fire and stir up crude minds with this lure of honor to ruin the discipline of the military? »

What Gallio gained from his calculated flattery was to be expelled immediately from the Senate, and subsequently from Italy. When it was said that he would live in too much luxury on Lesbos—the noble and pleasant island he had chosen for his exile—he was brought back to Rome and placed in the custody of magistrates.⁵ In the same letter, Caesar...

To hide this fear, the clever man turned the proposal into a joke. <note>The "Giantina" edition notes: "with pleasantry and modesty."</note>

**VI.** The beginning of that letter was remarkable: "What to write to you, or how, or what not to write at this time,

<note>The following are the translator's original footnotes from the bottom of the page.</note>

1 * *thought*. See at the end two first drafts of the translation of this and the previous chapter.

2 * *man-woman*. "Of uncertain virility" [incertæ virilitatis] not "incestuous" [incestæ]. To pair this joke about Gaius's dishonesty with the following one by Cotta, who called the dinner held for Tiberius's birthday a funeral feast, as he caused so many men to die. — Our translator follows the reading "of uncertain virility," which is derived from the Medicean manuscript. Others use "incestuous virility," following Suetonius, who records that Caligula committed incest with his sister Drusilla.

3 * *funeral*. The translator Davanzati inconsistently writes this as *essequie* and *esequie*. He uses the same graphic inconsistency in other words, like *dopo* and *doppo* [after], *publico* and *pubblico* [public], etc. See the *Warning at the beginning*.

4 * *annual funeral feast*. Latin: *novendialem cenam*; a mortuary dinner held during the funeral honors rendered to the dead nine days after the burning of the corpse; and therefore called "nine-day."

5 * *of Augusta*: I follow the Giuntina edition, which conforms to the Medicean manuscript reading: "the birthday of Augusta." Other editions read "of Augustus," following the conjecture of Lipsius, who observed that Livia's birthday was never celebrated after her death. But what forbids such a celebration being held during her life? Livia was "a mother burdensome to the republic" [gravis in rempublicam mater]: and hence the joke.

6 * *complaining.... had said etc.*; that is: and he was likewise accused that he, complaining.... said etc.

7 * *litigating over money*, he had a lawsuit for a certain sum of money.

8 * *Eager to convict him etc.* Translated according to Pichena's conjecture "and all those things" [*eaque cuncta*]. But the Medicean manuscript has "nor all things" [*neque cuncta*], and intends to signify, as Walther interprets, that two causes combined to prevent the success of the accusation: first, that not everything could be proven; second, the recourse to the prince. Hence one should translate: "Nor could those leading men prove everything; and since they gave him no rest, he appealed to the prince."

...with eccentric arguments, he moved on to more serious matters: stating that he had made enemies for the sake of the republic, he requested that <term>Macro</term><note>Naevius Sutorius Macro, the powerful Praetorian Prefect who replaced Sejanus.</note>, the prefect, along with some tribunes and centurions, should always enter the Senate with him. **XVI.** A frenzy of accusers broke out against the usurers, who were enriching themselves beyond what was permitted by the law of <term>Caesar the Dictator</term><note>Refers to Julius Caesar’s legislation concerning lending and land ownership in Italy, which had fallen into disuse.</note> regarding lending and property in Italy—a law long ignored, for private interest often kicks against the public good. Usury is an old sickness of the city, and a constant <gloss>¹</gloss> cause of uprisings and discord; therefore, even in ancient times when customs were less corrupt, it was subject to correction. To this end, the <term>Twelve Tables</term><note>The foundational legal code of ancient Rome, established around 450 BCE.</note> first capped interest at one percent per month, whereas previously it was set at the whim of the rich. Later, by a law of the tribunes, it was reduced to a half-percent; finally, all usury was forbidden. Through many plebeian decrees, attempts were made to block the clever tricks used to bypass these rules, yet usury always grew back, like a weed that had been cut down. Therefore, when the <term>Praetor</term> Gracchus had such accusations brought before him, he was troubled by the scale of the impending ruin and referred the matter to the Senate. The fearful senators (for who among them was innocent?) asked the <term>Prince</term><note>Tiberius</note> for a general pardon, and they obtained it; they were granted eighteen months to settle their personal finances <gloss>²</gloss> according to the law.

**XVII.** From this arose a violent shortage of money; for all debtors were pressed for payment at once, and because of so many convictions and the subsequent sale of properties, the <term>fisc</term><note>The imperial treasury.</note> and the public treasury had swallowed up all the available cash. Because of this, the Senate ordered that the usurers should accept two-thirds of their debt in Italian land; but the creditors demanded the full amount in cash, and those being asked did not find it honorable to fail in their obligations.

Thus there was a state of agitation,¹ and of pleading;² people appealed to the law. Yet the sales and purchases intended as a remedy only increased the scarcity of coin; for buyers hoarded their money, and the sheer number of sellers offering estates devalued them.³ Those most in debt sold with the greatest difficulty, and many were ruined, losing both property and their status and reputation. Eventually, Caesar provided aid by distributing two and a half million gold pieces <note>The Italian text specifies "due milioni e mezzo d'oro," referring to gold coins (aurei), which equates to the 100 million sesterces mentioned in the original Latin accounts of this bailout.</note> to the banks, to be lent without interest for three years to anyone who could secure the loan with estates worth double the amount. Thus credit returned, and gradually private individuals began to lend again, while the law requiring the purchase of land was no longer enforced. Matters that are handled with great rigor at the beginning are often neglected later.

**XVIII.** The initial fears returned with the accusation of <term>treason</term><note>The law of *maiestas*, or "diminished majesty," which covered crimes against the state or the emperor.</note> brought against Considius Proculus. While he was celebrating his birthday in complete security, he was suddenly seized, brought before the Senate, condemned, and executed—it all happened in <unclear>one</unclear> moment. His sister Sancia was "denied water and fire" <note>original: "levossi acqua e fuoco." This was the formal Roman ritual of banishment, effectively stripping a person of their citizenship and livelihood.</note>. The accuser was Quintus Pomponio, a restless spirit who claimed he did this and more to win the prince’s favor and free his brother, Pomponio Secondo. Additionally, Pompeia Macrina was driven into exile; her husband Argolicus and her father-in-law Laco, among the leading men of the Achaeans, had already been brought low by Caesar. Her father, an illustrious Roman knight, and her brother, who had been a <term>praetor</term><note>A high-ranking magistrate who served as a judge or provincial governor.</note>, committed suicide just as they were about to be condemned. Their "crime" was that their great-grandfather, Theophanes of Mytilene, had been an intimate friend of <term>Pompey the Great</term><note>The famous Roman general and rival of Julius Caesar.</note> and, after his death, had been worshipped as a god through Greek flattery.

...might reveal what he was asked. <note>This sentence fragment completes the thought that Tiberius executed his astrologers to keep his consultations secret.</note> ^1 Therefore, once Thrasyllus was led up those crags and questioned, he accurately predicted the empire and what was to happen to Tiberius. Tiberius, deeply moved, then asked him if he had studied his own birth ^2 and what fortune he might run into that year and that very day. After calculating the times and the aspects of the planets, Thrasyllus first became unsettled, then terrified; the more he scrutinized the charts, the more his hair stood on end. Finally, he cried out that he was in a moment of great crisis, perhaps even his last. Then Tiberius embraced him and rejoiced that he had correctly perceived his own danger, telling him he should not doubt. Ever after, Tiberius held whatever Thrasyllus said as an oracle, and kept him as an intimate friend.

XXII. Truly, because of this and other similar cases, I would not know how to judge whether the affairs of mortals happen by destiny and fixed necessity, or simply by chance. The greatest ancient sages and their sects <term>sects: schools of philosophy</term> disagree. Many hold ^3 that the gods take no account of our birth or death, nor, in short, of us men; therefore, the good suffer misfortune and the wicked prosper most of the time. Others ^4 say the opposite: that things carry their own fate, not from the planets ^5 but from natural principles and causes which, being intertwined, pull one another along. However, they believe we are left with the free will to choose what life we want; and once that choice is made, things follow their natural course. Nor are "good" and "evil" what they seem to the common people; on the contrary, many who are buffeted by adversity are blessed by enduring it with fortitude, while most of those with great wealth are utterly miserable because they use it poorly. "...And I (Attius boasts¹) struck him with these terrible words; and he, as he was dying, spat out the like:" and he recounts how at first, like a madman, he sent such foolish curses to Tiberius; then, despairing of life, he spoke with reason: saying that since he [Tiberius] had killed his daughter-in-law, his brother's son, and his grandsons, and filled the whole house with death, he should suffer the punishments due to the name and nobility of his ancestors and those to come. XXV. Tears were not yet dry when word came that Agrippina (who must have wanted to live after Sejanus's death, hoping for some better outcome), seeing that the cruelty persisted, had stopped eating—unless the food was taken from her so that her death would appear voluntary. **XXVI.** Shortly thereafter, Cocceius Nerva <note>A famous jurist and a long-time, loyal companion of Tiberius.</note>, who was always by the Emperor’s side, a man learned in all divine and human law,¹ healthy in body and in the prime of his life, decided to die. Tiberius remained at his bedside, pleading and asking: "Why is this? What guilt would I bear, what reputation would I have, if my dearest friend were to flee from life for no reason at all?" Nerva turned his back to him and refused to eat any more. Those who knew his mind said that because he saw the Republic in such a dire state, he wished—out of both anger and fear—to die while his honor was still pure and untarnished. The ruin of Agrippina (who would believe it?) led to the ruin of Plancina. She had been the wife of Gnaeus Piso and had made a public display of joy at the death of Germanicus. When Piso fell, the prayers of Augusta <note>Livia, the mother of Tiberius.</note>, and no less her status as an enemy of Agrippina, had protected her.² Once that hatred and that favor were gone, justice took its course: accused of crimes that were already well-known, she paid the penalty with her own hand—a punishment that was more delayed than it was undeserved.

**XXVII.** To so many sorrows and tears in the city, there was added the fact that Julia, the daughter of Drusus and former wife of Nero <note>Nero Caesar, the eldest son of Germanicus, not the later Emperor Nero.</note>,³ remarried Rubellio Blandus. He came from an honorable family, enjoyed a prosperous old age, and gained even more prestige because he had been prevented from actually going to govern his assigned province. After Pomponius Flaccus, the acting governor of Syria, died, a letter from Caesar <note>Tiberius</note> was read in which he complained that the most talented men, fit to lead armies, were refusing the provinces, and he was forced to beg the former consuls to accept them. He seemed to forget that Arruntius had already been prevented from going to Spain for ten years. Also in that year died Marcus Lepidus, of whose moderation and wisdom much has been said in previous books;⁴ as for his nobility, it is enough to say⁵ he was of the Aemilian house, a lineage⁶ rich in excellent citizens. There were some corrupt men among them, but they were still great.

<meta>This page transitions from the political suicides and social scandals of Rome to a miraculous natural event reported in the provinces—the appearance of the phoenix—before returning to the grim reality of the city's mounting death toll under Tiberius. -># THE SIXTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.<-

During the consulship of Paulus Fabius and Lucius Vitellius, after a long cycle of centuries had passed,¹ the phoenix came to Egypt. This provided the learned men of that land and of Greece much material to discuss regarding such a miracle. It is worthy to recount where they agree and where they differ. All write that this bird is sacred to the sun: in its beak and its variegated feathers, it is distinct from others. Regarding its years, the most common opinion is that it appears every five hundred years. Some affirm it is one thousand four hundred and sixty-one years, and that another flew into the city of Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt, a major religious center.</note> in the time of Sesostris, another in the time of Amasis, and a third in the time of Ptolemy, the third king of the Macedonian line, with a great following of other birds attracted by its strange form. Ancient history is very obscure: ² from Ptolemy to Tiberius was less than two hundred and fifty years; hence, some held that this phoenix was not real, nor did it come from Arabia. They argued it had done nothing of what ancient memory records,³ namely that when its years are finished and it is close to death, it builds a nest in its own land and pours its seed into it. Once the young phoenix is born and raised, its first duty is to bury its father. It does not do this randomly, but tests itself by carrying a weight of myrrh on a long flight; if it succeeds, it takes its father upon its shoulders, carries him to the altar of the sun, and burns him. These things are uncertain and embellished with fables.⁴ But it is not doubted that this bird is seen in Egypt from time to time.⁵

Labeo <note>Pomponius Labeo, a former governor of Moesia.</note>, who, as I said, governed Moesia, slit his veins; and Paxaea, his wife, did the same. So ready was the resort to suicide <gloss>1</gloss> to escape the executioner, and because those who were condemned were thrown into the pits <note>The Gemonian Stairs, where the bodies of executed criminals were displayed and then thrown into the Tiber.</note> and their property confiscated. But for those who died before being judged, their wills remained valid and their bodies were buried—a reward for an accelerated death. Caesar <note>Tiberius.</note> wrote to the senate, stating that he had forbidden Labeo from entering his house, and had merely intended to renounce their friendship according to the ancient custom. He claimed that Labeo, gnawed by a conscience burdened by his maladministration of the province and other crimes, had sought to cover them by inciting hatred against the Emperor, and had needlessly frightened his wife who, though guilty, was in no danger. Mamercus Scaurus was accused once more—a man of noble birth and a great orator, but of dissolute character. It was not his friendship with Sejanus that ruined him, but the no less pestilential hatred of Macro, who used the same arts as his predecessor but more covertly. They came to Rome in secret, led principally by Sinnaces, a man of great noble family and wealth, and Abdo, a eunuch; in Parthia, being a eunuch is no disgrace, but rather a path to power. These two, along with other grandees, found no one of the Arsacid <term>Arsacids: The ruling dynasty of the Parthian Empire, claiming descent from its founder, Arsaces I.</term> bloodline to make king—as Artabanus had murdered the adults or the rest were too young—and so they requested Phraates from Rome, the son of King Phraates. XXXII. Tiberius, who desired this outcome, honored Phraates and prepared him to take his father's throne. This followed his usual temperament: managing foreign affairs through cunning and counsel rather than by force of arms. When Artabanus learned of the conspiracy, he wavered between fear and a burning desire for revenge. To barbarians, hesitation is cowardice, while striking out is a kingly act; nevertheless, he held to what was advantageous <margin>he held to what was advantageous. In Syria, Phraates passed away. Having lived the delicate Roman life for so many years, he was no longer accustomed to the harsh Parthian lifestyle, and his health failed. **XXXIX.** Trebellienus Rufus died by his own hand; and Sestius Paconianus, because of verses he had written in prison against the prince <note>The "prince" refers to Emperor Tiberius.</note>, was strangled there. Tiberius remained not far from Rome, nor separated by the sea as he usually was, so that he could receive reports immediately and write his decrees to the consuls the same day or the next. It was as if he wished to see the blood flowing through the gutters, or the executioner's hand raised. At the end of the year, Poppaeus Sabinus died. He was a man of humble origins who had been honored by the emperors with the consulship, triumphal honors, and the governorship of major provinces for twenty-four years; this was not due to any great wisdom, but because he was competent enough for business, and no more. <gloss>1</gloss>

**XL.** [Year of Rome 789, Year of Christ 36.] In the following consulship of Quintus Plautius and Sextus Papinius <gloss>2</gloss> the death of Lucius Arruseus seemed like nothing, for people had grown so callous to such things. As he fell and gasped for breath, he was carried off by the attendants to prison, where, though he was already cold, the noose was tightened around his throat. <gloss>3</gloss> Not even a royal name could protect Tigranes, formerly the King of Armenia, who was then a defendant and suffered the punishment of a common citizen. They understood these to be signs of impending death and took their own lives. ...Lepidus her father. Then she was accused of having an affair with a slave; the evidence was undeniable, and so, without making a defense, she took her own life.

**XLI.** At this time, the Cietae <note>original: "Clitari"</note>, who were subjects of Archelaus of Cappadocia, were forced to undergo a census and pay tributes according to our Roman customs. They withdrew to the heights of Mount Taurus and, protected by the nature of the terrain, held out against the king's un-warlike troops. Marcus Trebellius, a lieutenant sent by Vitellius, the governor of Syria, with four thousand legionaries and a choice group of auxiliaries, besieged two hills where the barbarians had fortified themselves (the smaller called Cadra, the other Davara). He forced those who tried to break out to surrender by the sword, and the rest by thirst. Tiridates, with the support of the Parthians, reclaimed Nicephorium and Anthemusias, and other cities founded by the Macedonians with Greek names, as well as the Parthian cities of Halus and Artemita. They were all overjoyed to have traded the cursed cruelty of Artabanus—who had been raised among the Scythians—for the expected kindness of Tiridates, seasoned with Roman civility.

**XLII.** Tiridates found immense flattery in Seleucia, a powerful and walled city. It had not become "barbarized," but remained true to its founder, Seleucus; it is governed by a council of three hundred of its wealthiest and wisest citizens, like a senate. The common people also have their share of power: when they are in agreement, they mock the Parthians; but when they split into factions <gloss>1</gloss>, each side calls for outside help, and the one called in becomes the master of all. This had happened recently during the reign of Artabanus, who suppressed the commoners and empowered the nobles for his own benefit, for popular rule is close to liberty, whereas the rule of the few is akin to tyranny. Now that Tiridates had arrived, they praised him with honors used for ancient kings, along with newer, more elaborate ones. They insulted Artabanus, saying he was an Arsacid <note>The Arsacid dynasty was the ruling house of the Parthian Empire.</note> only through his mother, but degenerate in every other way. Tiridates left Seleucia to be governed by its people; while he was consulting on when to be crowned, he received letters from Phraates and Hiero, who held the strongest parts of the kingdom, asking him to wait a short while. He did not want to fail these high-ranking lords <gloss>2</gloss> and went to Ctesiphon, the seat of the empire. As they kept delaying from one day to the next, the Surena <note>The "Surena" was a hereditary title for the second-most powerful official in Parthia, who had the right to crown the king.</note> crowned him with the traditional ceremonies, in the presence of many who signaled their approval.

**XLIII.** And if he had immediately presented himself in the heart of the kingdom and to the other subject peoples <gloss>1</gloss>, there would have been no contest; they all would have yielded. But by dawdling <gloss>2</gloss> in the castle with the concubines and the treasure that Artabanus had left there, he gave his enemies time to change their minds. For Phraates and Hieron, and the others who had not been present at his coronation—some out of fear, others out of envy of Abdageses, who now controlled the court and the new king—turned back to Artabanus. They found him in Hyrcania, filthy, disheveled <gloss>3</gloss>, and feeding himself by the use of his bow <gloss>4</gloss>. At first, they terrified him, appearing as if they had come to kill him; but once they gave their word that they were actually there to restore his kingdom, he recovered his spirit and asked the reason for such a sudden change. Hieron replied: "Tiridates is but a boy; it is not an Arsacid who reigns, not a warrior, but a hollow name, a dying foreigner; Abdageses is the true king."

**XLIV.** Artabanus, being experienced in the ways of ruling, knew that false friends do not bother to feign such hatred. He immediately called for aid from Scythia and, without giving his enemies time to think or his friends time to reconsider, he rushed off, still in his filthy state, to stir up a sense of pity <note>original: "rancura"</note> <gloss>5</gloss> among the common people. He spared no prayers, no deceptions, and no artifice to win over the wavering and to strengthen his allies. As he approached Seleucia with a great host, Tiridates was struck down by the rumors of Artabanus's approach, and soon by his actual presence; he was thrown into confusion by his advisors. Some argued that he should face him and fight immediately: "These are a ragtag people, exhausted by the long journey; and not all of them truly want him. Those who favor him now were his traitors and enemies just a moment ago." But Abdageses advised returning to Mesopotamia; there, defended by the river, they could call for help from the Armenians and Elymaeans and others in the rear, and with those reinforcements and whatever the Roman captain <note>Referring to Lucius Vitellius</note> might send, they could test their fortune. ## XLVIII.
Therefore Domitius, thinking of his defense, and Marsus, who had almost decided to die of hunger, did not kill themselves. Arruntius, encouraged by his friends to do the same, replied:

> “The same things do not suit everyone: I have lived long enough; I have nothing to repent for other than having let myself be trampled upon first by Sejanus, now by Macro, and always by some powerful man; and for what? For not tolerating their wickedness. When these few days that Tiberius has left to live pass, how will I escape from the youth who succeeds him? If the nature of power had changed and corrupted Tiberius, even with all his experience; how could one expect better from Gaius Caesar <note>The future Emperor Caligula.</note>, a mere boy, ignorant and unruly, in the hands of Macro? He, who was chosen to destroy Sejanus as one more wicked than him, now torments the republic even more miserably. I foresee a more cruel servitude: therefore, I flee from the evils present and those to come.”

Thus he almost prophesied, and then opened his veins. How well he acted will appear from the things that followed. Albucilla struck herself lightly <note>original: "si dette piano." She wounded herself, but not mortally.</note>; the senate imprisoned her. As for those who facilitated her lusts, Grasidius Sacerdos, a former praetor, was exiled to an island; Pontius Fregellanus was expelled from the senate; Laelius Balbus suffered both punishments with applause, having been seen as a bloodthirsty orator <term>dicitor sanguinolento|A prosecutor who viciously pursues the innocent to win favor or political standing.</term> against the innocent.

L. Already his body and his strength were failing Tiberius, but not his capacity for dissimulation. With the same fierce spirit, expression, and speech—and sometimes with forced pleasantries—he tried to conceal his obvious decline. He changed locations frequently, and finally came to a halt ^3 <note>original: "si giudicò." An archaic Italian expression meaning to be bedridden or beyond hope of recovery. The Latin source merely says "consedit" (he settled/sat down), but the translator Davanzati uses a more terminal medical connotation.</note> at the Cape of Misenum, in the villa that once belonged to Lucullus. ^2 There, the arrival of his end was discovered in this manner: there was a famous physician named Charicles who was accustomed, during the prince’s illnesses, to give him advice even if he did not treat him directly. He came to Tiberius as if for his own business, and taking the Emperor's hand as if in a gesture of affection, he felt his pulse. Tiberius noticed this and perhaps grew angry; but to hide it, he ordered food to be brought and stayed at the table longer than usual, as if to honor his friend upon his departure. Charicles assured Macro that the pulse was failing and that he would not last two days. Therefore, everything was handled there through conferences among those present, and dispatched abroad <note>original: "quivi trattando, e fuori spacciando." LI. Such was the end of Tiberius^1 at seventy-eight years of age: he was the son of Nero, and of the Claudian house on his mother’s side as well, though she was adopted into the Livian and later the Julian families. From his earliest years, he navigated a precarious fortune, for he went into exile with his father. Having entered Augustus’s household as a stepson, he was obstructed by many rivals while Marcellus and Agrippa, and later Gaius and Lucius Caesar, were still living; furthermore, his brother Drusus enjoyed greater favor among the citizens. He was in a most wretched situation with his wife Julia <note>Julia the Elder, the daughter of Augustus, was notorious for her many affairs, which caused Tiberius great public and personal humiliation.</note>, being unable to either swallow or spit out her offensive dishonor. After returning from Rhodes, he was master of the prince's vacant house for twelve years, and emperor for twenty-three. His character shifted with the times: he was of excellent life and reputation as long as he lived as a private citizen or held command under Augustus; he was secretive and feigned virtues while Germanicus and Drusus lived; he was a mixture of evil and good while his mother was alive; and he was most cruel and full of hidden lusts while he loved or feared Sejanus. At the last, he gave himself over completely^2 to every wickedness and filth, once all fear and shame were removed and he followed his own nature.

---

^1 *Such was the end of Tiberius.* A parallel is found in a great man of our own times <note>Davanzati, the translator, often draws parallels between Roman history and 16th-century Italian events.</note> who, suffering from similar fainting spells, fell into one that lasted so long that the surgeons <term>cerusici: historical term for barber-surgeons who performed surgeries and autopsies</term> arrived to perform the necessary honors. At the first cut, he cried out; they continued regardless "for the best." Radamistus, as this author says in the twelfth book, smothered his sister and uncle in blankets. (*)
^2 *gave himself over completely etc.* Latin: <note>original: "in scelera simul ac dedecora prorupit." Meaning: he broke out into crimes and disgraces alike.</note> Dati <note>Carlo Dati, another noted translator/scholar</note> renders it: "he let himself go headlong into every sort of disgrace and wickedness."

(*) In the Giuntine edition belonging to Count Mortara, this note is shortened thus: "A parallel is found in a great man of our times who, upon dying, the surgeons came to perform the due honors. At the first cut he revived. They continued for the best." The incident of Radamistus is not cited in the Giuntina.

## GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

### SUMMARY.

**I.** Valerius Asiaticus, due to an infamous accusation by Messalina, dies by his own hand.— **IV.** A ruinous dream for certain Roman knights. — **V.** The Cincian law <note>A law from 204 BC that forbade advocates from receiving gifts or payments for legal services.</note> is invoked against treacherous lawyers. — **VI.** Their fees are regulated. — **VIII.** Discords among the Parthians. Gotarzes is defeated, but recovers. — **IX.** He reconciles with Bardanes, — **X.** who is then killed by his own people. — **XI.** The Secular Games. Domitius Nero is destined for the empire. — **XII.** Messalina goes mad with passion for Silius. — **XIII.** Claudius pays no attention. He enacts laws and invents new letters. — **XIV.** A discussion of the inventors of alphabets. — **XV.** A decree regarding the soothsayers <note>term: *Aruspices*—priests in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods by examining the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>. — **XVI.** A king is given to the Cherusci. — **XVII.** From which arises discord and war among them. — **XVIII.** Corbulo keeps the Chauci under control; he is harsh with the soldiers. — **XIX.** He reorganizes the Frisii and kills Gannascus. — **XX.** Claudius restrains him. He opens a canal between the Meuse and the Rhine; he receives a triumph. — **XXI.** Curtius Rufus does the same. — **XXII.** Nonius is ruined. On gladiators and quaestors. — **XXIII.** The Gauls seek citizenship and, through the sponsorship of the Prince <note>Emperor Claudius</note>, obtain it; the Aedui are the first. II. Not in the senate, but in the Emperor's bedchamber, with Messalina present, Suilius charged him with having corrupted the soldiers with money and lustful favors for every kind of filthiness, with committing adultery with Poppea, and with using his own body like a woman. Entering into his defense, he greatly moved Claudius’s spirit and brought tears to Messalina’s eyes. She left the room to dry them and commanded Vitellius <note>The father of the Vitellius who would later briefly become Emperor in 69 AD.</note> not to let the prisoner escape. This was done so entirely without the knowledge of Caesar <note>Claudius.</note> that a few days later, while dining with her husband Scipio, he asked why he had come without his wife. He replied that she was dead.

...and there was no merchandise more widely traded than the betrayals of lawyers. Thus Samius, a foremost Roman knight, having given Suilius ten thousand florins <note>original: *fiorini*. ### VI.

As those who expected shame from such a law shouted out, Silius spoke forcefully against Suilius: "The ancient orators saw that the true reward of eloquence is eternal fame. To turn the queen of the arts into a sordid shopkeeper's trade is too great a stain; nor can there be any loyalty in those who serve whoever pays the most. ³ If cases were defended without reward, lawsuits would decrease; whereas now, enmities, accusations, grudges, and injuries are nurtured so that, just as many diseases fill the doctors' purses, so the plague of litigation fills the lawyers'. Let them remember that Gaius Asinius and Messalla, ⁴ and among the moderns, Arruntius and Aeserninus, ⁵ rose to great heights through their eloquence and their blameless lives." This speech pleased everyone, and a decree was being prepared to condemn them under the law regarding illegally seized property. When Suilius, Cossutianus, ⁶ and the others saw that they were being judged not for their guilt, which was clear, but for their punishment, they surrounded Caesar <note>Emperor Claudius</note> and begged him to pardon the past. He bowed his head, and they began:

$^1$ *To profit*, to bring utility or gain. It comes from *pro*, meaning useful or advantageous. Dante, *Inferno* XXI: *what does it profit him? what use does it do him?* — Pietro Pietri, in his manuscript notes on this sentence ("No one would want to do anything unless they believed it would be profitable"), observes:
> "This is true; but if there were no lawsuits, there would be no lawyers and procurators, who would then be forced to learn another trade with less ruin to the republic. A dispute begins in the countryside, in a villa or village, over a stolen hen, a cut tree, a moved boundary stone, or two palms of usurped land: they enter into litigation. Whoever loses in the countryside appeals to the city; from the cities to the provinces, kingdoms, and empires; from one court to another until the supreme court, where it becomes immortal without hope of an end, unless the medicine works by itself—that is, the parties have nothing left to spend. Look at the Imperial Chamber of Speyer <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire, famous for cases lasting decades or centuries.</note> and see how many lawsuits are still pending there, how much expense is caused by this, and how many people have been reduced to poverty. And would to God that the evil stopped there, and did not crawl with its poison even to those who still have the shell on their heads—nay, those who are not even born yet! There the grudges return, the lawsuit is taken up where the ancestors left it, and until they too are finished and drained, the plague continues to trouble the world and scatter families. It is the duty of counselors to warn princes, and the duty of princes to vindicate us."

$^2$ *To go... in civil dress, in the attire of a citizen*. Latin: "*toga enitescere*."

$^3$ *Mithridates*. (See Annals VI, 32, 33.)

$^4$ *To Caesar*, to Caligula.

$^5$ *As I said*: certainly in the books where he wrote the history of Caligula, which are now lost.

XII. But the people brought ⁴ this enthusiasm from their memory of Germanicus <note>Germanicus was a beloved Roman general and the father of Agrippina the Younger; his memory made the public favor his grandson, Nero.</note>, whose lineage had no other male heir; their affection was further increased by compassion for his mother, Agrippina. She was so infatuated with him that, to enjoy her adulterous lover entirely, she forced him to divorce his wife, the noble Junia Silana. ¹ The *Troy Game* was an equestrian tournament traditionally performed in the circus by young aristocrats. The poet Virgil, in the *Aeneid*, Book V (translated here from Annibal Caro’s version), describes its origins:

> These tournaments and these jousts
> Ascanius later renewed, when he founded
> Alba Longa: the Latins learned them;
> The Albans maintained them, and from Alba to Rome
> They were transported, and they remain there today; and as
> Both the custom and Rome and the games derived
> Are from the Trojans, they now take the name of Troy.

² *seemed to predict his future*: A linguistic note on the original Italian phrasing (*predirgliele*), which suggests the people's favor was an omen of his eventual reign as Emperor.
³ *Fables and wonders*: See the historical accounts of Dio Cassius (Book LXI, 2) and Suetonius (*Life of Nero*, chapter 6).
⁴ *But the people brought*: The subject here is the Roman populace.
⁵ *tormented*: The original term *imperversata* suggests she was made a target of Messalina's cruelty and perversity.
⁶ *concealing*: The Italian *frodare* is used here in the sense of the Latin *fallere*, meaning to hide or keep a secret—in this case, his sin.
⁷ *clung to him*: The Latin phrase used by Tacitus is *egressibus adhaerescere*, meaning she followed him step-by-step whenever he left his house. This was a scandalous public display for an Empress.
