Additionally, he added new letters to the alphabet, having observed that even the Greek alphabet was imperfect at its beginning.

Demaratus of Corinth taught these letters in Italy to the Etruscans; and Evander of Arcadia taught them to the Aborigines <note>The "Aborigines" here refers to the earliest inhabitants of central Italy, according to Roman founding myths, rather than the indigenous peoples of Australia.</note>. We also had few letters at first, and then more were added; such as the three added by Claudius <gloss>2</gloss>, which were used while he ruled and later discarded. XV. In the Senate, he made a proposal concerning the college of Haruspices <note>Haruspices were diviners in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals, a practice of Etruscan origin.</note>, urging that such a science, which was ancient in Italy, should not be neglected. He noted that "in many times of trouble for the Republic, the masters of this art had been summoned to restore and better utilize it. The nobles of Tuscany <note>Etruria</note>, whether voluntarily or encouraged by the fathers of Rome, had preserved it and passed it down through their families. Now it is no longer esteemed, due to a common neglect of the noble arts and the preference for foreign superstitions. While everything currently prospers, we must thank the benevolent gods; we should not abandon the sacred rites in times of happiness that we strictly observed in times of adversity." The senators decreed that the high priests should determine what the Haruspices ought to retain and observe.

They asked for Italicus, the only remaining member of their royal line, born to Flavius <gloss>3</gloss> (the brother of Arminius) and a mother who was the daughter of Catumerus, prince of the Chatti. He was a handsome man, skilled with horses and weapons in both our manner and theirs. Caesar [Claudius] gave him money, an escort, and the encouragement to reclaim the greatness of his house. <gloss>1</gloss> *Linus the Theban.* "Linus was not the inventor of letters, but of rhythm and melody among the Greeks. He lived 500 years before the founding of Rome. See Diodorus Siculus, Book III." (R. Pastore.)

<gloss>2</gloss> *such as the three added by Claudius;* in the same way that Claudius added three. These were: 1st, the inverted Aeolic digamma (Ⅎ) which represented the sound of the aspirated 'v' or 'v', as in **sᴇʀᴠᴠs** <note>the Latin word for 'slave' or 'servant'</note>; 2nd, the antisigma (Ↄ) which replaced the Greek letter Psi; 3rd, the modified iota (Ⱶ) which shared the sound of both *i* and *u*, as in **ᴏᴘᴛɪᴍᴠs** <note>the Latin word for 'best'</note>. However, these attempts at graphic improvement, as much as they might seem based on good reasoning, always failed because they had to overcome long-established usage. Thus, what happened to [the scholars] Trissino, Salvini, and now the learned Gherardini, also happened to Claudius: even imperial authority was not enough to grant citizenship to new letters.

...born of a king <note>Italicus was the son of Flavius, the brother of the famous Germanic leader Arminius, but he was raised in Rome as a citizen.</note> but a citizen, to go out to a foreign empire. His first arrival was joyful to the Germans, especially because he, holding no factional ties, treated everyone equally. He was celebrated and respected; he practiced those courtesies and respects that displease no one. Often he gave himself over to wine and lusts, which are pleasing to the barbarians. His reputation already shone among those nearby and those far off; however, those who used to flourish through party factions, suspecting such great power, went to the neighboring states. They bore witness: "The ancient German liberty is gone; Roman power <margin>original: *Romani*; that is, the Roman power.</margin> rises again. XVII. Thus inflamed, they gathered a great host of people; nor did a smaller force follow Italicus, who said: "I did not enter by force, but was called. If I surpassed the others in nobility, I would also show through virtue whether I am worthy of my uncle Arminius and my grandfather Catumerus. I cannot be ashamed of my father, for he never broke that faith with the Romans with which he went to serve them by the will of the Germans. These men make a fine protest of liberty <margin>original: *pretender*, to flaunt or show off.</margin>, who, being vicious in private and harmful in public, cannot live except by discord." The common people favored him with a roar and boldness. The barbarians fought a great battle. The king won; he became proud due to his good fortune, and was later driven out. Refortified with Langobard <note>The Longobards or Lombards, a Germanic tribe that would later invade Italy.</note> forces, he troubled the Cherusci <note>A Germanic tribe located in the northern Rhine valley, famous for the defeat of Varus.</note> with victories and defeats.

**XVIII.** During this time the Chauci, who had been peaceful among themselves, became arrogant due to the death of Sanquinius;^1 when Corbulo^2 came to encounter them, they raided Lower Germany under Gannascus, a captain of the Canninefate^3 nation who had served a long time among our auxiliary forces. Later, as a fugitive, he began pirating with small vessels, mostly along the coasts of the Gauls, knowing them to be wealthy and not very warlike. Once Corbulo entered the province—with great diligence and to his own glory (which began in that military campaign)—he led the galleys through the Rhine; the other ships, as they were suited, through canals and marshes;^4 and he sank the enemy vessels. He drove out Gannascus; and, once things were quieted, he returned the legions—who were eager for plunder and unacquainted with labor or toil—to the ancient custom of not leaving the line of battle: not fighting unless commanded:^5 and performing the watches, the scouts, and the duties of day and night while fully armed. It is said that he punished two soldiers with death because they were digging at the trench, one without weapons, the other with only a dagger; stories which, whether true or false, originated from the severity of the commander, to show how attentive^6 and merciless he was regarding great sins, he who was so cruel and harsh^7 in the smallest ones.

**XIX.** This terror produced two different effects; it increased the courage of our soldiers^8 and diminished the ferocity of the barbarians; and the Frisians (who, after they defeated L. All things, O conscript fathers <note>The formal title for Roman senators</note>, which we now believe to be ancient, were once new.³ First the fathers <note>The patricians</note> held the magistracies: then the plebeians: then the Latins: then Italians of every sort; with the Gauls holding them now, even this will become ancient: and where we support it with examples, it will eventually be cited as an example itself.⁴"

**XXV.** The fathers <note>The Senate</note> decreed according to the speech of the Prince <note>The Emperor Claudius</note>. And the Aedui were the first to become Roman senators,⁵ because of their ancient treaty and because they alone among the Gauls are called "brothers of the Roman people." During these days, Caesar <note>Claudius</note> declared the oldest senators, or those descended from famous men, to be patricians: as few remained of those families that Romulus called the "greater clans" <term>Gentes maiores: the original noble families of Rome</term>, and of those that L. Brutus called the "lesser clans," and likewise of the additions⁶ made by Caesar the Dictator by the Cassian Law, and by Augustus by the Senian Law.⁷ Amidst these grateful public measures, Caesar, desiring to cleanse the Senate of certain shameful members, did so in a gentle and new way derived from ancient severity: he privately advised them to examine themselves and petition to no longer be senators. He would console them by saying they had left that order of their own will and with a good excuse, which was less shameful than being driven out by a formal judgment of the censors. For such actions, Vipsanius the consul proposed that Claudius should be hailed as "Father of the Senate."

> "Others have been called 'Fathers of the Country.' New merits toward the republic ought to be honored with unused titles."

But he shouted down the consul, as being too...

She did not value these words much—not out of love for her husband, but for fear that Silius, once in power, might despise her and recognize the crimes that had pleased him during their moment of crisis. However, she craved the name of marriage for the sake of the great infamy—the ultimate pleasure for those who have "lowered their visor"³ <note>original: "mandato giù la visiera"; a metaphor for losing all sense of shame</note>—and she held a solemn wedding as soon as Claudius had gone to Ostia for a certain sacrifice.

**XXVII.** I see that it will seem like a fable that anyone would dare so much in a city that knows everything and keeps nothing silent; that the consul-elect should find himself on the appointed day marrying the prince’s wife; that a contract should be made with witnesses, as if for the sake of children to be born; that she should hear the words of the augurs, say "I do," sacrifice to the gods, and spend the whole night in a banquet, with the kisses, embraces, and licenses of a wedding. But I, without exaggerating at all, shall relate what I have read and heard from the elders.

**XXXVIII.** Then she realized her fate and took the steel, pointing it at her throat and chest in vain, for her hand trembled: the tribune <term>a military officer of the Praetorian Guard</term> pierced her through with a sword thrust. The body was granted to her mother. To Claudius, who was dining, word was brought that Messallina was dead; it was not specified whether by her own hand or another's, nor did he ask; he requested a drink and continued his dinner as was his custom. In the days following, he showed no signs of hatred, anger, grief, joy, or any other human emotion: not when he saw her accusers rejoicing, nor when he saw his children weeping. The Senate further assisted him in forgetting her, for it decreed that her name and her image be removed from every public and private place. To Narcissus were given the insignia of a quaestor; a small thing to him,¹ who had become the foremost man of the court after Pallas² and Callistus; honorable nonetheless: but this victory brought about the most terrible consequences without any punishment.³

# GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

## SUMMARY.

**I.** Claudius resolves to remarry, uncertain between Lollia Paulina, Julia Agrippina, and Aelia Paetina. — **III.** Agrippina triumphs, aided by Pallas and her own charms. The Senate decides that marriage between an uncle and a niece is legitimate <note>Agrippina was the daughter of Claudius's brother, Germanicus, making this union incestuous by traditional Roman law until this decree.</note>. — **VIII.** Silanus kills himself; his sister Calvina is driven from Italy; Annaeus Seneca is recalled from exile <note>Seneca, the famous Stoic philosopher, was brought back to tutor Agrippina's son, Nero.</note>. — **IX.** Octavia, daughter of Claudius, is betrothed to Nero. — **X.** The Parthians ask Rome for King Meherdates, who is defeated in battle by Gotarzes; the latter dies; Vonones succeeds him, then Vologeses. — **XV.** Mithridates attempts to regain the Kingdom of Pontus; defeated, he is brought to Rome. — **XXII.** Lollia and Calpurnia fall into trouble due to Agrippina’s hatred. — **XXIII.** The Augury of Health <note>original Latin: "Augurium Salutis"; a ritual to ask the gods if it was permissible to pray for the state's safety.</note> is renewed; the *pomerium* <term>the sacred boundary of the city of Rome</term> is extended; its ancient borders. — **XXV.** Nero is adopted by Claudius. — **XXVII.** A colony is established in the land of the Ubii to honor Agrippina <note>This site became "Colonia Agrippinensis," known today as Cologne, Germany.</note>. The Chatti, turned into raiders, are defeated. — **XXIX.** Vannius, king of the Suebi, is driven from his kingdom. — **XXXI.** The deeds of Publius Ostorius in Britain: Caratacus is defeated, Ostorius dies, and Aulus Didius takes his place. — **XLI.** The *toga virilis* <term>the white toga signifying adulthood</term> is hurried upon Nero. Britannicus <note>Claudius's biological son</note> is pushed aside through Agrippina’s schemes. — **XLII.** Prodigies in Rome, and a famine. — **XLIV.** The Armenians and Iberians are at war. Parthians and Romans in great tumult with one another. — **LII.** Furius Scribonianus is exiled; soothsayers are expelled from Italy. — **LIII.** The Senate decrees a penalty for any woman who joins with a slave. A reward is given to Pallas, who was declared by Claudius to be the creator of the proposal. — **LIV.** Judea is quieted from its disturbances; Cumanus is condemned. — **LV.** Antiochus settles the turbulent Clitae. — **LVI.** After staging a naval battle, Claudius provides a drainage outlet for Lake Fucinus. — **LVIII.** Nero pleads the cause of the people of Ilium <note>The city of Troy, from which Rome claimed descent.</note> and the Bolognese; the burned colony of Bologna is aided; freedom is restored to the Rhodians; the tribute of the Apameans is suspended for five years. — **LIX.** Statilius Taurus is ruined by Agrippina. — **LX.** The authority of the procurators <term>financial agents of the Emperor</term> in the provinces is established. — **LXI.** Immunity granted to the people of Cos. — **LXII.** The Byzantines are granted five years of tribute relief. — **LXIV.** Frequent prodigies; death is decreed for Lepida. — **LXVI.** Claudius falls ill; Agrippina loses no time and kills him with poisoned mushrooms. — **LXIX.** Agrippina keeps Britannicus distracted with feigned kindness, and Nero is proclaimed Emperor. Divine honors are granted to Claudius.

**I.** The death of Messallina threw the court into turmoil, <note>original: "rivolse la corte". Dati: "the prince's court fell into discord."</note> as the freedmen <term>former slaves who rose to high administrative positions</term> competed over who should provide a wife for Claudius, who was prone to being unable to live without one and to being dominated by them <note>original: "e da quelle"; meaning, by his wives.</note>. An even more burning ambition resided in the women, each showing herself to be beautiful, noble, wealthy, and worthy of such a husband. The frontrunners were Lollia Paulina, <note>Pliny (Natural History IX, 35) tells incredible things of her luxury: "I saw," he says, "Lollia Paulina, who was the wife of the Emperor Gaius (Caligula), not even at some grave and solemn display of sacred ceremonies, but even at a simple wedding supper, covered in emeralds and pearls, with rich ornaments all over her head, in her hair, in her curls, on her ears, her neck, her arms, and her fingers: so much so that she had no less than four hundred thousand sesterces worth upon her; and she was always ready to show the receipts for them. And Narcissus proposed Aelia Paetina of the Tubero family. Claudius, turning now to one, now to the other according to what he heard, called them all to state their reasons.

**II.** Narcissus spoke of the former marriage, <note>original: "l’antico matrimonio". Aelia Paetina had already been the wife of Claudius, later repudiated for minor reasons. **III.** These reasons were the most persuasive, and were aided by art, as Agrippina made frequent visits to her uncle, as if out of duty <note>original: "quasi per obbligo." The Italian translator notes that the scholar Bernardo Davanzati made a slight error here: the Latin phrase "per speciem necessitudinis" does not mean "out of duty," but rather "under the pretext of kinship."</note>; and she captivated him so much more than the others that she began acting as his wife before she actually was. Once she was certain of her position, she looked further ahead, planning to marry her son Domitius (born of Gnaeus Ahenobarbus) to Octavia, the daughter of Claudius. This could not be done without scandal, as Claudius had already betrothed her to Lucius Silanus; Claudius had even made this son-in-law great in the eyes of the people, who loved him for his own sake, for his triumphal honors, and for the magnificent gladiatorial spectacles he had provided. But everything was easy with that good, bland prince, who was meant to be spoon-fed and commanded <note>original: "buono, scipito, da essere imboccato ec." The Latin text reads: "cui non iudicium, non odium erat, nisi indita et iussa," describing a man who had no judgment or hatred of his own, except what was suggested or ordered by others.</note>.

**IV.** Vitellius, therefore—covering his own malicious baseness under the mask of his role as <term>Censor</term> (a high official responsible for public morality)—sought to win the favor of Agrippina, whom he saw as the future mistress of the state. He meddled in her secret affairs and brought her rumors against Silanus and his sister Julia Calvina, who was beautiful and wanton, and had recently been the daughter-in-law of Vitellius himself. He eventually came to accuse Silanus, not of having committed a sin with his sister, but of having loved her too openly. Caesar [Claudius] was not deaf to these suspicions against his son-in-law, being pressured further by his daughter Octavia. But Silanus, unaware of these schemes <note>original: "non sapendo queste girandole." The translator explains this as "these raggiri" or tricks. The original Latin is "insidiarum nescius," meaning "unaware of the snares."</note> (and he was even a <term>Pretor</term>, a high-ranking magistrate, that year), found himself expelled from the Senate by an edict from Vitellius, despite having been confirmed during the recent selection of senators <note>Valeriani notes: "even though the senators had already been chosen and the ritual purification (lustrum) completed."</note>. At the same time, Claudius broke off the family alliance <note>referring to the engagement to Octavia</note>; Silanus was forced to resign his praetorship, and his term was finished by Eprius Marcellus <note>A famous informer or spy. See Tacitus's History II, 53 and Dialogue 5, 8, 13.</note>.

**VII.** There were those who protested that if Caesar wavered <note>original: "se... la tentennasse." From the Latin *si cunctaretur*. To "stay in the balance" means to be uncertain, to waver, or to doubt. Reference: Varchi, *Ercolano*.</note>, they would go and make him do it <note>original: "fargliele," to make him do that thing.</note> by force; they rushed out of the Senate in a fury. Various groups formed; a great crowd gathered there <note>original: "Vari mucchi; gran calca vi concorre." The Latin reads *conglobatur promiscua multitudo*; that is, a confused rabble crowded together, shouting, etc.</note>, crying out that the Roman people demanded the same. And Claudius, without delay, presented himself to them in the forum and accepted their support. He entered the Senate and urged the decree that marriages between an uncle and a brother’s daughter be considered legal, both now and in the future. Titus Alledius Severus, a Roman knight, seeking to gain favor (so they said, with Agrippina), was the only one to desire such a kinship <note>original: "fu solo a bramare tal parentado." He was the only one eager to follow Claudius's example by taking a niece. Suetonius, in *Life of Claudius*, chapter 26, notes: "Hardly a day passed from the aforementioned resolution before he celebrated the wedding; nor was any found to imitate him in this, except for a certain freedman and a primary centurion, at whose wedding he himself, with his Agrippina, was present."</note>. From then on, everything changed. A woman governed; but she did not play with the state out of indecency, like Messalina; instead, she demanded service, not as a woman would, but as if from slaves <note>original: "ma si facea servire, non come donna, e come da schiavi." Latin: *adductum, et quasi virile servitium*. That is, it was a bondage of rigor and austerity, almost masculine.</note>. In public she was severe, often proud; at home, she was most honorable, unless it served her goal to rule: she was (she said) most greedy for gold in order to support the kingdom.

**VIII.** Silanus killed himself on the day of the wedding <note>original: "s’ ammazò ec." Calvina, his sister, was driven out of Italy, and Claudius ordered that the sacrifices of King Tullus and the re-blessings of the <term>pontiffs</term> <note>Members of the highest council of priests in ancient Rome.</note> be performed...

...in the grove of Diana, on account of Silanus’s incest with his sister; everyone mocked the fact that, at such a time, incests were being punished and "purified" <note>original: "purgassero." This refers to the ritual cleansing of a religious or social stain.</note>. But Agrippina, to make herself known for good deeds as well, had the exile of Annaeus Seneca pardoned,¹ and had him made praetor. She thought this would be pleasing to the public because he was a renowned man of letters, and it would allow Domitius² to be raised by such a great master. She also intended to use his counsel to reach the principate <term>principate: the early period of the Roman Empire and the office of the Emperor</term>, believing Seneca would be faithful out of gratitude for the favor, yet hostile to Claudius because of the injury of his exile.

IX. It seemed there should be no delay: and with great promises, they induced Memmius Pollio, the consul-elect, to deliver his opinion that Claudius should betroth Octavia to Domitius. The age of the couple was suitable, and greater things would surely follow. Pollio performed this duty using almost the same words that Vitellius had used recently. The result followed quickly: thus Domitius, from a relative, was made a son-in-law and a groom. He was now equal to Britannicus thanks to his mother’s favors and the schemes of those who had accused Messalina, who feared that her son <note>Britannicus, the biological son of Claudius and the late Messalina</note> might one day punish them.

X. During this time, the ambassadors of the Parthians (sent to ask for Meherdates, as I mentioned previously³) entered the Senate and explained:

> "They came well aware of our alliance; they were not rebels against the house of the Arsacids, but sought to reclaim the son of Vonones and grandson of Phraates. He would free them from the tyranny of Gotarzes, which had become intolerable to both the nobles and the common people. Gotarzes had murdered his own brothers, his neighbors, and those far off; even pregnant women and infants were not spared, as he tried to hide with cruelty his own inadequacy at home and his lack of grace in war. They requested the ancient public friendship, asking that we aid our companions, who were rivals in power but yielded to Rome out of reverence. They gave the sons of their kings as hostages for no other reason than to be able, when they were ruled poorly, to turn to the Prince and the Senate <note>original: "padri," literally "fathers," referring to the Senators</note> for a good king who had been trained in the Roman school."

XI. Caesar, in response, spoke of Roman greatness and the respect shown by the Parthians. He noted that a king was being requested from him just as one had been requested from the divine Augustus.⁴ He did not say a word about Tiberius, who had also sent one.

->THE TWELFTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.<-

Meherdates, who was present, was warned "not to think of ruling those peoples as slaves, but rather to govern them as citizens, with clemency and justice: qualities that are all the more welcome to barbarians for being so little known to them." Turning then to the ambassadors, he praised to the heavens "this pupil of Rome, a man full of modesty; yet he added that one must make some allowances for kings, and that it was not useful to change them constantly. We are so filled with glory," he said, "that we wish to see every other state at peace." He then ordered Gaius Cassius,¹ the governor of Syria, to escort the young man to the banks of the Euphrates.

## XII.
In matters of law, Cassius was the most learned man of those times; for the arts of war lay dormant during the peace, which values the idle as much as the brave. Nevertheless, as much as was possible in a time without war,² he restored the ancient ways of training the soldiers—thinking, providing, and acting as if an enemy were about to attack. It seemed to him that this was consistent with the dignity of his ancestors and the Cassian family, which was still celebrated among those Eastern nations. Having then summoned those who had called for the king, he encamped at Zeugma,³ where the river crossing is easiest. When the Parthian grandees and Abbarus, King of the Arabs, arrived, Cassius reminded Meherdates to make haste with his enterprise; for barbarians are moved by sudden impulse, and if they delay, they grow weary or turn to treachery. This advice was not heeded⁴ due to the deception of Abbarus; he kept the unsuspecting youth—who believed that being a king consisted of living in great luxury—lingering for many days in the land of Edessa.⁵ And though Carenes called to them, saying that everything was ready if only they arrived quickly, they did not take the short route into Mesopotamia,⁶ but instead detoured through Armenia, a region that should have been avoided since winter was beginning.

## XIII.
Exhausted by the mountains and the snow, they joined together

...with the people of Carenes near the plain: they crossed the Tigris and passed through Adiabene, <margin>1. Adiabene, in modern Kurdistan.</margin> whose king Izates, <margin>2. Izates (Giuliate in the original text).</margin> who feigned friendship with Meherdates, was secretly siding with Gotarzes. On their journey they took the city of Ninus, <margin>3. The city of Ninus. <note>original: "la città di Nino"</note> According to the scholar Orelli, this is the Nineveh of Adiabene, which Tacitus confuses with the ancient capital of Assyria; a portion of those ruins were discovered in 1843 by Paul-Émile Botta, son of the historian.</margin> the most ancient seat of Assyria, and the famous fortress where Alexander fought Darius and overthrew the power of Persia. Meanwhile, on Mount Sambulos, Gotarzes was sacrificing to the local gods; Hercules is the one held in greatest devotion there. At certain times, this god appears in dreams to the priests, commanding them to ready their horses for the hunt and place them near the temple. These horses, laden with quivers full of arrows, gallop through the woods and return at night panting heavily, their quivers empty. The god then appears again in a dream to show them which forests they ran through, and the slaughtered game is found scattered upon the ground.

XIV. But Gotarzes, lacking a sufficient army, used the Corma river as a barrier. Though challenged to battle and provoked by trumpet blasts and insults, he stalled for time, changed locations, and sent bribes to the enemy to encourage betrayals. Among others, Izates <margin>4. Izates.</margin> the Adiabene and Abbarus the Arab king departed with their armies, following their own natural fickleness; <margin>5. *due to their inherent fickleness*. <note>original: "per loro poca levatura"</note> From the Latin: <term>levitate gentili</term>. A person is said to be of "little substance" when their spirit is easily moved, especially to anger, or stirred by any slight cause. The historian Varchi notes that "women usually have little substance... and are like children who get angry at every small thing." In Tuscan dialect, it refers to someone of little wit.</margin> it was clear by experience that barbarians are quick to request kings from Rome, and just as quick to reject them. Meherdates, stripped of such strong support and suspicious of those remaining, decided—having no other choice—to commit himself to fortune and fight. Gotarzes, emboldened by the reduced number of his enemies, accepted the challenge. The clash was bloody and the outcome remained in doubt until Carenes, having pursued a fleeing unit too far, was surrounded by a fresh force. **XX.** Claudius, though lenient toward foreign nobility, was uncertain whether it was better to receive the prisoner on such terms or to reclaim him by force of arms. He was weighed down by the grief of past injuries and the desire for vengeance; however, it was argued to him: "That this would be a war in deserted lands, on a sea without ports, against fickle kings and nomadic peoples, upon a sterile soil. It would be tedious if it lasted, and dangerous if hurried; there would be little glory in winning, and great shame if one lost. Why not accept him on these terms? Life would be a continued punishment for the wretch." For these reasons, he wrote to Eunones: "That while Mithridates deserved death and he had the power to inflict it <note>original: "dargliele"; a Florentine linguistic form using a feminine suffix regardless of gender.</note>, by ancient custom the Romans were as kind to suppliants as they were unyielding to enemies <note>original: "duri a’ nimici." This references Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI: "Roman, remember... To spare the conquered and to war down the proud."</note>; and triumphs are celebrated for the conquest of nations and kingdoms, not for a single man."

**XXI.** Mithridates was subsequently handed over and brought to Rome by Junius Cilo, the procurator of Pontus. It is said that he spoke to Caesar <note>The Emperor Claudius.</note> with a pride ill-suited to his fortune, and these words of his circulated among the people: "I have not been sent back to you, but have returned of my own will; if you do not believe it, set me free and you shall see." Even when he was displayed to the people from the rostrum <note>A raised platform used for public speaking.</note> surrounded by guards, his expression did not change. Cilo was awarded the insignia of a consul, and Aquila those of a praetor.

## XXV. ## [Year of Rome 803; 50 AD]

When Gaius Antistius and Marcus Suillius entered as consuls, the adoption of Domitius was hastened through the influence of Pallas. He was an intimate of Agrippina—having first been her agent in arranging her marriage and later becoming her lover—and he urged Claudius to think of the public good by providing a support for the childhood of Britannicus. He argued that the divine Augustus, though supported by grandsons, had elevated his stepsons <note>Drusus and Tiberius</note>; and Tiberius, despite having his own son <note>Drusus the Younger</note>, had adopted Germanicus. He suggested Claudius should likewise make use of this young man, shifting a portion of his burdens onto him. By these arguments, Claudius was persuaded to favor Domitius, who was only two years older than his own son, and he delivered a speech to the Senate which had been fed to him by his freedman <note>Pallas</note>. Experts noted that no other adoption could be found among the patrician Claudians, who had maintained a continuous natural lineage from the time of Attus Clausus <note>The founder of the Claudian house, whose name later became Appius Claudius</note> until then.

## XXVI. ##

The prince was thanked for this, and Domitius was exquisitely flattered. A law was passed granting him entry into the Claudian house and the name of Nero; Agrippina was also granted the title of Augusta. Once these things were done, there was no man so cold-hearted that he did not weep for poor Britannicus. Abandoned even by the lowliest servants, he became the object of mockery due to the inappropriate "affections" shown to them by Agrippina <note>A secondary interpretation suggests that Britannicus was gradually deprived of all his servants and mocked the ill-timed "kindness" of his stepmother, sensing the deception behind it.</note>. It was said that he was a boy of great intelligence; perhaps it was his perceived suffering that earned him such praise, before he could truly prove himself.

**XXVII.** To demonstrate her power even to allied nations, Agrippina established a colony in the land of the Ubii and gave it her own name,<sup>1</sup> as she had been born there. It so happened that this tribe, having crossed the Rhine, had previously submitted to the protection of her grandfather, Agrippa.

At that time, Upper Germany faced turmoil because the Chatti <note>A powerful Germanic tribe often at odds with Rome</note> had entered to plunder. L. Pomponius, the legate <note>A high-ranking military officer or governor</note>, dispatched the Vangiones and Nemetes,<sup>2</sup> our allies, along with a troop of cavalry, with orders to intercept the raiders or catch them while they were scattered and off guard. The soldiers added their own ingenuity to the commander's plan by dividing their forces. One group moved to the left and surrounded those returning from the raid, who were wallowing in their plunder or idling. To their great joy, they liberated several slaves who had been captured forty years earlier during the defeat of Varus.<sup>3</sup> <note>The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, where three Roman legions were destroyed.</note>

**XXVIII.** The other group, taking the shorter route to the right, encountered the enemy, who dared to fight but suffered a bloodier defeat. Burdened with loot and glory, the Romans returned to Mount Taunus,<sup>4</sup> where Pomponius waited with the legions to see if the Chatti would regroup for revenge. The Chatti, fearing they would be caught between the Romans on one side and their eternal enemies, the Cherusci, on the other, sent ambassadors and hostages to Rome. Triumphal honors <note>original: "le trionfali"</note> were decreed for Pomponius; however, he is rendered much more famous by his poetry.<sup>5</sup>

**XXIX.** During this same time, Vannio,<sup>6</sup> who had been made King of the Suevi by Drusus Caesar, was driven from his kingdom. Initially popular and beloved, he grew arrogant and earned the hatred of his people over time. He was betrayed by Vangio and Sido, his sister’s sons, and by Giubillius, King of the Hermunduri. Despite many pleas, Claudius did not wish to involve Roman arms in these barbarian disputes. He promised Vannio a safe refuge if he were ousted and wrote to P. Atilius Istrus, the governor of Pannonia, to station a legion and the best of the auxiliary troops along the Danube. This was intended to provide aid to those who lost and to restrain the vic—

These were the neighboring nations. They chose for the battle a place fortified by earthen ramparts, with an entrance so narrow that it was inaccessible to the cavalry. Ostorius, although lacking the full strength of the legions, set out to overwhelm them with his auxiliary troops; dividing the cohorts, he also put the horsemen to work on foot. At the signal, he broke through the ramparts, throwing the enemy into confusion <note>original: "sconfonde" — to throw into disarray</note>. Caught in their own "cage," and seeing that they were trapped as rebels with all exits blocked, they performed deeds that were truly memorable <note>original: "da dirsene" — literally "to be spoken of"; the translator notes this phrase is similar to a line from the poem *Malmantile*: ->He performed deeds to be written home about.<-</note>. In that skirmish, Marcus Ostorius, the son of the legate <term>Legate: a high-ranking Roman military officer and provincial governor</term>, earned the civic crown for saving a fellow citizen.

XXXII. The defeat of the Iceni <note>A tribe in eastern Britain, later famous for the rebellion of Queen Boudica</note> settled those who were wavering between war and peace <note>original: "i dubbii"</note>, and the army marched against the Cangi <note>A tribe inhabiting what is now northern Wales</note>. They devastated the land everywhere and gathered much loot, as the enemy did not dare to face them in open battle. Instead, they harassed the column with hit-and-run tactics <note>The Latin source states: "ex occulto carpere agmen tentarunt" (they tried to harass the army from hiding)</note>, which turned out poorly for them. Having approached the sea that looks toward Ireland <note>original: "Ibernia"</note>, the commander was forced to turn back by internal discords among the Brigantes <note>A powerful tribe in Northern England, modern Yorkshire and surrounding areas</note>. He was a man resolved not to attempt new conquests until the previous ones were secured. After killing the few who had taken up arms and pardoning the rest, he left them in peace. However, neither severity nor mercy could make the Silures <note>A fierce tribe in South Wales</note> lay down their arms; it became necessary to subdue them with permanent garrisons. To make this easier, a colony was established <note>The translator notes that the word "bisognò" (it was necessary) is implied here</note> in the conquered territory at Camalodunum <note>Likely modern Colchester, though the note suggests Maldon. It was the first Roman colony in Britain</note>. XXXIII. Then they marched against the Silures,<gloss>1</gloss> who were fierce by nature and emboldened by their great faith in Caratacus, their leader. He was the foremost warrior among the Britons, renowned for his many great exploits. Though he was at a disadvantage in terms of the number of trained soldiers, he held the upper hand in his knowledge of the terrain. With great cunning, he shifted the theater of war into the territory of the Ordovices <note>A tribe in North Wales</note>. There, joined by all those who feared the Roman "peace" <note>A common Roman euphemism for conquest and subjugation</note>, he decided to tempt fortune. He positioned his forces on a steep mountain where every entrance, exit, and path was to our disadvantage;<gloss>2</gloss> and wherever the slope could be climbed, he fortified it with piles of stones like a rampart. A treacherous river also protected the front, where his best soldiers stood ready before the defenses.

XXXIV. Caratacus rushed from place to place among the leaders and the ranks, encouraging them, heartening them, dispelling their fears, and offering hope and other incentives to fight. He cried out: "This is the day! This is the battle for the recovery of our liberty or for eternal servitude!" He invoked the names of their ancestors who had driven away Caesar the Dictator <note>Referring to Julius Caesar's invasions in 55 and 54 BCE</note>; it was by their courage, he said, that they had been spared the Roman axes and tributes, and the honor of their wives and children had been kept safe. At these words, the crowd shouted; each nation swore according to its own custom never to shrink from weapons or wounds.

XXXV. Such readiness—with the river in the middle, the reinforced ramparts, the looming mountains, and everything threatening to us but familiar to them—terrified our commander. But the soldiers cried out, "Battle! Valor conquers all!" The tribunes and the prefects echoed these same sentiments,<gloss>3</gloss> further inflaming the army’s spirit. Ostorius then, after scouting the reachable points, led them all easily across the river. When they reached the rampart and the skirmishing began with missile weapons, many of our men were wounded and fell. "...an immortal example of your mercy." At these words, Caesar <note>The Emperor Claudius</note> granted pardon to him, his wife, and his brothers. Once they were unbound, they offered their reverence, thanks, and praise to the prince, and the same to Agrippina, who sat on another nearby throne. It was a novel sight, and contrary to all ancient custom, for a woman to sit among the Roman military standards: but she presented herself as a partner in that empire which her own ancestors had acquired.

**XXXVIII.** The gathered fathers <note>The Roman Senate</note> spoke with great magnificence concerning the capture of Caratacus, claiming it was no less splendid than those displays made to the Roman people by Publius Scipio regarding Syphax <note>King of the Massylii in Numidia</note>, or by Lucius Paulus regarding Perseus <note>The last King of Macedon</note>, or by others who had displayed other enchained kings. They decreed triumphal honors for Ostorius for his happy successes; however, these successes did not endure. This was perhaps because Ostorius was less vigilant in the war once Caratacus was removed, believing it nearly won, or because compassion for so great a king had inflamed the enemies to seek vengeance. They surrounded the camp prefect and the Roman bands left among the Silures <note>A powerful and warlike tribe in ancient Wales</note> to build fortifications. Eight centurions and the most valiant soldiers died there; and they all would have perished had they not been quickly rescued from the neighboring villages and forts. Soon after, they routed our men who were out seeking provisions, as well as the cavalry sent to aid them.

**XXXIX.** Ostorius sent out light cohorts to them, but as they could not check the flight, he went there with the legions. With their strength, the battle was first leveled and then won; the enemy escaped with little damage because the day was ending. Frequent and small skirmishes followed, in the manner of bandits in the woods or marshes; occurring by chance or by design, through anger or for plunder, by command or without it. The Silures were particularly obstinate because of a rumor spread about the Roman Emperor: "that just as the Sugambri <note>A Germanic tribe that had been defeated and relocated to Gaul under Augustus</note> had been destroyed and transported into Gaul, so too must the seed of the Silures be extinguished." They therefore ambushed two auxiliary cohorts <note>Non-citizen troops supporting the Roman army</note> that were led by the greed of their commanders to go too far in looting; by giving away the spoils and prisoners from this victory, they drew other peoples into rebellion. Thus Ostorius, afflicted by so many heavy cares, died—to the joy of his enemies, who felt that the war, if not his sword, had extinguished a commander of such reputation.

Having arrived after a favorable voyage, he found things in a sorry state, as a legion under Manlius Valens¹ had been defeated, and the matter was being exaggerated to terrify the new commander; and he, in turn, exaggerated it further² to increase his own glory if he were to win, or to provide an excuse if he were to lose. A fierce battle followed: at first the outcome was uncertain, but in the end, it was successful. A legion under Caesius Nasica fought with similar success, for Didius, being old and full of honors, acted through subordinates and was content simply to keep the enemy at bay. I have not divided these events by individual years so that they may be better understood as a whole. Now I return to the chronological order.

### XLI.

During the fifth consulship of Tiberius Claudio <note>The Emperor Claudius</note> and Servius Cornelius Orfitus, the toga <note>The *toga virilis*, or toga of manhood, marking the transition from childhood to adult citizenship</note> was given to Nero early,⁴ so that he might appear ready for government. Caesar <note>Claudius</note> allowed himself to be led by the flatteries of the Senate to appoint Nero as consul for when he reached twenty years of age;⁵ in the meantime, he was to have proconsular authority outside of Rome and be titled the Prince of Youth <term>Princeps Juventutis: a title historically given to the designated heirs of the Roman Empire</term>. A bounty was also given in his name to the soldiers and a gift to the common people. During the Circensian games <note>Chariot races and spectacles in the Circus Maximus</note>, which were held to win the favor of the populace, Britannicus appeared in a child’s bordered toga <term>toga praetexta: the standard dress for high-born Roman boys</term>, while Nero appeared in triumphal robes <note>robes typically worn by a general during a formal victory parade</note>. This was done so that the people, seeing one dressed as an emperor and the other as a child, might judge for themselves who was to be the future ruler. ### XLII.

Therefore, by the advice of his wife—who claimed that the cohorts were dividing into factions due to the competition between two leaders, and could be better disciplined if commanded by one—the command of the Pretorians <note>The Praetorian Guard, the elite unit of the Imperial Roman army that served as the Emperor's personal bodyguards</note> was given to Burrus Afranius, who was considered a great soldier, but well aware of who had given him the position <note>Burrus knew he owed his elevation to Agrippina and was thus indebted to her</note>. Agrippina then rose to even greater heights of prestige: she began entering the Capitoline in a ceremonial carriage <term>Carpentum: A two-wheeled carriage traditionally reserved for priests and sacred objects</term>, an honor that had previously been granted only to the priesthood and sacred things. This increased the veneration for this woman, who was the daughter of a great commander <note>Germanicus</note>, and the sister, wife, and mother of three emperors <note>She was the sister of Caligula, wife of Claudius, and mother of Nero</note>: a unique example in history until today. Meanwhile Vitellius, who had championed her cause <note>original: "l’aveva presa per lei," meaning he had taken her side and defended her</note> more than anyone else and was highly favored though very old (so precariously do the great hang in the balance), was struck by an accusation of treason and of coveting the empire by the senator Junius Lupus. Caesar [Claudius] was inclined to listen, until Agrippina, using threats rather than prayers, turned him toward punishing the accuser with the "interdiction of fire and water" <term>Interdiction of fire and water: A Roman legal sentence of exile, where the person was deprived of the basic necessities of life within the community</term>; Vitellius was satisfied with this outcome.

### XLIII.
In that year, many omens appeared. Birds of ill omen <note>original: "mal' uria," meaning bad luck or a poor augury</note> perched upon the Capitoline Hill; earthquakes caused many houses to collapse, and in the crush of the terrified crowds fleeing, the weakest were smothered. There were poor harvests, which led to famine. Because of this, the people did not merely murmur against Claudius; but while he was administering justice <note>original: "rendendo ragione," a translation of the Latin "jus reddentem," referring to the Emperor's role as a judge</note>, the crowds deafened him with their cries. Pushing him into a corner of the Forum and mobbing him, the guards were forced to clear a path for his escape. It was discovered that there was only enough bread for fifteen days; but the kind gods and a mild winter saved the city. In the past, Italy used to feed distant lands, and even today it is not barren; but we prefer to cultivate Africa and Egypt, and entrust the lives of the Roman people to ships and to fortune.

### XLIV.
In the same year, a war broke out between the Armenians and the Iberians <note>Iberia here refers to an ancient kingdom in the Caucasus (modern-day Georgia), not the Spanish peninsula</note>, which also caused massive movements between the Parthians and the Romans. Vologases, born of a Greek concubine, was king of the Parthians by the will of his brothers. Pharasmanes was king of the Iberians by long possession, and Mithridates, his brother, was king of the Armenians, held in power by our [Roman] influence. Pharasmanes had a son named Rhadamistus, who was handsome, tall, and strong; he was skilled in the local customs and held a high reputation among those nations. This young man, who was often too fierce in revealing his ambitions, used to say:

> “We have but a tiny kingdom <note>original: "un dito di regno," literally "a finger of a kingdom." Latin: "modicum regnum"</note>, and an old dotard <note>original: "barbogio," a derogatory term for a senile or foolish old man</note> holds it.”

Pharasmanes, burdened by years and fearing this powerful, fierce young man who had a large following <note>original: "di seguito." Latin: "studio popularium accinctum," meaning he was surrounded by the support of the common people</note>, turned Rhadamistus’s attention toward the hope of taking Armenia. He reminded his son that he had previously given Armenia to Mithridates after driving out the Parthians, but suggested that before using force, he should see if he could take it back by deceit while the king suspected nothing. Thus, Rhadamistus went to his uncle, pretending to be enraged with his father over the insults of a stepmother. Received with fatherly affection, he secretly persuaded the Armenian nobles to join his plot; he was so discrete that Mithridates himself acted as a mediator to reconcile the boy with his father. Once Rhadamistus returned home, he told his father that he had prepared the matter through fraud, and it was now time to finish it with arms.

### XLV.
While he <note>Rhadamistus</note> was fighting against the King of Albania and asking the Romans for help, his brother worked against him; to avenge this injury, he intended to destroy him. Having given his son a large army, he immediately launched an assault and seized the countryside from a bewildered Mithridates, who saved himself in the fortress of Gornea,¹ which was strong and held a good guard of soldiers under the command of Caelius Pollio, the prefect, and Casperius, a centurion. Barbarians understand nothing less than taking lands through the use of siege engines and tactical skill; we Romans are masters of it. Rhadamistus, having assaulted in vain or with great loss, began a siege. Seeing no progress, he corrupted the prefect with bribes, despite Casperius’s protest: 
> "He should not so foully sell an allied king, nor Armenia, which is a gift of the Roman people." 

Pollio responded that there were too many enemies surrounding the fortress, and Rhadamistus cited his father's orders. Having declared a truce, Casperius departed to dissuade Pharasmanes from this war; if he failed, he intended to inform Titus Ummidius Quadratus, who governed Syria, of the state of affairs in Armenia.

### XLVI. 
Once the centurion had departed, the prefect, left as if without a pedagogue <note>original: "pedagogo," here meaning a moral guide or overseer</note>, advised Mithridates to reach an agreement, reminding him: 
> "Pharasmanes is your older brother, you are his son-in-law, and you are the father-in-law of Rhadamistus. The Iberians <note>Caucasian Iberians from the region of modern Georgia</note>, though currently the stronger side, do not refuse peace. It is well known how treacherous the Armenians are; you have no other security because this fortress is not provisioned. Do not choose war when you could have a bloodless treaty." 

Mithridates was slow to trust the prefect’s advice, as Pollio had been intimate with one of the King's concubines and was believed to be capable of any foul deed for money. Meanwhile, Casperius reached Pharasmanes and demanded that the Iberians lift the siege. Pharasmanes gave vague and often favorable-sounding answers, but secretly sent messengers to Rhadamistus, urging him to tighten the siege by every means. The deceit <note>original: "baratteria," meaning corrupt dealing or fraud</note> grew, and Pollio secretly bribed the soldiers to demand peace and threaten to desert. Driven to such a desperate position, Mithridates agreed to a meeting on the day and place appointed and left the fortress to surrender.

...confirm the peace, Rhadamistus said, in the presence of the gods, with sacrifices ordained within the temple. It is the custom of these kings, when they form a confederacy, to join their right hands and tie their thumbs tightly together; then, when the blood rises to the skin, they prick it and suck one another’s blood. Such a peace, consecrated as if by shared blood, they hold to be inviolable. But on this occasion, the man who was tying the bond let himself fall, and seizing Mithridates by the legs, he threw him down. Many rushed forward, clapped him in irons, and dragged him along by a chain at his feet (which is a great shame among the Barbarians). The mistreated people turned on him with insults and blows, though some were moved to pity by such a great reversal of fortune. His wife followed with their small children, filling the air with laments. They were placed in separate wagons and kept confined until the arrival of the order from Pharasmanes <note>King of Iberia and Rhadamistus’s father</note>; for the sake of that kingdom, he renounced both his brother and his daughter, and the villain resolved to have them murdered, provided he did not have to see it. And Rhadamistus, pretending to be an observer of his oath, used neither blade nor poison against his sister and uncle; instead, he threw them to the ground and smothered them under many heavy layers of cloth. He then slaughtered their children, simply because they were weeping for their parents.

### XLVIII.
Quadratus <note>Titus Ummidius Quadratus, Governor of Syria</note>, having learned of the betrayal of Mithridates and that the traitors were now reigning, called a council to present the facts and ask whether punishment should be meted out. Few in the council looked to public honor; most looked to their own security, saying, "We should cherish the rages of foreigners among themselves and sow discord. The Roman princes have often used this tactic, giving this blessed Armenia to one and taking it from another just to stir them up. It is better for us <note>original: "Farsi per noi," meaning to be of use to us</note> that Rhadamistus keeps what he gained through evil, burdened with hatred and infamy, rather than holding it with glory." This was the course decided upon; but so as not to appear to approve of such atrocity (and fearing Caesar <note>the Emperor Claudius</note> might be of another mind), they sent word to Pharasmanes that he and his son must clear out of the Armenian state.

### XLIX.
The procurator of Cappadocia was Julius Pelignus, a man of vile spirit and a ridiculous body, who was equally contemptible but a total favorite of Claudius. Back when Claudius was still a private citizen, he used Pelignus to pass the time <note>original: "passava mattana," an idiom for dispelling a dark mood or boredom</note> with people whose faces were made to provoke laughter <note>The scholar Valeriani notes: "when, as a private citizen, he refreshed his leisure with the conversation of buffoons."</note>. This man, wishing to recover Armenia...

He raised an army to restore his brother Tiridates to the throne, so that no member of his royal house should be without a kingdom.

### L.
When the Parthians arrived, they drove out the Iberians <note>The people from the Caucasus region supporting Rhadamistus</note> without a single battle. The Armenian cities of Artaxata and Tigranocerta submitted to their rule. However, a bitter winter, a lack of provisions, or perhaps a combination of both, gave rise to a plague. This forced Vologeses to leave Armenia empty of his troops. Rhadamistus immediately returned, now even more cruel than before, treating the people as if they were rebels and traitors. Though they were accustomed to being subjects, the people lost their patience and, taking up arms, besieged him within his own palace.

### LI.
Only the speed of his horses allowed him to save himself and his pregnant wife <note>Zenobia</note>. Out of fear of the enemy and love for her husband, she barely endured the first part of the flight. Then, as her womb was shaken and her internal organs were tossed about by the ride, she begged him to give her an honorable death so that she would not be left as prey and a victim of torture for the enemy. He embraced her, supported her, and comforted her: at one moment he was amazed by her courage; at another, he was driven mad by the thought that someone else might possess her. Finally, overcome by love, or perhaps simply accustomed to cruelty, having unsheathed... <note>The text ends here mid-action; historical accounts describe Rhadamistus stabbing her and throwing her into the river Araxes before fleeing.</note>

**LII.** In the year when Faustus Sulla <note>Sulla was the son-in-law of Emperor Claudius through his wife Antonia</note> and Salvius Otho <note>Otho was the brother of the man who would later briefly become Emperor</note> were consuls, Furius Scribonianus was sent into exile. His mother, Junia, was exiled with him for having violated her previous banishment. Camillus <note>Referencing the rebellion mentioned in earlier books</note>, the father of Scribonianus, had once taken up arms in Dalmatia, and Caesar <note>The Emperor Claudius</note> took credit for his own kindness in forgiving the son of his former enemy. Scribonianus died soon after; some claimed it was by poison. A strict law was then passed in the Senate to expel all soothsayers <note>astrologers and diviners</note> from Italy, though it was enacted in vain <note>The Roman authorities frequently banned astrologers, but the elite continued to consult them in secret</note>. The prince highly praised certain senators who had voluntarily resigned their rank due to poverty, while he stripped the rank from others who, though equally poor, sought to keep it.

**LIII.** A penalty was proposed and passed regarding free women who, without the permission of the master, cohabited with slaves: such women were to be reduced to slavery themselves, though their children would be born free. Barea Soranus, the consul-elect, moved that the insignia of a praetor and three hundred and seventy-five thousand florins <note>The Italian translator uses "fiorini" (florins) to represent the Roman sesterces</note> be awarded to Pallas, whom Caesar claimed was the author of this proposal. Cornelius Scipione added that Pallas should be thanked publicly because, despite being descended from the ancient kings of Arcadia <note>This was ridiculous flattery; it was common for the era to invent noble lineages for powerful former slaves. Claudius testified that the good Pallas was satisfied with the honor alone and preferred to live in his "poverty." Soon the Senate, by a decree engraved in bronze and posted in public, attributed the highest praises of ancient frugality to this freedman, who was actually worth seven and a half million gold pieces.

**LIV.** His brother, known as Felix, was not so restrained. Appointed earlier to govern Judea, he believed every whim was permitted to him, emboldened by his great power. <gloss>1</gloss> <note>Felix was the brother of Pallas, the Emperor's powerful freedman and advisor; his status at court gave him a sense of legal immunity.</note> Indeed, the Jews had shown signs of rebellion when, upon hearing of the death of Gaius <note>Gaius is the Emperor Caligula</note>, they failed to obey his orders: <gloss>2</gloss> they feared that a future prince might command the same atrocities. Felix and Ventidius Cumanus, using the wrong remedies, competed to see who could incite more wickedness. Cumanus governed Galilee while Felix ruled Samaria—two regions naturally at odds, and even more so then as they held their poor governors in contempt. They robbed one another, employed assassins, committed betrayals, and eventually came to open combat. They brought their plunder to these governors, whose eyes gleamed with delight at first; <gloss>3</gloss> but as the scandals grew, they sent in soldiers, who were killed in the fighting. The province would have been consumed by war if Quadratus, the governor of Syria, had not arrived; he executed those who had killed the soldiers without hesitation. As for Felix and Cumanus, since Claudius had written that Quadratus should also judge them as the causes of the rebellion, he hesitated; however, he made Felix sit beside him on the tribunal as one of the judges, so that the accusers would not speak against him. Thus, for the sins of two men, only Cumanus was punished, and the province became quiet.

**LV.** Shortly thereafter, the Clitae, rustic tribesmen of Cilicia often prone to uprising, moved under their leader Trosobore and camped in the rugged mountains. Descending from there to the cities or the coast, they murdered townspeople, farmers, merchants, and sailors. They besieged the city of Anemur and defeated Curtius Severus, who had been sent from Syria with cavalry, which was not as effective as infantry for fighting...

**LVI.** During this time, the mountain was cut through <gloss>1</gloss> between Lake Rossiglione <gloss>2</gloss> and the Garigliano river, <gloss>3</gloss> so that more people might witness the magnificent naval battle organized on that lake. Claudius armed galleys and light vessels with nineteen thousand combatants. He created a circle of floating beams so they could not escape, yet spaced widely enough to allow for maneuvering, steering, rowing, and fighting. Infantry and cavalry guards stood on the beams behind parapets equipped with catapults <gloss>4</gloss> and loaded crossbows. Marines <gloss>5</gloss> in decked ships held the rest of the lake. The hills, the shores, and the mountain peaks, arranged like a theater, were crowded with people arriving from the surrounding areas and from Rome, either to witness the sight or to pay court to the prince. They sat in state: the Emperor in imperial robes, and not far off, Agrippina in a cloak of gold. Although the combatants were criminals, they fought like brave and valiant men, and after many wounds, they were separated. <note>These "naval battles," known as naumachiae, typically involved prisoners of war or criminals fighting to the death for public entertainment.</note>

The **Sempronian laws** <margin>These were the laws of Gaius Gracchus, who in the year 632 from the founding of Rome [122 BC] transferred the right to preside over trials from the Senate to the Equestrian order.</margin> placed the equestrian order <gloss>the knights</gloss> in possession of the right to judge; and the **Servilian laws** <margin>Lucius Servilius Caepio, in the year 648 [106 BC], desired by law that judicial duties be shared between the senators and the knights.</margin> returned it to the senate. The wars between Marius and Sulla were fought for almost no other reason than this. <note>The commentator notes these wars arose mainly from the struggle between the senatorial and equestrian orders for judicial control. After so much bloodshed, Claudius took this right from both to give it to the procurators of the imperial treasury.</note> One side favored one order, the other side the other, and whichever side conquered, took the right to judge. Under the arm of Caesar, Gaius Oppius and Cornelius Balbo were the first who were able to decide matters of peace and war according to their own will. **LXI.** He proposed to make the people of **Kos** <term>Coo: An island in the Aegean Sea famous for its medical school.</term> exempt from all taxes, speaking at length about their ancient history:

The people of Kos had undoubtedly aided the Roman people in many victories; but Claudius, sweet-natured as usual, did not embellish the favor by reminding them of these deeds.

**LXIV.** In the year when Marcus Asinius and Marcus Acilius were consuls [54 AD], many prodigies <gloss>omens or supernatural signs</gloss> showed that the state of affairs was destined to worsen. But more than anything, Agrippina was terrified by a biting remark <note>original: "un mal bottone," literally a "bad button," meaning a harsh or ominous word. **LXVI.** Claudius, under the weight of so many worries, fell ill and went to seek recovery in the healthy air and baths of Sessa <note>Ancient Sinuessa, a resort town famous for its medicinal waters.</note>. Agrippina, already determined to poison him and seizing this opportunity—and having no lack of agents—deliberated on which poison to use. A rapid one would be too obvious; a slow and lingering one might allow Claudius to notice the plot, and as he neared death, his fatherly love might be rekindled, prompting him to leave the empire to his own son, Britannicus. She decided on a poison that would cloud his mind and cause a slow death. It was prepared by Locusta <note>Locusta was later put to death by the Emperor Galba.</note>, who had already been condemned as a sorceress and then kept for a long time among the "tools of the state" <note>original: "masserizie di stato." Latin: *instrumenta regni*; people whose hands the court used to remove anyone who caused them trouble.</note>.

**LXVII.** It was later known with such precision that the writers of those times record that the poison was given to him in mushrooms <note>The Italian text uses "uovoli," referring to the *Amanita caesarea* mushroom, a delicacy in ancient Rome.</note>, of which he was very fond:<sup>2</sup> and Claudius, either drunk or senseless, did not notice it. His nature helped him, and his bowels were relieved, so it seemed he might recover. Agrippina was terrified; and seeing everything at stake, she cast aside all caution and hurried to Xenophon the physician, who was already part of the conspiracy. He, under the pretense of helping the Emperor vomit, thrust a feather into his throat that had been dipped in a fast-acting poison. He did this knowing that the greatest crimes are begun with danger but completed with great rewards.

**LXVIII.** The Senate is convened; the consuls and priests offer up prayers for the prince's recovery, even while he was already dead;<sup>3</sup> he was hidden under warm cloths and poultices<sup>4</sup> to buy time to arrange matters to secure the empire for Nero. Meanwhile, Agrippina, as if overcome by grief and seeking comfort, held Britannicus <note>Claudius's biological son and the rightful heir, whom Agrippina needed to sideline.</note> in a tight embrace, calling him the very image of his father. By various tricks, she kept him from leaving the chamber. She also locked in his sisters, Antonia and Octavia, and placed guards at every door. She frequently put out word that the Prince was improving, to keep the soldiers in good hope and to wait for the auspicious moment calculated by the astrologers <note>The text refers to them as "caldei" (Chaldeans), a common term for court astrologers in Rome.</note>.

**LXIX.** At midday on the thirteenth of October, the palace gates were thrown open, and Nero emerged with Burrus <note>Sextus Afranius Burrus, the prefect of the Praetorian Guard and Nero's tutor.</note> and went to the cohort,

<sup>1</sup> **performed the tasting.** <note>Original Latin: *explorare gustu solitus* (accustomed to testing by taste). See the following book, chapter 16. To "make the credence" means to taste the food before it is placed on the table to assure the lord that there is no poison. From this practice, the sideboard where the food was placed for this tasting came to be called a "credenza."</note>

<sup>2</sup> **of which he was very fond.** <note>Suetonius, in his *Life of Claudius*, writes: "All agree that he was poisoned, but they do not agree on where or by whom. Some write that it was in the Citadel while dining with the priests; others that it was Halotus, his taster; still others that Agrippina put the poison in a mushroom, a dish he loved. Nor do they agree on what followed: because some affirm that immediately after taking the poison he lost his speech, and after a night of great pain, died at daybreak. Others write that at first he fell asleep; then, as the food swelled in his stomach, he vomited it out, and was poisoned again. They are also uncertain if this second dose was in the broth they gave to restore him, or if they poisoned the enema administered to relieve his fullness."</note>

<sup>3</sup> **dead.** <note>The original Italian uses the word *basito*.</note>

...who stood, according to custom, on guard. At this point, the soldiers—prompted by Burrus <note>Sextus Afranius Burrus, the prefect of the Praetorian Guard and a key ally of Agrippina.</note>—received him with joyful shouts and placed him in a litter. It is said that some hesitated, asking where Britannicus <note>Claudius's biological son, who was younger than Nero and the legitimate heir.</note> was; but since there was no one to suggest otherwise, they accepted the choice presented to them.

Nero was then brought to the camp <note>The Praetorian camp, the military heart of Rome, where the guard's loyalty was secured.</note> and spoke fitting words. He promised a bounty <term>donative: a large monetary gift given by a new emperor to the soldiers to secure their allegiance</term> equal to that which his father <note>original: "padre"—referring to his adoptive father, Claudius.</note> had given, and he was hailed as Emperor. The decision of the soldiers was followed by the decrees of the Senate, and soon after, the provinces accepted the change without hesitation. 

Divine honors were decreed for Claudius, and his funeral was conducted with the same ceremony as that of Augustus, with Agrippina striving to match the magnificence of her great-grandmother Livia <note>Livia Drusilla, the wife of Augustus, who had been the most powerful woman in the early Empire.</note>. However, his will was not read aloud, lest the public be provoked by the injustice and spite of a father who had preferred a stepson over his own son.

## GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

### SUMMARY.

I. G. Silanus poisoned through Agrippina’s <note>Agrippina the Younger, Nero's mother, who was at the height of her power at the start of this book.</note> plot. The Senate discusses the frauds of freedmen and whether to return them to slavery: yet no general change is made to the law. — XXVIII. Vipsanius Laenas condemned. L. Volusius dies. — XXXI. Magistrates elected to the Provinces are forbidden from giving public games. — XXXII. <meta>This page transitions from the death of Claudius to the first actions of Nero's reign in 54 AD. It establishes the power struggle between Nero’s mother, Agrippina, and his advisors, Seneca and Burrus, while detailing the first political assassinations of the new era.</meta>

# THE THIRTEENTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

I. [Year of Rome 807, Year of Christ 54.] The first person killed under the new principate was Junius Silanus,¹ proconsul of Asia. This was done without Nero’s knowledge through the treachery of Agrippina. It was not because Silanus was particularly feared for his temperament—in fact, he was sluggish and held in such contempt by previous emperors that Gaius Caesar <note>The Emperor Caligula.</note> used to call him the "golden ox"²—but because Agrippina, who had plotted the death of his brother Lucius Silanus,³ feared his vengeance. The common people were whispering that Nero, barely out of his youth and made emperor through foul play, should be passed over for Silanus, a man of mature age, integrity, and noble birth who was—a key factor at the time—of the blood of the Caesars, being the great-grandson of Augustus. This was his death warrant. The agents of the crime⁴ were Publius Celer, a Roman knight, and Helius, a freedman, who both served as the prince’s procurators in Asia. They poisoned him at a banquet, so openly that everyone noticed. Just as quickly, Narcissus, the freedman of Claudius whose bitter arguments with Agrippina I mentioned earlier,⁵ was forced to die in a harsh prison through extreme hardship. This was against the will of the prince <note>Nero.</note>, who shared Narcissus's vices of greed and extravagance—though the prince's nature was not yet fully revealed—and therefore found him a kindred spirit.

II. Many more would have died had Afranius Burrus and Annaeus Seneca not intervened. These two governed the young emperor together with equal power but different methods: Burrus with military discipline and gravity of character, and Seneca with lessons in eloquence and courtly grace. They assisted one another to more easily keep the prince's impressionable age in check with permitted pleasures, if they could not guide him toward virtue. Their only struggle was against the ferocity of Agrippina, who burned with every tyrannical desire and was aided by Pallas, the man who had induced Claudius to ruin himself⁶ through an incestuous marriage and a disastrous adoption. However, Nero was not in the mood to let himself be governed by slaves, and Pallas, with his arrogance exceeding the con—

III. And while he recounted the ancient lineage, the consulships, and the triumphs of his ancestors,¹ the attention of the crowd was great. The mention of his <note>Claudius's</note> scholarship and noble arts, and how, during his reign, no harm was received from any foreign enemy, was well-received. But when Nero entered into the topics of his wisdom and foresight, no one could keep from laughing—even though the speech, composed by Seneca, was highly polished by that graceful wit² and tailored to the ears of those times. Idle elders, who enjoy comparing ancient things with modern ones, noted that Nero was the first of all the rulers of Rome to speak with borrowed words <note>original: "imboccato," literally meaning "fed by the mouth," referring to a speech written by someone else.</note>; for Caesar the Dictator vied with the greatest orators. Augustus spoke clearly and fluently,³ in a manner befitting a prince. Tiberius possessed the art of weighing his words; his thoughts were vivid, or sometimes intentionally obscure. Nor did Gaius Caesar’s <note>The Emperor Caligula.</note> madness take away his power of speech.⁴ Even Claudius, when he spoke with preparation, was elegant. Nero’s talent in his tender years was directed toward painting, carving, singing, and horsemanship, though he showed some seeds of learning in his verse-making.

IV. The mourning period completed, he came to the Senate and, after a speech about the authority of the fathers <note>The Senators.</note> and the unity of the soldiers, he spoke excellently of his intentions and examples for good governance. He noted that he was not a youth raised in civil arms or domestic discord; he did not—

Footnote 1: Nero's intent was not to be the sole judge of all matters, nor to allow the powerful few to prevail by keeping accusers and the accused enclosed within a private house.</note> His own household would be one thing, and the republic another. V. And he observed all these things, and many orders were made as the Senate desired: That advocates should not be bought for pay or gifts; that even the quaestors-elect should not be required to put on gladiatorial shows—even though Agrippina <note>Nero's mother, who sought to maintain the policies of the late Emperor Claudius</note> opposed this, as it went against the orders of Claudius. She used to have the Fathers <note>the Senators</note> gather in the palace, and she would listen at the door behind a veil so as not to be seen. And while the Armenian ambassadors were presenting their case before Nero, she was coming forward to ascend the dais and sit beside him; but Seneca, while the others stood astonished, told him <note>Nero</note> to go out and meet her. Thus, by showing her reverence, he averted the shame of the situation.

VI. At the end of the year, news arrived that Armenia had been overrun again by the Parthians, and Radamistus had been driven out—who, having entered and fled many times before, was now completely abandoned. Many in that gossiping city asked: “In what way could that prince, a boy of seventeen years, bear such a weight or unburden himself of it? What help can be given by one who is ruled by a woman? Will the battles, the assaults, and other actions of war be entrusted to tutors?” Others said: “He will endure the hardships of war better than that foolish old man Claudius, who was commanded by servants; of Burrus and Seneca, there are many experiences to draw from. And as for the Emperor, how much is he lacking in maturity...”

...of these important new enterprises, traveling swiftly, he met Quadratus in Aegeae,¹ a city of Cilicia. Quadratus had moved there ahead of him out of jealousy, fearing that if Corbulo—a man of great power, magnificent speech, and possessing not only experience and wisdom but the ability to move others by his very presence—entered Syria to receive the troops, he would cause all eyes to turn toward himself.

IX. Both commanders sent messages urging King Vologases to choose peace over war: to provide hostages <term>hostages: "statichi," noble captives given as security for a treaty</term> and to continue the reverence shown by his predecessors to the Roman people. Vologases, either to gain time to prepare his forces for the war or to remove potential rivals for the throne, handed over the leading members of the Arsacid family as hostages to Insteius² the centurion, whom Vinidius <note>Gaius Ummidius Durmius Quadratus, often referred to by his family names</note> had by chance sent to the king earlier for that purpose. When Corbulo heard of this, he sent Arrius Varus, a prefect of a cohort, to take them. The centurion and the prefect came to bitter words over the matter. To avoid making a scene³ in front of the foreigners, they left the choice to the hostages and their escorts. These men preferred Corbulo because of his recent glory and the respect even his enemies held for him. This caused discord between the commanders; Vinidius complained that what he had earned through his own efforts was being snatched away, while Corbulo boasted that the king had not resolved to offer hostages until he knew he had to deal with him, turning his hope into fear. To reconcile them, Nero decreed that the emperor's fasces <note>bundles of rods symbolizing authority</note> should be wreathed in laurel in honor of the successful deeds of both Quadratus and Corbulo. These events took place in the following year.

And against the will of the senators, who wanted the month of December—in which he was born—to be the start of the year, he maintained the ancient religious tradition of the first of January <note>original: "calende di gennaio"</note>.
