**XI.** [Year of Rome: 808, Year of Christ: 55.] When Nero and Lucius Antistius entered office as consuls, and the magistrates took the customary oath to uphold the acts of the emperors, Nero forbade his colleague Antistius from swearing an oath to his own acts. The senators praised him greatly, hoping that this youthful spirit, which found pleasure in these small gestures of modesty, would continue on toward greater glory. He showed kindness to Plautius Lateranus—who had been expelled from the senatorial order for his affair with Messalina—by restoring him to his rank. He frequently promised clemency in his speeches, which Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and Nero's tutor</note> composed and published under the prince's name, both to showcase the virtues he was teaching him and to display his own literary talent.

**XII.** The mother's <note>Agrippina the Younger, Nero's mother</note> influence began to decline little by little, as Nero had become infatuated <note>original: "intabaccato," an old-fashioned term for being "hooked" or deeply in love</note> with Acte, a freedwoman. He shared this secret with two handsome young men: Otho, from a family of consular rank, and Claudio Senecio, the son of one of the emperor's freedmen. Through their shared lusts and dangerous secrets, these two became his close confidants. Once Agrippina learned of this, she was unable to stop it. The prince's advisors thought it better to let him vent his passions with this woman without harming anyone, rather than having him pursue noble ladies. This was especially true since Nero could not stand his wife Octavia—despite her noble birth and excellent character—perhaps by some misfortune of fate or because forbidden things are always more attractive.

**XIII.** Agrippina seethed with rage that a freedwoman should be her rival and a servant her daughter-in-law, among other such complaints. She did not wait for her son to regret his actions or grow bored; instead, the more she shamed him, the more she fueled his passion. Overwhelmed by this love, Nero cast off all obedience to his mother and turned instead to Seneca. To hide the young prince's affair at first, one of Seneca's close associates, Annaeus Serenus, pretended to be the one in love with the freedwoman; gifts were sent in Serenus's name. At this point, Agrippina changed her tactics and began to tempt the youth with flatteries, even offering him her own bedroom to secretly indulge in whatever desires his youth and supreme power might suggest. She confessed that she had been too strict with him. She offered him all her wealth, which was nearly as great as the emperor’s own: where previously she had scolded him harshly, she now humbled herself before him. Of such...

Nero reached the end of this change <note>his shift in attitude toward his mother</note>, and his friends feared it and begged him to guard himself against that woman, who was always cruel and now felt betrayed. One day, while reviewing the robes and jewels of past empresses, he sent the richest and most precious items to his mother as a gift, without hesitation. She cried out loudly that "her son was not sustaining her with such honors, but taking all others away; and of the empire she gave him in its entirety, he was merely returning this small slice." <gloss>1</gloss> There was no lack of people to report everything to him, and even worse.

**XIV.** Nero, who could not tolerate those who fueled the woman's pride, stripped Pallas <note>an extremely wealthy and powerful freedman who had been the imperial treasurer</note> of the management given to him by Claudius, through which he governed nearly the entire realm. It is said that as Pallas was leaving with a great retinue, Nero jokingly remarked that he was going to "swear out of office." <gloss>2</gloss> It is true that he had negotiated a deal: that without his public accounts being audited, they would be considered settled and balanced. With him she would go to the military camp, where the daughter of Germanicus <note>Agrippina herself, who traded on her father's immense popularity with the soldiers</note> would be heard on one side, and Burrus and Seneca—a maimed man and a schoolmaster—on the other, claiming to govern the human race." She thrashed her hands; <gloss>4</gloss> she spoke every evil; she called upon Claudius in heaven and the souls of the Silani <gloss>5</gloss> in hell, and all the many horrific sins she had committed to no avail.

**XV.** Nero was unsettled by this, and as Britannicus was turning fourteen within a few days, he considered now his ruinous mother, now the spirited youth, who had shown his character and gained favor during those Saturnalia festivals <note>a December festival where social roles were often reversed</note>. ...[Nero ordered] him to go into the middle and sing an impromptu song. He hoped to make the people laugh at the boy, who was not used to refined gatherings, let alone drunken ones. But he, singing with great presence of mind, alluded to how "he had been cast out from his seat and supreme power"; this moved the guests to a more obvious pity, as the night and the merriment had stripped away their usual restraints. Nero, seeing himself disliked in favor of his brother, felt his hatred grow; spurred by Agrippina’s threats, he hastened to find a way to have him killed. He did not dare to do it openly; instead, he planned a deception, seeking to poison him through Julius Pollio, a tribune of a guard cohort who held Locusta¹ in custody. She had been condemned for many poisonings and was a famous mistress of that art. Indeed, every one of Britannicus's attendants was already prepared to commit any betrayal against him. These first gave him a poison that merely moved his bowels and passed through him, being either too weak or diluted at the time. But Nero, unable to wait, threatened the tribune and ordered the woman to be punished; he complained that while they worried about public opinion and making excuses, they kept the Emperor in danger. They promised him a death swifter than a knife to the heart. In his own antechamber, they brewed a most violent poison from several others already proven to be lethal.

**XVI.** It was the custom for the children of princes to sit in the sight of their elders at the foot of the tables with other nobles of their own age, at a separate and less lavish table. While Britannicus was eating in this manner, one of his attendants performed the tasting <term>credenza|The "credenza" was the official ritual of a servant tasting food or drink before serving it to a royal to ensure it was not poisoned.</term> of his food and drink. To avoid omitting this custom,² or revealing the poison by having both the taster and the boy die, this trick was devised: a drink was brought to Britannicus without poison and tasted for him, but it was served too hot; he refused it, and it was then cooled with water that contained the poison. It immediately rushed through all his limbs, taking away his voice and breath. The young guests were terrified and some fled, but those who understood the situation fixed their eyes on Nero. He, without rising, acting as if nothing were wrong, said: "He is suffering from that illness³ which from his infancy..."

**XVII.** That same night Britannicus died, and he was cremated with a meager funeral that had been prepared in advance. He was buried in the Field of Mars <note>The Campus Martius, a public area in Rome used for military exercises and later for monumental tombs.</note> during such a tempestuous rainstorm that it seemed the gods were enraged, though many people excused Nero’s actions. They blamed the natural discord between brothers and the nature of sovereign power, which brook no partners. Many writers of those times claim that Nero had frequently abused the childhood of Britannicus before this; therefore, his death might not seem premature or cruel, even though it was given at a sacred table, without even allowing him to be embraced by his sisters³ <note>The original Italian says "sister," but the Latin source "complexum sororum" refers to both Octavia and Antonia.</note>, and right before the eyes of his enemy—who thus extinguished the last bloodline of the Claudii, a bloodline corrupted by shame before it was destroyed by poison. Caesar <note>Referring to Nero.</note> excused the hasty funeral in a public edict, saying: «That it was the custom of the ancestors to remove from sight those who died an untimely death <note>original: "acerbe," meaning immature or premature.</note>, and not to linger over such bitter events with processions and funeral orations. Having lost the support of his brother, all his hope now rested in the Republic. As the sole survivor of a family born to supreme command, he should be held all the more dear by the senators and the people.»

**XVIII.** He gave lavish gifts to his closest friends, and some—who affected a stern honesty <note>original: "che faceano il grave," from the Latin "gravitatem asseverantes."</note>—were reproached⁵ for having divided among themselves houses and villas like spoils of war in such a season. [Agrippina’s] fear was such that no amount of wealth or generosity could now soothe it. She began to draw Octavia <note>Nero’s wife and the sister of the murdered Britannicus.</note> close to her; she held secret meetings with her confidants. Driven by an avarice rooted in her very bones, she seized money from every possible source as if to build a war chest for her protection. She courted tribunes and centurions, and she honored the names and virtues of the remaining nobles as if she were searching for a leader and a faction to support her. When Nero realized this, he removed the sentinelles she had been granted first as the wife [of Claudius] and later as the mother of the emperor. He also took away her German bodyguard <note>The *Corpus Custodum Germanorum*, an elite private guard of Germanic soldiers loyal to the imperial family.</note>. Furthermore, to ensure fewer people came to pay her their respects, he forced her to move out of the palace and return to the house that had belonged to Antonia <note>Antonia the Younger, Nero's grandmother; this was a move from the center of power to a private residence.</note>. Whenever he visited her there, he arrived surrounded by a crowd of centurions, gave her a cold kiss, and then left immediately.

**XIX.** No mortal thing is as fleeting or unstable as the reputation of great power when it lacks its own foundation. Agrippina’s doorstep suddenly grew cold:¹ <margin>It was no longer frequented; no one went to visit Agrippina anymore.</margin> no one came to console or see her, except for a few women—whether out of love or hatred, it is unknown. Among these was Junia Silana, once the wife of Gaius Silius, whom Messalina <note>The previous empress and wife of Claudius.</note> had forced him to divorce, as we mentioned;² <margin>See Book XI, chapter 2.</margin> she was of noble blood and provocative beauty. She had once been very close to Agrippina, but later they were no longer on speaking terms³ <margin>There was no longer any good blood between them; they hated each other.</margin> because Agrippina had blocked her marriage to Sextus Africanus, a noble youth. Agrippina had described her as indecent and old—not because she wanted the man for herself, but to prevent a husband from inheriting the wealth of a woman who was both rich and childless. 

Silana, seizing the moment for revenge, arranged for Iturius and Calvisius, her dependents <term>creature: clients or subordinates who owe their position to a patron</term>, to accuse Agrippina. They did not bring up old, exhausted grievances like mourning the death of Britannicus or listing the mistreatment of Octavia. Instead, they accused her of plotting a revolution with Rubellio Plautus—who was descended from Augustus through his mother in the same degree as Nero—with the plan of taking him as her husband and seizing control of the state once more. Iturius and Calvisius revealed this plot to Atimetus, a freedman of Domitia (Nero’s paternal aunt). Atimetus was delighted by the news (for Agrippina and Domitia were fierce rivals), and he urged the actor Paris, who was also a freedman of Domitia, to rush to Nero and report this conspiracy in the most terrifying terms.

**XX.** It was deep into the night, and Nero was spending it drinking heavily. Where they agree, we shall state it as fact; where they differ, we shall cite them. Consider that, in the night and amidst wine, deliberations can easily turn out to be indiscreet and reckless."

**XXI.** Once the prince's fear had subsided and day had broken, Burrus was ordered to go and examine Agrippina to either clear her or condemn her. Pallas's innocence was not as notable as his arrogance was nauseating; it was said that when he heard his freedmen named as witnesses, he claimed that in his house he commanded only by gestures or nods, and if things needed further explanation, he wrote them down to avoid making himself an equal to his servants by speaking. Burrus, although an accused party, still cast his vote among the judges. Paetus was banished, and the tax records were burned where he had been reviving <gloss>3</gloss> the debts of those who had already paid.

**XXV.** [Year of Rome 809, Year of Christ 56.] The year of the consuls Q. Volusius and P. Scipione was quiet abroad, but shameful within the city. Nero, disguised as a slave, roamed the streets, taverns, and alleys with wicked companions, stealing <gloss>original: "correva," meaning he robbed</gloss> goods set out for sale and causing such brawls while unrecognized that he himself was often struck, bearing the marks upon his face. He turned the license of favoring different pantomime actors into something like a battle, failing to punish and even rewarding the disruption, while he watched, sometimes hidden and sometimes openly. This discord among the people and the danger of an uprising was remedied by banishing the actors from Italy and returning the military guard to the theater.

"...that the senate was content with it; let him command the decision, as it was between few and disagreeing opinions." Some grumbled, "Liberty has made them so insolent that, whether they act rightly or wrongly, they confront their masters eye-to-eye <note>original: "stanno a tu per tu col padrone," meaning they speak back without respect or enter into direct conflict. The Latin text notes: "whether they should act on equal legal footing with their patrons."</note>, and when the master wishes to punish them, they repel him or strike him. And what else can a poor, offended master do to his freedman but banish him twenty miles away to the Land of Labor <note>original: "Terra di Lavoro"; a historical name for the fertile region of Campania in southern Italy.</note>? In all else they proceed as equals, and it is necessary to put a bit in their mouths so that they may fear it. It is not a burden to maintain liberty with the same reverence with which they obtained it. Let him who errs return to being a slave, and let fear restrain those whom kindness does not change."

**XXVII.** On the other hand, it was said, "The guilt of a few should harm only those individuals, and not prejudice the whole body of others—a body so large that the majority of the tribes, the decuries <term>decurie: administrative or official subgroups in Roman society</term>, the ministers of magistrates and priests, the soldiers guarding the city, countless knights, and very many senators have come from no other source. If you remove the descendants of freedmen, few other free people would remain. It was not by chance that our ancestors honored each rank with its own specific powers <note>original: "di sue proprie podestà." The commentator Valeriani explains that while dignity was divided by rank, liberty was intended to be shared by all.</note>, and made liberty common to everyone. Furthermore, they ordained that liberty be granted in two ways to leave room for repentance or for a new benefit. Those who were not made free through a magistrate remain almost in servitude; let their merits then be examined, and let us not rush to grant freedom when it cannot be revoked." This opinion prevailed. And Caesar <note>Referring to the Emperor Nero.</note> wrote back to the senate: "that in particular, justice should be done for anyone who complained about their own freedmen; in general, nothing should be changed." Shortly thereafter, not without bringing blame upon Nero, the actor Paris was stripped from the legal control of his aunt Domitia, after the Emperor first had him declared free-born <term>ingenuo: a person born free, as opposed to a "liberto" or freed slave; Nero did this to legally sever Paris's obligations to his aunt.</term>

**XXVIII.** There still remained a small semblance of the Republic, because after Vibullius the praetor <term>praetor: a high-ranking official responsible for the administration of justice</term> had imprisoned certain partisans of actors, and Antistius, the tribune of the plebs <term>tribune: an official elected to protect the rights of the common people</term>, ordered that they should be...

->### THE THIRTEENTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.<-

...they were left; the fathers <note>The "fathers" refers to the Roman Senators (Patres).</note>, having approved the action, scolded Antistius. They likewise forbade the tribunes from encroaching upon the authority of the consuls and praetors, or from summoning cases from across Italy to themselves. Lucius Piso, the consul-elect, added that they should not exercise their power to condemn within their own homes, and that the questors should delay recording the fines they imposed for four months: during that time, an appeal could be made, and the consuls would judge the matter. Furthermore, the authority of both the curule and plebeian aediles was restricted, and limits were placed on the amounts they could seize as collateral <term>pegnorare: the legal right of a magistrate to seize property or a "pledge" to ensure payment of a fine</term> or fine. Because of this, Helvidius Priscus, a tribune of the plebs who held a private grudge against the treasury questor Obultronius Sabinus, accused him of auctioning off the goods of the poor with excessive cruelty. The prince [Nero] then took the public records out of the hands of the questors and entrusted their care to prefects.

**XXIX.** This arrangement changed frequently; Augustus had the prefects elected by the senate, but later, fearing the influence of personal favors, they were chosen by lot from the number of praetors. This method did not last either, because many incompetent men were selected. Claudius returned the responsibility to the questors, and so they would not act too cautiously for fear of giving offense, he promised them extraordinary <note>original: "fuor d'ordine," meaning they would skip the usual mandatory career steps</note> praetorships for later <note>original: "per poi," meaning after they finished their term as questors</note>. However, because those holding that first office were quite young <note>The questorship was the entry-level position in the Roman political career (the *cursus honorum*)</note>, Nero eventually chose tested individuals <note>original: "persone cimentate," meaning experienced or proven men</note> who had already served as praetors.

**XXX.** This year, Vipsanius Laenas was condemned for having governed Sardinia with rapacity. For a similar charge, Cestius Proculus was acquitted when his accusers withdrew. Clodius Quirinalis, commander of the fleet at Ravenna, who had mistreated Italy with debauchery and cruelty as if it were the most worthless of nations, poisoned himself before his sentence was passed. Gaius Caninius Rebius <note>The text reads "Aminio Rebio," a variant transcription of the legal scholar Caninius Rebius</note>, a man of the highest standing in legal doctrine and wealth, cut his veins in his old age to escape his pains; such courage was not expected from that lustful old man, who was considered as infamous as a woman. Lucius Volusius died with an excellent reputation at the age of ninety-three, having lived justly...

...enriched, without falling into disgrace under so many wicked emperors.

**XXXI.** [Year of Rome 810, Year of Christ 57.] In the second consulship of Nero and Lucius Piso, there was little worth recording, unless one wished to clutter the pages by praising the grand foundations and timber of the amphitheater that Caesar <note>Referring here to Nero</note> built in the Field of Mars; but for the dignity of the Roman people, it is customary to write of illustrious matters in the Annals, and of such trivialities in the daily journals. The colonies of Capua and Nocera were replenished with veteran soldiers, and ten florins <note>The original Italian uses the word *fiorini* (florins), the currency of the translator’s own 16th-century Florence, to represent the Roman *sesterces*.</note> per head were donated from the public funds to the common people, and a million in gold <term>millión d'oro: likely referring to a million sesterces or a specific weight of gold used to stabilize the state treasury</term> was placed in the treasury to maintain the public credit. The four percent tax on the sale of slaves was abolished, more in appearance than in effect; for since the seller was required to pay it, they simply increased the price to cover the cost. An edict was also issued that no magistrate or provincial governor should host spectacles of hunts, gladiators, or the like; for previously, they afflicted the people with such games no less than by plundering them, using these displays of "generosity" to mask their crimes.

**XXXII.** A decree was issued by the senate for both punishment and security: that if a master were murdered by his slaves,¹ those freed by his will² who were living under that roof should suffer the same penalty.³ Lucius Varius, a former consul who had previously been accused of extortion and dismissed,⁴ was reinstated as a senator. Pomponia Graecina, an illustrious woman and wife of Plautius⁵—who had returned from Britain with an ovation—was accused of a foreign superstition.⁶ She was handed over to her husband to be judged; he, following the ancient custom, examined her life and honor in the presence of her relatives and declared her innocent. She lived a long life in continual sadness because of Julia, daughter of Drusus,⁷ who was killed through the malice of Messalina. For forty years, she wore the garments of mourning...

**XXXIII.** Many were accused this year; from Asia, **P. **XXXIV.** [Year of Rome 811, Year of Christ 58.] **Nero** was consul for the third time with **Valerius Messalla**, whose great-grandfather **Corvinus**, the orator, the old men (now few) remembered having been a colleague in that same magistracy with **Augustus**, the great-great-grandfather of **Nero**. And to further honor such a noble family, he was given twelve thousand five hundred florins <note>The translator uses 16th-century "florins" to represent Roman sesterces</note> a year to sustain his innocent poverty. The prince assigned other provisions to **Aurelius Cotta** and **Aterio Antonino**, even though they had squandered their ancient ancestral wealth.

At the beginning of this year, the war with the **Parthians** for the possession of **Armenia**, which had started slowly and remained suspended, turned bitter. This was because **Vologases**, who had given the kingdom to his brother **Tiridates**, did not want him to lose it nor to hold it as a gift from any other power; and to **Corbulo**, it did not seem honorable for the Roman people to fail to retake the conquests previously made by **Lucullus** and **Pompey**. And the **Armenians**, of doubtful loyalty, called upon the arms of both sides: but being related to the **Parthians** by marriage, and more similar in country and customs, and knowing nothing of liberty, they were more inclined to serve them.

**XXXV.** But **Corbulo** was more troubled by the laziness of his soldiers than by the treachery of his enemies. The legions brought from **Syria**, having become "broken-winded" <gloss>meaning they had become weak and lazy; "bolso" is a term for a horse with a cold or cough, used here metaphorically for troops who have lost their edge</gloss> during the long peace, panted at the slightest labor...

Roman affairs. In that army were found veteran soldiers who had never stood watch or guard; they looked upon a rampart or a trench as a strange new thing. They wore neither helmets nor breastplates; instead, being finely dressed and busy with trade, they had spent their years of service in the fortified towns. Therefore, having dismissed the old and the sickly, **Corbulo** requested new troops, which were raised in Galatia and Cappadocia; additionally, a legion of fine horsemen and infantry came to him from Germany. He kept the entire army outside under tents, though to pitch them it was necessary to dig up the ground, which was frozen solid by a most cruel winter. Because of the cold, many men's limbs shrivelled up, and some sentinels froze to death on watch. One soldier, who was carrying a bundle of wood, found his hands so frozen to it that they fell off, leaving him stump-armed. The captain himself, **Corbulo**, poorly dressed and bare-headed <note>original: "in zucca," meaning without a hat or helmet despite the cold</note>, was always among them at their labors and at the drills: he gave praise to the brave, comfort to the sick, and an example to all. And because many fled from that harshness of climate and military life, severity was his remedy. He did not forgive, as was done in other armies, the first failure <gloss>1</gloss> or the second; instead, anyone who left the standards was immediately beheaded. This proved to be the true medicine, more effective than showing mercy, for fewer men deserted that camp than those where pardons were granted.

**XXXVI.** **Corbulo** kept our men inside the camp until mid-spring. He stationed the auxiliary forces in several locations with orders not to be the first to engage in battle; he placed them under the command of **Pacius Orphetus**, who had held the rank of first centurion <note>term: "primipilo," the highest-ranking centurion of a legion</note>. Although this man wrote that "the barbarians are off their guard, and there is an opportunity to achieve something good," he was commanded not to leave his position and to wait for more troops. He did not obey; when a few horsemen arrived from nearby outposts <note>term: "castella," small fortified military positions</note> asking recklessly for battle with the enemy, he joined the fight and was defeated. The others, who should have helped them, were frightened by the loss of their comrades and fled back to their own quarters. **Corbulo** took this very badly; after harshly rebuking **Pacius**, the officers, and the soldiers, he forced them all to camp outside the safety of the ramparts, and he did not relieve them of that shame until the entire army pleaded on their behalf.

**XXXVII.** **Tiridates**, supported by his own followers and those of his brother **Vologeses**, no longer acted in secret but began to harass Armenia with open war. He plundered those whom he believed were faithful to us, and if troops were sent against him, he would dodge them, moving here and there—

...pretending not to have heard him, he replied that it would be better to consult on matters concerning everyone with the entire army gathered together. In the center, he placed the **Sixth Legion**, along with three thousand soldiers from the **Third Legion** who had been brought in by night from other camps; these were all kept under a single eagle <note>The "eagle" or *aquila* was the primary standard of a Roman legion, and using only one made the combined force look like a single legion.</note> to give the appearance of a single legion. **Tiridates** appeared late, and at such a distance that he could be seen more than heard. XXXIX. The king departed in haste, either fearing a stratagem (seeing that our forces were moving in many places at once), or to cut off the supplies coming to us from the **Black Sea** <note>original: "mar maggiore"</note> and **Trabzon**; but those supplies were carried through the mountains and were well-guarded by our men. To force the **Armenians** to defend their own property, **Corbulo** set about the siege of their villages, choosing for himself **Volandum**¹, the strongest; the smaller ones he assigned to the legate **Cornelius Flaccus** and the camp prefect <term>Insteius Capito</term> <note>The *praefectus castrorum* or "master of the camp" was a high-ranking professional officer.</note>. He divided the army into four parts: one, under the protection of the <term>testudo</term>² <note>The "tortoise" formation where shields were interlocked over the heads of the soldiers.</note>, to dig trenches; another to scale the walls; many others to launch fire and arrows with siege engines. He placed hand-throwers and slingers in positions where they could hurl stones from afar; and thus, by making every spot dangerous, he prevented any aid from reaching the defenders. This army fought with such fervor that before the third part of the day was over, the walls were cleared, scaled, the forts taken, the gates battered down, and all the adult males³ <note>original: "barbati", meaning men of military age</note> killed. Few of our men were wounded, and none killed. Those unfit for war were sold at auction; all other plunder was given to the victorious soldiers. The legate and the camp prefect met with equal fortune: they took three fortresses in one day; the others surrendered...

**XL.** It was a matter of shame for Tiridates not to aid the city, yet a danger to entangle his cavalry in such rugged terrain. He decided to show himself, and in the morning² begin the fray, or by pretending to flee, lead our men into an ambush. He therefore suddenly surrounded the Roman army, which was marching in battle formation according to the commander's foresight. The **Third Legion** marched on the right flank, the **Sixth** on the left, and the flower of the **Tenth** in the center; the baggage was placed between the lines, and a thousand horsemen brought up the rear with orders to fight if confronted, but if lured away by a feigned retreat, to let them go <note>The Latin original says "refugos non sequerentur," meaning they should not pursue those who fled.</note>.³ On the wings were the foot-archers and the rest of the cavalry; the left wing was extended further along the foot of the hills so that, if the enemy entered there, they could turn and surround him. Tiridates circled around, staying more than a bowshot's distance away, now threatening, now appearing to retreat in fear, hoping to make us spread out and then attack our men once they were scattered. Seeing that everyone stayed in their place—except for one decurion⁴ of the cavalry who advanced too far and, being showered with arrows, taught the others by his example to obey—he [Tiridates] departed as night approached.

...he <note>Tiridates, King of Armenia</note> had taken the long road¹ <note>original: "aveva preso la lunga"; the text implies he took a circuitous route or fled.</note> toward the Medi or the Albani. He <note>Corbulo</note> waited for the day, and sent forward light-armed troops to either surround the walls or begin battering them from a distance. But the local inhabitants opened the gates and surrendered themselves and all their possessions to the Romans: this act saved their lives. **Artaxata** was burned and razed to the ground, because it could not be held without a large garrison due to its vast circumference, and we did not have sufficient forces to both occupy it and continue the war; furthermore, if it were left abandoned, what profit or glory would there be in having captured it? And, as if by a miracle, a dark cloud (while the sun shone outside the walls) kept the city in total shadow;² it flashed with such lightning that it truly seemed the angry gods had destined it for desolation.

Following these successes, **Nero** was hailed as Emperor. The Senate decreed processions, statues, arches, and continuous consulships for **Nero**; they also established holidays for the days the victory was won and for when the news arrived, as well as for the Senate session held on the matter. These honors were so excessive that **Gaius Cassius** <note>A famous Roman jurist and senator known for his traditionalist views.</note>, who had remained silent during the other honors, remarked: "If every day the gods have favored us must be spent in thanksgiving, the whole year would not suffice; therefore, it is necessary that days be divided: some sacred for divine worship, and some secular for human business; the one must not be spoiled by the other."

**XLII.** After various turns of fortune, a man much hated with good reason was accused, though not without casting some blame on **Seneca**. This was **P. Suillius**,³ who during the reign of **Claudius** was a terrible and venal informer <note>Informers, or "delatores," made their fortunes by accusing wealthy citizens of crimes to seize their property.</note>. With the change of times, his influence had waned, but not as much as his enemies desired; and it bothered him less to be proven guilty than to humble himself. It is believed that to bring about his ruin, the Senate's decree and the <term>Cincian Law: a law revived to prevent advocates from taking fees or gifts for legal services</term> were renewed. He complained of this, being fierce by nature and made bold by his advanced age; he spoke ill of **Seneca**, claiming "that he persecuted the friends of **Claudius** because that Emperor had rightfully exiled him, and that, being accustomed to teaching young men playful letters <note>A disparaging reference to Seneca’s philosophical and rhetorical lessons for the young Nero.</note>, he envied those who defended citizens with living and real eloquence." He <note>Suillius</note> claimed to have been the quaestor of **Germanicus**, while **Seneca** was the adulterer of that same house <note>Suillius is referencing Seneca's alleged affair with Julia Livilla, the sister of Caligula and niece of Claudius.</note>. Which is worse: to accept a kindness from a client for honest labor, or to haunt the beds...

XLIV. During this time, **Octavius Sagitta**, a <term>tribune of the plebs</term><note>A high-ranking magistrate elected to represent the common people.</note>, driven mad with love for the married **Pontia**, purchased her favors with great gifts, and then secured a promise from her to reject her husband and take him instead. The woman, once she was free <note>Having divorced her first husband, she was still hesitant to marry her new lover.</note>, delayed him, making excuses that her father was unwilling; and hoping for <note>The original Latin would suggest: "and having found another wealthier man."</note> another richer suitor, she began to withdraw. **Octavius**, now weeping and now threatening, declared that he had lost his reputation and his wealth; "only his life remained; she could do with it what she willed," yet she remained steadfast in her refusal. He begged her for the contentment of just one final night, so that he might then resign himself to patience. The appointment being made, she ordered a trusted servant to guard the bedchamber. He entered with a freedman and a dagger hidden beneath his clothes. There, as happens where there is both resentment and love, there followed disputes, pleas, reproaches, reconciliations, and part of the night spent in embraces. Then, with his anger rekindled, he ran her through with a sword-thrust while she suspected nothing. He frightened away the servant who rushed in by giving her a light wound <note>original Latin: *vulnere absterret*, "he scares her off with a wound."</note>, and fled. In the morning the rumor spread; the killer was obvious, as it was proved he had been there. But the freedman claimed that he had killed her to avenge the insult to his master. Some were moved by this noble act; however, the servant recovered and told the truth. **Octavius**, having left the tribunate, was summoned by the father of the deceased before the consuls and was condemned by the senate under the <term>Cornelian law on assassins</term><note>The *Lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis*, a law established by Sulla to punish murderers and poisoners.</note>.

...like her mother, she was the most beautiful woman of that age; she possessed wealth sufficient for her noble lineage; her speech was sweet; she was of loose character, yet knew how to play the modest woman; she rarely went out in public; she kept part of her face covered, either because it suited her better or to excite desire;¹ she cared nothing for her reputation; nor did she distinguish between husbands and lovers; she was never bound by her own love nor by that of others. XLVI. **Otho** did not cease to praise the beauty and grace of this wife of his to the prince: either he was foolish through too much love, or perhaps he intended to make the prince fall in love and enjoy her, using this as another ladder to climb higher. ### XLVII. 
Until now, Nero tried to conceal his wicked deeds, suspecting Cornelius Sulla most of all, whose slow wit he attributed to deep cunning. Caesar's freedman Graptus, an old courtier from the time of Tiberius, increased this suspicion with this lie. The Milvian Bridge <gloss>2</gloss> was then the gathering place for every late-night revelry. Nero went there to roam more freely outside the city. Returning by the Flaminian Way to the Sallustian Gardens, Graptus ran to tell him that fate had helped him avoid Sulla's ambush (even though some rowdy pranksters <gloss>3</gloss> had only jokingly frightened the prince's servants as they returned by the usual route, as is often done): nor was any servant or follower of Sulla recognized there; he was a despised man, and not at all capable of such daring. Nonetheless, as if he had been convicted, he was ordered to leave Rome and not go beyond the walls of Marseille.

### XLVIII. 
In that same year, opposing ambassadors were sent from Pozzuoli to complain: the senators about the violence of the common people, and the common people about the greed of the magistrates and the elite; and they had come to throwing stones and threats of fire, which meant weapons and blood. Gaius Cassius, chosen to quiet them, seemed too severe to them, and at his request, the task was given to the two Scribonii brothers with a Praetorian cohort, whose terror and the punishment of a few brought the people of Pozzuoli to an agreement.

...to judge,
> "If he believes that the republic requires its senators to speak freely, why does he trouble himself with such trivial matters? Why does he not speak instead of war or peace, of revenues, of laws, and of other Roman matters of importance, and what should or should not be done? The fathers <note>The "fathers" (Latin: *patres*) refers to the members of the Roman Senate.</note>, who have a voice in the Senate, are allowed to propose whatever they wish and ask that it be put to a vote: does he have nothing else to correct but the excessive spending on festivals in Syracuse? Is everything else throughout the empire so well and perfectly ordered, as if Thrasea were the ruler instead of Nero? If he shuts his eyes to the great matters, why does he pay so much attention to the vain ones?"

Thrasea responded to his friends that he had corrected this minor error not out of ignorance of serious matters, but for the honor of the senators, so that it might be seen that those who attend even to the smallest things are clearly mindful of the great ones.

**L.** In this year, with the people pestering him <note>original: *rompengogli la testa il popolo*; literally "the people breaking his head," meaning they were making frequent and persistent demands</note> regarding the abuses of the tax collectors, Nero took it into his mind to abolish all duties and give this beautiful gift to the world. But the elders <note>original: *i vecchi*; referring to the senators</note>, while praising his greatness of soul to the heavens, held back his impulsive fury. They showed him that the empire could not sustain itself if the "nourishment"—effectively the harvest—of the republic were diminished. They argued that if these duties were removed, there would soon be demands to remove regular taxes as well. Furthermore, the tax-farming companies were mostly created by consuls and tribunes during the height of Roman liberty, balancing public revenue with expenses. Instead, the tax collectors <note>original: *pubblicani*; these were private contractors or companies who bid for the right to collect taxes for the Roman state, often using predatory methods to ensure a profit</note> should be restrained <note>original: *doversi dare in su le mani*; meaning their excessive greed must be checked</note>, so that they do not cause the public to curse, through new cruelties, things that have been tolerated since ancient times.

**LI.** Nero therefore decreed that the tax rates of all the tax-farming companies, which had been hidden until then, should be made public. He also ruled that claims not pursued within a year could not be revived; that in Rome, the Praetor, and abroad, the Vice-Praetor or Vice-Consul, should judge complaints against these companies summarily; and that soldiers should maintain their tax exemptions, except in cases where they engaged in trade like merchants. He made other just provisions as well, which lasted only a short time before they vanished.

However, the "fortieth," the "fiftieth," and the other greedy names <note>These refer to specific tax rates—1/40th and 1/50th—applied to various transactions.</note> devised by the tax collectors were not repealed: the duties on grain exported to overseas provinces were reduced: and merchant ships were not taxed a tenth.¹ ²

**LII.** Sulpicius, Camerinus, and Pomponius Silvanus were acquitted of the complaints brought by the province of Africa, which they had governed. Camerinus had few accusers, and they charged him with private acts of cruelty rather than the theft of public funds. Silvanus had a world of accusers: they asked for time to bring witnesses, but the defendant demanded to be defended immediately. He succeeded because he was old and had no heirs; however, those who plotted against him in hopes of inheriting his wealth died before he did.

**LIII.** Matters in Germany remained quiet <note>original: *si stavano*; meaning the region was at peace</note>,³ by the will of Paulinus Pompeius and Lucius Vetus, who were the commanders there. At that time, because triumphal honors were being granted so liberally, they believed that maintaining peace brought greater glory. But to prevent the soldiers from becoming idle, Pompeius finished the embankment⁴ on the Rhine which Drusus had begun sixty-three years earlier. Vetus ordered the digging of a canal from the Moselle to the Saône,⁵ so that armies brought by sea into the Rhone and the Saône could be ferried through that canal into the Moselle, then the Rhine, and finally the Ocean. By avoiding the many difficulties of land travel, this would make the northern and western coasts navigable in both directions. Out of envy for such a grand work, Aelius Gracilis, the legate of the Belgians, warned Vetus not to lead his legions into another’s province and not to try to win the favor of the Gauls, as this would make the Emperor suspicious. Thus, honorable enterprises are often hindered.

**LIV.** Because of the continuous idleness of the armies, a rumor spread that the commanders had been stripped of the authority to move against the enemy. Therefore, the Frisians <note>A Germanic tribe from the coastal regions of the modern-day Netherlands</note> led their youth through woods and marshes, and the elderly across the lakes, to the riverbank. He then turned toward the sun and the stars as if they were present, asking: "Do they wish to see this land laid to waste? Let the sea rather overflow it, in defiance of those who deprive men of the earth."

**LVI.** Avitus was moved by this and spoke to the Ampsivarii <note>original: "Ansibarii"</note> in public, stating: "One must obey one's superiors; it has pleased the gods they invoke that the power to give and to take away resides with the Romans, without their having to answer to Boiocalus." He offered Boiocalus lands for his own personal use as a reward for his past merits; but Boiocalus, viewing this as a bribe for his betrayal, refused, saying: "We may lack land on which to live, but land in which to die cannot be lacking." And so they departed in a fury, calling upon the Bructeri, the Tencteri, and other distant allied nations for aid. Avitus wrote to Curtilius Mancia, commander of the Upper Army, to cross the Rhine and show them his weapons from the rear. Avitus then led his legions into the territory of the Tencteri, threatening to wipe them out if they took up the troubles of others. They abandoned the alliance, and out of the same fear, so did the Bructeri and the others. The Ampsivarii, left alone, retreated <gloss>turned back</gloss> toward the Usipi and Tubantes. Driven from there, they went to the Chatti, then to the Cherusci; after long wandering, without shelter, and exhausted in enemy territory, their young men were cut to pieces and the rest were taken as spoils.

**LVII.** In that same summer, the Hermunduri and the Chatti, both desiring by force the dominion of the river that divides them and produces much salt, met in a great battle. This was driven both by their desire to decide things by arms...

...settling everything with arms, both out of superstition <note>original: "ubbía," meaning a false religious apprehension or irrational fear.</note>—believing that site to be the closest to heaven and the place from which the gods most readily hear human prayers. "Therefore, they possess that river and those woods, blessed with salt that is not produced like that of other nations from flooded and dried seawater, but is instead poured from the river itself onto a burning pile of specific trees, causing it to condense through the struggle of opposing elements <note>The reaction between the cold water and the fire</note>."

The war was prosperous for the Hermunduri and brought extermination to the Chatti; for the victors had made a vow to Mars and Mercury <term>Mars and Mercury: The translator uses Roman names for the Germanic gods, likely Týr and Odin, to whom the tribes dedicated their "spoils of war."</term> to sacrifice their enemies to them should they win. Thus, horses, men, and everything captured were made into victims, and the threats the enemies had made fell back upon their own heads <note>original: "tornavano loro in capo," meaning the destruction they planned for others became their own ruin.</note>. But the community of the Ubii <note>original: "Ivoni"</note>, our allies, suffered an unexpected wound. Fires erupted from the earth, catching the fields, villas, and farmsteads, and even reached the walls of the new colony <note>Modern-day Cologne</note>. Neither falling rain, nor poured water, nor any other moisture could extinguish them. Certain peasants, lacking any other remedy and driven by anger at the damage, threw stones at the flames from a distance, which caused them to subside. Approaching then with poles and sticks, they beat the flames as if they were wild beasts; finally, they stripped the clothes from their bodies and threw them on top—the more worn and dirty the rags, the more effective <note>original: "più il caso," meaning more suitable for the purpose.</note> they were at smothering those fires.

**LVIII.** In the said year, the Ruminal fig tree <term>Ruminal fig tree: A sacred tree in the Roman Forum, traditionally associated with the spot where the wolf nursed Romulus and Remus.</term> located in the Comitium—under which Romulus and Remus were suckled eight hundred and forty years ago—lost its branches and its trunk began to wither. This was taken as a bad omen, until it began to put forth new shoots once more.

### SUMMARY.

**I.** Nero, increasingly inflamed by Poppea, kills his mother Agrippina. — **XI.** He writes to the senate making excuses for the deed. — **XII.** Religious processions are established; Thrasea, no longer able to endure it, leaves the senate. — **XIII.** Nero dissolves into all manner of lusts. — **XVII.** Great bloodshed between the colonists of Nuceria and Pompeii <note>A famous riot in the amphitheater of Pompeii that led to the city being banned from holding games for ten years.</note>. — **XVIII.** The state of Cyrene; notable deaths. — **XX.** A five-year festival instituted in Rome. — **XXII.** Rubellius Plautus removed from the city. — **XXIII.** Corbulo acts like Mars <note>Refers to his military prowess and aggression</note> in Armenia; having taken Tigranocerta, he installs Tigranes as king. — **XXVII.** Laodicea, leveled by an earthquake, rises again by its own efforts; poor provisions for populating the colonies. — **XXVIII.** The elections of the Praetors proceed in agreement. — **XXIX.** Ruin of our forces in Britain while Suetonius Paulinus attacks Mona <note>Modern-day Anglesey</note>; almost the entire province is lost, then recovered by Suetonius with singular constancy in a single day. — **XL.** Horrendous crimes: the Prefect of Rome is killed by one of his slaves; the entire household pays the penalty <term>pays the penalty: under Roman law, if a slave murdered their master, the entire slave household (familia) could be executed.</term>. — **XLVI.** Tarquitius Prisco condemned. Censuses for Gaul. — **XLVII.** Memmius Regulus dies; a gymnasium is dedicated. — **XLVIII.** The law of the state <note>specifically regarding treason (maiestas)</note> is renewed. — **LI.** At the height of the public's misfortunes, Burrus dies. — **LII.** After Burrus's death, Seneca's influence is diminished; to escape envy and accusations, he speaks to Nero, who answers with cunning. — **LVII.** Tigellinus, rising further in favor, procures the deaths of Plautus and Sulla. — **LX.** Nero casts out Octavia and recalls Poppea. The people riot, which hastens Octavia's exile; she is later killed on the island of Palmarola <note>ancient Pandateria</note>.

...at every turn she scolded or mocked him, saying he was still a ward under a guardian, and merely followed orders;¹ he had neither power nor freedom.² "Why else did he delay marrying her? Did he find her ugly? Lacking triumphant ancestors? Did he fear she was sterile,³ or of small spirit, or that as his wife she would dare to reveal his father's injuries, or the people's anger at his mother's pride and greed?⁴ If she [Agrippina] could not endure a daughter-in-law unless she was hateful to her son, let them return her to her Otho;⁵ she would vanish to the ends of the earth to hear of the Emperor’s humiliations rather than witness them at her own peril." These stabs at his proud mother, delivered with tears and the art of a mistress, pleased everyone—not because they believed the son would kill her out of any amount of hatred, but because they wished to see her power reduced.

II. Cluvius⁶ relates "that the passion for maintaining her greatness drove Agrippina to present herself several times to Nero when he was drunk at midday. While he was heated with wine and food, she appeared finely groomed and ready for incest. Already their caresses and lewd kisses, noted by those standing by, were leading to the act, had Seneca not intervened by sending the freedwoman Acte to him. For the sake of her own danger and Nero’s honor, she was to tell him that his mother was boasting of having enjoyed him, and that the soldiers would not endure such a profane emperor." Fabius Rusticus⁷ says that "Nero, and not Agrippina, felt such a desire, and that Acte diverted him with cunning." But others write as Cluvius does, and it is believed that such depravity was more likely to have come from her; as a young woman, in her hope for power, she had slept with Lepidus, then submitted herself even to Pallas, and, as the wife of her uncle [Emperor Claudius], had become hardened to every shame.

III. **Nero** therefore avoided being alone with her. He would praise her for seeking recreation in her gardens and villas at **Antium** and **Tusculum**. Finally, unable to endure her presence anywhere, he resolved to kill her. He only hesitated over whether to use poison, the sword, or some other form of violence. He first favored poison; but it could not be hidden at his table, **Britannicus** <note>Nero’s stepbrother, whom he had famously poisoned during a banquet in 55 AD.</note> having been killed in that very way. It seemed difficult to administer, for she was well-accustomed to such treachery and guarded herself by taking various antidotes. Killing her with a blade could not be kept secret, and he feared he would not find an executioner willing to carry out such a great crime. **Anicetus**, a freedman and commander of the fleet at **Misenum**, found a way. He had been a tutor to **Nero** when he was a boy, and he and **Agrippina** hated each other to death. <note>original: "sarebbonsi egli e Agrippina manicati col sale," an idiom for intense mutual hatred. The Latin source states: "mutuis odiis Agrippinae invisus" (he was hated by Agrippina with mutual loathing).</note> He showed that a section of a ship could be engineered to open, making her fall suddenly into the sea, which is capable of making any accident believable. <note>original: "Non v' ha caso fortuito che il mare non possa render credibile"—there is no accidental event that the sea cannot make plausible.</note> If she were to drown, who would ever blame anyone but the winds and the waves? The prince could then build her temples, altars, and perform other pious honors.

IV. This clever plan was pleasing, and the timing was right as **Nero** was going to **Baiae** for the five-day festival, <note>The Quinquatria, a festival held in March in honor of the goddess Minerva.</note> to which he invited her. He went about saying "that the resentments of mothers must be tolerated and pacified," in order to spread the rumor that he had reconciled with her, and to welcome **Agrippina** who was coming (as women are quick to believe such things) to rejoice in the peace. When she arrived from **Antium** at the shore, he met her, took her by the hand, embraced her, and led her to **Bauli**, <note>Bauli was formerly the villa of the orator Hortensius. Some ruins remain between the Port of Baiae and the Dead Sea (Mare Morto); others identify it with modern Bacoli, specifically the ruins known as the "Hundred Small Rooms" or the "Prisons of Nero."</note> a villa on the sea that curves from the Cape of **Misenum** to the Lake of **Baiae**. A ship, more decorated than the others as if to honor her, was waiting there—for she was accustomed to being carried in a galley or other rowed vessel. He then invited her to dinner, so that the night might cover the crime. It was said that the deception was discovered by her. Whether she believed it or not, she had herself carried to **Baiae** in a sedan chair. There, her fear was dispelled by the endearments **Nero** showed her; he placed her in the seat of honor, and while chatting...

...with youthful playfulness, and then by raising his eyebrows as if conferring on grave matters, he prolonged the dinner. When she departed, he could not stop gazing at her and pressing her to his chest—either to complete the deception, or because the final sight of her so close to her death restrained that soul, although it was the soul of a tiger.

V. It seemed that the gods provided that starry night and a quiet sea to expose the deed. The ship had not traveled far. Among those accompanying **Agrippina**, **Crepereius Gallus** stood near the helm, and **Aceronia** (at the feet of the Empress as she reclined) spoke joyfully of the son’s repentance and the mother’s return to favor. Suddenly, at a given signal, the roof in that section, which had been weighted with lead, collapsed and crushed **Crepereius**. **Agrippina** and **Aceronia** were saved by the projecting sides of the couch platform, <note>The Italian translator uses "getto," which refers to a raised platform or reinforced structure. See the note below on the textual debate between "roof" and "bed."</note> which were high and sturdy enough to resist the weight. The ship did not immediately break apart, as everyone was in total confusion, and those who were not in on the secret plan <note>original: "ordine," referring to the conspiracy or the secret instructions given to the saboteurs.</note> hindered the others. The rowers tried to tilt the ship to one side <note>original: "alla banda," to capsize it.</note> to sink it, but they could not agree on the timing immediately, and the others, by pushing in the opposite direction, caused the fall into the sea to be gentler. **Aceronia**, playing a dangerous game of reverse-irony, <note>original: "giuocando a rovescio." By pretending to be the Empress to seek rescue, she inadvertently made herself the primary target of the assassins.</note> cried out, "I am **Agrippina**, help the Emperor's mother!" She was struck down with poles, oars, and whatever came to hand. **Agrippina**, remaining silent and thus less easily recognized, was nevertheless wounded in the shoulder. By swimming, she came upon a small boat and was carried to **Lake Lucrinus** at her own villa.

VI. There she reflected on the situation: "that she had been invited by that treacherous letter and honored more than usual; that the ship, near the shore and moved by neither wind nor rock, had collapsed from above like a siege engine; <note>original: "terrestre machina," literally a land-machine or a building designed to fall.</note> that **Aceronia** had been killed; and that she herself was wounded."

...and seeing no other remedy for these snares <note>The Italian "lacci" refers to the literal and metaphorical traps Nero set for her.</note> than to pretend she did not recognize them, she sent word to her son through her freedman **Agerinus**, "that by the grace of the gods and his own good fortune, she had escaped a great danger. He should not trouble himself to come see her for now; she wished to rest." Then, showing herself to be completely calm, she attended to the dressing of her wound and to her recovery. She ordered that the will of **Aceronia** be found and her belongings sealed; this was the only thing she did without pretense.

VII. **Nero**, who was waiting for news of the sinking, instead heard of her escape with only a slight wound, and that the circumstances were such that the author of the crime was obvious. He fainted from fear,¹ crying out "that she would soon come for her revenge, arming slaves, inciting the soldiers, calling upon the Senate and the people, shouting about the shipwreck, her wound, and her dead friends. What remedy would he have? Unless **Burrus** and **Seneca** might sharpen their wits a little;"² for whom he immediately sent; and perhaps they already knew of the situation. They stood silent for a long while, so as not to advise him in vain, seeing that the case had reached such a point that, if **Agrippina** were not overcome by hand,³ **Nero** was finished. Then **Seneca**, being the first to resolve the matter, looked **Burrus** in the face, as if asking him, "should soldiers be sent to finish her?" He replied: "The Praetorian guards have obligations to the entire house of the Caesars and a cherished memory of **Germanicus** <note>Agrippina’s father and a celebrated Roman general; his popularity made the soldiers loyal to his daughter.</note>: they would not dare to touch his blood. Let **Anicetus** finish it, since he had already set the plan in motion." — "Leave it to me," he⁴ said immediately. At this voice, **Nero** exclaimed: "Today, from you, O my freedman, I receive my empire: run with the boldest men and carry out the deed." Having heard that **Agerinus**, **Agrippina’s** messenger, had arrived, **Anicetus** suddenly staged a theatrical scene: while the messenger was delivering his news, he dropped a dagger at the man's feet. Then, as if the messenger had been caught in the act, he had him bound, claiming he had been sent by the mother to kill the prince; this was done so he could spread the word that she, out of shame for the discovery of her plot, had killed herself.

...fortunate escape from danger: everyone runs to the sea; some climb onto the pier, others into boats; others wade as far as they can, while others stretch out or reach out their hands. The whole shore¹ was filled with laments, shouts, and cries; various questions and uncertain answers. A great crowd rushes there with lights. And when it was understood that she had escaped, they pushed forward to congratulate her, until they were threatened and driven away by armed men. **Anicetus** surrounds the villa with soldiers and, having broken down the door, seizes whatever servants he encounters. Reaching the bedchamber, the servants had nearly all fled due to the noise. Inside was a small light and one maidservant, and **Agrippina** was increasingly terrified, seeing neither **Agerinus** nor anyone else returning from her son; the shore was now cleared, not crowded as before, with sudden noises and signs of ultimate disaster. As the maidservant was leaving, she said, “Do you also abandon me?” She saw **Anicetus** in the company of **Herculeus**, a captain of the galleys, and **Oloaritus**, a centurion of the fleet, and said: “If you come to see me, tell him that I have recovered; if to kill me, I do not believe that my son has commanded it of you.” As they approached the bed, **Herculeus** first struck her on the head with a club. To the centurion, who was drawing his sword, she offered her belly, crying out, “Strike here!” <note>original: “Ventrem feri.” This famous exclamation suggests she invited the blow to the womb that had carried Nero.</note> and she died from many wounds.

**IX.** All authors write of these things. Whether **Nero** saw her dead and praised her beauty, some say yes and others no. She was burned that same night on a dining couch with a poor funeral; she had no tomb while **Nero** lived. Later, those of her household made her a small one along the road to **Misenum**, near the villa of **Julius Caesar** the Dictator, which sits very high and looks out over the bays. **Mnesterus**, a freedman, lit the funeral pyre and then ran himself through with a sword; whether out of love for his mistress or fear for himself is not certain. **Agrippina** had heard of this end of hers many years before, but had not heeded it; she had asked the **Chaldeans** <note>Astrologers from Mesopotamia who were popular in Rome for predicting the future.</note> about **Nero’s** future, and they said he would be Emperor and would kill his mother. “Let him kill me,” she said, “so long as he reigns.” <note>original: “Occidat, dum imperet.”</note>

<meta>This page follows the account of Agrippina the Younger's murder. Nero, having successfully ordered her death, now faces the psychological and political consequences of matricide, attempting to justify the act to the Roman Senate through a letter written by his advisor, Seneca.</meta>

...he waited for the light of day to bring his ruin. The first to encourage him were certain centurions and tribunes sent to him by **Burrus** <note>Sextus Afranius Burrus, the commander of the Praetorian Guard and Nero's advisor.</note> to kiss his hand and rejoice that he had escaped his mother's unexpected treachery. Then his friends ran to the temples; and following them, the nearby cities of **Campania** <note>Original: "Terra di lavoro," a historical region of Italy.</note> showed their joy with sacrifices and embassies. He, on the contrary, made himself appear sad and almost grieving for his own escape, weeping for his mother. But because landscapes do not wear masks as men do, he could not bear to look at that sea and those shores; and some believed they heard the sound of trumpets from the neighboring hills and wailing from his mother's grave. He departed for Naples and wrote to the Senate:

**XI.** "Agerinus, a principal freedman of Agrippina, was found with a weapon, having been sent to kill me; she then punished herself out of remorse for the wickedness she had ordered." He added old sins: "She had hoped to become my co-ruler, and to have the Praetorians swear obedience to her; she sought the same disgrace from the Senate and the people. When every design failed her, she turned her fury against the soldiers to stop their bonuses and against the common people to stop their gifts, seeking to ruin the great men and making an enemy of everyone. How much effort it took to keep her from entering the Senate and from answering ambassadors?" Indirectly, he blamed the era of **Claudius**, attributing every evil to his mother, claiming she was extinguished (as he put it) by public good fortune; he even recounted the shipwreck as it happened. But who would have been so dull-witted <note>original: "sì tondo," or the Latin "adeo hebes," meaning someone so foolish or slow of mind.</note> that they would believe it was an accident? Or that a woman who had just been fished out of the sea would send a single armed man to break through the Emperor's guards and armies? Reproaches were cast <note>original: "levavansi... i pezi," meaning shameful insults or vitriol were directed at someone.</note> therefore, not at **Nero**, who was already dismissed as an infamous monster, but at **Seneca**, for having written that confession of sin in that letter.

Many omens also appeared, though they yielded no results. A woman gave birth to a snake; another died from a lightning strike while lying with her husband; the sun suddenly darkened; and lightning bolts fell in all fourteen <note>original: "tutt' a quattordici." A linguistic note in the original points out a regional pronunciation where the article is swapped.</note> districts of Rome. These things occurred with so little concern from the gods <note>original: "senza cura degl' iddii." To make his mother seem more hated and to appear more merciful now that she was removed, he allowed **Junia** and **Calpurnia**, high-born women, to return to their homeland, along with **Valerius Capito** and **Licinius Gabolus**, men of rank who had been exiled by her. He also ordered that the ashes of **Lollia Paulina** <note>A wealthy noblewoman and former rival of Agrippina.</note> be found and a tomb built for her. He granted a pardon to **Iturius** and **Calvisius**, whom he had recently <note>original: "dinanzi." A textual note suggests the correction "dianzi," meaning recently.</note> banished. **Silana**, returning from a distant exile, had died at **Taranto**, finding some comfort in seeing the fall or the calming of Agrippina, whose enmity had been her ruin.

### XIII.

Nero lingered among the estates of **Campania** <note>original: "Terra di lavoro," the historic region surrounding Naples.</note>, confused about how to enter Rome: whether he should demand a meeting with the Senate or seek the applause of the common people. The most wretched men—of whom that court was the most fertile supply in the world—told him: "The name of Agrippina is hated, and by her death, the people's love for you has been rekindled; go safely, for you will see yourself adored." They urged him to set out on the road, and they found him even more ready than they had promised. The tribes came out; the Senate appeared in festive robes; ranks of women and children were arranged according to age and sex; tiers of seats were built to watch him pass, as if at a triumph. Thus, emboldened and triumphing over the public's servitude, he went to the **Capitoline Hill** to give thanks—and then plunged into every form of lust, which had been held back for a short time by some shred of respect for his mother.

XIV. He had a long-held urge <note>original: "umore antico"; an old inclination or disposition.</note> to race four-horse chariots, and an equally disgraceful desire to sing to the lyre in the manner of a wandering performer while at dinner. He claimed that this was the custom of ancient kings and leaders, praised by poets and used to honor the gods: music was sacred to Apollo, and that great god and oracle was depicted as a lyre-player not only in Greek cities but also in the temples of Rome. **Burrus** and **Seneca** <note>Nero’s primary advisors; Burrus was the prefect of the Praetorian Guard and Seneca was the famous Stoic philosopher.</note>, unable to cure him of both these follies, decided to allow him one. An enclosed space was built in the Vatican <note>original: "in Vaticano." The Latin text says "valle Vaticana." The scholar Luigi Canina notes that this valley between the Janiculum and Vatican hills was the site of the Circus of Caligula and Nero. Soon, however, the Roman people were invited there, and they praised him to the heavens, being a crowd fond of entertainment and easily driven to madness if the Prince himself invited them. And where his advisors had hoped that by satisfying his appetite in public he might grow weary of the disgrace, his hunger was instead sharpened. Thinking he could hide his own shame by staining the reputation of others, he induced many fallen nobles to act on stage for money. They are dead now and I will not name them, so as not to dishonor their families, for the shame was truly his; he ought to have paid them *not* to disgrace themselves. He even induced prominent Roman knights to fight in the amphitheater with great gifts; however, such "gifts" carry the weight of necessity when they come from one who has the power to command.

Never were morals more corrupted than among that rabble. Even through honest practices, it is difficult to maintain chastity, modesty, or skill—let alone when competing in vice. These were strong and vigorous youths, some joining out of eccentricity, others hoping to advance themselves by applauding the Prince's beauty and voice day and night with divine titles: they were treated as great and honored men, as if for some great virtue.

**XVI.** To avoid appearing merely as a stage performer <note>original: "strione"; an actor or buffoon, a profession considered socially degrading for a Roman citizen.</note>, this emperor also turned to composing verses. He gathered amateur poets and sat among them,¹ helping them piece together, revise, and patch up his verses. This is evident in their strained and broken style, which lacks a natural flow or the mark of a single author. After meals, he would also listen to philosophers who revealed their disagreements by bickering; there were even some among the Prince’s pastimes who wished to be seen with a severe expression and voice <note>referring to philosophers who tried to maintain a facade of Stoic or Cynic dignity while entertaining the emperor.</note>.

**XVII.** During this time, a minor dispute between the people of **Nuceria** and **Pompeii** erupted into great bloodshed during a gladiatorial festival <note>original: "festa degli accoltellanti"; literally "festival of the stabbers."</note> hosted by **Livineius Regulus**, who, as I mentioned, had been expelled from the Senate. Beginning with small-town insults, they moved to verbal abuse, then to stones, and finally to weapons. The Pompeian plebeians, who were hosting the festival, emerged victorious. Many Nucerians were carried back to Rome wounded, maimed, or dead, and were mourned by their fathers and children. The Prince referred the case to the Senate; the Senate to the consuls; and it returned to the senators <note>original: "padri"; literally "the fathers," a standard term for the Senate.</note>, who banned the Pompeians from holding such festivals for ten years, dissolved their illegal associations, and exiled Livineius and the other ringleaders of the riot.

**XX.** [Year of Rome 813, Year of Christ 60.] In the fourth consulship of **Nero** and **Cornelius Cossus**, the quinquennial festival <note>known as the "Neronia." **XXI.** This license pleased many, and they covered it with honorable terms. They argued that "Even the ancients did not abhor the pleasures of spectacles suited to their times, with actors summoned from **Tuscany** and horse races from **Thurii**;<sup>4</sup> <note>Thurii was a city on the Gulf of Taranto, built near the ruins of the ancient city of Sybaris.</note> once **Achaia** and **Asia** were conquered, these shows became more magnificent. Furthermore, with a permanent theater, great expenses have been saved, as it does not need to be rebuilt every year; and if the state itself pays for the games, the magistrates will not be impoverished, nor will the people have reason to demand Greek-style festivals from them. The prizes awarded for fine oratory and poetry would sharpen the wits, and the judges would gladly listen to honorable studies and permitted pastimes. For the sake of joy and not for lewdness, only a few nights in five years are granted; where, among so many lights, what indecency could possibly occur?" Indeed, the festival passed without notable indecency or riots from the partisan commoners. This was because the actors, although returned<sup>6</sup> <note>The actors were "returned" because they had been banished from Italy four years prior.</note> to the stage, did not participate in the sacred games. No one was declared the winner for the finest speaker, as the prize was awarded to **Nero**; and the Greek garments, which had begun to be seen in those days, were put away.

...driven out, there was talk of a replacement. ...or to save themselves in the mountains when they are driven back, Corbulo sent the Iberians <note>The Caucasian Iberians from modern-day Georgia, who were Roman allies.</note> to defeat them; and with foreign blood, he took vengeance for the enemy's boldness.

**XXIV.** Neither he nor the army suffered damage from battles, but rather from famine and exhaustion; they sustained themselves on the meat of sheep. There was a shortage of water, the heat of summer was burning, and the marches were long: they were consoled only by the endurance of the commander, which was greater than that of any common foot soldier. They arrived in a settled land and harvested the grain. Of the two fortresses where the Armenians had taken refuge, one was taken at the first assault; the other, which held out, was captured by siege. From there he passed into the land of the Tauranti,¹ where he faced an unexpected danger from a barbarian of no small status, who was found with a weapon just outside the general's tent. Under torture, he confessed the details of his betrayal, naming his accomplices and those who, acting as friends, were leading him; they were convicted and punished. Shortly after, ambassadors arrived from Tigranocerta <note>One of the two traditional capitals of the Kingdom of Armenia.</note>, who opened the gates to him, the people being ready to obey; and they presented him with a golden crown, as if to a welcome guest. He accepted it with honorable words and changed nothing in the city’s status, so that they might serve him more willingly.

**XXV.** But a fortress was defended by fierce young men on behalf of the king, first before the walls and then within the defenses. Finally, it yielded to force. These things proceeded more easily because the Parthians <note>The great empire to the East, Rome's primary rival.</note> were distracted by a war with the Hyrcanians <note>A people living southeast of the Caspian Sea.</note>, who had sent envoys to the Roman prince <note>Emperor Nero.</note> to request an alliance, boasting as a sign of friendship that they were keeping Vologases <note>The King of the Parthians.</note> occupied. Upon their return, so that they would not be captured by enemy guards while crossing the Euphrates, Corbulo had them escorted by a strong guard to the Red Sea <note>In this context, the Persian Gulf.</note>, by which route, avoiding Parthian territories, they returned home.

**XXVII.** In that year Laodicea, a great city of Asia <note>The Roman province of Asia, located in modern-day Turkey.</note>, was ruined by earthquakes and rebuilt itself with its own resources,¹ without our help. In Italy, Puteoli <note>Original: "Pozuolo".</note>, an ancient land, was re-established as a colony and renamed by Nero. Veterans were assigned to Tarentum <note>Original: "Taranto".</note> and Antium; but even so, they did not populate these places, as many returned to the provinces where they had served. The others, not being used to marriage or raising children, let their families die out. This was because colonies were no longer replenished by entire legions with their tribunes, centurions, and ranks, as in the past, to create a united and affectionate community; instead, they were brought in bit by bit, from various companies, without a leader, without knowing or loving one another—a motley multitude gathered as if from another world, rather than a colony.

**XXVIII.** The election of the praetors <note>High-ranking Roman magistrates.</note> fell to the Senate; but due to the pressure² of the candidates, the Emperor satisfied three who exceeded the usual number by making them heads of three legions. He granted another honor to the Fathers <note>The Senators.</note>: that anyone appealing a case from a private judge to the Senate (for which there had been no penalty) would, if they lost, be subject to the same penalty as those who appeal to the Emperor <note>A fine intended to prevent frivolous or stalling appeals.</note>. At the end of the year, Vibius Secundus, a knight, accused by the Moors of unjust governance, was driven out of Italy as a minor punishment, thanks to the influence of his brother, Vibius Crispus.

**XXIX.** [Year of Rome 814; Year of Christ 61.] In the consulship of Caesennius Paetus and Petronius Turpilianus, a great defeat was suffered in Britain, where the legate Avitus had done nothing more than maintain what had already been acquired. His successor, Veranius, raided slightly, plundering the Silures <note>A powerful and warlike tribe in ancient Wales.</note>, but was prevented from advancing further by death.
