**XXX.** The enemies stood on the shore, armed and in tight ranks. Among them ran women with disheveled hair, in black robes and with torches in hand like furies. And the Druids, their priests, with hands raised to heaven, prayed for horrible things; and so much did this novel sight stun the soldiers that they stood motionless like statues, letting themselves be wounded. But encouraged by their general, and urging one another not to be afraid of women and madmen, they charged in, striking those they met and rolling them into their own flames. Guards were placed in the villages, and the groves sacred to their horrid devotions were cut down, where they incensed the altars with the blood of prisoners and sought to divine their own fates from human entrails. While Suetonius was doing these things, he received word that the province had suddenly rebelled.

**XXXI.** Prasutagus, King of the Iceni <note>The Iceni were a Brittonic tribe in the area of modern Norfolk.</note>, a man of famous wealth, left his two daughters as heirs, and Caesar <note>The Emperor Nero.</note> for the other half: thinking that such a courtesy would protect both his kingdom and his house. He guessed wrong: the centurions plundered the kingdom, and the slaves the house, as if they were prey. Boudicea <note>Commonly known today as Boudicca.</note> his wife was beaten: the daughters violated: the leading Iceni (as if the legacy included the whole country) were stripped of their ancestral goods: the king's relatives were put among the slaves. ...people conspired to reclaim their liberty, hating with a deadly passion the veterans recently settled in the colony of Camalodunum <note>Modern-day Colchester, the first capital of Roman Britain.</note>. These veterans were driving the locals from their homes and lands, calling them captives and slaves; the regular soldiers encouraged this insolence because they shared the same lifestyle and hoped for the same license for themselves. Also before their eyes was the temple built to the Emperor Claudius, which was regarded as a pledge of eternal servitude, while the priests, under the pretext of religion, devoured everyone’s wealth. It did not seem a difficult task to destroy that colony, as it was not fortified; our commanders had focused more on making it a pleasant place than a useful stronghold.

**XXXII.** The statue of Victory fell there <gloss>1</gloss> without any apparent cause, its back turned as if it were yielding to the enemy. Frenzied women cried out that the end of the world was at hand; strange foreign noises were heard in their senate-house; the theater echoed with howls; a phantom appeared in the river Thames; shapes of human bodies were left behind by the receding tide; and the ocean itself appeared blood-red. All these were signs that the colony was doomed, giving hope to the Britons and terror to the colonists. Because Suetonius <note>The Roman Governor, Suetonius Paulinus.</note> was far away, they asked for help from Catus Decianus, the procurator <term>Procurator: A Roman official in charge of a province's financial affairs.</term>. He sent no more than two hundred men, and poorly armed at that; there were only a few other soldiers present, as they trusted that the temple would serve as a defense. Secret conspirators within the town sabotaged their plans, and they failed to dig a ditch or raise a rampart. They did not send away those unfit for war, nor did they keep only the youth for defense; having planned nothing, as if they were in the lap of peace, <gloss>2</gloss> a multitude of barbarians surrounded them. Everything was plundered, burned, and besieged in a fury. In two days, the rebels took the temple where the people had retreated. The victorious rebels then confronted Petilius Cerialis, commander of the Ninth Legion, who was coming to the rescue; they broke the legion and slaughtered the infantry. Cerialis escaped with his cavalry and took refuge in his camp. Catus the procurator, terrified by this defeat and by the intense hatred of the province—which had been driven to war by his own greed—fled to Gaul.

**XXXIV.** Suetonius, having already under arms the fourteenth legion with the <term>vessillari</term> <note>Vexillarii: veteran soldiers or detachments serving under their own banner (vexillum).</note> of the twentieth and nearby auxiliaries—totaling about ten thousand men—did not think he should waste any time; and so he ordered the battle. He arranged the legion in many ranks, with the light-armed troops around them and the cavalry on the flanks. The British army, spread out in bands and groups of horsemen, boasted in greater numbers than ever before, and were so fierce that they brought their women in wagons, arranged in a circle around that plain, to witness the victory.

Forget about looting; once you win, everything will be yours." The soldiers were so inflamed by their captain's words, and those veteran soldiers, tested <gloss>experienced</gloss> in many battles, prepared themselves so well to cast their javelins, that Suetonius, certain of the outcome, sounded the signal for battle.

**XXXVII.** First, the legion remained motionless, using the narrowness of the place as a defense; when the enemy was close enough for the javelins to strike, and having exhausted their supply, they burst forward in a wedge formation <gloss>Politi: "it closes between them in the manner of a wedge." The cavalry, with their lances, overthrew every strong point of resistance; the rest turned their backs and fled. But their own wagons <note>The Britons had brought their families to the battlefield in wagons to witness their expected victory; these now blocked their escape route</note> formed a barrier to their flight, and the Roman soldiers did not even spare the women; even the pack animals, pierced through, added to the mountains of corpses. The victory that day was glorious and equal to the great victories of ancient times. There are some who say <gloss>So in the Nestiana and Cominiana editions. **XXXVIII.** The army was mustered and encamped to bring the war to an end. Caesar <note>Nero</note> sent two thousand legionary soldiers from Germany, eight cohorts of auxiliaries, and a thousand cavalry; upon their arrival, the Ninth Legion was replenished with legionaries. Infantry and cavalry were stationed in new garrisons, and all the neutral or hostile locals were put to fire and sword. But their greatest suffering was hunger, as they had been negligent in sowing crops, and people of every age had rushed to war, counting on our supplies. This wild people moved even more slowly toward peace because Julius Classicianus—who had been sent to succeed Cato <note>Catus Decianus, the previous procurator whose greed helped spark the rebellion</note> and was at odds with Suetonius—allowed private hatred to undermine the public good. He spread rumors that the Britons should wait for a new legate <note>A high-ranking Roman official; in this case, a military governor</note> who would treat them with kindness, having neither the wrath of an enemy nor the pride of a conqueror. He also wrote to Rome that they should never expect an end to the war while Suetonius was in command;¹ attributing every setback to Suetonius’s malice and every success to the good fortune of the republic.

**XXXIX.** Consequently, Nero sent the <term>freedman<note>A "liberto" was an enslaved person who had been granted legal freedom; under Nero, many rose to positions of immense political power.</note></term> Polycletus² to survey the state of Britain, with great hope that his authority could not only reconcile the governor with the procurator but also establish peace with the barbarians and rebels. Polycletus crossed the sea with a vast retinue, a heavy burden to Italy and Gaul, and appeared fearsome even to our own soldiers. However, the enemy—still burning with the spirit of liberty and unaware of the power freedmen held in Rome—laughed at the fact that a general and an army who had won such a great war would obey a man who had been a slave. Nevertheless, the situation was reported back to the Emperor in a more favorable light. Later, after Suetonius lost a few ships and their crews upon the shore while attending to his duties, he was ordered to hand over the army (as if the war were still continuing) to Petronius Turpilianus,³ who had recently finished his term as consul. By simply leaving the enemy alone and being left alone in return, he gave the honorable name of peace to his own cowardly idleness.

[...he was a man of] praetorian rank <note>A former high-ranking magistrate, just below the level of consul</note>, very old, childless, and wealthy; and thus he was vulnerable to schemes. **XLI.** And Pompeius Aelianus, a young man who had served as quaestor <note>A junior magistrate responsible for financial administration</note>, did not escape unscathed that day; as he was found complicit, he was banished from Italy and from Spain, where he was born. Valerius Ponticus suffered equal shame; to avoid a trial before the Prefect of Rome <note>The official responsible for maintaining order in the city</note>, he had accused the defendants before the Praetor so they might escape punishment, first under the pretense of law and then through collusion. Consequently, a decree was issued stating that anyone who engaged in such barratry <note>A legal term for the fraudulent manipulation of the justice system</note> would be subject to the same penalties as those for false accusations.

**XLII.** Shortly thereafter, a slave of Pedanius Secundus, the Prefect of Rome, murdered him, either because he had been denied the freedom he had purchased, or because he could not bear him as a rival in his love for a young man. Now, according to ancient custom, the entire slave household <note>The *familia*, which included every enslaved person living in the victim's house</note> that lived under that roof had to be put to death. The common people rushed to defend so many innocent lives, and a riot broke out. Even within the Senate itself, some did not approve of such severity, but the majority wanted no changes made to the law. Among these, Gaius Cassius <note>A famous jurist known for his strict adherence to traditional law</note> gave his opinion, saying:

**XLVIII.** [Year 815 of Rome, 62 AD.] During the consulship of **P. Marius** and **L. Asinius**, the praetor **Antistius**, who had been (as I previously mentioned) <gloss>3</gloss> a rowdy tribune of the plebs, composed **lampoons** <gloss>4</gloss> against the prince and published them at a dinner party hosted by **Ostorius Scapola**. **Cossutianus Capito**, who had been restored as a senator <gloss>5</gloss> through the influence of his father-in-law **Tigellinus**, accused him of treason. It seemed this law was revived at that time not so much to bring ruin to **Antistius**, but rather to bring glory to the emperor; the goal was that once the Senate had condemned him to death, he would be saved by the emperor's intervention. **Ostorius** testified that he had heard nothing; however, credit was given to the opposing witnesses. **Julius Marullus**, the consul-elect, moved that the accused be stripped of his praetorship and his life, according to the ancient custom. While the others were in agreement, **Thrasea Paetus**, with great honor toward **Caesar**, sharply rebuked **Antistius** and said: « Under a good prince, and unless the Senate is forced by absolute necessity, we should not deliberate on every punishment the guilty man might deserve. The noose and the executioner were done away with long ago; <gloss>6</gloss> and penalties have been established by law to provide punishment <gloss>7</gloss> without making the judges appear cruel or the era infamous. It is better to confiscate his goods and confine him to an island, where his own life will be miserable, but his survival will serve as a great public example of mercy. »

**XLIX**. The boldness of **Thrasea** broke the silence of the others, and they moved to his opinion with the consul's permission; except for a few, among whom was **A. Vitellius**, who was most ready to flatter and biting in his words against the virtuous, but silent when anyone showed their teeth...

The others who had followed him did not change their minds either—some to avoid making the prince appear even more hateful, and most because they felt safe in their numbers.

**L.** Fabricius Veiento suffered a similar hardship for a similar sin; he had composed certain books titled *Codicils*, <gloss>2</gloss> which were full of insults against priests and senators. Furthermore, his accuser, Talius Geminus, claimed that he had sold the prince's favors and the distribution of magistracies. For this reason, Nero took up the case himself. Once Veiento was convicted, Nero banished him from Italy and ordered that his books be burned. While it was dangerous to possess them, people sought them out and read them; later, once the permission to keep them was granted, they fell into neglect.

**LI.** Public misfortunes grew daily, while the remedies for them diminished. Burrus died of <term>quinsy</term> <gloss>3</gloss> which swelled and blocked his throat; or, as most claimed, Nero had his palate smeared with poisoned oil under the guise of medical treatment. Burrus, sensing the treachery when the prince came to visit him, turned his face away; when asked how he felt, he simply said, «I am well.» He left behind a great longing for himself in Rome, both for the memory of his virtue and by comparison to his two successors: one was good but ineffective, while the other was most wicked and dishonest. ...deserved ample rewards: but I, in exchange for such great generosity, what could I give you other than studies, so to speak, nurtured in the shade? <note>Seneca refers to his life as a scholar and philosopher, which he views as "cloistered" or "in the shade" compared to the "sunlight" of active political or military service.</note> These studies have given me the distinction of having instructed your youth: which is worth much; but you have returned to me immeasurable favors and infinite wealth. Wherefore I often reflect, and say to myself: "I, born a simple knight <note>original: "cavaliere." Seneca refers to his status as a member of the Equestrian order, the lower of the two aristocratic classes in Rome.</note> outside of Rome, have I become one of the city's foremost men? Do I shine among the nobles and those prized for ancient honors, I, a newcomer? Where is that spirit once content with little, that now desires such beautiful gardens? Does it wander through such comfortable villas? Does it possess so many lands and so much money at interest?¹" I will answer nothing else, except that I should not have resisted your generosity.

**LIV.** "But each of us has filled our measure:² you by giving as much as a prince can to a friend; I by receiving as much as a friend can from a prince. This excess has increased envy; which, like all mortal things, stands below your greatness but crushes me. I must be relieved. Just as I, weary in war or travel, would ask for help, so in this journey of life—finding myself old and weak even for the lightest cares, and falling under the weight of my riches—I pray you to unburden me. Hand them over to your agents as your own property. I do not mean that I wish to live as a beggar; but, having cast away the splendors that harm me, the time that is lost in the care of gardens and villas I will give entirely to my spirit. You are in your peak vigor, strengthened by so many years of governing; we old friends ask for rest. You will have this further glory: of having raised to the highest heights those who are content with moderation."

**LV.** To these things Nero replied roughly thus: "To your considered speech I will respond spontaneously: by your grace, for you have taught me how to do both. My great-great-grandfather Augustus granted Agrippa and Maecenas rest from their labors, but at an age when his authority justified³ this and everything he had granted them; and he did not take from them the rewards earned in war and in the perils in which he was always engaged as a young man.

...and fear, he was terrified and inflamed with anger. But the evidence against her involving a slave was not believable, and the torture of her handmaidens had cleared her name. It seemed necessary, then, to find someone who would confess to a crime, and to forge a new weapon against her with a manufactured plot. <note>original: "appiccarlesi un altro ferro di cercata novità"; this refers to inventing a new slander, specifically a charge of political subversion.</note> There was no better candidate for this than Anicetus—the man who killed Nero's mother and was, as I have said, the Admiral of the Misenum fleet. Nero promised him rewards—secret for the time being, but great later—and pleasant villas; should he refuse, he would be put to death. Nero then called his friends together as if for a council and had Anicetus examined. This man, wicked by nature and already practiced in evil-doing, easily confessed to more than he was asked—things never even dreamed of. Consequently, he was confined to Sardinia, where he lived in relative wealth and eventually died.

LXIII. Nero then proclaimed that Octavia had seduced the Admiral to bring the fleet over to her side and that she had terminated her pregnancies to hide the fact that they were bastards—conveniently forgetting that shortly before this, he had banished her for being sterile. He claimed he had seen the evidence with his own eyes. Therefore, he confined her to the island of Palmarola. <note>Palmarola refers to the island of Pandataria.</note> No woman ever went into exile with such great sorrow from those who watched. Some remembered how Tiberius had banished Agrippina, and more recently, how Claudius had banished Julia; but those were grown women who had experienced some joy in their lives, and the memory of happy times served to console them in their misery. <note>The translator notes a contrast here with the poet Dante, who famously wrote in the *Inferno* that "there is no greater sorrow than to recall happy times in misery."</note> For Octavia, her very wedding day was like a funeral: she entered the house weeping for her father and soon after for her brother, both poisoned. In that house, the servant [Poppaea] held more power than the mistress; and for no other reason than for her...

...to extinguish her, Poppaea was married; and lastly, a crime more grave than a thousand deaths was attributed to her.

**LXIV.** Only twenty years old, she was placed among centurions and soldiers. Already certain of her doom, she was essentially snatched from life, yet she found no peace even in the prospect of death;¹ the order for which arrived a few days later. She protested that she was now a widow and only a sister to him; she invoked the shared name of Germanicus <note>Octavia was the granddaughter of the beloved general Germanicus, making her Nero’s cousin as well as his stepsister.</note>, and then that of Agrippina, who, though she lived a miserable marriage, at least was not murdered while her husband lived. She was tightly bound and her veins were opened; but because her blood, frozen by fear, would not flow, she was placed in a blistering hot bath until she suffocated. Her head was then severed and carried to Rome, where Poppaea—to add to the atrocity—insisted on seeing it. Offerings were ordered at the temples for this "success." I say this so that whoever reads of the events of these times, written by me or others, may be certain that for every exile or murder the prince commanded, people ran to thank the gods. Those things that used to be signs of public happiness were now signs of public misery. Nor will I remain silent when the Senate passes new decrees out of the most novel flattery or the most abject servility.

**LXV.** In this year, it is believed that Nero caused the deaths of two of his most prominent freedmen by poison: Doryphorus, as if for having opposed his marriage to Poppaea, and Pallas, because by living too long he kept the Emperor from his overflowing treasury.² Romanus secretly accused Seneca of conspiring with Gaius Piso. But Seneca poured this burning lye back onto his head even more fiercely;³ from this, Piso grew fearful, and there was born a conspiracy against Nero—great in scale, but ill-fated.

## OF

# GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

### SUMMARY.

**I.** Vologeses, King of the Parthians, invades Armenia, but is restrained by Corbulo with caution and force. — **VI.** Caesennius Paetus is appointed as a separate General for Armenia: through ignorance and recklessness, he fails; Corbulo comes to his aid too late. — **XVIII.** A trophy for the victory over the Parthians is decreed in Rome, while the war still rages. — **XIX.** A law of the Senate regarding fraudulent adoptions. <note>It was common for childless Romans to adopt someone briefly to qualify for certain political privileges reserved for fathers.</note> — **XXIII.** Poppaea bears Nero a daughter: there is great joy, but it is brief. Dying in her fourth month, the infant receives divine honors. — **XXIV.** Parthian envoys in Rome seek to retain Armenia: they depart dissatisfied; Corbulo is authorized to continue the war. He invades Armenia again: the Parthians, terrified, come to a parley; peace is established, and it is agreed that Tiridates shall place his crown before the statue of Nero, and not take it back except from Nero's hand. — **XXXII.** The Maritime Alps are granted Latin rights. — **XXXIII.** Nero sings publicly in Naples: Rome becomes a sinkhole for his luxury and lust. — **XXXV.** Torquatus Silanus is forced to his death. — **XXXVIII.** Rome is in flames, whether by chance or by Nero’s order remains unknown: he uses the ruins of the fatherland to build himself a "Golden Palace." <note>The *Domus Aurea*, a vast landscaped palace complex built by Nero in the heart of Rome after the fire.</note> — **XLIV.** The Christians are slandered as arsonists and endure pitiless torments and mockery. — **XLVII.** Prodigies. — **XLVIII.** The conspiracy of Gaius Piso against Nero is discovered. Death of the most illustrious men, among whom are Lucan and Seneca. — **LXXIV.** Gifts and thanksgivings are decreed to the gods: the month of April is renamed "Nero."

**I.** At this time¹ Vologeses, King of the Parthians, having seen the successes of Corbulo; and seeing that² a foreign king, Tigranes, had been given to Armenia, and that the pride of the Arsacid dynasty <note>The Arsacids were the ruling house of the Parthian Empire.</note> was being scorned because his brother Tiridates had been driven out; he thought of vengeance, yet, on the other hand, he considered Roman greatness and his respect for their long-standing friendship.

### **III.**

### **VI.**
Many magnified these events, as if they had occurred through the agreement of the king and the bravery of Corbulo. Others commented that they had come to an understanding between themselves so that Vologeses would depart without war, and Tigranes would afterwards leave Armenia:
> “Otherwise, why remove the Roman army from Tigranocerta? Why abandon in peace what was defended <note>Refers to the provinces defended during the conflict.</note> with war? Was it perhaps better to winter with more ease on the borders of Cappadocia, in wretched huts, than in the seat of the kingdom held until then? <meta>This page continues the narrative of the Roman-Parthian conflict over Armenia. Following the previous page's description of Vologeses' failed siege of Tigranocerta and the subsequent diplomatic standoff, the focus now shifts to the arrival of a new Roman commander, Cesennius Paetus, whose arrogance creates a rift in the Roman leadership and leads to a series of ill-omened military maneuvers.</meta>

# THE FIFTEENTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

As I mentioned <note>See chapter 3.</note>, Corbulo had requested a general specifically for Armenia, and word arrived that Cesennius Paetus was coming. Upon his arrival, the forces were divided: the Fourth, Twelfth, and Fifth legions (recently brought from Moesia <note>A Roman province located in the Balkans, along the Danube.</note>), along with the auxiliary troops from Pontus, Galatia, and Cappadocia, were to obey Paetus. The Third, Sixth, and Tenth legions, along with the veteran <note>The original "di prima" refers to long-serving, experienced soldiers.</note> soldiers from Syria, remained under Corbulo's command. The other allied nations were to be shared or assigned according to necessity. However, Corbulo could not tolerate a rival, and Paetus—who should have been honored to serve as second-in-command—belittled <note>The original "sfatava" implies a scornful dismissal of someone's reputation.</note> Corbulo’s achievements, claiming they were "won without blood or plunder" and that cities were "taken in name only" <note>Meaning they were captured through diplomacy or show of force rather than actual combat.</note>. Paetus boasted that he would impose actual taxes, laws, and the Roman yoke upon the defeated, doing away with that "shadow of a king."

**VII.** The ambassadors I mentioned, whom Vologeses had sent to the prince <note>Emperor Nero.</note>, returned without a resolution. Consequently, the Parthians resumed the war, and Paetus accepted the challenge. Leading two legions—the Fourth, then commanded by Funisulanus Vettonianus, and the Twelfth, under Calavius Sabinus—he entered Armenia under dark omens. As they crossed the Euphrates by bridge, the horse carrying the consular regalia took fright for no apparent reason, bolted backward, and escaped. A sacrificial beast, tied near some tents being pitched, fled while the work was half-finished and leaped over the ramparts. Furthermore, the soldiers' javelins caught fire; a particularly grim sign, as the Parthian enemy fights primarily by throwing such weapons.

**VIII.** Yet Paetus, disregarding these signs, failed to properly fortify his winter quarters or secure food supplies. He hurried his army across Mount Taurus, intending, as he said, to retake Tigranocerta and devastate the regions Corbulo had left untouched. He captured some fortresses, and might have gained some glory and spoils if he had maintained the former with moderation and the latter with diligence. With long-distance raids <note>The original "cavalcate" refers to rapid cavalry incursions or sorties.</note>, he attempted the impossible and wasted the supplies he had seized. With winter already arriving, he withdrew his army and wrote to Caesar as if he had already won the war—words full of pride but empty of results.

**IX.** Corbulo, meanwhile, maintained a strong guard along his well-defended bank of the Euphrates. To ensure that the enemy cavalry—which was already hovering about <gloss>original: *volitabant*. "With great show" implies they were trying to appear as a vast multitude</gloss> in those plains with a great show of force—did not hinder the construction of a bridge, he placed large ships in the river, bound together with beams and topped with towers <gloss>original: *torre*, meaning towers</gloss>. From these, mangonels and ballistae <term>Ancient siege engines; mangonels launched stones, while ballistae were like giant crossbows for firing bolts.</term> threw the barbarians into disorder, spitting stones and spears further than the enemy's arrows could reach. The bridge was completed and crossed; the auxiliary troops took the hills, and the legions established their camp <gloss>The text follows the Nestiana edition here, using "posero" (placed/established) rather than "presero" (took).</gloss> with such speed and display of force that the Parthians, losing heart for their campaign in Syria, turned all their hopes toward Armenia.

**X.** Paetus, ignorant of the looming dangers, had his Fifth legion far away in Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea.</note> and had weakened the others by granting leave to anyone who asked. Upon hearing that Vologeses was approaching with a threatening force, he called for the Twelfth legion; however, while he wanted this to give the impression of a reinforced army, the summons only revealed how diminished his ranks were. Even so, he could have defended himself in the camp and frustrated the Parthians by drawing out the war, if only Paetus had possessed any resolve in following his own or others' counsel. But whenever experienced soldiers warned him during urgent situations, he would do the exact opposite—and poorly—simply to avoid appearing as though he needed their advice. He then marched out of the camp shouting that he had not been given ditches or palisades to hide behind, but men and weapons to fight the enemy. He drew up his troops as if for a set battle; however, after losing a centurion and a few soldiers sent to scout the enemy host, he returned inside, terrified. Then, because Vologeses did not advance with quite the heat expected, Paetus regained a hollow confidence and stationed three thousand elite infantry on the nearby Mount Taurus to block the pass. He placed the Pannonians—the core of his cavalry—down on the plain, and sent his wife and son to the fortress of Arsamosata <gloss>A fortified city near the Euphrates, mentioned by Pliny and Polybius.</gloss>, guarded by a single cohort. Thus, he scattered the forces that, if united, could have better sustained the enemy's raids. It is said he was barely persuaded <gloss>literally: "pulled with winches" (*tirato con gli argani*). Latin: *aegre compulsum*.</gloss> to—

**1** **hovered about**. Also in the Latin, "*volitabant*." — *With great show*: understand this to mean appearing as a great multitude.

**2** **towers**, plural.

**3** **established**. Thus the Nestiana edition, and correctly so. It was not necessary for Mr. Volpi to correct it to *took*.

**4** **Arsamosata**. Pliny (Book VI, 9) and Polybius (Book VIII, 25) write *Armosata*, which is a land near the Euphrates.

**5** **pulled with winches**, induced with great difficulty. Latin: "*aegre compulsum*."

...confessed to Corbulo that the enemy was upon him <note>original: *che gli era addosso*. The author clarifies that the enemy was pressing Paetus, and that Corbulo did not want to rush the rescue so that the increased danger would make the eventual relief more glorious.</note>: Corbulo, not being in a hurry—in order that the rescue might be more glorious as the dangers grew—dispatched three thousand infantry (one thousand from each of the three legions) <note>original: *per una*</note>, eight hundred cavalry, and an equal number from the auxiliary cohorts.

**XI.** Vologeses, although informed of the mountain passes Paetus had occupied—on one side with infantry, on the other with cavalry—pressed forward. He routed the cavalry and crushed the legionaries, so that only the centurion Tarquitius Crescens dared to defend himself in the tower entrusted to him; he frequently charged out and killed the barbarians who approached, until he was overcome by the many fires thrown at him. The infantry fled; if any escaped unharmed, they did so by going off-road <note>original: *fuor di strade*, meaning by traveling through unused or cross-country paths.</note> and into the distance. The wounded remained in the camp and, out of fear, told tales of the wonders of the King’s valor and the cruelty and numbers of the enemy; those who were already frightened easily believed them. Paetus, making no attempt to remedy the disorder, abandoned all military duties and sent word again, begging Corbulo to come quickly to defend the standards, the eagles, and the name of the small, wretched army that remained; he promised that as long as he lived, he would maintain <note>original: *manterrebbe*. The translator notes that the Nestiana edition uses a single 'r' here, a spelling variation seen elsewhere.</note> his loyalty.

**XII.** Corbulo, with a bold spirit, left a portion of his men in Syria to hold the forts along the Euphrates. Taking the shortest route well-supplied with provisions, he arrived in Commagene <note>Commagene was a region of Syria; its capital was Samosata, known today as Samsat.</note>, Cappadocia, and Armenia. Along with the usual baggage, a great number of camels laden with grain accompanied the army to drive away both the enemy and hunger. The first of the terrified men to encounter him was the centurion Paccius, a *primopilus* <term>The "first file" or highest-ranking centurion of a Roman legion.</term>, followed by many others. When they offered various excuses for their flight, Corbulo told them to return to their standards and to Paetus, to see if he would forgive them; for his part, he said he only forgave those who were victorious. He visited his legions, comforted them, reminded them of past deeds, and pointed toward new glory—the recovery of honor and the reward for their labors, saying they were not seeking "the villages or small castles of Armenia, but the camp..."

"If for a single common soldier, for a single citizen saved, a man would receive his crown from the hand of the emperor, how much glory will it be to see an equal number of those crowned and those saved?¹" Fired by such words, and especially those who had brothers or relatives there, they marched day and night, rushing without rest.

**XIII.** And Vologeses pressed the besieged even more closely: he attacked now the camp, now the fort² where the weak forces were, approaching more closely than is the custom of the Parthians, hoping that through such excessive daring he might draw the enemy out to fight. ---

¹ *of those crowned and those saved?* The original Latin text says: <note>original: "si singulis manipularibus praecipua servati civis corona imperatoria manu tribueretur, quod illud et quantum decus, ubi par eorum numerus apisceretur... qui attulissent salutem et qui accepissent!"</note> This passage, quite difficult and interpreted in so many different ways, is translated very well by Burnouf: "how glorious would be the day when there would be as many civic crowns to distribute as there had been citizens in peril!" It is useful to translate the note with which he supports his interpretation and corrects Davanzati <note>Bernardo Davanzati was a famous 16th-century Italian translator of Tacitus.</note>. "I have translated this phrase," he says, "as literally as I could, and I believe I have derived a clear and satisfying sense from it: — He who saves a citizen deserves a civic crown; those whom we are going to liberate are in danger of all perishing, and must be saved. If it were possible for the general to give to each man who deserved it a special and individual crown (*praecipua*), what a great day of triumph and glory would it be, in which this noble prize was distributed to as many soldiers of the liberating army as there were members of the liberated legions! — Nonetheless, it seems that in this antithesis—*those who had brought safety and those who had received it*—Tacitus has leaned a bit on artifice; and Ernesti <note>Johann August Ernesti, a noted 18th-century classical scholar.</note> asks what this equality of number between the saviors and the saved matters to glory. But he has not caught Tacitus's concept: the equality of number is not between the two armies, but between a part of one and the totality of the other—between the part of Corbulo’s soldiers who would receive the civic crown, and the totality of Paetus’s legions, who would be saved from death. Moreover, *those who had brought safety* designates not the liberating soldiers specifically, but the liberating army in general: in this army, as many soldiers would obtain the civic crown (*par numerus apisceretur*) as there were citizens who owed them their own preservation (*et qui salutem accepissent*), which is to say, as many as there were legionaries in the besieged army. Thus disappears that coldness of style that offended Ernesti, and which is seen in Davanzati's translation: *How much glory will it be to see an equal number of those crowned and those saved.*"

This despair within the army forced Paetus to write the first letter to the king, which was not humble in tone, but almost a grievance: "That the King proceeded as an enemy against the Armenians, a people who were always either vassals of the Roman empire or under a king appointed by the Emperor. Peace," he argued, "would be equally useful to both sides. The King should not look only at the present; while he had come against two legions with all the forces of his kingdom, the rest of the world remained at the Romans' disposal to support this war."

**XIV.** Vologeses did not respond directly to the point: "He was waiting there from hour to hour for Pacorus and Tiridates, his brothers, to decide what should be done with the Roman legions and with Armenia, which the gods had added to the Arsacid <note>The Arsacids were the ruling dynasty of the Parthian Empire.</note> dignity." Later, Paetus requested a face-to-face meeting with the King through messengers. The King instead sent Vasaces, his general of the cavalry. To him, Paetus recalled the triumphs of Lucullus and Pompey <note>Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Pompey the Great were famous Roman generals who had conducted successful campaigns in the East decades earlier.</note>, and other captains who had held or granted the kingdom of Armenia. Vasaces replied that the Romans had held and given it only as a matter of ceremony <gloss>in appearance</gloss>; whereas the Parthians held it in actual fact. They argued at length, and the following day, in the presence of Monobazus of Adiabene <note>A king of a semi-independent region who acted as a witness</note> who was called as a witness, they came to an agreement: "That the siege of the legions be lifted; all soldiers must evacuate Armenia; they must surrender the fortresses and all provisions to the Parthians. Once these conditions were met, Vologeses would be permitted to send ambassadors to Nero."

**XV.** In the meantime, Paetus built a bridge over the river Arsania <margin>The Arsania is today known as the Arsen, a tributary of the Euphrates. The Nestiana manuscript calls it the Arsametus.</margin>, which flowed in front of the camp, supposedly to facilitate his departure. However, the Parthians commanded its construction as a symbol of their victory, because they were the ones who actually used it, while our troops were forced to take another path <note>The translator Dati notes: "But the Parthians had commanded this of him as a sign and memory of that victory; for the bridge was used by them, and our men departed by another road."</note>. Rumor further added that the legions were forced to pass under the yoke <note>A "yoke" was a frame made of spears that defeated soldiers were forced to crawl under as a supreme act of humiliation.</note>. They even went as far as stripping the soldiers of their clothes and weapons, while our men yielded for the sake of peace <gloss>showing themselves timid and yielding so as not to provoke a fight</gloss> <note>original Latin: "pavido milite et concedente, ne qua praelii..." meaning "the soldiers being fearful and giving way, lest any cause for battle arise."</note>.

Corbulo met him at the banks of the Euphrates with his own men. Their weapons and standards were somber ² out of respect, so as not to mock the defeated by the contrast of their own splendor. The soldiers, moved by pity for their comrades, could not hold back their tears; they could barely greet each other through their weeping. There was no rivalry for bravery or desire for glory—feelings found in a joyful heart—only compassion, which was felt even more deeply by the common soldiers.

**XVIII.** In Rome, the arches and trophies ordered by the Senate for the victory over the Parthians were still being erected on the Capitoline Hill even as the war raged on, for they had more regard for appearances than for the truth. He appointed three former consuls to manage the public revenue: Lucius Piso, Ducennius Geminus, and Pompeius Paulinus. He criticized past emperors for spending more than their income, while he himself donated one and a half million gold pieces to the state every year.

XXI. “In the past, besides the praetor or consul, visitors were sent to the provinces who, by reporting on how each man conducted himself, kept the people in check. Today, we observe <gloss>1</gloss> the subjects and flatter them; and at their whim, we rush to offer thanks for good service, or to bring accusations. Let this be granted to them, and let them show their power in such a way. But false praises, or those obtained through begging, should be restrained no less than wickedness and cruelty. More often one sins by failing to do good than by doing evil. Indeed, we even hate certain virtues: constant severity and a spirit that despises seeking favors. Because of this, we are better at the beginning of our magistracies than at the end, when we go about recommending ourselves, much like those seeking office do. If these practices were abolished, the provinces would be ruled with more justice and a better reputation. And just as the fear of the law against extortion <note>The *Lex Repetundarum*, a Roman law intended to prevent provincial governors from plundering their territories for personal gain.</note> curbed avarice, so will these intrigues be ended by prohibiting public votes of thanks.”

> "I pardon you right now <margin>Immediately. Latin: *statim*.</margin>; for if I delayed even a little, you would faint from fear."

**XXVI.** In Syria, Corbulo assigned the fourth and twelfth legions, which seemed poorly suited for combat since their best men were lost and the remainder were terrified. In their place, he drew out and led into Armenia the sixth and the third legions, which were at full strength and hardened by many successful campaigns. To these he added the fifth, which had been in Pontus and was untouched by the disaster <margin>Latin: *expers cladis*.</margin>, and the fifteenth, which had arrived recently. He also gathered the cohorts of chosen cavalry and infantry from Egypt and Illyria, along with the auxiliary forces of the allied kings. He assembled the army <margin>He gathered the military force.</margin> at Melitene <margin>Melitene, today known as Malatya in modern Turkey.</margin>, where he intended to cross the Euphrates. Then, after performing the customary review of the entire army, he addressed them, speaking highly of serving under such an emperor and recounting his own past achievements. He remained silent regarding the unfortunate ignorance of Paetus, speaking with a natural authority that, for a soldier, served as well as eloquence.

**XXVII.** He then followed the route once taken by Lucius Lucullus <note>A Roman general who campaigned in the same region against Mithridates and Tigranes nearly a century earlier.</note>, reopening the mountain passes that time had closed. He did not disdain the ambassadors who arrived from Tiridates and Vologeses to discuss peace, but sent them back accompanied by his own centurions with a measured response:

> "It is not yet necessary to resort to a final battle; the Romans have had many successes, and the Parthians some; therefore it is not..."

**XXVIII.** Corbulo's name was still more respected by the barbarians than it was hated: therefore, they trusted his advice. It was concluded that Tiridates would place the royal crown beside the image of Caesar, and would not take it back except from the hand of Nero. Then, having kissed, they departed. **XXXI.** He departed and found Pacorus in Media and Vologeses in Ecbatana <note>Modern Hamadan, Iran; the ancient capital of the Median Empire and a summer residence for Parthian kings.</note>, who was concerned for his brother. This request came because Vologeses, accustomed to foreign pride, did not know that we Romans care for the reality of power and disregard the empty vanities of empire.

**XXXII.** In that same year, Caesar <note>Referring here to Emperor Nero.</note> granted Latin rights <term>Latin Rights: A set of legal privileges intermediate between full Roman citizenship and the status of a non-citizen.</term> to the tribes of the Maritime Alps. XXXIII. [Year of Rome 817, Year of Christ 64.] In the consulship <term>Consulship: The highest elected political office in the Roman Republic and Empire; two consuls were elected annually to serve as heads of state.</term> of Gaius Laecanius and Marcus Licinius, Nero’s desire to sing in all the theatrical plays grew every day; for until then he had sung only at home or during the Juvenile Games <note>original: "giuochi giovenali." Immediately, the theater of Naples was filled with people who flocked there at the news from nearby lands and colonies, along with those who followed Caesar to pay him court or for other business, and even squads of soldiers.

XXXIV. There, an event occurred which most considered mournful, though he viewed it as a lucky omen: after all the people had left, the empty theater collapsed without harming anyone. He gave thanks to the gods for this through musical songs, and while singing of the fortune of this recent event and making his way toward the Adriatic Sea, he stopped at Benevento. There, Vatinius hosted a most beautiful gladiatorial festival. This man was one of the most infamous monsters of that court—the student of a tailor, hunchbacked, and a crude jester <note>original: "buffon magro," a plebeian and foolish jester. Latin: *facetiis scurrilibus* (scurrilous wit).</note>. He was first received as an object of ridicule, but later, by slandering the best men, he gained such power in favors, money, and the ability to cause harm that he surpassed even the worst of men.

XXXV. The pleasure of this festival did not distract Nero’s mind from his wicked deeds; he forced Torquatus Silanus to die because, in addition to the nobility of his Junian blood, he recognized the divine Augustus as his great-great-grandfather. Accusers were instructed to charge him with being so lavish in his gift-giving that he could only hope for a revolution <note>original: "novità," literally "novelty," but used here in the political sense of a coup or regime change.</note>. He was accused of keeping nobles as secretaries, accountants, and chancellors—titles and roles belonging to a prince. When his principal freedmen <term>Freedmen: Former slaves who had been granted their freedom and often served as high-level administrators for Roman aristocrats.</term> were seized and bound, and his sentence was drawn up, Torquatus cut the veins in his arms. Nero then repeated his usual refrain: that even though the man was guilty and had despaired of his defense, Nero would have granted him his life if he had only waited for the Emperor's mercy.

**XXXVI.** Not long afterward, having postponed his journey to Achaia <term>Achaia: A province in southern Greece where Nero intended to perform as a singer and lyre player.</term> for reasons unknown, he returned to Rome. He harbored secret designs for the eastern provinces, and most especially for Egypt. Through a public edict, he announced
> "that his absence would not be long, and that everything would remain stable and prosperous for the state," <note>original: "che l' assenza sua non sarebbe lunga, e ne seguirebbe ogni cosa ferma e prospera alla republica." and he went to the Capitol <term>Capitol: The Capitoline Hill, the most important temple site in Rome, where the Temple of Jupiter stood.</term> to commend this journey to the gods. Upon entering the Temple of Vesta <term>Vesta: The goddess of the hearth and home; her temple held the eternal fire of Rome.</term>, a trembling took hold of all his limbs; perhaps he was terrified by the goddess herself, or by the memory of his great crimes, which kept him in a state of constant fear. Consequently, he abandoned the enterprise, saying
> "that his love for his country surpassed every other thought; seeing the sorrowful faces of his citizens and hearing their secret complaints about the long journey he intended to take—he, whom they could not bear to lose sight of; for his presence was accustomed to comfort them in times of adversity. Just as private individuals are bound by their most precious family ties, so too did the Roman people compel him to console them by not departing." <note>The commentator Politi explains: "Just as in private families the closest blood relatives prevail, so in Nero the affection of the Roman people prevailed."</note>

This was what the common people <term>plebe: The common citizens of Rome.</term> wanted, for they loved their pleasures and feared a shortage of food <note>original: "del caro." This refers to the high cost of grain or a potential famine.</note> (which is their greatest concern) should he be absent. The Senate and the leading men doubted whether he would be more cruel while far away or while present; but then, as often happens with great fears, they believed that what had actually occurred—his staying—was the worse of the two.

**XXXVII.** In order to make it believed that he saw nothing more joyful than the city of Rome, he began to eat in public and treated the entire city as if it were his own house. **XXXVIII.** There followed the gravest and most atrocious ruin that ever happened in Rome by the violence of fire; it is unknown whether it was by chance or by the fraud of the prince, for there are authors who support both. The fire broke out in the Circus <term>Circus: Specifically the Circus Maximus, the massive arena for chariot racing located in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills.</term> adjacent to the Palatine and Caelian hills, where, in shops full of merchandise that served as fuel, a great flame immediately arose. Aided by the wind, the fire ran through the whole length of the Circus without hindrance from walls, temples, or any other obstacles. It spread across the flat ground, climbed the hills, then descended again, seizing everything before any defenses could be mounted against its fury. That old Rome, with its narrow, winding alleys and lanes, was suddenly turned into a bonfire. <note>original: "un falò." The translator notes that this same term was used in the *Life of Agricola* to describe the public burning of books.</note> Attempts to extinguish it were hindered by women, the elderly, and children, terrified and screaming, and by those who scrambled to save themselves and others; dragging the weak, waiting for them, or running, so that often while looking behind them, they were overtaken from the front or the side. Even those who fled further away found the flames already burning there. No longer knowing what to flee or seek, they crowded the streets <note>Older editions incorrectly transcribed "calcavan le vie" (crowded the streets) as "cavalcavan le vie" (rode the streets).</note> or lay in the fields. <note>original: "campora," meaning fields.</note> Some, having lost everything, even food for a day, perished; others, because they could not pull their dearest ones from the fire, remained there by choice and died with them. ...to try to extinguish it, as many people threatened those who attempted to stop the flames; others openly threw torches, crying out that they were following orders—either to facilitate their looting or because they had actually been commanded to do so.

**XXXIX.** Nero was staying in Antium <note>Antium, modern-day Anzio, was Nero's birthplace and a favorite seaside retreat.</note>, and he did not return to Rome until the fire approached his house, which he had built to connect the palace with the gardens of Maecenas. However, it was impossible to prevent the fire from swallowing the palace, the house, and everything surrounding it. To comfort the frightened and fleeing people, he opened the Campus Martius, the monuments of Agrippa, and even his own gardens. He ordered temporary shelters to be built quickly to house the impoverished; provisions were brought from Ostia and the neighboring towns. He even lowered the price of grain to three sesterces <note>original: "un carlino," an Italian coin used by the translator to represent the Roman "ad ternos nummos" or three sesterces.</note>. These acts of kindness, however, were spoiled by a rumor that, while the city was burning, he had gone onto his private stage and sang of the "Destruction of Troy," comparing the present disaster to that ancient calamity.

**XL.** On the sixth day, the fire finally stopped at the foot of the Esquiline Hill; it found only open ground and empty air because a vast number of buildings had been leveled to create a gap. Before the fear had passed, the fire broke out again, though with fewer deaths and less damage, as the streets in that area were wider. It ruined divine temples and porticos built for beauty. This second fire was even more hated because it began in the Aemilian gardens belonging to Tigellinus <note>Ofonius Tigellinus was the powerful and ruthless prefect of the Praetorian Guard.</note>, and because Nero seemed to want the glory of rebuilding the city entirely anew and naming it after himself. Of the fourteen districts into which Rome is divided, only four remained intact; three were leveled to the ground, and seven were reduced to a few charred ruins.

**XLI.** It is not easy to count the number of houses, blocks <term>Insulae: Literally "islands," these were the multi-story apartment blocks where the majority of Rome's population lived.</term>, and temples ruined. The most venerable for their antiquity were burned: the temple consecrated by Servius Tullius to the Moon; the Great Altar and temple dedicated by Evander of Arcadia to Hercules; the temple of Jupiter the Stayer vowed by Romulus; the palace of Numa; and the temple of Vesta with the household gods <note>The Penates, the sacred protective spirits of the Roman state.</note> of the Roman people. The spoils of so many victories, the masterpieces of Greek artists, and the ancient, preserved works of great minds were lost—many things that the elders remembered and which were impossible to replace, even with the beauty of the city rising again. It was noted that the fire began on the nineteenth of July...

**XLII.** But Nero took advantage of the ruins of his homeland to build a house so <note>original: "cotale," meaning so great or of such a kind</note> stupendous that the miracle of its gems and gold was nothing compared to the fields, woods, lakes, and "wildernesses" <note>original: "eremi," described as groves styled after solitary places. Latin: "in modum solitudinum silvae."</note>—openings and vistas created by Severus and Celer. These were architects of such talent and daring that they attempted to use art to achieve things beyond nature and to mock the resources of the prince. They promised him they could dig a navigable canal from Lake Avernus <note>A volcanic crater lake near Naples, which the ancients believed was the entrance to the Underworld.</note> to Ostia, through arid shores and mountains. No other waters were to be found there to fill it except for the Ufente <note>The Ufente river, located in the Pontine Marshes.</note> to be diverted into it; the rest of the terrain is dry earth or solid rock that cannot be broken, and would not have been worth such intolerable labor. Nonetheless, Nero, always hungry for the incredible, attempted to cut through the mountain near Avernus; the traces of such folly remain to this day.

**XLIII.** Those houses in Rome not occupied by his palace were rebuilt—and not haphazardly <note>original: "a vanvera," meaning without design or confusedly.</note> as they were after the fire of the Gauls—but according to a plan: the heights were limited, the streets were wide, the cross-streets <note>original: "traverse," a term still used by the common people for side-roads.</note> were measured, the squares were larger, and in front of every isolated block of houses, they were protected by a loggia <note>A covered porch or gallery.</note> on the front. Nero offered to build these loggias at his own expense and to return the ground to the owners beautiful and clear. He also offered to pay a reward, according to each person's means and rank, to whoever finished rebuilding their house or block within a set time. For the ships <note>original: "vasselli," an older form of "vascelli." The translator notes Dante's use of the word: "Upon a vessel [vassello] swift and light."</note> that carried grain from Ostia to Rome along the Tiber, he ordered that on their return trip, they should carry away the rubble and debris to be dumped in the marshes of Ostia. Furthermore, he ordered that certain parts of the houses be built without wooden beams, instead being reinforced with Gabine and Alban stone <note>Types of volcanic tuff (peperino) that were known to be fire-resistant.</note>, and that buildings should not share common walls, but each should be isolated and independent. He placed guards over the water supply, which had previously been diverted by many private citizens for their own use, to ensure it flowed abundantly in public places for fighting fires and was accessible <note>original: "manesca," meaning ready at hand for everyone.</note> to all. These useful measures also added beauty to the new city. Nevertheless, some held that the old form of the city was healthier, because...

**XLIV.** After human aid, recourse was made to the divine; and having consulted the Sibylline Books <note>A collection of oracular utterances, sought by the Roman Senate in times of crisis.</note>, supplications were made to Vulcan, Ceres, and Proserpina. Juno was propitiated by matrons, first on the Capitoline Hill, then at the nearest sea <sup>1</sup>, and from that water the temple and the image of the goddess were sprinkled; then married women held sacred banquets <sup>2</sup> and vigils. But neither human effort, nor divine prayers, nor the prince’s largesse could diminish the infamous rumor that he himself had burned Rome. Therefore, to divert this suspicion, he prosecuted and punished with exquisite cruelty those hated evildoers whom the common people called Christians; <sup>3</sup> named after Christ, who, during the reign of Tiberius, was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate. This pestiferous seed <note>The original Italian "semenza pestifera" translates the Latin *exitiabilis superstitio*, meaning "deadly or destructive superstition."</note> <sup>4</sup> was suppressed for a time; but it sprang up again not only in Judea, where the malady was born, but in Rome, where all atrocious and shameful things from everywhere gather and are celebrated. Therefore, those who first confessed were seized, and then, based on their information, a vast multitude was convicted, not so much for the crime of arson as for their hatred of the human race. <sup>2</sup> **the couches.** Latin: "lectisternia." <note>A Roman religious ritual where images of gods were placed on couches and offered a meal.</note> This is how our author reads it; but perhaps incorrectly. Because for goddesses, the *sellisternium* (ritual chairs) was prepared rather than the *lecti* (couches), upon which the images of gods were placed.

<sup>3</sup> **Christians.** Suida <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> in the article *Christianoi* says "that under the Roman Emperor Claudius, when the apostle Peter ordained Evodius in Antioch, those who were previously called Nazarenes and Galileans were named Christians." This occurred, according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, in the year of Christ 45.

<sup>4</sup> **pestiferous seed.** To see how much Tacitus betrays the truth here, let us look at what Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, a friend of Tacitus and governor of Bithynia.</note> said—his dear friend, who was appointed by Trajan to investigate and punish the Christians. "The only thing I discovered," (he says to the emperor) "was a perverse and unbridled superstition." And the superstition was this: "They affirmed they were accustomed to gather on a fixed day before dawn; to sing hymns among themselves alternately to Christ, as if to a God; to bind themselves by an oath, not to commit any crime, but to abstain from robbery, murder, and adultery, to keep their word, and when called upon, to return what was deposited with them: which done, it was their custom to depart; then to gather again for a meal, which was public and innocent; from which they had nonetheless abstained after my edict, which, following your orders, forbade any such gatherings. I therefore deemed it all the more necessary, even by torturing two female slaves who were called ministers, to clarify the truth." (Letters X, 97). But the truth is clarified by Tacitus himself, who was unable to bring forward any fact to confirm his grave accusations.
</note>

...clad in the skins of wild beasts, so that dogs might tear them apart alive; or they were nailed to crosses, or set ablaze to serve as lamps at night. Nero offered his own gardens for this spectacle and hosted a circus festival, dressed as a charioteer upon a chariot, or mingling with the common people as a spectator. Thus, although these wretches were guilty and deserved the harshest punishments, a sense of pity arose for them, as they were dying not for the public good, but to satisfy the cruelty of one man.

**XLV.** Meanwhile, extortions and taxes <margin>forced loans and taxes; today called impositions.</margin> devastated Italy. Subjects, allies, and cities that were free in name—even the gods themselves—were not exempt from such looting; the temples of Rome were stripped, and all the gold was carried off <margin>taken/pried loose. In the second book of the Annals, ch. 38, we saw "prying open the treasury" to take money by force.</margin> that the Roman people had ever consecrated for triumphs, prayers, celebrations, or in times of fear. Throughout Asia and Achaia, our two commissioners seized not just gifts but the very statues of the gods: Acratus, a freedman and the height of villainy, and Carinas Secundus, who had some Greek learning on his lips <margin>Latin: *græca doctrina ore tenus exercitus*, meaning his education was superficial, "only to the edge of the lips."</margin> but no goodness in his soul. It was said that Seneca, to distance himself from the burden of these sacrileges, begged to retire to a distant villa; and not obtaining permission, he confined himself to his room, pleading a case of gout. Some write that Nero had poison prepared for him by his freedman Cleonicus; warned of this, or suspicious of it, Seneca avoided it by living on simple foods, fruit from his own gardens, and running water.

**XLVI.** At this time, the gladiators held in Praeneste <margin>Praeneste, modern Palestrina.</margin> <note>Praeneste was a popular resort town for Romans, famous for its massive Temple of Fortune.</note> attempted to escape; the soldiers guarding them held them back. Already the common people, fearful and eager for any novelty, began to recall Spartacus <note>A Thracian gladiator who led a major slave uprising against the Roman Republic (73–71 BC).</note> and the evils of old. # THE FIFTEENTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS.

...the southwest wind <note>original: *libeccio*, a strong Mediterranean wind</note> battered them on the coast of Cuma, resulting in the loss of many galleys and a great number of smaller vessels.

**XLVII.** At the end of this year, portents occurred, serving as announcements of the impending evils. Never had there been so many lightning strikes. A comet appeared, which Nero always sought to appease with the blood of some nobleman <note>In Roman times, comets were viewed as omens of the death of a ruler or a change in the state.</note>. Two-headed infants and wild beasts were found in the streets, or discovered inside sacrificed pregnant animals; and in the territory of Piacenza, a calf was born along the road with its head attached to one of its legs. The soothsayers declared that the world would soon have another "head" <note>meaning a new leader or emperor</note>, but one that would not last and would not be hidden—because this head had been twisted within the womb and was born right on the public way.

**XLVIII.** [Year of Rome 818, AD 65.] When Silius Nerva and Atticus Vestinus entered their consulship, a conspiracy of senators, knights, soldiers, and even women was born and grew suddenly. They competed to join out of hatred for Nero and love for Gaius Piso. Piso, of the House of Calpurnia, was related to the highest nobility of Rome and held a great reputation among the people for his virtues—or things that resembled them. He was an eloquent advocate for the citizens, a generous giver to his friends, and pleasant and sociable even with strangers. He was tall and handsome, yet his character lacked seriousness; he was devoted to pleasure, refined, magnificent, and sometimes even a spendthrift. This pleased many, for in such a corrupt age, people did not want an emperor who was stingy or austere.

**XLIX.** The conspiracy did not spring from Piso's own greed; nor could I say who first invented such an undertaking, which was then joined by so many. The most eager were Subrius Flavius, a tribune of a guard cohort, and Sulpicius Asper, a centurion, as their brave ends would later prove. Annaeus Lucan <note>The famous author of the epic poem *Pharsalia*.</note> joined with a fierce hatred <note>The Italian text uses the idiom "Co’ denti la presero," literally "they took it with their teeth." Latin: *vivida odia intulere*, meaning "they brought a lively or fierce hatred."</note> because Nero, out of vain jealousy, had disparaged and banned his poetry. Plautius Lateranus, the consul-elect, joined not out of personal offense, but out of love for the fatherland. Among the first were Flavius Scaevinus and Afranius Quintianus, both senators, though they were not held in high regard. Scaevinus was lost in luxury and sleep. Quintianus, more effeminate in his habits than a woman, wanted revenge because Nero had insulted him in shameful verses.

...to hold him; they drew into the conspiracy Tullius Senecio, Cervarius Proculus, Volcatius Araricus, Julius Tugurinus, Munatius Gratus, Antonius Natalis, and Marcius Festus, all Roman knights. Among these, Senecio, who was very intimate with Nero, faced more danger as he remained constantly in the Emperor’s circle. Natalis was a confidant of Piso; the others hoped for a change in government. Besides those mentioned, they summoned men of war: Subrius and Sulpicius, Granius Silvanus and Statius Proximus, who were tribunes of two guard cohorts; and the centurions Maximus Scaurus and Paulus Venetus. They also brought in Faenius Rufus, the prefect—which was of great importance—a man of good life and reputation, who had been pushed out <margin>pushed out of the prince's favor; the original Latin text says that Tigellinus was surpassing him (*anteibat*) in influence.</margin> of the Emperor's favor by the cruelty and filthiness of Tigellinus. Rufus had been weighed down <margin>meaning he was being burdened with accusations.</margin> by many charges, including the false claim that he was an adulterer of Agrippina <note>Nero’s mother, whom Nero had murdered years earlier; being linked to her was politically fatal.</note>, and because of his devotion to her memory, he was intent on revenge. When the conspirators learned, even from his own words, that the prefect was on their side, they took greater heart <margin>meaning they took greater courage.</margin> and discussed when and where to carry out the assassination. It was said that Subrius had the idea of attacking Nero while he was singing on stage, or while his house was burning at night and he was running here and there without his guards. In the former case, the Emperor would be alone; in the latter, the very sight of so many witnesses would have fired up that noble spirit, had it not been cooled by the desire for self-preservation, which is always contrary to noble daring.

### LI.
While these men wavered and delayed between fear and hope, a certain woman named Epicharis revealed <margin>The translator refers here to a previous note in Book VI, chapter 8 of the *Annals* regarding the word "spilled" or "leaked."</margin> the matter, though it is unknown how, as she had never before been a woman concerned with honorable thoughts. She urged them on and reproached them for such slowness; finally, unable to endure it any longer while staying in Campania, she began to subvert and draw in <margin>She began to incite and bring the leaders into the conspiracy. "Contaminate" is used here in the sense of corrupting the loyalty of the soldiers.</margin> the commanders of the fleet at Misenum <note>Misenum was the base of the primary Roman naval fleet in the Tyrrhenian Sea.</note>. One of these was Volusius Proculus, who had been involved in the murder of Nero's mother, but felt he had not been promoted as highly as he deserved for such a crime. Having confided <margin>meaning he opened up or shared a secret. See also *Annals* II, 12 and IV, 68.</margin> his grievances to her, as she was a friend of his, whether old or new...

...and having complained of having served Nero so much to no avail, she threatened to take revenge when the time and place were right. From this, she took hope in drawing him and many others into the conspiracy, to which the fleet could provide great assistance and opportunity, because Nero often took his pleasure in the sea near Pozzuoli and Miseno <note>Coastal towns near Naples where the Roman elite had villas and the imperial fleet was stationed.</note>. Thus, she began to recount to him all the wickedness of the prince, and that the Senate was not standing idle; rather, they had found a way to avenge the ruined Republic. She urged him to join in, to do his part, and to bring his most ferocious soldiers; it would be for his own good. However, she kept the names of the conspirators secret. Proculus reported everything to Nero, but when he was brought face-to-face with Epicharis, he could produce no witnesses and was dismissed <note>The original Italian *riprovato* here means his testimony was rejected or confuted for lack of proof.</note>. But she was placed <note>The original text uses *messa* as a shorthand for "she was put in prison."</note> in prison, as Nero suspected that what could not be proven might still be true.

LII. Therefore, to avoid being discovered, it seemed best to the conspirators to hasten to kill him at Piso’s villa in Baia, where Nero often went for the beauty of the place; there he would enter the baths and eat, having left behind his great retinue <note>The original Italian *traino* refers to his suite or guard. The Latin source says: *omissis excutiis et fortunæ suæ mole*, meaning "having set aside his guards and the weight of his high station."</note> and his court. But Piso did not wish to bear the burden of defiling the sacred tables and the gods of hospitality with the blood of a prince, however guilty he might be. It would be better, he argued, to complete the enterprise for the Republic in Rome, either in that hateful palace built from the spoils of the citizens, or in public. This is what he told them; but in his heart he feared that Lucius Silanus—a man of the highest nobility, raised by Gaius Cassius and elevated to every splendor—might seize the empire for himself with the ready help of those who were untainted <note>Original: *de' non intinti*, referring to those not yet compromised or involved in the conspiracy.</note> and who might feel compassion for Nero, seeing his death as a wicked murder. It was also believed that Piso feared the consul Vestinus, a fierce man who might wish to restore liberty or give the empire to someone who would acknowledge him as its source. Vestinus knew nothing of the conspiracy, though Nero later used it as an excuse to vent his long-standing hatred against him.

LIII. They finally resolved to carry out the deed in the Circus <note>The Circus Maximus, the great chariot-racing stadium in Rome.</note> on the day of the feast of Ceres <note>The *Cerialia*, a festival held in mid-April.</note>, because Caesar <note>Nero.</note> rarely left his house or gardens, and when he did go to the Circus to enjoy the spectacles, it was easier to get close to him.

The plan was as follows: Lateranus <note>Plautius Lateranus, a consul-elect known for his great physical strength.</note>, under the pretext of begging for financial help for his livelihood, would throw himself at the Emperor's knees. Once he had knocked him down—being a man of great size and spirit—he would pin him to the ground. Then the tribunes and centurions, according to each man's courage, would rush in and kill the Emperor while he was down and entangled. Scaevinus asked for the honor of dealing the first blow with a dagger taken from the Temple of Salus in Tuscany; others say it came from the Temple of Fortune in Ferentum <note>An ancient town in Etruria.</note>. He carried it as if it were consecrated for a great work. Meanwhile, Piso was to wait at the Temple of Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>, from where Faenius <note>Faenius Rufus, a commander of the Praetorian Guard who secretly joined the plot.</note> and the others would collect him and bring him to the military camp, accompanied by Antonia, the daughter of Claudius Caesar, to win over the favor of the people. So says Gaius Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and historian.</note>, and I have not wished to omit it; however, it does not ring true to me—neither that Antonia would lend her name to such a risky and uncertain venture, nor that Piso, who was in love with his wife, would pledge himself to another woman. That is, unless the desire for power outweighs all other affections.

LIV. Amid such a diversity of backgrounds, ranks, social statuses, genders, and ages—among the rich and poor alike—the secrecy was marvelous, right up until the first clue emerged from the house of Scaevinus. The day before the planned assassination, Scaevinus had a very private meeting <note>The original Italian *molto alle strette* translates to "a very close or private talk."</note> with Antonius Natalis. Upon returning home, he made his will. He unsheathed the aforementioned dagger, which was eaten by rust, and gave it to his freedman <note>A former slave who had been granted legal freedom.</note> Milichus to sharpen and polish it <note>The original Latin source says *in mucronem ardescere iussit*, which means "he ordered the point to glow or sparkle."</note>. He prepared a banquet more lavishly than usual; he granted freedom to his most beloved slaves and gave money to others. He appeared somber and lost in deep thought, though he tried to feign joy through various conversations. Finally, he ordered Milichus to prepare bandages to staunch the flow of blood. Milichus may have already been aware of the conspiracy and was trusted until then; or, as some writers suggest, he became suspicious of these movements. Thinking with his servile mind of the rewards, money, and power that betrayal would bring him, he cast aside his duty, his master's safety, and the memory of the freedom he had been given. He even took counsel from his wife—advice that was womanly and worse still—as she frightened him by pointing out that many slaves and freedmen had seen these things, and that it would benefit...

LV. At dawn, Milichus went to the Servilian gardens; <gloss>1</gloss> and not being admitted, he claimed he brought a matter of great and terrible importance. The gatekeepers led him to Epaphroditus <note>A powerful freedman and secretary to Nero; he would later assist Nero in his suicide.</note>, Nero's freedman, and he to the Emperor. He told him of the urgent danger, the vast conspiracy, and what he had heard and surmised. He showed him the dagger that was intended to kill him, and he demanded that Scaevinus be brought there. Having been seized by soldiers, Scaevinus defended himself by saying:

> "That he had kept that dagger in his chamber as an ancient relic of his family, from which the wicked freedman had stolen it; that he had made many wills without favoring one day over another; that he had granted freedom and money to his slaves on other occasions, but more generously then because, since he was leaving them their liberty by his will while having more debt than assets, the creditors would have priority. He had always lived a life of splendor and cheer, which was little approved by strict censors. He had not requested bandages for wounds; this vanity had been added by the informant to bolster his other lies and make himself a witness."

To these words he joined a fierce spirit, expression, and voice, calling the man a villain and infamous, with such efficacy that the evidence was vanishing. But Milichus's wife warned that Antonio Natalis <note>A Roman knight and close confidant of the conspiracy's leader, Piso.</note> and Scaevinus, both soul and body devoted to Gaius Piso, had held a long conversation in secret.

LVI. Natalis was sent for; they were questioned separately about what they had discussed; since their stories did not match, they became suspicious and were bound. At the sight of torture and the sound of threats, they yielded. <gloss>2</gloss> Natalis, who was more knowledgeable of the plot and better at convincing, first named Piso, then Seneca—either because he had carried messages between him and Piso, or to gain favor with Nero, who, having grown weary of Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the famous Stoic philosopher and Nero's former tutor.</note>, sought every means to crush him. Scaevinus, hearing that Natalis had confessed, out of similar weakness or believing everything was discovered and that silence was useless, named the others. Lucan <note>The famous poet and nephew of Seneca.</note>, Quintianus, and Senecio held out for a long time; then, having been broken <gloss>3</gloss> by the promise of pardon,
