as an excuse for their delay <gloss>1</gloss>, they named: Lucan named Atilla, his mother; Quincianus named Glicius Gallus; Senecio named Annius Pollio; all their dearest friends.

**LVII.** Nero remembered Epicharis, who was still held on the information given by Proculus; and believing that a woman's body could not withstand the pain, he ordered her to be subjected to every kind of torment. But neither the lash nor fire, nor the fury of the torturers—who were enraged at being unable to defeat a woman <gloss>2</gloss>—could force a confession from her: and so she overcame the first day. On the following day, as she was being carried back to the same tortures in a chair (since she could no longer stand on her mangled limbs), she took a band from her breast, tied it in a noose to the canopy of the chair, and placed her neck within it. By putting the weight of her body against it, she choked out what little breath remained in her. This was a memorable example: that a freedwoman, in such agony, would seek to protect strangers and people she hardly knew, while high-born men, Roman knights and senators, would betray their nearest and dearest without even being touched by torture. Indeed, Lucan, Senecio, and Quincianus did not stop naming others at length. Because of this, Nero’s fear grew ever greater; he doubled his guards.

**LVIII.** Sentinels held the city and the walls; squads of infantry and cavalry swarmed through the squares, houses, villas, and fields, even to the sea and the river. Among them were Germans, whom Nero trusted most because they were foreigners. Ropes of prisoners <gloss>3</gloss> were dragged toward the aforementioned gardens, waiting in lines on the ground to be called to the torture. Having celebrated with anyone in the conspiracy, or having spoken to them, met them, dined with them, or attended a festival together, were now considered mortal sins. In addition to the cruel questioning by Nero and Tigellinus <note>Ofonius Tigellinus was the powerful and ruthless prefect of the Praetorian Guard, known as Nero's most brutal advisor.</note> against the conspirators, Fenius Rufus—who had not yet been named—conducted the interrogations with extreme atrocity against his own companions to avoid appearing as one of them. And Subrius Flavius, who stood before him, signaled to him with a gesture that he should kill Nero right there; but Fenius shook his head, and his courage failed him.

**LIX.** Once the conspiracy was uncovered, there were those who advised Piso that while Milichus was being heard and Scaevinus was still wavering, he should go to the military camp or climb the rostra <note>The speaker's platform in the Roman Forum</note> to test the favor of the soldiers and the people:
> "If the companions of your enterprise gathered together, even the others would follow them; and in the great noise of a rebellion, which carries much weight in times of change, Nero has not prepared for this. Sudden events terrify even brave men, let alone that guitar-player with Tigellinus <note>The ruthless commander of the Praetorian Guard and Nero’s favorite</note> and his women. Take up arms. Many things, by setting to work <note>original: "mettendovisi," to apply oneself with ardor. Latin: "experiendo."</note>, turn out well, though they seem daunting to those who stand still. Silence and loyalty cannot be hoped for in so many minds aware of the secret; torture and rewards force every door. Soon men would appear to chain even you, and kill you indignively. How much more praised would you die by embracing the republic, calling for aid in the name of liberty, and—should the soldiers fail you and the common people abandon you—becoming more justified in the eyes of those past and those to come?"

He did not move. After remaining a short time in public, he shut himself in his house and prepared to die. Then, a group of young and new soldiers arrived from Nero; he feared the veterans, believing them to be inclined toward Piso. He cut the veins of his arms. He left a will full of ugly flatteries toward Nero for the sake of his wife, Aria Galla—a woman who was beautiful and nothing else, whom he had taken from his friend Silio Domizio. His patience and her lack of virtue brought infamy upon Piso.

**LX.** The second to die was Plautius Lateranus, the consul-elect, killed with such haste that he was not given time to embrace his children or choose the manner of his death. Dragged away and murdered where slaves are executed <note>In the place called the Sestertium, about two and a half miles outside Rome.</note> by the tribune Statius—who was himself one of the conspirators—Lateranus did not breathe a word <note>original: "non fiatò." He did not want to reproach the tribune for being a fellow conspirator. Latin: "nec tribuno obiiciens eamdem conscientiam."</note>. Next followed the death of Seneca, to the great joy of the prince, so that he might finish him with the blade since the poison had failed, and not because he was truly convicted of the conspiracy:

...because Natalis alone said exactly <note>original: "disse appunto," meaning he said no more than this and nothing further.</note> "that Piso sent him to visit the sick Seneca and to complain that Seneca did not wish to see him; it would be better if, by speaking together, they could enjoy their friendship <note>Dati explains: "it would have been better if they had spent time and reasoned together informally and as the good friends they were."</note>." And he claimed that Seneca responded "that frequent conversations between them were not beneficial <note>original: "non far," meaning they were not useful or advantageous.</note> to either one; but that his own health and safety depended upon that of Piso." Nero then sent Granius Silvanus, a tribune of a guard cohort, to question Seneca on whether Natalis had visited him and if he had indeed responded with those words. On that day, whether by chance or by design <note>original: "a studio," meaning on purpose or with careful intent.</note>, Seneca had returned from the countryside to his villa four miles outside of Rome. Towards evening, the tribune surrounded the villa with soldiers. Finding Seneca at dinner with his wife, Pompeia Paulina, and two friends, the tribune delivered the Emperor's command.

**LXI.** Seneca replied "that Piso had sent Natalis to him to complain of not being allowed to visit; and he had excused himself on the grounds that he was ill and required rest; nor did he have any reason to value the health of a private citizen above his own. He did not know how to flatter, nor did anyone know this better than Nero, who had many times found him to be a free man rather than a slave." When the tribune reported this, Tigellinus <note>Ofonius Tigellinus, the ruthless commander of the Praetorian Guard</note> and Poppaea <note>Nero’s wife, known for her influence over his cruelest decisions</note> were present; these two formed the inner council for the Emperor's cruelties. Nero asked if Seneca had resolved to kill himself. The tribune replied that he had detected neither fear nor melancholy in Seneca's words or expression. "Well then," said Nero, "go back and tell him he must die." Fabio Rustico <note>A Roman historian and contemporary of Seneca</note> relates that the tribune did not return by the same path, but turned aside to Fenius Rufus, the prefect, to ask if he must obey such a command. Rufus replied that he should; such was the cowardice that had become fatal to everyone. Although Silvanus was <note>The annotator of the Nestian copy by G. Capponi, not having understood "benchè" (although) used in the Latin style with the present tense, incorrectly corrected "benchè" to "perchè" (because).</note> one of the conspirators and was fostering the very wickedness he had already agreed to avenge, he nevertheless did not have the face or the voice to deliver the death sentence to Seneca personally; instead, he sent in a centurion.

**LXII.** Seneca calmly asked for his will: when the centurion refused him, he turned to his friends and said: "Since I am forbidden from rewarding your merits, I leave you the only beautiful jewel <note>original: "un bel gioiello," referring to the "imago vitae" or the image/example of his life.</note> remaining to me: the example of my life. By remembering its goodness, you will gain the reputation for such steadfast friendship." As they began to weep, he comforted or rebuked them, asking: "Where is your philosophy? Where are the remedies against looming disasters that you have studied for so many years? Who was unaware of Nero's cruelty? After the murder of his mother and brother, what was left for him to kill but his tutor and teacher?" <note>Seneca had served as Nero's tutor (aio) and advisor for many years, attempting to guide the young Emperor’s education and morality.</note>

**LXIII.** Having said such things to almost everyone, he embraced his wife, and feeling somewhat softened, he warned and begged her "to temper her grief; in time, move past it; and endure the loss of your husband with the honorable pleasure of contemplating his virtuous life." She declared that she wished to die with him and called for the executioner <note>original: "feditore," meaning the one to strike the blow or make the cut.</note>. Then Seneca, so as not to rob her of her glory, nor to leave so beloved a woman a prey to insults, said: "I had shown you the comforts of life; you prefer the splendor of death; I shall not deny it to you. Our deaths shall be equally courageous; yours shall be the more illustrious." Having said this, they had the veins of their arms cut at the same time. Seneca also cut the veins in his legs and behind his knees, because the blood struggled to flow from a body withered by old age and a meager diet. Overcome by those terrible pains, and so as not to frighten his wife—nor to be unsettled himself by seeing her suffering—he persuaded her to go into another room. Frequently calling for scribes,<gloss>1</gloss> he dictated, with his eloquent spirit, concepts so famous (since copies have been widely published) that I will not repeat their substance here.

**LXIV.** Nero, because he did not harbor personal ill-will toward Paulina and to avoid increasing the public hatred against him, sent soldiers to prevent her from dying. At their urging, slaves and freedmen bandaged her arms and stopped the bleeding; it is not known if she was conscious of this. Since the public always tends toward the worst interpretation, there were those who believed that while she despaired of pardon, she sought the honor of dying with her husband; but when she saw a hope of life...

Seneca, struggling to die, prayed to Annaeus Statius, his faithful friend and physician, to give him a certain hemlock <term>hemlock: a poison used for state executions in ancient Athens, most famously used by the philosopher Socrates</term> long kept in reserve, with which poison the condemned in Athens used to die. LXV. It was said that Subrius Flavius, together with his centurions, held a secret council (with Seneca's knowledge) that once Nero was killed with the help of Piso, Piso should also be murdered, and the empire should be given to Seneca, as one who was innocent and chosen for his most illustrious virtues for the highest rank. And this motto of Subrius went around: "To remove a lyre-player and put in a tragic actor does not diminish the shame." Because Nero sang with the lyre, and Piso sang dressed in the robes of a tragic actor.

LXVI. The soldiers involved in the conspiracy could no longer maintain the deception; those who had already confessed were disgusted to see themselves being interrogated by Faenius Rufus, who was secretly their own companion in the plot. As Rufus threatened and squeezed Scaevinus hard to speak up, Scaevinus laughed and said, "no one knows more than you do;" and he urged him "to return the favor to such a good prince" <note>This is a sarcastic remark; Scaevinus is exposing Rufus's hypocrisy by suggesting he should be as "loyal" as the rest of them.</note>. LXVII. And they turned to Subrius Flavius, the tribune, who 
> "first alleged the absurdity that a brave soldier would never have joined such an enterprise with those no better than women." <note>Flavius initially tried to deflect suspicion by using the sexist Roman trope that the conspirators (specifically referring to Epicharis) were weak, and thus beneath a soldier's dignity to associate with.</note>

Afterward, being pressed further, <sup>1</sup> he resolved to make a noble confession. When asked by Nero for what reasons he had forgotten the oath he had sworn to him, he said:
> "I hated you; and you had no more faithful soldier than me as long as you deserved to be loved. I began to be unable to endure you when you murdered your mother and your wife; when you became a charioteer, an actor, and burned Rome." <note>To the Roman elite, Nero’s public performances as a singer and charioteer were considered as shameful and criminal as his murders.</note>

I have included his exact words because they are not widely known like those of Seneca; nor is it any less worthwhile to know the words of a soldier, which are rough but fierce. Nothing from that conspiracy so disturbed Nero, who was always ready to commit crimes but was unaccustomed to hearing them thrown back in his face. He entrusted the execution of Flavius to Veianus Niger, a tribune. This man had a pit dug in the nearby field. Flavius, criticizing it as being too small and narrow, said to the surrounding soldiers:
> "He could not even manage to do this right."

When he was told to offer his neck bravely, he replied:
> "Would that you might strike as bravely." <sup>2</sup>

The executioner, trembling, barely managed to cut it in two blows; and to boast of having made him suffer, he later reported that he had severed the head with a stroke and a half.

LXVIII. There followed another courageous example from Sulpicius Asper, a centurion. When asked by Nero why he wished to kill him along with the others, he replied briefly:
> "Because there was no other way to provide a remedy for your many horrors."

He then suffered his punishment with a strong spirit, and the other centurions did not falter in their character. Faenius Rufus did the opposite, filling even his last will and testament with cowardly lamentations. Nero expected that Vestinus the consul would also be named, as he considered him a violent enemy; but the conspirators did not want him—some because of old enmities, others because they considered him too reckless and unsuitable. However, Nero's hatred for him was born from too much intimacy, which allowed Vestinus to know and despise the prince's cowardice; and the prince feared the ferocity of his former friend.

...who often mocked him with bitter jokes; which, when they touch a raw nerve, stick in the memory. A new cause was added: Vestinus, though he knew Caesar <note>Nero</note> was one of the lovers of Statilia Messalina, married her.

LXIX. Therefore, since there was no crime or accusation, and no appearance of a trial could be made, Nero acted by sheer authority. He commanded Gerelanus the tribune to take a cohort of soldiers to preempt the consul by seizing his palace, which overlooked the forum like a fortress. He was to crush that band of chosen youths whom Vestinus kept in his service, who were all handsome and of the same age. Having finished his consular duties that day, Vestinus was hosting a banquet, either entirely without fear or seeking to hide it. The soldiers entered; it was said the tribune was waiting for him. Rising and shutting himself in a room, a physician came; his veins were cut and he was placed in a warm bath. It was all over quickly, without him speaking a word or showing any grief. His guests were seized and detained until midnight, until Nero—imagining the <term>terror</term> <note>original: "battisoffiola," a colorful Florentine term for a state of trembling anxiety.</note> of those poor wretches awaiting death—said laughing that they had <term>paid the price</term> <note>original: "pagato lo scotto," a metaphor for paying the penalty.</note> for their consular delicacies.

LXX. Next, he ordered the death of Marcus Annaeus Lucanus <note>Lucan, the famous poet of the *Pharsalia* and nephew of Seneca.</note>. Seeing his blood pour out, his hands and feet growing cold, and his spirit gradually departing from his extremities while his chest was still warm and his mind sound, he recited some of his own verses about a wounded soldier dying just as he was; and with this last utterance, he expired. Afterward, Senecio, Quintianus, and Scaevinus, who had lived effeminate lives, died manfully; the others died without any memorable word or deed.

LXXI. Rome was full of funerals; the Capitol was full of sacrificial victims. Those who had lost a son, a brother, a relative, or a friend gave thanks to the gods, adorned their houses with laurel, threw themselves at Nero's knees, and exhausted him with kisses on his hands. He, believing these actions sprang from joy, pardoned Antonius Natalis and Cervarius Proculus as a reward for the evidence they had so quickly revealed. Milichus was made rich and took that Greek name which signifies "Savior" <note>The Greek name is *Soter*.</note>.

...perhaps because Gaius Caesar <note>The emperor Caligula, nephew of Claudius.</note>, who was a wanderer, <margin>a wandering hunter of uncertain lust.</margin> dallied with his mother.

**LXXIII.** Nero, having delivered his speech to the fathers <note>The Roman Senate.</note>, issued a proclamation to the people regarding those who had been condemned. He also had the records of their trials and their own confessions entered into the public journals. This was done to quiet the rumors that attacked him, claiming he had destroyed so many honorable men out of personal hatred or fear. However, the origin, progress, and ultimate end of this conspiracy was never doubted at the time by anyone who cared to know the truth; and it was later confirmed by those who returned to Rome after Nero's death. Meanwhile, those senators who had the most cause for grief were the ones who most indulged in flattery. Julius Gallio <note>The brother of the philosopher Seneca; he is also mentioned in the Bible (Acts 18) as the proconsul of Achaia.</note>, Seneca’s brother, was pleading for his own life, full of terror. Salienus Clemens attacked him, calling him an enemy and a parricide; but the other fathers spoke out against Salienus, warning him not to exploit public misfortunes to settle private grudges, nor to prick and re-inflame the wound <margin>To make it raw again, or to poison it.</margin> of the prince's anger, which had already begun to heal.

**LXXIV.** Offerings and thanksgivings were decreed to the gods, with special honors paid to the Sun in his ancient temple near the Circus <note>The Circus Maximus, the Great Racing Track of Rome.</note>, where the assassination was to have taken place; for it was believed the Sun's divine light had uncovered the plot. It was also decreed that more horse races should be run in the Circus in honor of Ceres; that the month of April should be renamed "Nero"; and that a temple to Salvation <term>Salus: the Roman goddess of safety and public well-being.</term> should be built on the spot where Scaevinus had drawn the dagger. Nero himself consecrated this dagger in the Capitol, inscribing it: **TO JUPITER THE AVENGER** <note>original: "A GIOVE VINDICE" / Latin: "Iovi Vindici."</note>. At the time, this inscription was not given much thought, but after the later rebellion of Julius Vindex <note>Vindex's name means "avenger" in Latin; he led the revolt that eventually triggered Nero's downfall.</note>, it was viewed as an omen of the emperor’s future punishment. I find in the Senate records that Cerialis Anicius, the consul-elect, proposed that a temple be built at public expense as quickly as possible to the "Divine Nero"—implying that Nero should be worshipped by men as more than a mere mortal. However, this was later interpreted as a bad omen of his death, <margin>It was interpreted as a presage of his death.</margin> because no prince is honored as a god while he still lives among men.

# THE SIXTEENTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS

->BY<-

## GAIUS CORNELIUS TACITUS.

### SUMMARY.

**I.** Fortune mocks Nero through Cesellius Bassus, a madman who boasts of discovering treasures in Africa. — **III.** Luxury increases due to this vain hope. — **IV.** The Quinquennial Festival <note>A festival held every five years.</note>: Nero sings to the great annoyance of the people and at the risk of Vespasian <note>The future emperor Vespasian reportedly fell asleep during Nero's performance, nearly costing him his life.</note>. — **VI.** Poppaea dies: her body is not buried but embalmed; she receives a public funeral. — **VII.** Gaius Cassius and Lucius Silanus are exiled: Lepida is left to Nero's judgment. — **X.** Lucius Vetus, Sextia, and Pollutia meet their deaths. — **XII.** The names of the months are changed. — **XIII.** Storms and diseases. — **XIV.** Anteius and Ostorius are put to death. — **XVII.** Annaeus Mela, Anicius Cerealis, Rufius Crispinus, and Gaius Petronius <note>The famous author of the Satyricon.</note> go with them to their deaths. — **XX.** Silia is exiled. — **XXI.** Nero, enraged against virtue itself, piles up serious charges against Thrasea Paetus and Barea Soranus: Servilia, daughter of Soranus, is joined to her father's fate: their courage remains unconquered: they are given the choice of how to die: the accusers Eprius Cossutianus and Ostorius Sabino are rewarded. — **XXXV.** Death of Thrasea, Soranus, and Servilia: exile of Paconius and Helvidius.

---

->*The course of a year.*<-

Year of Rome 819. (A.D. 66). — **Consuls.**
{ GAIUS SUETONIUS PAULINUS.
{ GAIUS LUCIUS TELEZINUS.

**I.** Fortune then wished to make a mockery of Nero,¹ who was so weak that he believed the dream of a half-mad Carthaginian named Cesellius Bassus. This man came to Rome and, having purchased an audience with the prince, revealed to him that he had found on his land a cavern of immense depth, filled with gold that was not coined, but raw and in the ancient style; there were massive ingots there, and in another part, upright columns. He claimed all this had been hidden for so long a time to increase Nero's own fortune. He believed that Dido of Phoenicia <note>The legendary founder and first queen of Carthage.</note>, having fled from Tyre after she built Carthage, had hidden that treasure so that the new people would not become insolent from too much wealth, or so that the greed of the kings of Numidia <note>A neighboring North African kingdom.</note>—who were enemies for other reasons²—would not be sparked into making war to steal it.

**II.** Nero, therefore, without investigating who this man was or

### XV.
Ostorius was then vacationing on the borders of Liguria, where a centurion was sent to kill him immediately. This was because Nero—a coward by nature and at that time terrified by the conspiracy—seemed to always see that formidable man before him. Ostorius had been decorated in Britain with the civic crown <note>The *corona civica*, one of the highest military honors, awarded for saving the life of a fellow citizen in battle.</note>, was of great stature, very robust, and highly skilled in arms. When the centurion arrived at the villa, he seized the gates and delivered the Prince's <note>The Emperor Nero</note> command to Ostorius. Ostorius then turned his own fortitude, so often used against enemies, upon himself. Because little blood flowed from his veins despite them being opened, he had a slave hold a dagger high and steady—not to strike, but to keep it firm—then he took the slave's right hand and cut his own throat upon the blade.

### XVI.
I would be tedious and unpleasant to myself and others were I to recount so many similar and continuous cases of sorrow, even if they were from foreign wars or deaths for the Republic, let alone such servile patience and so much blood wasted at home; it troubles me and chills my heart. But I will offer no other excuse to the reader than this: no hatred has moved me against those who died so wretchedly. Nor could that divine wrath against the Romans be described all at once and then passed over, as when armies are defeated and cities are taken by force. Let it be granted to the descendants of these great personages that, just as they have their own tombs and are not buried in common with others, so they may have a particular memory of their end in history.

### XVII.
A few days later, Annaeus Mella, Cerialis Anicius, Rufius Crispinus, and Gaius Petronius died almost in a batch. Mella and Crispinus were distinguished knights <note>Members of the *Equites*, the social class just below the Senators</note>, equal in standing to senators. Crispinus had been the prefect of the Praetorians and had received the consular insignia; recently exiled to Sardinia <gloss>1</gloss> because of the conspiracy, upon hearing he was to die, he killed himself. Mella, the brother of Gallio and Seneca, did not seek honors out of a vain glory for power; though a knight, he felt equal to those of consular rank and believed that managing the Prince's business was a shorter path to enrichment. He was the father of Annaeus Lucan <note>The famous poet and author of *Pharsalia*</note>, which added greatly to his prestige. When Lucan was dead, while Mella was minutely inventorying his estate, he provoked Fabius Romanus—an intimate friend of Lucan—to report him as a conspirator as well...

XVIII. I shall begin the account of Gaius Petronius <note>Traditionally identified as the author of the *Satyricon*, a famous Roman novel.</note> from further back. He spent his days in sleep and his nights in the duties and pleasures of life. While others gained fame through industry, he earned his through idle neglect. He did not squander his fortune in gluttony and debauchery like most spendthrifts, but rather on the refinements of a sophisticated nature. The more his words and deeds appeared free and natural, the more they were liked for their lack of affectation. As proconsul in Bithynia, and later as consul, he proved himself energetic and capable. Returning then to a life of vice—or perhaps the imitation of it—he became one of Nero’s most intimate companions. He was appointed the "Master of Elegance" <term>Arbiter Elegantiae: The supreme authority on matters of taste and fashion at the imperial court.</term>. Nero found no pleasure or luxury sufficiently refined unless Petronius had first given it his approval. This sparked a deep envy in Tigellinus, who saw Petronius as a rival and a superior master of pleasure. Therefore, by appealing to the Emperor’s cruelty—which was more powerful than any of his other appetites—Tigellinus bribed a slave to report that Petronius was a close friend of Scaevinus. Petronius was given no chance to defend himself, and almost his entire household was dragged off to prison.

XIX. Caesar <note>Nero</note> had by chance traveled to Campania <note>original: *Terra di lavoro*; a historical region of southern Italy.</note>, and Petronius, having reached Cumae, was detained there. But he did not rush to take his own life. He had his veins opened, then bound up again, so that he could reopen them at his whim. Meanwhile, he spoke with his friends, but not on serious topics, nor did he seek the fame of a "constant" or stoic death. He chose to listen not to discourses on the immortality of the soul or the teachings of philosophers, but to light and pleasant poetry. He rewarded some of his slaves and had others punished; he went out for a walk and even slept, so that his death, though forced, might appear natural. Unlike many of those who died at that time, he did not use his will to flatter Nero or Ti-

...Tigellinus or any other man in power; instead, he sent the Prince <note>The Emperor Nero</note> a written account of his debaucheries, detailing all his shameful acts with young men and women. He sealed it and then broke his signet ring, so it could not be used later to forge documents and endanger others.

**XX.** While Nero wondered how his nocturnal inventions were being discovered, he remembered Silia. She was a woman of some status as the wife of a senator, but she was also a mistress to the Emperor and had participated in every kind of depravity; she was also very close to Petronius. Nero sent her into exile out of hatred, though under the pretext that she had revealed what she had seen and endured in his company. To satisfy the wrath of Tigellinus, he sacrificed Numicius Thermus, a former praetor; a freedman of Thermus brought a foul accusation against Tigellinus, for which the freedman paid the price with cruel tortures, and his master with an unjust death.

**XXI.** After such a cruel slaughter of so many great men, Nero wished to uproot virtue itself by killing Barea Soranus and Thrasea Paetus. They had long been disliked, but Thrasea was now targeted for new reasons: for having walked out of the Senate when the matter of Agrippina <note>Nero’s mother, whom he had murdered; Thrasea’s walkout was a silent protest against the Senate's sycophancy.</note> was discussed, as I related,¹ and for having shown little interest in the *Juvenalia* <note>The "Youth Games" established by Nero in which elites were forced to perform.</note>. This stung Nero even more because Thrasea, in his native Padua, had sung in tragic costume at the Games of the Cestus <note>Ancient boxing matches.</note> established by the Trojan Antenor. On the day when the praetor Antistius² was being condemned to death for verses composed against Nero, Thrasea had proposed a milder sentence and carried the vote. Furthermore, when divine honors were being decreed for Poppaea <note>Nero's wife; her death was officially mourned as a national tragedy.</note>, he refused to attend the funeral. Cossutianus Capito³—a man prone to wrongdoing and an enemy of Thrasea—reminded Nero of these things; Capito hated him because Thrasea had supported the ambassadors⁴ of Cilicia, who had complained of Capito's extortions, and had used his authority to see him condemned.

**XXII.** In addition, he reproached Thrasea for "avoiding the oath taken at the start of every year. Though a member of the priesthood of fifteen,⁵ he did not come to make the vows, nor did he ever sacrifice for the health of the Prince and his 'heavenly voice.' This man, who used to be so tireless in guiding even the smallest debate in the Senate, has not entered the House for three years..."

...Armenia, so that the noise of foreign affairs would drown out the crimes committed at home, or perhaps to display the greatness of the Empire by killing great men as if it were a royal duty.

**XXIV.** When the whole city had rushed out to pay court to the prince and meet the King <note>Referring to Tiridates I of Armenia, who traveled to Rome to be crowned by Nero in a massive display of imperial power.</note>, Thrasea was forbidden from attending. He did not lose heart, but wrote to Nero, stating that if he were shown the charges and allowed to defend himself, he would justify his actions. Upon reading that letter, Nero immediately thought that Thrasea, out of fear, had resolved to bolster the Prince’s fame and glory while diminishing his own. When this did not happen, Nero grew afraid of that free and innocent spirit and countenance, and he summoned the Senate. Thrasea consulted with his circle of friends on whether he should attempt a defense or treat the summons with contempt; and their opinions were divided.

**XXV.** There were those who wanted him to appear in person; "they were confident in his constancy: he would say nothing that would not increase his glory. Only the weak and cowardly die in obscurity; let the people see him face his end. Let the Senate hear those superhuman words, spoken almost as if by a god. Such wonder might even move Nero himself; and if not, posterity will judge very differently those who die gloriously and those who die by keeping a shameful silence."

**XXVI.** Those who wanted him not to leave his house confirmed the same virtues in him, but argued: "What if he suffers mockery and insults? It is better to spare him from such treatment. It is not only Eprius and Cossutianus <note>Eprius Marcellus and Cossutianus Capito, the professional informants and accusers who led the prosecution against Thrasea.</note> who are there, but others perhaps ready to lay violent hands on him. Even good men follow Caesar’s brutality out of fear. He should rather protect the Senate itself, which he has always honored, from the shame of condemning him; let it remain uncertain what the fathers <term>padri: referring to the *Patres*, the Roman Senators</term> would have decided had they seen Thrasea before them as an accused man. It is a foolish hope to think Nero will feel shame for his cruelties; indeed, one must fear that he may become even more cruel toward Thrasea’s wife, his family, and his other loved ones. Let him make a noble end, unviolated and unstained, following the examples of those wise men who adorned his life." In that council was Arulenus Rusticus, a fiery young man who, out of a desire for praise, offered—as a tribune of the plebs <term>tribuno della plebe: a Roman magistrate with the power to veto the actions of the Senate</term>—to oppose the Senate's deliberation. Thrasea restrained him, "lest he enter into vanities that would not help the accused and would be ruinous to himself. At the end of his life, he must not change the..."

**XXIX.** While Marcellus was saying these things, he threw himself forward, his voice, face, eyes, and threats all ablaze; the Senate saw itself overwhelmed, not by the usual melancholy brought on by so many dangers, but by a deeper and newer terror at the sight of the soldiers' hands and weapons upon them. **XXX.** Ostorius Sabino entered the field to accuse Soranus <note>Barea Soranus, a former governor of Asia known for his integrity, which made him a target for Nero.</note>, starting with his friendship with Rubellius Plautus, and the seditions he allegedly nurtured in the cities of Asia when he was proconsul there, seeking to make himself great against the public good. She, out of devotion to her father and because of her simple age, had asked them for nothing more than whether her house would remain standing, whether Nero would be appeased, and whether the Senate's judgment would not be rigid. She was brought into the Senate before the tribunal of the consuls: the old father stood facing his daughter, who was less than twenty years old; recently married to Annius Pollio and then abandoned when he was driven into exile; standing like a desolate widow, not even daring to look at her father, who was burdened because of her.

Money brought these hidden evils to light, and made him an example of how much one must guard against the wicked and the treacherous who masquerade as good men and friends.

**4.** in the logic of "reason of state" <note>The principle that the interests of the state may justify actions that would otherwise be considered illegal or immoral.</note>, the accounts never balance unless they are settled with one person alone.

**12.** Gaius Turranius, prefect of the grain supply; <note>The official responsible for the grain distribution (*annona*) in Rome.</note>

(1) *Friuli*. An error by the translator. It should say *Frejus*. The same error recurs in the *Life of Agricola*. <note>The "Foro giulio" (Forum Iulii) in the original Latin refers to modern Fréjus in France, not the Friuli region in Italy.</note>

(2) Here he places the following marginal note which was removed with the correction read opposite: "This was properly the selling of justice and public affairs, just as *simony* <note>the act of selling church offices or roles</note> is for sacred things. This word has remained in the writings of the security of merchants, where the insurers obligate themselves for every barratry <note>original: "baratteria"; in maritime law, this refers to fraudulent acts by a ship's master or crew</note> of the master, and it implies fraud and foul play. Frequent disputes arise over this word *barratry*, because it is not well understood today, and it is placed in those writings as a public form given to them in the times when it was used and understood; which form of the writing and the other Florentine statutes of security would have great need of reform."

(1) And here too he adds a note: "To pronouns placed after the verb *to be* and after adverbs, the oblique case is given: *if I were you* <note>original: "s' io fussi te"</note> — *go where he is* <note>original: "va' dove lui"</note> — *do as I do* <note>original: "fa come me"</note> — 'And that which is not her,' said Petrarch — *if I were you* <note>original: "s' io fussi tu"</note> — *go where he is* <note>original: "va' dov' egli"</note> — *do as I do* <note>original: "fa' com'io"</note> would be said in jest. The year that Rubellius and Fufius were consuls, both Gemini, Julia Augusta died at a very old age, of the most illustrious nobility, born of the Claudii, adopted into the Livii and the Julii.
Then Caesar
and without giving her a pause to give birth,
but as she was joined with the blood of Augustus through the marriage of Agrippina with Germanicus, he held as his own their children, the great-grandchildren of Augustus.
manageable wife,
she took hold of her husband with wiles, and let her son do as he pleased.
he retained few of them
having forbidden her heavenly honors.
biting
seducer of women
Thereafter the government rushed headlong, because she had provided a remedy for things; (1)
(Count Mortara's copy: "it fell into ruin and violence").
read it was.
but not arms,
the loves of youths.
fainted with fear.
(Count Mortara's copy: "by harming").
he stood tense, ready to let fly his atrocious sentence:
(Count Mortara's copy: "to let fly the sentence").
secretary
seeing the coming evil.
and the consuls
and shouted, that letter was (with respect to Caesar) false:

(1) Here appears the following marginal note: "Revised: it fell into ruin and violence, following the opinion of the secretary Picchena <note>Curzio Picchena (1553–1626) was a scholar and Tuscan diplomat famous for his edition of Tacitus.</note>, that the word *urgens* <note>original: "urgens"; Latin for 'pressing' or 'driving forward.'</note>, which functions well and is common to all texts, should not be changed to *vergens* <note>original: "vergens"; Latin for 'sloping' or 'declining.'</note>."

<page-num>479</page-num>

# FIRST ATTEMPTS AT THE TRANSLATION

## OF TACITUS:

---

### I.

1 *To prove through deed the false claim of Henri Estienne <note>original: "Arrigo Stefani," the French scholar and printer who had criticized the Italian language</note>, who said that the Italian tongue is long-winded and cold, I began to translate into our Florentine speech Cornelius Tacitus in this manner:*

I. Rome first had kings: Lucius Brutus established liberty and the consulship: dictatorships were temporary: the power of the Ten <note>The Decemviri, a ten-man commission established to codify Roman law</note> lasted little more than two years, and the authority of the military tribunes with consular power did not long endure: neither Cinna nor Sulla ruled for long. The power of Pompey and Crassus soon fell to Caesar, and the armies of Lepidus and Antony to Augustus: who, under the title of Prince <note>original: "capo" (head/leader), translating the Latin "Princeps"</note>, made himself master of the whole state, which had been shattered by civil wars. But the successes and misfortunes of the old Republic have been recorded by famous writers; nor were noble minds lacking to narrate the times of Augustus, until growing flattery drove them away. The histories of Tiberius, Gaius <note>Caligula</note>, Claudius, and Nero were falsified while they lived, out of fear; and after their deaths, they were written with recent resentment. Therefore, I intend—having touched upon a few final events of Augustus—to recount the reign of Tiberius and the other three without bitterness or favor, having no reason for either.

II. Once the public armies were gone—Brutus and Cassius being slain; the younger Pompey crushed in Sicily; and no other leader remaining...

<margin>1 This fragment was published by Abbot Cesare della Croce, custodian of the Ambrosian Library (where this autograph manuscript is found), in the final volume of the *Translation of Tacitus*, printed in Milan, 1800. Davanzati addressed it to Giovanni Vincenzo Pinelli. See the letter in volume III of this edition.</margin>

<summary>This page contains Bernardo Davanzati’s introduction to his translation of Tacitus, where he defends the Italian language against French criticism, followed by his concise translation of the opening of Tacitus's Annals.</summary>
<keywords>Bernardo Davanzati, Tacitus, Henri Estienne, Florentine dialect, Roman History, Augustus, Tiberius, translation theory, Ambrosian Library</keywords>

--- Page 576 ---
<meta>This page continues the "First Attempts" at the translation of Tacitus' Annals by Bernardo Davanzati. Having established his intent on the previous page to prove the expressive power of the Italian language, Davanzati now moves into the narrative of Augustus's rise to power and the complex web of his intended successors.</meta>

<page-num>480</page-num>

<header>->FIRST ATTEMPTS<-</header>

nothing remained—with Lepidus stripped of power and Antony killed—but Caesar as the sole leader <note>original: "capo," translating the Latin "Princeps"</note>. Calling himself no longer a triumvir but consul, and content with the authority of a tribune to defend the common people, he won over the populace with abundance, the soldiers with rewards, and all men with the sweetness of peace. He began, step by step, to elevate himself, and to appropriate the functions of the senate, the magistrates, and the laws, with no one opposing him. The most fierce had been extinguished in battle or at the borders; of the remaining nobles, whoever was more eager to serve was made richer and greater; and having remade themselves under the new state, they preferred the present and secure situation over the past and dangerous ones. Such a state was not rejected even by our provinces, which were suspicious of the rule of the Senate and the People due to the struggles of the powerful and the greed of the magistrates; as the laws there were of no effect <gloss>¹</gloss>, being ultimately overturned by force, manipulation, and money.

III. Now Augustus, to strengthen the state, elevated Claudius Marcellus—his sister's son—to the priesthood and to the <term>curule edileship</term> <note>A high-ranking magistracy in Rome responsible for public buildings and games</note> while still a very young man; and Marcus Agrippa, a man of low birth but a good soldier and companion in victory, to two consecutive consulships; and when Marcellus died, he took him [Agrippa] as his son-in-law. To Tiberius Nero and Claudio Druso, his stepsons, he added the titles of <term>Imperator</term> <note>At this time, a title of military honor rather than the sole title of the ruler</note>, even though his house was not yet diminished by Gaius and Lucius, the sons of Agrippa. These two he had adopted into the family of the Caesars; and while pretending to refuse, he had ardently desired that they be called "Princes of Youth" and destined as consuls while still children wearing the <term>toga praetexta</term> <note>The purple-bordered toga worn by Roman boys before reaching adulthood</note>. When Agrippa died, Lucius Caesar—while traveling to the armies of Spain—and Gaius—returning wounded from Armenia—were taken from life, their brief hour having come <gloss>²</gloss>, or by the schemes of their stepmother Livia. Drusus had died previously. Thus, Nero <note>Referring to Tiberius Nero, the future Emperor Tiberius</note> remained the sole stepson. Upon him <gloss>³</gloss> everything turned: he was adopted as a son, made a partner in the empire and in the tribunician power, and acknowledged by all the armies; no longer through the intrigues of his mother, as before, but openly, as the old Augustus was spurred on by her.

---

<gloss>¹</gloss> *being of no effect;* having no force or authority, being useless.

<gloss>²</gloss> *their brief hour having come.* Meaning: they died, either because the hour of their short life had arrived, or because Livia hastened it with poison.

<gloss>³</gloss> *Upon him;* that is, upon Nero [Tiberius].

<summary>This page describes how Augustus consolidated power by taking on the roles of consul and tribune, while neutralizing the Senate and nobility. It also details the tragic deaths of his intended heirs—Marcellus, Agrippa, Gaius, and Lucius—leaving Tiberius as the sole successor, potentially due to Livia's influence.</summary>

<page-num>481</page-num>

<header>## ON THE TRANSLATION OF TACITUS.</header>

...so lost in his love <note>For his wife, Livia</note>, that he banished his only grandson, Agrippa Postumus, to the Island of Pianosa; a man truly coarse and dull <note>original: "soro," an archaic term meaning a bird not yet fully trained or a person lacking refinement</note>, and awkwardly fierce in his physical strength; yet he was guilty of no crime that could be charged against him. As General of the eight legions on the Rhine, he appointed Germanicus, the son of Drusus, and had him adopted by Tiberius, even though Tiberius already had a grown son of his own; but it is clear that Augustus wished to strengthen his position with multiple layers of succession.

In that time there was no other war except <gloss>¹</gloss> for the one against the Germans, intended more to erase the shame of the army lost under Quintilius Varus <note>The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, a catastrophic Roman defeat</note> than out of a desire to expand the empire, or for any other worthwhile reason. The city was at peace: the names of the magistrates remained the same: the young had been born after the victory at Actium; the old had lived through the civil wars: and who was there left who could have seen the Republic?

### IV.

With the state thus transformed, no good ancient custom remained: everyone, made lower than the prince, watched only for his commands without any other thought; meanwhile, Augustus, while vigorous in age, sustained himself, his household, and the peace. When great old age came, along with troublesome illnesses and death at his bedside, new hopes arose; some, out of season, discussed how beautiful liberty was: many feared war; others desired it: most spoke ill of the oncoming masters in various ways. "Agrippa is a brute <note>original: "bestione"</note>, embittered by shame: neither in age nor experience is he fit for such a heavy burden. Tiberius Nero is mature in years and tested in war, but full of that Claudian pride <note>A reference to the *gens Claudia*, known for being haughty and arrogant</note>: many signs of his cruelty erupt, though he restrains them: he was raised in a reigning house: consulships and triumphs were heaped upon him in his youth: even during the years he stayed in exile at Rhodes (he called it a 'retreat'), he had no better thoughts than anger, pretense, and secret debaucheries: then there is that mother, the most insolent of women; we shall serve a woman and two boys, who will now ruin and one day dismember this state."

### V.

While people were reasoning thus, Augustus’s condition worsened: some suspected poison from his wife; for a rumor had spread that Augustus, a few months earlier, having confided in a few, had gone with Fabio Massimo...

---

<gloss>¹ *ma' che*, except for, if not, etc. Dante, *Inferno*:

> -> There was no weeping except for sighs. <-</gloss>

<meta>Signature I. at bottom left indicates the physical gathering of the printed sheets.</meta>

--- Page 578 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of the transition of power from Augustus to Tiberius as described in Tacitus’s Annals, translated by the historian Bernardo Davanzati. The previous page established Augustus's failing health and the strategic positioning of Tiberius as his successor, despite the existence of Augustus's biological grandson, Agrippa Postumus.</meta>

<page-num>482</page-num>

<header>FIRST ATTEMPTS</header>

Accompanied by no one else, he <note>Augustus</note> sailed to Pianosa to see Agrippa: where the embraces and tenderness were great on both sides; from which it was expected that the grandfather would bring the young man back home. Maximus revealed this to his wife: she to Livia: Caesar <note>Augustus</note> found out: and not long after, Maximus died—perhaps helped along—as Marcia was heard at the funeral saying through her sobs, "I, wretched one, am the cause of my husband's death." Whatever the truth of it, Tiberius, having barely entered Illyria, turned back, recalled by his mother’s letters with the greatest urgency. He found Augustus in Nola, though whether still alive or having breathed his last was not known, because of the strict guards Livia had placed at the palace and the roads. From time to time she spread word that he had improved; and when everything <gloss>1</gloss> the situation required had been provided for, a single announcement reported that Augustus was dead and Nero <note>Tiberius, whose full name was Tiberius Claudius Nero</note> was in full possession of power.

### VI.

The first business of the new principate was the murder of Agrippa Postumus, whom the centurion—though brave—only finished with difficulty, as the youth was caught unaware and unarmed. Tiberius did not breathe a word of it in the Senate: he acted as if this were his father's doing; claiming that Augustus had commanded the tribune who guarded him to kill him immediately once he himself had closed his eyes. It is true that Augustus had made the Senate decree <gloss>2</gloss> the young man's exile with many cruel words; but he never proceeded to the point of putting anyone of his own blood to death. It does not seem believable that the grandfather would kill the grandson to secure his stepson; it is more likely that Tiberius out of fear, and Livia out of a stepmother’s hatred, hurried to remove a youth who was a source of such suspicion and annoyance. When the centurion reported to him, in soldierly fashion, that he had done as he commanded, Tiberius replied that he had not commanded him and that he must render an account to the Senate. When Sallustius Crispus—who knew the secrets and was the one who sent the written commission to the tribune—heard this, he feared he might be examined, facing no less danger by telling the truth than by lying. He warned Livia that broadcasting household secrets, the advice of friends, and the services of soldiers was not wise; nor should Tiberius make himself a "prince in name only" by referring everything to the Senate: for the nature of...

<note>original: "quantunque, tutto ciò che" — meaning everything or whatever the time demanded.</note>
<note>original: "vincere, decretare" — used here in the sense of prevailing upon the Senate to issue a decree.</note>

...peculiar to a prince, that no account is valid unless it is rendered to him alone.

### VII. 

In Rome, consuls, senators <note>original: "padri", literally "fathers"</note>, and knights all rushed into servitude to their master. Those of the highest rank were the most hurried, their faces masked with deception and composed so as to appear neither too joyful at the death of the old man, nor too sorrowful at the arrival of the new prince; they mixed tears with gladness and lamentations with flattery. Sextus Pompeius and Sextus Apuleius, the consuls, were the first to swear obedience to Tiberius Caesar. Next followed Seius Strabo, captain of the guard, and Gaius Turanius, commissioner of the <term>grain supply</term> <note>original: "grascie", referring to the Annona or food provisions of Rome</note>, then the Senate, the military, and the people; for Tiberius let the consuls initiate every action, as if the ancient republic were still standing, or as if he himself were undecided about ruling. Even the edict by which he summoned the senators to council spoke only of Tiberius as a <term>Tribune of the Plebs</term> <note>A powerful office representing the common people, which gave him the right to convene the Senate</note>, a title granted to him by Augustus; the summons was brief and very modest: "He wished to deliberate on the honors for his father; he would not leave the body; he would take on no other public care." 

Meanwhile, Augustus being dead, he had already given the watchword to the Praetorian Guard as their emperor. Sentries, weapons, and the other trappings of a court were not lacking; soldiers accompanied him to the courts and the Senate. He wrote to the armies as the new prince; he never hesitated, except in his words before the Senate. The reasons were these: on one hand, he feared that Germanicus—with so many legions under his command, infinite foreign auxiliary forces, and wonderful favor with the people—might choose to seize the empire rather than wait for it. On the other hand, he wanted it to be known that he had been called by the republic to lead, and not smuggled in through a wife's flattery or an adoption by an old man in his dotage <note>original: "barbogio adottamento"</note>. Ultimately, it was understood that he also performed these pretenses <note>original: "lustre"</note> to see what faces and words the great men would make; and by this means, he penetrated and marked down their ill-disposed hearts.

### VIII. 

On the first day of the Senate, he would allow no business to be discussed but the will of Augustus, which was presented by the Vestal Virgins. It named Tiberius and Livia as heirs. Livia was to be adopted into the Julian family and granted the title of Augusta. He designated grandchildren and great-grandchildren as substitutes; in the third degree, he named the leading men of the city, most of whom he hated, but he wished to leave this reputation <note>original: "nomèa"</note> out of vanity. He made bequests like a private citizen, except to the people and the plebs...

...four hundred and thirty-five [hundred thousand] he bequeathed:¹ to the soldiers of the guard, one thousand sesterces² each; to the legionaries, three hundred³ per head. 

Then came the awarding of honors: the principal ones proposed were by Asinius Gallus, who suggested the funeral procession pass through the Triumphal Gate; and by Lucius Arruntius, who proposed that the titles of the laws Augustus had enacted and the names of the nations he had conquered be carried before the body. Valerius Messala added that the oath of allegiance to Tiberius should be renewed every year. When Tiberius asked him, “Did I command you to say this?” Messala replied: “The interests of the Republic told me to do it, and they will never let me wait for advice from anyone, even if it might displease you.” Only this sort of refined flattery was missing. The senators <note>original: "padri", the "fathers" of the Senate</note> cried out: “Let us carry him to the funeral pyre on our own shoulders!” Caesar <note>Referring here to Tiberius</note> granted them this favor with a very haughty air, and then issued a proclamation that the people should not disrupt these funeral rites as they had those of the divine Julius <note>Julius Caesar, whose funeral turned into a riot where the public burned his body in the Forum</note>, for out of excessive affection they might wish to burn Augustus in the Forum rather than in his designated tomb in the <term>Campus Martius</term> <note>The "Field of Mars," a public area in Rome used for military training and monuments</note>. On the day of the funeral, soldiers stood by as if on guard; this provoked laughter from those who had seen, or heard from their fathers, of that other day <note>The funeral of Julius Caesar</note> when independence was attempted but failed, and who now felt the swallowed but not yet digested servitude rising in their stomachs. To some, the spectacle of the dead Caesar, once a dictator, seemed a terrible thing, while to others it seemed most beautiful. “Indeed!” <note>original: "Gnaffe!", an old Italian exclamation of surprise or emphasis</note> they said, “There is great need today for soldiers to let an old prince be buried in peace—a man of ancient power, with heirs already provided with sharp claws sunk deep into the Republic.”

### IX. 

Consequently, there was much talk about Augustus himself. Many marveled at trivial coincidences: “On the same day that he first took command, he left this life; he died in Nola, in the same house and the same room as his father. He was consul as many times as Valerius Corvinus and Gaius Marius combined; he held the power of <term>Tribune of the Plebs</term> for thirty-seven years in a row; he was hailed as <term>Imperator</term> twenty-one times,” along with other honors heaped upon him...

...granted <gloss>1</gloss> or new ones." But the prudent divided their opinions: some placed him in heaven, others in the abyss. "Filial piety <note>The duty Augustus felt to avenge his adoptive father, Julius Caesar</note> and the necessity of the Republic, which was by then without laws, dragged him by the hair into the civil wars; and these can neither be provoked nor maintained through honorable means. To take vengeance upon his father’s assassins, he conceded many things to Antony and many to Lepidus. After the latter paid the price for his sluggishness and the former for his lusts, the fractured fatherland had no other remedy than to be governed by one man—not yet as a king or a dictator, but as a Prince <note>original: "capo," meaning head or leader; Augustus used the title *Princeps* to avoid the hated title of King</note>. He left the ocean or distant rivers as the boundaries of the empire. The legions, the provinces, the fleets—everything was well-linked together. He provided justice to the citizens and moderation to the allies. He made the city beautiful and magnificent. He used force in only a very few instances, and then only to ensure the peace of the rest."

X. On the reverse side, it was said: "Filial piety and the misfortunes of the Republic were merely fine excuses. It was a lust for power that drove him to stir up the veteran soldiers with bribes. As a private youth, he raised an army; he corrupted the legions belonging to the consul; he feigned to be a supporter of Pompey's faction. Having snatched the <term>fasces</term> <note>Bundles of rods symbolizing a magistrate's power</note> and the authority of a praetor through a decree of the Senate, and after Hirtius and Pansa were killed—whether by the enemy in the field, or by Pansa having his wound poisoned and Hirtius being betrayed by his own soldiers—he seized both their armies. He made himself consul despite the Senate's wishes, and turned the arms given to him against Antony against the Republic itself. He exiled so many citizens and oversaw so many distributions of land—acts which displeased even those who carried them out. Let the deaths of Brutus and Cassius be forgiven <note>original: "vadano con Dio," literally "go with God"</note>, for they were his father's enemies, even if private hatreds ought to be set aside for the public good; but he also deceived the younger Pompey with a mask of peace and Lepidus under the guise of friendship. Antony, too, was lured in by the treaties of Taranto and Brindisi and by marriage to Augustus’s sister, only to find death as the dowry of that deceitful kinship. We have had peace since then, yes, but a bloody one: the disasters of Lollius and Varus <note>Military defeats in Germania</note>, and the executions of the Varros, the Egnatii, and the Julii right here in Rome." Nor did they spare him for his domestic affairs: how he stole Nero’s wife <note>Livia Drusilla, who was pregnant when Augustus took her from her husband, Tiberius Claudius Nero</note> and mockingly asked the pontiffs if she could be married while pregnant... leav-

the ways of Tedius and Vedius Pollio. <gloss>1</gloss> Livia, finally, was a bad mother to the Republic, and a worse stepmother to the house of the Caesars: what worship is left for us to offer to the gods, since she demands temples, images, priests <note>original: "flamini," referring to the *flamines*, a category of priests in Roman religion</note>, and clergy? XI. Then, pleas were turned to Tiberius to accept the rule. He argued that "the empire was vast, and he himself modest; only the mind of the divine Augustus was capable of such a burden: having been called by him to share his thoughts, he had learned how arduous and precarious a weight it is to rule everything: they should not, given the city was founded by so many illustrious men, give the whole burden to one man; the united labors of many would conduct the affairs of the Republic more easily." There was more pomp than truth in this speech. And Tiberius’s words—by nature or by habit double-edged and dark, even when he wished to be understood—now that he sought the complete opposite, were all the more entangled and doubtful. But the fathers, for fear of appearing to recognize his ruse (for woe to them if they did), threw themselves into laments and tears...

...labored to the great pleasure of the fathers <note>The Roman Senators</note> Sextus Paconianus <note>original: "Sestio Pogiano." A former praetor who was an informant for Sejanus.</note>, a former praetor, bold and malicious, who spied on everyone’s secrets, chosen by Sejanus <note>The powerful and treacherous commander of the Praetorian Guard under Tiberius.</note> to administer poison to Gaius Caesar <note>The future emperor Caligula.</note>. When this was discovered, the hatred held for him burst forth, seeking to deliver him to the ultimate punishment, had he not become a whistleblower.

**IV.** A most welcome spectacle then was Latinius Latiaris <note>original: "Latino Laziare"</note>, who was likewise hated, when Haterius entered to give him cause for accusation. Latinius was the leader, as I have said, in leading Titius Sabinus to the mace <note>A reference to execution or the lictor's tools of punishment.</note>, and was then the first to be punished for it. Haterius Agrippa <note>original: "Aterio Agrippa"</note> attacked the former consuls: "If they have accused one another, why do they now stay silent? Fear and the gnawing of guilt have made them reach an accord: but the fathers must not let what has been heard pass in silence." Regulus <note>Publius Memmius Regulus</note> replied: "That time would not take away the punishment; and that the prince [the Emperor] would grant it." Trio <note>Fulcinius Trio</note> said that the disputes of colleagues and slanders should rather be forgotten. As Agrippa grew heated, Sanquinius <note>Sanquinius Maximus</note>, the oldest of the consuls, begged the senate: "Of your grace, let us not give the emperor more trouble by poking at festering wounds: let us leave them for him to heal, as he is the one who can." This was the salvation of Regulus, and it prolonged the ruin of Trio. Haterius became more hated than usual among the few: wasting away in sleep and lazily wallowing in lust, he did not fear the prince’s cruelty, and always plotted the downfall of the great while in taverns and brothels <note>original: "chiassi." Literally "noises," but historically referring to narrow alleys or houses of ill repute.</note>.

## SECOND DICTATION.

**III.....** What Gallio gained from his calculated flattery was to be expelled then from the senate, and afterwards from Italy; and as it was being said that he was living too comfortably in Lesbos—a noble and pleasant island he had chosen for his exile—he was brought back to Rome and given over to the guard of magistrates. In the same letter, Caesar struck—to the great joy of the fathers—Sextus Paconianus <note>original: "Sesto Paconiano." Note the correction of the name from the "First Dictation" above.</note>, a former praetor, bold and harmful, a spy of everyone’s secrets, and a tool of Sejanus to set the snare for Gaius Caesar. When this was known, the hatreds already harbored burst forth, and he was condemned to the ultimate punishment; but he said that he held a confession within him.

**IV.** And once [the sentence] was given to Latinius Latiaris <note>original: "Latino Laziare." An informant who famously trapped Titius Sabinus.</note>, it was a fine sight to see the spy and the guilty man together, each more wretched than the other. Latiaris, as I have said, was the leader in bringing Titius Sabinus to the mace <note>The "mace" refers to the lictor’s axe, the symbol of capital punishment.</note>, and he was now the first to be punished. During this, Haterius Agrippa <note>original: "Aterio Agrippa"</note> attacked the former consuls:

> “If they accused one another, why are they now silent? The worm <note>original: "il baco"</note> of conscience and fear has united them; but the Fathers <note>The Roman Senators.</note> must not allow the things they have heard to pass in silence.”

Regulus <note>Publius Memmius Regulus.</note> replied:

> “That delay does not remove punishment: the need [for justice] would be well-served when the Prince <note>The Emperor Tiberius.</note> is present.”

And Trio <note>Fulcinius Trio, another notorious informant.</note> [replied] that regarding the disputes and slanders between colleagues, it was better to stifle them. As Agrippa grew more heated, Sanquinius Maximus <note>original: "Sanquinio Massimo"</note>, a former consul, begged the Senate:

> “Of your grace, let us not add to the Prince’s troubles by poking at festering wounds: he will be well able to heal them himself.”

This gave Regulus an escape from death and bought time for Trio. Haterius was even more hated than they were, for he was rotting away in sleep and lust; because of his foolishness, he did not fear the Prince, cruel though he was; and he was always seeking the ruin of great men amidst taverns and dens of vice <note>original: "ma’ luoghi," literally "bad places."</note>.

mine, 110. — He rebuilds the burned Theater of Pompey, 152. — He pays for the houses burned on the Caelian Hill; where his image in the midst of the flames was not harmed, 194, 195. — He pays two and a half million <note>likely sesterces</note> for the houses similarly burned on the Aventine Hill, 238. — He aids and consoles twelve cities in Asia ruined by an earthquake, 90.

He has his son Drusus declared Tribune, which is to say, the emperor-elect, 143.

His government was initially good, 158, 17, 159, 52, 91, 110, 144, 179, 203.

Later it worsened, and why, 203.

His very strong spirit during the illness and death of his son, 160. — He praises him from the rostrum <note>original: "ringhiera," referring to the public speaking platform in the Forum</note>, 163.
